Volume 2

Architecture and APIs

Choosing a system shape, clean design and patterns, domain-driven design, and API design people can live with — REST, GraphQL and gRPC.

Part 5 — Software Architecture

Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to change later. Which process runs which code, which database owns which table, which team can deploy without asking another team, how a request travels from the load balancer to the row on disk. Everything else (naming, formatting, which HTTP client library you use) is a detail you can refactor on a Tuesday afternoon. Architecture is what you live with for years.

This part walks through the architectural styles you will meet in real backend work, always with the same stack in mind: a NestJS application in front of PostgreSQL and Redis, with Kafka or RabbitMQ carrying events to background workers. For each style we look at the shape of the code, the shape of the deployment, and, most importantly, what breaks at 02:00 when it goes wrong.

A warning before we start. Every style below is a tool. None of them is a goal. The senior engineer's job is not to "do microservices" or "do clean architecture"; it is to pick the least amount of structure that lets the current team ship the current product safely, while leaving a door open for the next stage. Keep that in mind as you read.

5.1 The monolith

Concept

A monolith is a single deployable unit. One repository, one build, one process (or many identical copies of the same process behind a load balancer), one database. Every feature of the product lives inside it: user registration, product catalog, cart, checkout, payments, notifications, admin reports.

In NestJS terms: one main.ts, one AppModule, and every other module imported into it. npm run build produces one dist/ folder, and docker build produces one image.

Why does it exist?

The monolith exists because it is the natural first shape of any system. You do not design a monolith; you get one by writing code. It solves the most important early problem: getting a working product in front of users with a team of one to ten people, without paying for infrastructure you do not need yet.

What breaks without it? Nothing; it is the baseline. The question is what breaks with it, and when. We will get there.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant with one kitchen. Every dish, from starters to desserts, comes out of the same room. The chefs walk over and talk to each other; nobody sends a courier across town to ask if there are still tomatoes. Communication is fast and cheap. But if the kitchen catches fire, every dish stops. And when the restaurant grows to two hundred tables, one kitchen becomes crowded, chefs bump into each other, and one slow station (the grill) holds up every order.

A monolith is that single kitchen.

How it works

  1. A request hits the load balancer and is forwarded to one of N identical Node.js processes.
  2. The NestJS router matches the route to a controller inside the process.
  3. The controller calls a service; the service calls other services and repositories by plain method calls, all in the same memory space. A "call" costs nanoseconds, never a network round trip.
  4. All repositories talk to the same PostgreSQL database through one connection pool.
  5. A single database transaction can span any tables you like, because they are all in the same database.
  6. Deployment replaces the whole process. There is no such thing as "deploying only the payments part".
                 +----------------------------------------+
   Client -----> |  NestJS process (one image, one build)  |
                 |                                          |
                 |  UsersModule  OrdersModule  PaymentsModule|
                 |  ProductsModule  NotificationsModule     |
                 |          \       |        /              |
                 |           +------+-------+               |
                 |                  |                       |
                 +------------------|-----------------------+
                                    v
                            PostgreSQL (one DB)

Practical example

An e-commerce startup with four engineers. The product has users, a catalog, a cart, checkout, and order emails. Traffic is 20 requests per second at peak. The entire system is one NestJS app with a PostgreSQL database on RDS and a Redis instance for sessions.

Checkout is a single method that, inside one transaction, decrements inventory, creates the order, records the payment intent, and enqueues an email. If any step fails, the transaction rolls back and nothing half-happens. That is the monolith's superpower: local transactions across the whole domain.

NestJS example

A typical early-stage layout. Note that nothing stops OrdersService from injecting InventoryRepository directly; there are no boundaries yet.

src/
  main.ts
  app.module.ts
  users/
    users.controller.ts
    users.service.ts
    users.module.ts
    user.entity.ts
  products/
    products.controller.ts
    products.service.ts
    product.entity.ts
  orders/
    orders.controller.ts
    orders.service.ts
    order.entity.ts
  payments/
    payments.service.ts
  notifications/
    email.service.ts
// src/orders/orders.service.ts
import { Injectable, ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository, DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { Product } from '../products/product.entity';
import { PaymentsService } from '../payments/payments.service';
import { EmailService } from '../notifications/email.service';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Order) private readonly orders: Repository<Order>,
    private readonly dataSource: DataSource,
    private readonly payments: PaymentsService,
    private readonly email: EmailService,
  ) {}

  async checkout(userId: string, productId: string, qty: number): Promise<Order> {
    // One local transaction spans inventory, orders and payment intent rows.
    return this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const product = await manager
        .getRepository(Product)
        .createQueryBuilder('p')
        .setLock('pessimistic_write') // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the hot row
        .where('p.id = :id', { id: productId })
        .getOne();

      if (!product || product.stock < qty) {
        throw new ConflictException('Insufficient stock');
      }
      product.stock -= qty;
      await manager.save(product);

      const order = manager.create(Order, { userId, productId, qty, status: 'CREATED' });
      await manager.save(order);

      await this.payments.createIntent(manager, order); // same transaction
      await this.email.queueOrderConfirmation(order.id); // Redis queue, fire-and-forget
      return order;
    });
  }
}

This is good code for a small team. It is honest, it is transactional, and a new engineer can read the whole checkout in one file.

PostgreSQL example

One database, one schema, foreign keys everywhere. That is fine; it is a feature at this stage.

CREATE TABLE products (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  name        text NOT NULL,
  stock       integer NOT NULL CHECK (stock >= 0),
  price_cents integer NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  product_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  qty         integer NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  status      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'CREATED',
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX orders_user_created_idx ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);

The CHECK (stock >= 0) constraint is the last line of defence against overselling; it will reject a bad decrement even if application code has a bug.

Production scenario

A well-built monolith carries a surprising amount of traffic. A single Node.js process handling mostly I/O-bound work comfortably does 1,000 to 3,000 requests per second if the database is not the bottleneck. Ten replicas behind an ALB give you 10,000 to 30,000 RPS. Many companies never need more than that. Shopify famously ran a modular Rails monolith at enormous scale for years, and Stack Overflow serves billions of page views a month from a small number of large servers.

The real limits of a monolith are organisational, not technical:

  • Build and test time. At 400,000 lines of TypeScript, a full tsc plus Jest run creeps past 20 minutes. Every pull request waits.
  • Deployment coupling. A one-line fix to the email template deploys the checkout code too. If a release is bad, everything rolls back.
  • Blast radius. One unbounded query in the reports module can exhaust the connection pool and take checkout down with it.
  • Ownership blur. With forty engineers, "who owns OrdersService?" has no answer, and it grows to 2,000 lines.

Failure scenario

At 14:20 on a Monday, the marketing team launches a campaign. Traffic triples. The admin dashboard's "sales by hour" report runs a query that does a sequential scan over 30 million orders rows and holds a connection for 40 seconds. Three admins refresh it repeatedly. Within two minutes, the shared PostgreSQL pool (max 20 connections per replica) is full of report queries. Checkout requests wait for a connection, time out at 30 seconds, and the load balancer starts marking replicas unhealthy. Revenue drops to zero for eleven minutes.

Nothing in the checkout code was wrong. The failure was architectural: a low-value, heavy workload shared a resource (the pool) with a high-value, light workload, and there was no boundary between them.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Noisy neighbour inside the process. A CPU-heavy task (PDF generation, image resize) blocks the event loop for everyone. Node.js has one main thread per process.
  • Memory leak in one module kills the whole process; Kubernetes restarts it and the checkout is gone for 15 seconds each time (OOMKilled loops).
  • Migration lock. One ALTER TABLE on a large table locks the table for the whole app, not just one feature.
  • Test suite coupling. A flaky test in notifications blocks a payments hotfix.
  • Dependency upgrade friction. Upgrading TypeORM affects every module at once.
  • Circular imports creep in because nothing forbids users from importing orders and vice versa.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior engineer does not apologise for a monolith. They ask: Is the team small? Is the domain still being discovered? Is the traffic within one database's capacity? If yes to all three, the monolith is the correct answer, and adding services would be waste.

What they refuse to do is let the monolith become a ball of mud. From day one they enforce module boundaries inside the monolith, which is exactly the modular monolith we discuss next. They also refuse to run heavy analytical workloads on the same pool as transactional traffic; they route reports to a read replica with a separate pool.

To a product manager: "We are one application today. That lets us ship features fast and keep the bill low. We are building it in separate rooms so that when a room needs its own building, we can move it without knocking down the house."

Common mistakes

  • Treating "monolith" as a slur and starting a new product with eight services and three engineers. This is the single most expensive mistake in modern backend engineering.
  • No boundaries at all. Every service injects every repository. After two years, no change is safe.
  • One connection pool for everything. Reports, cron jobs and checkout share 20 connections.
  • Running background jobs inside the web process. A job that takes 5 minutes blocks graceful shutdown and gets killed mid-way on every deploy.
  • Skipping the read replica because "it's just one database".

Interview questions

  1. When is a monolith the right architecture? Expected: small team, evolving domain, traffic within one database's capacity, need for fast iteration. Follow-up: what signals would make you reconsider?
  2. What is the blast radius of a bug in a monolith and how do you reduce it? Expected: the whole process; reduce with bulkheads (separate pools, separate worker processes), timeouts, circuit breakers on outbound calls.
  3. How do you scale a monolith horizontally? Expected: stateless processes behind a load balancer, sessions in Redis, sticky sessions avoided, database read replicas, connection pooler like PgBouncer.
  4. Why can a monolith have simpler consistency guarantees than microservices? Expected: single database, local ACID transactions span the whole domain; no sagas or outboxes needed.
  5. What is the difference between a monolith and a "big ball of mud"? Expected: a monolith is a deployment shape; a ball of mud is a code shape with no boundaries. You can have a clean monolith or a muddy set of microservices.

Practical exercise

Take an existing NestJS monolith (or generate one with nest new). Add a ReportsModule with a deliberately slow query. Configure two TypeORM DataSources: one for transactional modules with max: 20, and one for reports with max: 3 pointing to a read replica (or the same database on a different pool for the exercise). Load-test checkout with autocannon while hammering the report endpoint.

Acceptance criteria: checkout p99 latency stays under 200 ms while the report endpoint is saturated; the report endpoint returns 503 or queues when its own pool is exhausted, never touching the transactional pool.

5.2 The modular monolith

Concept

A modular monolith is still one deployable unit and (usually) one database, but the code inside is divided into modules with enforced boundaries. A module exposes a small public interface and hides everything else. Modules talk through that interface or through in-process events, never by reaching into each other's tables or internal classes.

The word "enforced" is the whole point. Every monolith has folders. A modular monolith has walls.

Why does it exist?

It exists to get most of the organisational benefits of microservices (clear ownership, independent evolution, testability, a path to extraction) without paying the operational cost of a distributed system (network calls, partial failure, N pipelines, distributed tracing).

Without it, a growing monolith turns into a ball of mud: any class can call any class, tables are joined across domains in ad-hoc queries, and no one can change anything with confidence. The usual response is to "break it into microservices", which does not fix the problem; it distributes it.

Mental model

Imagine an office building. One address, one electricity bill, one front door. Inside, each team has its own room with a door and a reception desk. If Payments needs something from Inventory, they go to Inventory's reception and ask; they do not walk in and rummage through Inventory's filing cabinets. Because each room has a defined door, moving a team to a separate building later means re-routing the reception desk, not untangling desks that grew into each other.

How it works

The building blocks, in NestJS terms:

  1. One NestJS module per business capability, not per technical layer. OrdersModule, PaymentsModule, InventoryModule, NotificationsModule. Not ControllersModule and ServicesModule.
  2. Encapsulation via exports. A NestJS module can only inject providers that another module explicitly exports. If InventoryModule does not export InventoryRepository, then OrdersService cannot inject it. The DI container enforces this at startup, with a hard error.
  3. A public facade per module. Each module exports one or two application services (for example InventoryFacade) with a deliberately small API. Everything else stays internal.
  4. Schema-per-module in PostgreSQL. Each module owns a PostgreSQL schema (orders.*, payments.*, inventory.*). Cross-schema foreign keys are avoided; cross-module references are by id only. This is the single most important decision for later extraction.
  5. In-process events with @nestjs/event-emitter. When an order is paid, OrdersModule emits order.paid. InventoryModule and NotificationsModule subscribe. Orders does not know they exist.
  6. A shared kernel for truly shared, stable things: Money, UserId, base error classes, the event contract types. Kept tiny and versioned carefully.
  7. Contracts folder holding the public DTOs and event payloads each module publishes, so consumers depend on contracts, not on internals.
  8. Lint-level enforcement using eslint-plugin-boundaries or dependency-cruiser, so import ... from '../inventory/internal/...' fails CI.
flowchart TB
  subgraph App["NestJS process"]

Practical example

The same e-commerce company, now with twenty engineers in four squads: Orders, Payments, Inventory, Growth (notifications and marketing). Each squad owns one module and one schema. They still deploy one image, several times a day. When Payments needs to add Razorpay alongside Stripe, they change files only under modules/payments/; the Orders squad does not even review the PR.

Checkout now looks different from the naive monolith. OrdersService does not touch the inventory.stock table. It calls InventoryFacade.reserve(), which is the only door.

NestJS example

Folder layout designed for later extraction:

src/
  main.ts
  app.module.ts
  shared-kernel/
    money.ts
    ids.ts
    domain-error.ts
  contracts/
    events/
      order-paid.event.ts
      stock-reserved.event.ts
    inventory/
      reserve-stock.dto.ts
  modules/
    orders/
      orders.module.ts
      public/
        orders.facade.ts          <- the ONLY exported provider
      application/
        checkout.use-case.ts
      domain/
        order.ts
        order-status.ts
      infrastructure/
        order.entity.ts           <- schema: orders
        order.typeorm-repository.ts
      presentation/
        orders.controller.ts
        dto/create-order.dto.ts
    inventory/
      inventory.module.ts
      public/
        inventory.facade.ts
      application/
        reserve-stock.use-case.ts
        on-order-paid.handler.ts
      infrastructure/
        stock.entity.ts           <- schema: inventory
    payments/
      payments.module.ts
      public/
        payments.facade.ts
      infrastructure/
        payment.entity.ts         <- schema: payments

The module definition enforces the boundary:

// src/modules/inventory/inventory.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { StockEntity } from './infrastructure/stock.entity';
import { StockTypeormRepository } from './infrastructure/stock.typeorm-repository';
import { ReserveStockUseCase } from './application/reserve-stock.use-case';
import { OnOrderPaidHandler } from './application/on-order-paid.handler';
import { InventoryFacade } from './public/inventory.facade';

export const STOCK_REPOSITORY = Symbol('STOCK_REPOSITORY');

@Module({
  imports: [TypeOrmModule.forFeature([StockEntity])],
  providers: [
    { provide: STOCK_REPOSITORY, useClass: StockTypeormRepository },
    ReserveStockUseCase,
    OnOrderPaidHandler,
    InventoryFacade,
  ],
  // Only the facade leaves the module. Repositories and use cases stay private.
  exports: [InventoryFacade],
})
export class InventoryModule {}

If a developer in OrdersModule writes constructor(@Inject(STOCK_REPOSITORY) repo: StockRepository), NestJS fails at boot with Nest can't resolve dependencies of OrdersService (?). The wall is real.

The facade is a thin, intention-revealing API:

// src/modules/inventory/public/inventory.facade.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ReserveStockUseCase } from '../application/reserve-stock.use-case';
import { ReserveStockDto } from '../../../contracts/inventory/reserve-stock.dto';

@Injectable()
export class InventoryFacade {
  constructor(private readonly reserveStock: ReserveStockUseCase) {}

  // Returns a reservation id; throws InsufficientStockError (from shared-kernel).
  reserve(dto: ReserveStockDto): Promise<{ reservationId: string }> {
    return this.reserveStock.execute(dto);
  }
}

Cross-module reactions go through in-process events:

// src/modules/payments/application/confirm-payment.use-case.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { EventEmitter2 } from '@nestjs/event-emitter';
import { OrderPaidEvent } from '../../../contracts/events/order-paid.event';

@Injectable()
export class ConfirmPaymentUseCase {
  constructor(private readonly events: EventEmitter2) {}

  async execute(orderId: string, amountCents: number): Promise<void> {
    // ... persist payment row in schema payments ...
    // Emit AFTER commit. Emitting inside the transaction risks listeners
    // reading data that is later rolled back.
    await this.events.emitAsync(
      OrderPaidEvent.name,
      new OrderPaidEvent({ orderId, amountCents, paidAt: new Date().toISOString() }),
    );
  }
}

// src/modules/inventory/application/on-order-paid.handler.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OnEvent } from '@nestjs/event-emitter';
import { OrderPaidEvent } from '../../../contracts/events/order-paid.event';

@Injectable()
export class OnOrderPaidHandler {
  private readonly log = new Logger(OnOrderPaidHandler.name);

  @OnEvent(OrderPaidEvent.name, { async: true, promisify: true })
  async handle(event: OrderPaidEvent): Promise<void> {
    this.log.log(`Committing reservation for order ${event.orderId}`);
    // convert reservation into a hard decrement, idempotently by orderId
  }
}

EventEmitter2 is in-memory. If the process dies between the payment commit and the listener finishing, the event is lost. That is acceptable for a modular monolith only if the listener's work is recoverable (a reconciliation job, or the outbox pattern from Part 5.6). Do not pretend in-process events are durable.

PostgreSQL example

Schema-per-module with search paths and no cross-schema foreign keys.

CREATE SCHEMA orders;
CREATE SCHEMA payments;
CREATE SCHEMA inventory;

CREATE TABLE inventory.stock (
  product_id  uuid PRIMARY KEY,           -- reference by id, NO FK to products schema
  available   integer NOT NULL CHECK (available >= 0),
  reserved    integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (reserved >= 0),
  version     integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0  -- optimistic locking
);

CREATE TABLE inventory.reservations (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  order_id    uuid NOT NULL,              -- id only, owned by orders schema
  product_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  qty         integer NOT NULL,
  status      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'HELD',
  expires_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (order_id, product_id)           -- idempotency: one reservation per line
);

-- Each module's DB role can only touch its own schema.
CREATE ROLE inventory_svc LOGIN PASSWORD '...';
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA inventory TO inventory_svc;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA inventory TO inventory_svc;

Giving up the cross-schema foreign key feels wrong at first. It is the price of extraction: the day inventory moves to its own database, there is no constraint to drop and no join to rewrite.

TypeORM example

TypeORM entities carry the schema name, so the module owns its tables explicitly:

// src/modules/inventory/infrastructure/stock.entity.ts
import { Entity, PrimaryColumn, Column, VersionColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ schema: 'inventory', name: 'stock' })
export class StockEntity {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid') productId!: string;
  @Column('integer') available!: number;
  @Column('integer', { default: 0 }) reserved!: number;
  @VersionColumn() version!: number; // TypeORM bumps this on save; stale writes throw
}

For a per-module DataSource (a stepping stone to a separate database), register named connections with TypeOrmModule.forRoot({ name: 'inventory', schema: 'inventory', ... }) and TypeOrmModule.forFeature([StockEntity], 'inventory'). Most teams start with one DataSource and a schema per module, and only split the DataSource when the extraction is real.

Sequelize example

The Sequelize equivalent uses the schema option on the model:

// src/modules/inventory/infrastructure/stock.model.ts
import { Table, Column, Model, PrimaryKey, DataType } from 'sequelize-typescript';

@Table({ tableName: 'stock', schema: 'inventory', timestamps: false, version: true })
export class StockModel extends Model {
  @PrimaryKey @Column(DataType.UUID) productId!: string;
  @Column(DataType.INTEGER) available!: number;
  @Column({ type: DataType.INTEGER, defaultValue: 0 }) reserved!: number;
}

version: true turns on Sequelize's optimistic locking; a stale save() throws OptimisticLockError.

Production scenario

A modular monolith with eight modules, twenty engineers, 2,500 RPS peak, one db.r6g.2xlarge PostgreSQL primary and two read replicas. Deploys happen 10 to 15 times a day from one pipeline that runs 12 minutes. Each module has its own Jest project, so a change under modules/payments runs only the payments tests plus a small contract suite in the pre-merge stage; the full suite runs on main.

Observability is easy: one process, one trace, one log stream. A checkout request that touches four modules shows up as one trace with four spans, no context propagation to worry about.

When the Payments squad grows to twelve people and needs to deploy hotfixes at a different cadence than everyone else, they extract PaymentsModule into its own service. Because the module only ever spoke through PaymentsFacade and order.paid events, the extraction is:

  1. Move modules/payments to a new repository with its own main.ts.
  2. Replace PaymentsFacade in the monolith with an HTTP or gRPC client with the same interface.
  3. Replace EventEmitter2 for order.paid with a Kafka topic, using the same contract type.
  4. Point the new service's DataSource at a new database and migrate the payments schema with pg_dump --schema=payments.

That is a two-week project, not a six-month rewrite.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 on release day, a new engineer on the Growth squad needs the customer's email inside NotificationsModule. Instead of calling UsersFacade.getContact(userId), they add a TypeORM relation from NotificationPreference to UserEntity and write a join across users.users and growth.preferences. It works. Six months later, the Users squad extracts their module to a separate service and drops the users schema from the shared database. The notifications join fails in production for 3 hours before anyone realises the cause; there was no compile error because TypeORM relations are strings and metadata, not imports.

The lesson: schema-per-module must be enforced by database roles and lint rules, not by convention. A convention is a suggestion; a GRANT is a wall.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lost in-process events when the process crashes between commit and listener. Mitigate with an outbox table or make listeners idempotent and re-runnable from a reconciliation job.
  • Synchronous listener slowing the request. A @OnEvent handler that calls a slow third-party API inline adds its latency to the emitter's request unless async: true is used.
  • Shared kernel bloat. If shared-kernel/ grows to 200 files, every module depends on everything again. Keep it tiny; treat every addition as a versioned public API.
  • Cross-module transactions. OrdersService opening a transaction and passing the EntityManager into InventoryFacade couples the two modules at the storage level. Prefer reservations and compensation over shared transactions across module boundaries, so extraction remains possible.
  • Hidden coupling via database views or triggers that read another schema.
  • Module import cycles (OrdersModule imports PaymentsModule imports OrdersModule). NestJS supports forwardRef, but a cycle between business modules is a design smell; introduce events instead.
  • Test leakage. Module tests that spin up the whole AppModule become slow and defeat the purpose. Each module's test should bootstrap only that module with fakes for other facades.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior engineer's default for a new product with more than three engineers is the modular monolith. They ask: What are the natural capabilities of this business? Which of them will change most? Which ones have a different scaling profile? Those questions define the modules.

They insist on three non-negotiables: facades as the only exports, schema-per-module with database roles, and a lint rule that fails the build on deep imports. Without enforcement, a modular monolith decays into a plain monolith within a year.

They also resist premature extraction. "We could split it" is not a reason to split it. They keep a written list of the signals that would trigger an extraction (see 5.13) and check it quarterly.

Common mistakes

  • Modules per technical layer (ControllersModule, ServicesModule, RepositoriesModule). This gives you the ceremony of modules with none of the benefit.
  • Exporting repositories. Once OrdersRepository is exported, every module queries orders directly and the boundary is gone.
  • Cross-schema foreign keys and joins "because it's the same database anyway".
  • Fat shared kernel that contains entities, services and half the business logic.
  • Treating EventEmitter2 as a message broker. It is not durable, not distributed, and not ordered across processes.
  • Global modules everywhere (@Global()), which reintroduces "anything can inject anything".

Interview questions

  1. How do you enforce module boundaries in a NestJS monolith? Expected: exports in module metadata, facade providers, lint rules against deep imports, separate PostgreSQL schemas and roles, per-module test bootstrapping.
  2. Why avoid foreign keys across module schemas even in one database? Expected: they make extraction impossible without a rewrite and create hidden coupling. Follow-up: how do you maintain referential integrity without them? Answer: validate through the owning module's facade; accept eventual consistency; reconciliation jobs.
  3. What is a shared kernel and what belongs in it? Expected: tiny set of stable, cross-cutting types (ids, money, base errors, event contracts). Not entities, not services.
  4. How do modules communicate in a modular monolith? Expected: synchronous facade calls for queries and commands that need an immediate answer; in-process events for reactions; never direct repository access.
  5. What happens to in-process events if the process crashes? Expected: they are lost; discuss outbox pattern, idempotent handlers, reconciliation.
  6. Describe how you would extract one module into a service. Expected: facade becomes a client, events move to a broker, schema moves to its own database, contracts stay the same.

Practical exercise

Build a modular monolith with three NestJS modules: orders, inventory, notifications. Each module owns a PostgreSQL schema and exports exactly one facade. Implement checkout so that orders calls InventoryFacade.reserve() synchronously and emits order.paid through EventEmitter2; inventory and notifications react to the event. Add dependency-cruiser with a rule forbidding imports from any path containing /application/, /domain/ or /infrastructure/ of another module.

Acceptance criteria: a deep import causes the CI lint step to fail; removing InventoryFacade from exports makes the app fail to boot with a clear DI error; the orders module's tests run with a fake InventoryFacade and no database.

5.3 Microservices

Concept

Microservices split a system into multiple independently deployable processes, each owning one business capability and its own data. orders-service, payments-service, inventory-service, each with its own repository (or folder in a monorepo), its own pipeline, its own database, and its own on-call rotation.

Communication happens over the network: HTTP/REST, gRPC, or messages through Kafka or RabbitMQ. There is no shared memory and no shared transaction.

Why does it exist?

Microservices exist to let many teams deploy independently and to let different parts of a system scale and fail independently. When forty engineers share one deployment pipeline, every release becomes a negotiation. When the image-processing path needs 40 CPUs and the checkout path needs 2, one autoscaling group cannot serve both efficiently. Microservices solve organisational and scaling problems.

They are not a code-quality tool. A messy monolith split into services becomes a messy distributed system, which is strictly worse.

Mental model

Imagine a food court instead of one restaurant kitchen. Each stall has its own kitchen, staff, menu and cash register. A customer who wants a burger and a bubble tea walks to two stalls. Each stall can open, close, expand or change its menu without asking the others. But now there is no single bill, no single kitchen to walk over to, and if the bubble tea stall runs out of ice, the burger stall cannot help. Coordination happens by walking (network calls) or by shouting across the hall (events).

How it works

  1. Each service is a separate NestJS application with its own main.ts, image and Helm chart.
  2. An API gateway (or a BFF, "backend for frontend") is the single entry point for clients; it routes to services and handles auth, rate limits and TLS.
  3. Services call each other synchronously (REST/gRPC) when they need an answer now, and publish events (Kafka/RabbitMQ) when they want others to react later.
  4. Service-per-database rule. Each service owns its data. No other service reads its tables. Data needed by another service is obtained via API or by consuming events and keeping a local copy.
  5. Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) propagates a trace id in headers and message metadata so one user request can be followed across five processes.
  6. Service discovery (Kubernetes DNS, Consul) and client-side timeouts, retries and circuit breakers handle the fact that any call can fail.
flowchart LR
  C["Client"] --> GW["API Gateway"]
  GW --> O["orders-service"]
  GW --> P["payments-service"]
  O -->|"gRPC reserve"| I["inventory-service"]
  O -->|"HTTP createIntent"| P
  P -->|"order.paid"| K[("Kafka")]
  K --> I
  K --> N["notifications-service"]
  O --> ODB[("orders DB")]
  P --> PDB[("payments DB")]
  I --> IDB[("inventory DB")]

Production-first questions:

  • How do I implement it? One NestJS app per service, @nestjs/microservices for the transport layer or plain HTTP controllers, Kafka client for events.
  • What can go wrong? Everything in a monolith, plus network partitions, partial failures, duplicated messages, inconsistent data between services, version skew between deployed services.
  • How do I monitor it? Distributed tracing is mandatory, not optional. Per-service RED metrics (rate, errors, duration). Consumer lag per topic.
  • How do I scale it? Per service, independently, by HPA on CPU/RPS/lag.
  • When should I NOT use it? Fewer than about 15 to 20 engineers, or when the domain boundaries are still unclear.

Practical example

A marketplace with 120 engineers in 14 teams. checkout-service is deployed 30 times a day by a team of eight. search-service runs on memory-heavy nodes with Elasticsearch and deploys weekly. payments-service is PCI-scoped, runs in an isolated VPC, and only three people have production access. These three capabilities have different deploy cadence, different scaling profile and different compliance regime. That is exactly when microservices are justified.

NestJS example

@nestjs/microservices supports several transports: TCP, Redis, NATS, MQTT, gRPC, RabbitMQ (Transport.RMQ) and Kafka (Transport.KAFKA). A hybrid application exposes HTTP for the gateway and a Kafka consumer for events.

// apps/inventory/src/main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { MicroserviceOptions, Transport } from '@nestjs/microservices';
import { InventoryModule } from './inventory.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(InventoryModule);

  // Kafka consumer for domain events from other services.
  app.connectMicroservice<MicroserviceOptions>({
    transport: Transport.KAFKA,
    options: {
      client: { clientId: 'inventory', brokers: process.env.KAFKA_BROKERS!.split(',') },
      consumer: { groupId: 'inventory-consumer', allowAutoTopicCreation: false },
      run: { autoCommit: false }, // commit offsets only after successful handling
    },
  });

  // gRPC server for synchronous reserve() calls from orders-service.
  app.connectMicroservice<MicroserviceOptions>({
    transport: Transport.GRPC,
    options: { package: 'inventory', protoPath: 'proto/inventory.proto', url: '0.0.0.0:50051' },
  });

  await app.startAllMicroservices();
  await app.listen(3002); // HTTP for health checks and admin endpoints
}
bootstrap();

A Kafka event handler:

// apps/inventory/src/presentation/order-events.controller.ts
import { Controller, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Ctx, EventPattern, KafkaContext, Payload } from '@nestjs/microservices';
import { CommitReservationUseCase } from '../application/commit-reservation.use-case';
import { OrderPaidEvent } from '@company/contracts'; // shared, versioned package

@Controller()
export class OrderEventsController {
  private readonly log = new Logger(OrderEventsController.name);
  constructor(private readonly commit: CommitReservationUseCase) {}

  @EventPattern('orders.order-paid.v1')
  async onOrderPaid(@Payload() event: OrderPaidEvent, @Ctx() ctx: KafkaContext) {
    // Idempotent: the use case checks a processed_events table keyed by event.id.
    await this.commit.execute({ orderId: event.orderId, eventId: event.id });

    // Manual offset commit after success so a crash mid-handler replays the message.
    const { offset } = ctx.getMessage();
    const partition = ctx.getPartition();
    const topic = ctx.getTopic();
    await ctx.getConsumer().commitOffsets([{ topic, partition, offset: (Number(offset) + 1).toString() }]);
  }
}

And a gRPC client in orders-service with a timeout, because every network call must have one:

// apps/orders/src/infrastructure/inventory.grpc-client.ts
import { Inject, Injectable, OnModuleInit, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ClientGrpc } from '@nestjs/microservices';
import { firstValueFrom, timeout, catchError, throwError } from 'rxjs';
import { InventoryPort } from '../domain/ports/inventory.port';

interface InventoryGrpc {
  reserve(req: { orderId: string; lines: { productId: string; qty: number }[] }): import('rxjs').Observable<{ reservationId: string }>;
}

@Injectable()
export class InventoryGrpcClient implements InventoryPort, OnModuleInit {
  private svc!: InventoryGrpc;
  constructor(@Inject('INVENTORY_PACKAGE') private readonly client: ClientGrpc) {}

  onModuleInit() {
    this.svc = this.client.getService<InventoryGrpc>('InventoryService');
  }

  async reserve(orderId: string, lines: { productId: string; qty: number }[]) {
    return firstValueFrom(
      this.svc.reserve({ orderId, lines }).pipe(
        timeout(800), // p99 of inventory is 120 ms; 800 ms is a generous budget
        catchError((err) => throwError(() => new ServiceUnavailableException(`inventory: ${err.message}`))),
      ),
    );
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Service-per-database means orders-service cannot join to products. It keeps the data it needs, denormalised, from events:

-- orders DB: a local, read-only projection of product data, fed by product.updated events
CREATE TABLE product_snapshot (
  product_id   uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  name         text NOT NULL,
  price_cents  integer NOT NULL,
  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
  source_event_id uuid NOT NULL      -- for idempotent upserts
);

-- Idempotent projection update
INSERT INTO product_snapshot (product_id, name, price_cents, updated_at, source_event_id)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5)
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE
  SET name = EXCLUDED.name, price_cents = EXCLUDED.price_cents, updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
  WHERE product_snapshot.updated_at < EXCLUDED.updated_at;  -- ignore out-of-order events

The WHERE updated_at < EXCLUDED.updated_at guard is what protects you when Kafka delivers an older event after a newer one (different partitions, consumer restarts).

The other unavoidable table is the outbox, which makes "write to my DB and publish an event" atomic (detailed in Part 5.6 on event-driven architecture):

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  topic         text NOT NULL,
  payload       jsonb NOT NULL,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at  timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished_idx ON outbox (created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

Production scenario

The honest operating cost of microservices, with numbers from a 25-service system:

Cost Monolith 25 microservices
CI/CD pipelines to maintain 1 25 (plus shared templates)
Helm charts / deployment manifests 1 25
Dashboards and alert rules ~10 ~250
Distributed tracing optional mandatory
p99 checkout latency (same hardware) 90 ms 240 ms (4 hops at 30 to 40 ms each)
Cross-domain consistency one ACID transaction saga + outbox + idempotent consumers
Local dev setup docker compose up with 2 containers 25 containers or a shared dev cluster
Engineers needed for platform work 0 to 1 3 to 6 (a platform team)
Contract management TypeScript compiler versioned schemas, consumer-driven contract tests

A senior engineer says this out loud in the planning meeting: "Adopting microservices means hiring a platform team." If the company cannot afford that, it cannot afford microservices.

Distributed transactions deserve their own paragraph. In a monolith, checkout is one BEGIN ... COMMIT. Across services, there is no COMMIT that spans orders DB and inventory DB. Two-phase commit (XA) exists but is slow, fragile, and unsupported by most cloud messaging. The practical answer is the saga: a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions (reserve stock, then charge card; if the charge fails, release the reservation). Sagas are eventually consistent, and every step must be idempotent because the coordinator will retry.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 the on-call gets paged: checkout error rate 35%. Traces show orders-service calling pricing-service calling promotions-service calling users-service to check loyalty tier. users-service is doing a deploy; two of its five pods are restarting. Calls to it time out after the default 30 seconds. promotions-service has no timeout of its own, so its threads pile up, and its own health check starts failing. Kubernetes restarts promotions-service pods. Now pricing-service is timing out. The cascade reaches the gateway. A routine deploy of a leaf service has taken down checkout because nobody set timeouts and nobody had a circuit breaker.

The fix is not "fewer services". The fix is the discipline that microservices demand: per-hop timeout budgets, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and default values (assume "no loyalty discount" when users-service is unavailable).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Partial failure. Payment succeeded, inventory decrement timed out. Was it applied? You do not know. Idempotency keys and reconciliation are mandatory.
  • Duplicate messages. Kafka is at-least-once; consumers must dedupe by event id.
  • Out-of-order events across partitions; projections must compare timestamps or versions.
  • Version skew. orders-service v42 sends a field that inventory-service v17 does not know. Contracts must be backward-compatible; add fields, never rename or remove without a deprecation window.
  • Retry storms. Every caller retries three times; a slow dependency now gets 27x the load from a 3-hop chain.
  • Chatty calls. Loading an order page triggers 40 sequential HTTP calls. Use batch endpoints or a local projection.
  • Data ownership disputes. Who owns customer_email? Users-service. Everyone else caches it and must handle staleness.
  • Consumer lag after a burst; inventory falls minutes behind and oversells.
  • Rebalance storms when consumers restart during deploy; long handlers get cut off. Use manual commits and idempotent handlers.
  • Clock skew between services makes "latest event wins" unreliable; prefer version numbers over timestamps.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask three questions before splitting anything: Do we have teams that need to deploy independently? Do we have workloads with different scaling profiles? Do we have a regulatory or security boundary that requires isolation? If none applies, they do not split.

They refuse to let two services share a database. They refuse synchronous chains deeper than two hops on the critical path. They insist on tracing, timeouts and idempotency before the second service exists.

To a product manager: "Microservices let each team ship without waiting for others, but every feature that touches two teams now takes longer and needs more careful design. We are trading feature speed for team independence. Let's be sure we need the independence."

Common mistakes

  • Nano-services. Fifty services for ten engineers. Each engineer owns five pipelines and nothing gets maintained.
  • Splitting by technical layer ("the database service", "the auth service everyone calls synchronously on every request").
  • Shared database between services; the distributed monolith.
  • No timeouts, no circuit breakers, then blaming the network.
  • Synchronous request/response for everything, turning a cheap in-process call into a 30 ms hop with failure modes.
  • Ignoring idempotency until the first duplicate charge.
  • Skipping the contracts package. Each service copies the DTO and they drift.

Interview questions

  1. What does "service per database" mean and why is it non-negotiable? Expected: each service is the only writer and reader of its tables; shared DBs couple schemas and deploys and make independent scaling impossible. Follow-up: how do services get data they do not own? Projections from events, or API calls with caching.
  2. How do you handle a transaction spanning two services? Expected: saga with compensations, outbox for reliable publishing, idempotent steps. Discuss orchestration vs choreography.
  3. A leaf service deploy caused a checkout outage. Walk through the cascade and the fixes. Expected: missing timeouts, no circuit breaker, no fallback; fixes with numbers (timeout budgets per hop).
  4. What are the operational costs of microservices that people underestimate? Expected: pipelines x N, tracing, contract management, local dev, platform team, cross-team feature latency.
  5. How do you version an event schema? Expected: additive changes only, topic name with version suffix for breaking changes, consumers tolerant of unknown fields, schema registry.
  6. When would you choose gRPC over REST between services? Expected: strict contracts via protobuf, lower latency and payload size, streaming; REST when browser clients or simplicity matter.

Practical exercise

Split the inventory module from your modular monolith into a separate NestJS service. Expose reserve() over gRPC with an 800 ms client timeout, consume orders.order-paid.v1 from Kafka with manual offset commits, and keep a processed_events table for idempotency. Kill the inventory service during a load test.

Acceptance criteria: checkout returns a clear 503 within 1 second when inventory is down (no 30-second hangs); after inventory restarts, no order-paid event is processed twice (verify by row count in processed_events vs events sent); a replayed event with an older timestamp does not overwrite newer stock data.

5.4 Service-oriented architecture (SOA)

Concept

SOA is the older sibling of microservices. It also splits a system into services, but the classic SOA of the 2000s organised them around an Enterprise Service Bus (ESB): a central middleware that routed messages, transformed formats, applied business rules and orchestrated multi-step processes. Services were typically large ("the Customer service", "the Billing service") and communicated through SOAP/XML over the bus.

Why does it exist?

SOA was born inside large enterprises that had dozens of legacy systems (mainframe billing, a CRM bought from a vendor, a home-grown ERP) that needed to talk to each other. Point-to-point integrations between 30 systems mean up to 435 adapters. The ESB reduced that to 30 adapters, one per system, with the bus in the middle.

Mental model

Imagine an airport hub. Instead of every small city having a direct flight to every other city, all flights go through the hub. Fewer routes to maintain, but the hub becomes the bottleneck, the single point of failure, and the place where every delay originates. That hub is the ESB.

How it works

  1. Each system exposes a service interface (WSDL contract, SOAP endpoint).
  2. The ESB receives messages, transforms them (XML from system A into the schema system B expects), routes them, and often contains orchestration logic (BPEL processes).
  3. A registry lists available services.
  4. Governance boards approve contract changes because a change on the bus affects everyone.

How it differs from microservices

Aspect Classic SOA Microservices
Service size Large, coarse-grained Small, single capability
Integration Smart bus (ESB), dumb endpoints Dumb pipes (Kafka, HTTP), smart endpoints
Data Often shared enterprise databases Service per database
Protocols SOAP, XML, WS-* standards REST, gRPC, JSON, protobuf
Ownership Central integration team Product teams own end-to-end
Deployment Coordinated releases Independent releases
Logic location Business rules inside the ESB Business rules inside the services

The critical difference is where the intelligence lives. SOA put it in the middle. Microservices put it at the edges and keep the middle simple. The ESB became a monolith of its own: a giant, vendor-locked, hard-to-test blob of routing and transformation rules owned by a team that every product team had to queue for.

Production scenario

You still meet SOA in banks, insurers, telcos and government. A NestJS service you write may need to call a SOAP endpoint on an ESB to fetch a customer's policy. The senior approach is the anti-corruption layer: a NestJS adapter that speaks SOAP to the ESB and translates into your clean domain types, so the legacy schema never leaks into your code.

// src/modules/policies/infrastructure/esb-policy.adapter.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HttpService } from '@nestjs/axios';
import { firstValueFrom } from 'rxjs';
import { PolicyPort, Policy } from '../domain/ports/policy.port';

@Injectable()
export class EsbPolicyAdapter implements PolicyPort {
  private readonly log = new Logger(EsbPolicyAdapter.name);
  constructor(private readonly http: HttpService) {}

  async findByCustomer(customerId: string): Promise<Policy[]> {
    const envelope = `<soapenv:Envelope xmlns:soapenv="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/">
      <soapenv:Body><GetPolicies><CustomerId>${customerId}</CustomerId></GetPolicies></soapenv:Body>
    </soapenv:Envelope>`;
    const res = await firstValueFrom(
      this.http.post(process.env.ESB_URL!, envelope, {
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'text/xml', SOAPAction: 'GetPolicies' },
        timeout: 5000, // the ESB is slow; budget accordingly and cache upstream
      }),
    );
    return this.parse(res.data); // XML into Policy[]; legacy field names stop here
  }

  private parse(xml: string): Policy[] {
    // use fast-xml-parser; map PolicyNbr -> policyNumber, EffDt -> effectiveFrom, etc.
    return [];
  }
}

Edge cases & failure modes

  • ESB as single point of failure; when it is down, every integration is down.
  • Governance latency. A contract change takes six weeks to approve.
  • Transformation logic drift. Business rules hidden in bus mappings that no product team knows about.
  • XML payload bloat. A 2 KB JSON becomes 40 KB SOAP; latency and cost follow.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see SOA's core idea (services with contracts) as correct and the ESB as the mistake. When integrating with an ESB, they isolate it behind an adapter, cache aggressively, set tight timeouts, and never let SOAP types cross into the domain.

Interview questions

  1. How do SOA and microservices differ? Expected: smart pipes vs smart endpoints; shared vs owned data; coarse vs fine services; central vs product-team ownership.
  2. What was wrong with the ESB? Expected: it became a monolith of integration logic, a bottleneck and an organisational chokepoint.
  3. How do you integrate a modern service with a legacy SOAP system? Expected: anti-corruption layer adapter, timeouts, caching, contract tests against a recorded WSDL.

5.5 Serverless

Concept

Serverless means you deploy functions, not processes. The cloud provider (AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, Azure Functions) starts an execution environment when a request or event arrives, runs your handler, and freezes or destroys the environment afterwards. You pay per invocation and per millisecond of execution, not per hour of a running server.

Why does it exist?

It exists to remove server management and to make cost proportional to usage. A webhook handler that runs 200 times a day should not cost a 24/7 container. A batch job that runs once a night should not need a Kubernetes node. For spiky, event-driven, low-average-load workloads, serverless is dramatically cheaper and simpler to operate.

Mental model

Imagine a taxi versus owning a car. The taxi costs nothing while you sleep. It arrives when you call it, but there is a wait (the cold start). If you need a ride every three minutes all day, the taxi is more expensive and less convenient than a car you already own. Serverless is the taxi.

How it works

  1. You package your NestJS app as a Lambda handler. The @codegenie/serverless-express package (formerly @vendia/serverless-express) wraps an Express-compatible app so API Gateway events become HTTP requests.
  2. On the first invocation in a fresh environment, Lambda downloads the package, starts Node.js, runs your module-level code (this is where NestJS bootstraps and builds its DI graph), then calls the handler. This is the cold start: typically 800 ms to 3 seconds for a NestJS app with TypeORM, depending on bundle size and the number of providers.
  3. The environment is kept warm for a while (minutes). Subsequent requests reuse it: warm start, a few milliseconds of overhead.
  4. Concurrency scales by creating more environments. 500 concurrent requests means up to 500 environments, each with its own cold start and, critically, its own database connection.
  5. The environment is frozen between invocations. Timers and background promises do not run. Anything not awaited before the handler returns may never complete.

NestJS example

// src/lambda.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ExpressAdapter } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import serverlessExpress from '@codegenie/serverless-express';
import { Handler, Context, Callback } from 'aws-lambda';
import express from 'express';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

// Cache the server across warm invocations; this is the whole cold-start game.
let cachedHandler: Handler | undefined;

async function bootstrap(): Promise<Handler> {
  const expressApp = express();
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, new ExpressAdapter(expressApp), {
    logger: ['error', 'warn'], // less logging during bootstrap shaves cold start time
  });
  app.enableCors();
  await app.init(); // NOT app.listen(); Lambda owns the socket
  return serverlessExpress({ app: expressApp });
}

export const handler: Handler = async (event, context: Context, callback: Callback) => {
  // Let Lambda freeze the environment without waiting for open DB sockets.
  context.callbackWaitsForEmptyEventLoop = false;
  cachedHandler = cachedHandler ?? (await bootstrap());
  return cachedHandler(event, context, callback);
};

Cold start reductions that actually work: bundle with esbuild into one file (no node_modules scanning), lazy-load heavy modules with NestJS LazyModuleLoader, keep the DI graph small, use Provisioned Concurrency for latency-sensitive paths, and use Lambda SnapStart-style features where available for your runtime.

PostgreSQL example: the connection problem

PostgreSQL forks a process per connection; each costs about 5 to 10 MB of RAM and a few milliseconds to establish (more with TLS). A db.t3.medium RDS instance defaults to roughly 400 max connections. If 1,000 Lambda environments each open their own connection, the database refuses new connections (FATAL: too many connections) and the entire API fails, including the warm ones.

RDS Proxy solves this. It is a managed connection pooler that sits between Lambda and PostgreSQL. Lambdas open cheap connections to the proxy; the proxy multiplexes them onto a small pool of real database connections.

 1,000 Lambda envs --(1,000 light conns)--> RDS Proxy --(50 real conns)--> PostgreSQL

Configure TypeORM for it:

// typeorm datasource for Lambda + RDS Proxy
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

export const dataSource = new DataSource({
  type: 'postgres',
  host: process.env.RDS_PROXY_ENDPOINT, // proxy endpoint, not the DB host
  port: 5432,
  username: process.env.DB_USER,
  password: process.env.DB_PASSWORD,
  database: 'shop',
  ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: true },
  extra: {
    max: 1,                      // ONE connection per environment; the proxy pools
    idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,
    connectionTimeoutMillis: 3_000,
  },
  entities: [__dirname + '/**/*.entity.js'],
});

Two constraints to remember: RDS Proxy pins a session to a real connection when you use session-level features (SET, prepared statements, advisory locks, temporary tables), which reduces the multiplexing benefit; and it adds about 1 to 3 ms per query. Sequelize configuration is equivalent: pool: { max: 1, min: 0, idle: 30000 }.

Production scenario

Where serverless shines, with realistic numbers:

  • Webhook receivers (Stripe, Razorpay, Shopify): 5,000 events a day, bursts of 200 per second when a batch settles. Cost: under a dollar a month. A container would cost 30 to 60 dollars a month and sit idle 99% of the time.
  • Image and file processing triggered by S3 uploads: 40,000 images a day, 2 seconds each, needs 1 GB memory. Lambda scales to 300 concurrent without any capacity planning.
  • Scheduled jobs (EventBridge cron): nightly reports, cleanup, invoice generation.
  • Internal tooling and low-traffic admin APIs.

Where it hurts:

  • A core API at 500+ RPS sustained. Costs exceed containers, and the p99 is dominated by cold starts unless you pay for Provisioned Concurrency, at which point you are paying for servers again.
  • Long-running work. Lambda caps execution at 15 minutes.
  • WebSockets and long-lived connections. Possible through API Gateway WebSocket APIs, but awkward.
  • Kafka consumers. Possible with event source mappings, but the batching and error semantics are different from a long-running NestJS consumer.

Cost comparison for a 100 RPS API with 50 ms average execution at 512 MB: Lambda is roughly 130 to 180 dollars a month plus API Gateway (around 350 dollars a month at 260 million requests); two small Fargate tasks behind an ALB cost around 70 to 90 dollars a month. Serverless wins on low or spiky traffic, loses on steady traffic.

Failure scenario

Friday 18:00, flash sale. Traffic on the product API jumps from 20 RPS to 900 RPS in one minute. Lambda scales to 700 concurrent environments. Each opens a TypeORM pool of max: 10 (the default someone copied from the container config). PostgreSQL hits its 400-connection limit within seconds. Every function, warm or cold, fails with too many connections. The team scales RDS vertically (a 10-minute reboot) which makes it worse. The fix that worked: set max: 1, put RDS Proxy in front, and add reserved concurrency on the function so it cannot exceed what the proxy can handle. Total outage: 42 minutes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Cold start p99 spikes of 2 to 4 seconds; clients with 3-second timeouts see errors on every scale-out event.
  • Frozen background work. A setImmediate log flush or a fire-and-forget email promise never runs; the environment is frozen at return. Await everything, or use SQS.
  • Connection exhaustion without a proxy.
  • Duplicate invocations. Lambda retries asynchronous invocations; handlers must be idempotent.
  • 15-minute limit and payload limits (6 MB synchronous request/response).
  • Vendor lock-in of the deployment model; NestJS mitigates by keeping the app framework-portable.
  • Observability gaps. Logs are per invocation in CloudWatch; you need structured logging and a trace id per request.
  • Local development needs SAM or the Serverless Framework to emulate events.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They use serverless for the edges (webhooks, file processing, cron, glue) and containers for the core API, unless the whole product is low-traffic. They keep the NestJS app portable so the same code runs in a container tomorrow. They never deploy a Lambda that talks to PostgreSQL without a pooler, and they set reserved concurrency to protect the database.

To a product manager: "Serverless means we pay only when the code runs and we never manage a server. It is perfect for the webhook and the nightly reports. For the main API, it would cost more and be slower at peak, so that stays on containers."

Common mistakes

  • Copying the container pool configuration (max: 10) into a Lambda.
  • Calling app.listen() in a Lambda handler.
  • Forgetting callbackWaitsForEmptyEventLoop = false, so every invocation waits for the idle DB socket to close and hits the timeout.
  • Fire-and-forget promises that never complete.
  • Putting a 300 MB node_modules in the deployment package and wondering about 6-second cold starts.
  • Running a Kafka consumer loop inside a Lambda.

Interview questions

  1. What is a cold start and how do you reduce it for a NestJS app? Expected: environment bootstrap plus DI graph construction; reduce with bundling, lazy modules, smaller graphs, provisioned concurrency.
  2. Why is PostgreSQL a problem for Lambda and what is the fix? Expected: per-environment connections exhaust the server; RDS Proxy or PgBouncer, max: 1, reserved concurrency.
  3. When is serverless more expensive than containers? Expected: steady high traffic; give a rough break-even.
  4. What happens to a promise you did not await in a Lambda handler? Expected: the environment freezes; it may run later on the next invocation or never.
  5. How would you run a NestJS app both in Lambda and in a container? Expected: separate entry points (lambda.ts, main.ts), same AppModule, config from environment.

Practical exercise

Deploy a NestJS webhook receiver to Lambda with @codegenie/serverless-express, writing to PostgreSQL through RDS Proxy (or PgBouncer in a container for a local exercise). Configure TypeORM with max: 1. Fire 500 concurrent webhook calls with a load tool.

Acceptance criteria: PostgreSQL pg_stat_activity never shows more than the proxy's configured pool size; no too many connections errors; duplicate webhook deliveries (same event id) produce exactly one row.

5.6 Event-driven architecture

Concept

In an event-driven architecture (EDA), components communicate by publishing facts about what happened ("an order was paid") rather than by telling each other what to do ("send the confirmation email"). Producers write events to a broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SNS/SQS). Consumers subscribe and react. The producer does not know who consumes, or whether anyone does.

An event is a record of something that already happened, named in the past tense: OrderPaid, StockReserved, UserRegistered. A command is a request to do something, named in the imperative: ReserveStock, SendEmail, ChargeCard. A command has exactly one handler and can be rejected. An event has zero or many consumers and cannot be rejected; it is history.

Why does it exist?

EDA exists to decouple the thing that happened from the things that must happen next. When checkout emits OrderPaid, the checkout code does not change when marketing wants a new "first purchase" campaign, when finance wants a ledger entry, or when the warehouse wants a pick list. Each of those is a new consumer.

It also absorbs load. A burst of 10,000 orders in a minute does not have to be processed by the email service in that minute. The broker holds the backlog; consumers drain it at their own pace.

Without EDA, every side effect is a synchronous call inside the request, the request grows slower with every feature, and one slow side effect fails the whole thing.

Mental model

Imagine a newspaper. The reporter writes a story about what happened. The paper is delivered to every subscriber. The reporter does not call each reader. Readers who are on holiday get their papers when they return (the backlog). If a reader misreads the story, the reporter is not involved. Compare this with a phone tree, where each person must call the next and wait for an answer: that is synchronous request/response.

How it works

  1. A service performs a local state change (insert the order, mark it paid).
  2. In the same database transaction, it writes an event row to an outbox table. This is the transactional outbox pattern; it guarantees that the event exists if and only if the state change committed.
  3. A relay (a polling job, or Debezium reading the write-ahead log) publishes outbox rows to the broker and marks them published.
  4. The broker persists the event in a topic (Kafka) or routes it to queues (RabbitMQ exchanges).
  5. Each consumer group reads the event, checks a processed_events table to skip duplicates, performs its own local transaction, and commits its offset.
  6. Consumers that fail retry; after N failures the event goes to a dead-letter topic for human inspection.
sequenceDiagram
  participant O as OrdersService
  participant DB as OrdersDB
  participant R as OutboxRelay
  participant K as Kafka
  participant I as InventoryConsumer
  participant N as NotificationsConsumer
  O->>DB: BEGIN, UPDATE orders SET status PAID, INSERT INTO outbox, COMMIT
  R->>DB: SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL
  R->>K: produce orders.order-paid.v1
  R->>DB: UPDATE outbox SET published_at=now()
  K-->>I: OrderPaid
  I->>I: dedupe by event id, commit reservation
  K-->>N: OrderPaid
  N->>N: dedupe by event id, send email

Choreography vs orchestration. In choreography, there is no central coordinator: OrderPaid triggers inventory, which emits StockCommitted, which triggers shipping, and so on. It is simple to start and hard to follow at scale (who decides the order is "complete"?). In orchestration, a saga orchestrator (a state machine, often in the orders service) sends commands and waits for events, holding the full picture. Choreography for three steps, orchestration for anything with compensation logic or a meaningful "process state".

Eventual consistency. After OrderPaid is published, there is a window (usually milliseconds, sometimes minutes during lag) in which orders says PAID and inventory has not yet decremented. Every read that crosses that boundary can see a stale state. The product must accept this: "your order is confirmed; stock is being allocated" is a UX statement of eventual consistency.

Event schemas. An event is a public contract. It needs: a unique id (for dedupe), type and version, occurredAt, the aggregate id, and a payload. Payloads should be self-contained (a consumer should not need to call back to get the data), but not bloated with the whole aggregate. Schema evolution rules: only add optional fields; never rename or change types; for breaking changes, publish a new versioned topic and run both for a deprecation window.

Practical example

Food delivery. When a restaurant marks an order as ready, the orders service emits OrderReady. Consumers: dispatch (find a rider), notifications (push to the customer), analytics (kitchen prep time), restaurant billing (commission ledger). Four teams, zero changes to the orders service when a fifth consumer appears.

NestJS example

Writing to the outbox inside the same TypeORM transaction:

// src/modules/orders/application/mark-paid.use-case.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { OrderEntity } from '../infrastructure/order.entity';
import { OutboxEntity } from '../infrastructure/outbox.entity';

@Injectable()
export class MarkOrderPaidUseCase {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}

  async execute(orderId: string, paymentId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
      const result = await manager
        .createQueryBuilder()
        .update(OrderEntity)
        .set({ status: 'PAID', paymentId })
        .where('id = :orderId AND status = :expected', { orderId, expected: 'CREATED' })
        .execute();

      // Idempotent: a second call for the same order updates 0 rows and emits nothing.
      if (result.affected === 0) return;

      await manager.insert(OutboxEntity, {
        id: randomUUID(),
        aggregateId: orderId,
        topic: 'orders.order-paid.v1',
        payload: {
          id: randomUUID(),
          type: 'OrderPaid',
          version: 1,
          occurredAt: new Date().toISOString(),
          orderId,
          paymentId,
        },
      });
    });
  }
}

The relay, using @nestjs/schedule and KafkaJS:

// src/modules/outbox/outbox-relay.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Producer } from 'kafkajs';
import { OutboxEntity } from '../orders/infrastructure/outbox.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OutboxRelayService {
  private readonly log = new Logger(OutboxRelayService.name);
  private running = false;

  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource, private readonly producer: Producer) {}

  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_SECOND)
  async relay(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.running) return; // never overlap runs
    this.running = true;
    try {
      // SKIP LOCKED lets several replicas relay in parallel without double-sending.
      const rows: OutboxEntity[] = await this.dataSource.query(
        `SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL
         ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`,
      );
      for (const row of rows) {
        await this.producer.send({
          topic: row.topic,
          messages: [{ key: row.aggregateId, value: JSON.stringify(row.payload) }],
        });
        await this.dataSource.query(`UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = $1`, [row.id]);
      }
    } catch (err) {
      this.log.error(`relay failed: ${(err as Error).message}`);
    } finally {
      this.running = false;
    }
  }
}

Note that this relay is at-least-once: if the process dies after producer.send but before the UPDATE, the event is sent twice. Consumers dedupe by payload.id. This is why the event carries its own id.

The Kafka key is the aggregate id, so all events for one order land on the same partition and are consumed in order.

PostgreSQL example

The consumer side, idempotent by event id:

CREATE TABLE processed_events (
  event_id     uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  consumer     text NOT NULL,
  processed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- In the consumer's transaction:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id, consumer) VALUES ($1, 'inventory')
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
-- If the insert affected 0 rows, this event was already handled: ROLLBACK and ack.
UPDATE inventory.stock SET reserved = reserved - $2, available = available - $2
WHERE product_id = $3 AND reserved >= $2;
COMMIT;

Check rowCount after the first insert. If it is zero, skip the work and still acknowledge the message. This gives you exactly-once effects on top of at-least-once delivery.

Production scenario

Kafka topic orders.order-paid.v1 with 12 partitions, 400 events per second at peak, retention 7 days. Three consumer groups. Consumer lag is the key metric: kafka_consumergroup_lag per group, alert when it exceeds 5,000 messages or 60 seconds. Outbox table is pruned nightly (DELETE WHERE published_at < now() - interval '3 days') to keep the partial index small.

Latency budget from commit to consumer effect: relay poll up to 1 second, Kafka produce 5 ms, consumer poll and handle 10 to 50 ms. Typical end-to-end under 1.2 seconds. With Debezium instead of polling, under 200 ms.

Failure scenario

At 11:05 a deploy of the notifications consumer ships a bug: it throws on events with a null couponCode. The consumer library retries the same message forever (no dead-letter configured). The partition stalls. Lag on that partition climbs to 180,000 messages over two hours. Customers on that partition get no confirmation emails. The other 11 partitions are fine, so dashboards showing average lag look healthy. The on-call notices only when support tickets spike.

Fixes: per-partition lag alerts, a dead-letter topic after 5 attempts, a consumer that treats malformed events as poison rather than transient failures, and a replay tool that can reprocess a partition from an offset.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Event storms. A bulk price update emits 2 million ProductUpdated events; every projection recomputes. Batch or coalesce, and rate-limit consumers.
  • Out-of-order events across partitions or after a rebalance; use per-aggregate version numbers.
  • Duplicate events from at-least-once relays; dedupe table.
  • Poison messages stalling a partition; dead-letter after N tries.
  • Schema drift; producer adds a required field, old consumers crash. Enforce compatibility with a schema registry and contract tests.
  • Consumer lag hiding in averages; alert per partition.
  • Lost in-process events if you use EventEmitter2 as if it were a broker.
  • Large payloads (an event carrying a 4 MB PDF); store the blob, emit the reference.
  • Fan-out loops. Service A emits X, B reacts and emits Y, A reacts to Y and emits X again. Track causation ids.
  • Replays with side effects. Replaying OrderPaid to rebuild a projection also resends 200,000 emails unless the email consumer distinguishes replays.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They separate the two questions: Does this caller need an answer now? (command, synchronous) and Do others need to know this happened? (event, asynchronous). They never publish an event without the outbox, never consume without idempotency, and never deploy a consumer without a dead-letter topic and per-partition lag alerts.

They design the event schema as carefully as a public REST API, because it is one.

Common mistakes

  • Publishing to Kafka then committing the database transaction (or the reverse) without an outbox; the two get out of sync on the first crash.
  • Events that are really commands in disguise (SendEmailEvent), coupling producer to consumer.
  • Consumers with no dedupe.
  • One consumer group doing three unrelated things; one bug blocks all three.
  • Treating eventual consistency as a bug to be hidden rather than a product decision to be designed.

Interview questions

  1. Event vs command: explain the difference and the consequences for coupling. Expected: fact vs request; many consumers vs one handler; cannot be rejected vs can.
  2. How do you guarantee an event is published if and only if the state change committed? Expected: transactional outbox, relay, at-least-once with consumer dedupe.
  3. Choreography vs orchestration: when each? Expected: choreography for simple flows, orchestration when there is compensation and process state.
  4. How do you evolve an event schema without breaking consumers? Expected: additive optional fields, versioned topics for breaking changes, tolerant readers, registry.
  5. A partition is stalled. How do you detect it and recover? Expected: per-partition lag alert, DLQ, skip poison offset, replay.

Practical exercise

Implement the outbox pattern in a NestJS orders module with TypeORM. Add a relay using @nestjs/schedule with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, and a Kafka consumer in another module with a processed_events table. Kill the relay process randomly during a 10,000-event load test.

Acceptance criteria: every committed order produces at least one Kafka message; the consumer's side effects happen exactly once per order (row counts match); running two relay replicas does not double-publish beyond what the consumer dedupes.

5.7 Layered architecture

Concept

Layered architecture organises code into horizontal layers, each of which may only call the layer directly below it. The classic three: presentation (HTTP controllers, DTOs, validation), business logic (services), and data access (repositories, ORM). Sometimes a fourth, the database itself, is drawn underneath.

This is the architecture NestJS's generator gives you by default: controller -> service -> repository.

Why does it exist?

It exists to stop HTTP details from leaking into business rules and SQL from leaking into controllers. When a controller contains SELECT statements, you cannot test the business rule without an HTTP server and a database, and you cannot reuse the rule from a Kafka consumer or a cron job.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel. The front desk (presentation) takes your request. It does not clean rooms; it calls housekeeping (business logic). Housekeeping does not manufacture towels; it takes them from the storeroom (data access). Each floor knows only the floor below. The guest never walks into the storeroom.

How it works

  HTTP request
      |
      v
  +-----------------------------+
  | Presentation                |  controllers, DTOs, pipes, guards, filters
  +-----------------------------+
      | calls (method call)
      v
  +-----------------------------+
  | Business / Service          |  OrdersService, PaymentsService
  +-----------------------------+
      | calls
      v
  +-----------------------------+
  | Data access                 |  Repository<Order>, QueryBuilder, Sequelize models
  +-----------------------------+
      | SQL
      v
  PostgreSQL

Rules: a layer depends only on the layer below. Data flows down as parameters and up as return values. Cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth, transactions) are applied at the edges with NestJS interceptors, guards and middleware.

NestJS example

// presentation
@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Post()
  @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
  create(@CurrentUser() user: AuthUser, @Body() dto: CreateOrderDto) {
    return this.orders.create(user.id, dto); // no logic here; translate and delegate
  }
}

// business
@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Order) private readonly orders: Repository<Order>,
    private readonly products: ProductsService,
  ) {}

  async create(userId: string, dto: CreateOrderDto): Promise<Order> {
    const product = await this.products.getActive(dto.productId); // throws NotFound
    if (dto.qty > product.maxPerOrder) throw new UnprocessableEntityException('qty too high');
    return this.orders.save(this.orders.create({ userId, productId: product.id, qty: dto.qty }));
  }
}

This is clean, readable and correct for most CRUD-heavy services. Most NestJS code in the world looks like this, and that is fine.

Where it breaks
