Layered architecture has a direction problem: the business layer depends on the data layer. OrdersService imports Repository<Order> from TypeORM. The most important code in your system (the rules) depends on the least important (which ORM you chose). Consequences:

  1. Testing the rules needs the ORM. You mock Repository<Order> with its 40 methods, or you spin up a database. Unit tests become slow or brittle.
  2. Entities become the domain model. Order is a TypeORM @Entity with @Column decorators, no behaviour, public mutable fields. Business rules end up in services as procedural code over anaemic data bags.
  3. The ORM leaks upward. A service returns a TypeORM entity; the controller serialises it; lazy relations, circular references and password_hash columns end up in JSON.
  4. Fat services. With no place for domain logic, OrdersService grows to 1,500 lines that mix validation, orchestration, persistence and side effects.
  5. Multiple entry points strain it. The same business rule needed from an HTTP controller, a Kafka consumer and a cron job; the "presentation layer" was designed for HTTP only.
  6. Transaction boundaries are awkward. Who opens the transaction: the controller, the service, or the repository? Usually the service, which now holds a DataSource and knows about QueryRunner.

Layered architecture works well until the domain has real rules. The moment "can this order be cancelled?" depends on status, payment state, shipping state and a refund policy, you want a domain object that answers that question with no database in sight. That is where hexagonal, clean and onion architectures come in (next section): they keep the layers but flip the dependency direction so the domain depends on nothing.

Production scenario

A 60,000-line NestJS layered service handling 800 RPS. Over three years, OrdersService accumulates 38 injected dependencies. Every unit test file starts with 80 lines of mocks. A change to the refund rule takes two days because the rule is spread across OrdersService.cancel(), PaymentsService.refund() and a database trigger. The team's velocity is one third of what it was in year one.

Failure scenario

A developer adds @Get(':id') that returns the TypeORM User entity directly. The entity has passwordHash and an eager relation to Sessions. Every user lookup now serialises session tokens to the client. It ships on a Thursday; a security researcher reports it on Saturday. The root cause is architectural: there was no boundary between the persistence model and the API response.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Entities returned directly from controllers (data leaks, over-fetching).
  • Services depending on Repository<T> make swapping or testing storage painful.
  • Business rules duplicated between HTTP and messaging entry points.
  • Transactions opened in controllers (or worse, in interceptors that do not know the business step).
  • Circular service dependencies (OrdersService needs PaymentsService needs OrdersService).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They use plain layering for services that are mostly CRUD with light rules, and they draw a hard line at the API boundary: controllers return response DTOs, never entities. When the rules get thick, they introduce a domain layer with no framework imports and invert the dependency. They do not add that ceremony to a 12-endpoint admin service.

Common mistakes

  • Logic in controllers ("just a small if").
  • Returning entities from controllers.
  • Services that are just pass-throughs to repositories (no value) alongside services that are 1,500 lines (too much value).
  • Believing "layered" and "clean" are opposites; clean architecture is layering with inverted dependencies.

Interview questions

  1. What is the dependency direction problem in layered architecture? Expected: business depends on data access; inversion fixes it.
  2. Why should a controller never return an ORM entity? Expected: data leaks, coupling API to schema, serialisation surprises.
  3. Where do you open a transaction in a layered NestJS app? Expected: at the use-case/service boundary, never in controllers; see Unit of Work in Part 6.
  4. When is plain layering enough? Expected: CRUD-dominant, thin rules, small team; know the signals for moving on.

Practical exercise

Take a layered NestJS module where the controller returns entities. Introduce response DTOs with class-transformer @Exclude()/@Expose() and ClassSerializerInterceptor, and move one business rule ("orders over 10 items require manual approval") out of the service into a plain TypeScript class with no imports from typeorm or @nestjs/*.

Acceptance criteria: no endpoint returns a field not declared in a DTO; the rule class has a unit test with no mocks and runs in under 5 ms.

5.8 Hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)

Concept

Hexagonal architecture, proposed by Alistair Cockburn, puts the application's core (domain model plus use cases) in the middle and surrounds it with ports and adapters. A port is an interface the core defines: "I need something that can save orders", "I need something that can charge a card". An adapter is a concrete implementation of a port using a specific technology: a TypeORM repository, a Stripe client, a Kafka consumer, an HTTP controller.

The core knows about ports. It never knows about adapters. The dependency arrows all point inward.

Why does it exist?

It exists to make the most valuable code in the system (business rules) independent of the most changeable code (frameworks, databases, third-party APIs). You can test the core with no database, no HTTP, no network, in milliseconds. You can swap Stripe for Razorpay by writing a new adapter. You can drive the same use case from REST, GraphQL, a Kafka message or a CLI without touching the core.

Without it, every business rule is entangled with TypeORM decorators and NestJS exceptions, and "let's add a second payment provider" means editing forty files.

Mental model

Imagine a laptop. The motherboard (core) exposes standard sockets: USB-C, HDMI, a headphone jack (ports). Any keyboard, monitor or headset (adapters) that fits the socket works. The motherboard does not care which brand of monitor you plug in, and the monitor manufacturer never sees the motherboard's schematics. Your business logic is the motherboard. TypeORM is one brand of monitor.

How it works

flowchart LR
  subgraph Driving["Driving adapters (inbound)"]
    HTTP["HTTP Controller"]
    KC["Kafka Consumer"]
    CLI["CLI / Cron"]
  end
  subgraph Core["Application core"]
    UC["Use cases\nPlaceOrder, CancelOrder"]
    DOM["Domain\nOrder, Money, OrderStatus"]
    IP["Inbound ports\nPlaceOrderPort"]
    OP["Outbound ports\nOrderRepository, PaymentGateway, EventPublisher"]
  end
  subgraph Driven["Driven adapters (outbound)"]
    TO["TypeORM OrderRepository"]
    SQ["Sequelize OrderRepository"]
    ST["Stripe PaymentGateway"]
    KP["Kafka EventPublisher"]
  end
  HTTP --> IP
  KC --> IP
  CLI --> IP
  IP --> UC
  UC --> DOM
  UC --> OP
  TO -.->|implements| OP
  SQ -.->|implements| OP
  ST -.->|implements| OP
  KP -.->|implements| OP
  1. Inbound (driving) ports are the use-case interfaces: PlaceOrderPort { execute(cmd): Promise<Result> }. Controllers and consumers call them.
  2. Outbound (driven) ports are the interfaces the core needs from the outside world: OrderRepository, PaymentGateway, EventPublisher, Clock.
  3. The domain contains entities and value objects with behaviour (order.cancel() enforces the rules), and domain errors.
  4. Use cases orchestrate: load through a port, call domain behaviour, save through a port, publish through a port.
  5. Adapters implement the outbound ports (TypeORM, Stripe, Kafka) or call the inbound ports (HTTP, Kafka consumer).
  6. Wiring happens in the NestJS module, using injection tokens: { provide: ORDER_REPOSITORY, useClass: TypeormOrderRepository }.

The rule that makes this real in NestJS: the domain/ and application/ folders contain no imports from @nestjs/*, typeorm, sequelize, stripe or kafkajs. Only plain TypeScript. A lint rule enforces this.

Practical example

Orders in an e-commerce system. PlaceOrderUseCase needs to reserve inventory, create the order, and charge the customer. It depends on three ports. In production the adapters are TypeORM, a gRPC inventory client and Stripe. In tests they are in-memory fakes. In a load-test environment the payment adapter is a fake that always approves. None of that changes a line of the use case.

NestJS example

The domain, with no framework imports:

// src/modules/orders/domain/order.ts
import { Money } from '../../../shared-kernel/money';
import { DomainError } from '../../../shared-kernel/domain-error';

export type OrderStatus = 'CREATED' | 'PAID' | 'SHIPPED' | 'DELIVERED' | 'CANCELLED';

export class OrderLine {
  constructor(readonly productId: string, readonly qty: number, readonly unitPrice: Money) {
    if (qty <= 0) throw new DomainError('ORDER_LINE_QTY', 'qty must be positive');
  }
  get total(): Money { return this.unitPrice.multiply(this.qty); }
}

export class Order {
  private constructor(
    readonly id: string,
    readonly customerId: string,
    private _status: OrderStatus,
    readonly lines: OrderLine[],
    readonly createdAt: Date,
  ) {}

  static create(id: string, customerId: string, lines: OrderLine[], now: Date): Order {
    if (lines.length === 0) throw new DomainError('ORDER_EMPTY', 'order needs at least one line');
    return new Order(id, customerId, 'CREATED', lines, now);
  }

  static rehydrate(props: { id: string; customerId: string; status: OrderStatus; lines: OrderLine[]; createdAt: Date }) {
    return new Order(props.id, props.customerId, props.status, props.lines, props.createdAt);
  }

  get status(): OrderStatus { return this._status; }
  get total(): Money { return this.lines.reduce((sum, l) => sum.add(l.total), Money.zero('INR')); }

  markPaid(): void {
    if (this._status !== 'CREATED') throw new DomainError('ORDER_NOT_PAYABLE', `cannot pay order in ${this._status}`);
    this._status = 'PAID';
  }

  cancel(): void {
    if (this._status === 'SHIPPED' || this._status === 'DELIVERED') {
      throw new DomainError('ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE', `cannot cancel order in ${this._status}`);
    }
    this._status = 'CANCELLED';
  }
}

The outbound ports:

// src/modules/orders/application/ports/order.repository.ts
import { Order } from '../../domain/order';

export const ORDER_REPOSITORY = Symbol('ORDER_REPOSITORY');
export interface OrderRepository {
  findById(id: string): Promise<Order | null>;
  save(order: Order): Promise<void>;
}

// src/modules/orders/application/ports/payment.gateway.ts
import { Money } from '../../../../shared-kernel/money';

export const PAYMENT_GATEWAY = Symbol('PAYMENT_GATEWAY');
export interface PaymentGateway {
  charge(input: { orderId: string; amount: Money; idempotencyKey: string }): Promise<{ paymentId: string }>;
}

The use case, which depends only on ports and the domain:

// src/modules/orders/application/place-order.use-case.ts
import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; // the ONLY framework import, for DI wiring
import { ORDER_REPOSITORY, OrderRepository } from './ports/order.repository';
import { PAYMENT_GATEWAY, PaymentGateway } from './ports/payment.gateway';
import { EVENT_PUBLISHER, EventPublisher } from './ports/event.publisher';
import { Order, OrderLine } from '../domain/order';
import { Money } from '../../../shared-kernel/money';

export interface PlaceOrderCommand {
  orderId: string; customerId: string;
  lines: { productId: string; qty: number; unitPriceMinor: number }[];
}

@Injectable()
export class PlaceOrderUseCase {
  constructor(
    @Inject(ORDER_REPOSITORY) private readonly orders: OrderRepository,
    @Inject(PAYMENT_GATEWAY) private readonly payments: PaymentGateway,
    @Inject(EVENT_PUBLISHER) private readonly events: EventPublisher,
  ) {}

  async execute(cmd: PlaceOrderCommand): Promise<{ orderId: string }> {
    const existing = await this.orders.findById(cmd.orderId);
    if (existing) return { orderId: existing.id }; // idempotent on client-generated id

    const lines = cmd.lines.map((l) => new OrderLine(l.productId, l.qty, Money.of(l.unitPriceMinor, 'INR')));
    const order = Order.create(cmd.orderId, cmd.customerId, lines, new Date());
    await this.orders.save(order);

    const { paymentId } = await this.payments.charge({
      orderId: order.id, amount: order.total, idempotencyKey: `order:${order.id}`,
    });
    order.markPaid();
    await this.orders.save(order);
    await this.events.publish({ type: 'OrderPaid', orderId: order.id, paymentId });
    return { orderId: order.id };
  }
}

Some teams keep even @Inject out of the application layer by using a small custom decorator re-export or by wiring with useFactory. That is a matter of taste; the important line is that nothing from typeorm or stripe appears here.

The TypeORM adapter, which maps between the persistence entity and the domain object:

// src/modules/orders/infrastructure/typeorm/typeorm-order.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRepository } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { Repository } from 'typeorm';
import { OrderRepository } from '../../application/ports/order.repository';
import { Order, OrderLine } from '../../domain/order';
import { OrderEntity } from './order.entity';
import { Money } from '../../../../shared-kernel/money';

@Injectable()
export class TypeormOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(OrderEntity) private readonly repo: Repository<OrderEntity>) {}

  async findById(id: string): Promise<Order | null> {
    const row = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { lines: true } });
    if (!row) return null;
    return Order.rehydrate({
      id: row.id, customerId: row.customerId, status: row.status, createdAt: row.createdAt,
      lines: row.lines.map((l) => new OrderLine(l.productId, l.qty, Money.of(l.unitPriceMinor, 'INR'))),
    });
  }

  async save(order: Order): Promise<void> {
    const entity = this.repo.create({
      id: order.id, customerId: order.customerId, status: order.status, createdAt: order.createdAt,
      lines: order.lines.map((l) => ({ productId: l.productId, qty: l.qty, unitPriceMinor: l.unitPrice.minor })),
    });
    await this.repo.save(entity); // upsert by primary key
  }
}

And the module, which is the only place that knows both sides:

// src/modules/orders/orders.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { OrderEntity } from './infrastructure/typeorm/order.entity';
import { OrderLineEntity } from './infrastructure/typeorm/order-line.entity';
import { TypeormOrderRepository } from './infrastructure/typeorm/typeorm-order.repository';
import { StripePaymentGateway } from './infrastructure/stripe/stripe-payment.gateway';
import { KafkaEventPublisher } from './infrastructure/kafka/kafka-event.publisher';
import { PlaceOrderUseCase } from './application/place-order.use-case';
import { ORDER_REPOSITORY } from './application/ports/order.repository';
import { PAYMENT_GATEWAY } from './application/ports/payment.gateway';
import { EVENT_PUBLISHER } from './application/ports/event.publisher';
import { OrdersController } from './presentation/http/orders.controller';
import { OrderEventsConsumer } from './presentation/kafka/order-events.consumer';

@Module({
  imports: [TypeOrmModule.forFeature([OrderEntity, OrderLineEntity])],
  controllers: [OrdersController, OrderEventsConsumer],
  providers: [
    PlaceOrderUseCase,
    { provide: ORDER_REPOSITORY, useClass: TypeormOrderRepository },
    { provide: PAYMENT_GATEWAY, useClass: StripePaymentGateway },
    { provide: EVENT_PUBLISHER, useClass: KafkaEventPublisher },
  ],
})
export class OrdersModule {}

Swapping to Sequelize means one line: useClass: SequelizeOrderRepository. Testing the use case means passing fakes to the constructor, no NestJS test module required.

Sequelize example

A second adapter for the same port, demonstrating that the core does not care:

// src/modules/orders/infrastructure/sequelize/sequelize-order.repository.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectModel } from '@nestjs/sequelize';
import { OrderRepository } from '../../application/ports/order.repository';
import { Order, OrderLine } from '../../domain/order';
import { OrderModel } from './order.model';
import { OrderLineModel } from './order-line.model';
import { Money } from '../../../../shared-kernel/money';

@Injectable()
export class SequelizeOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
  constructor(@InjectModel(OrderModel) private readonly model: typeof OrderModel) {}

  async findById(id: string): Promise<Order | null> {
    const row = await this.model.findByPk(id, { include: [OrderLineModel] });
    if (!row) return null;
    return Order.rehydrate({
      id: row.id, customerId: row.customerId, status: row.status, createdAt: row.createdAt,
      lines: row.lines.map((l) => new OrderLine(l.productId, l.qty, Money.of(l.unitPriceMinor, 'INR'))),
    });
  }

  async save(order: Order): Promise<void> {
    await this.model.sequelize!.transaction(async (t) => {
      await this.model.upsert({ id: order.id, customerId: order.customerId, status: order.status, createdAt: order.createdAt }, { transaction: t });
      await OrderLineModel.destroy({ where: { orderId: order.id }, transaction: t });
      await OrderLineModel.bulkCreate(
        order.lines.map((l) => ({ orderId: order.id, productId: l.productId, qty: l.qty, unitPriceMinor: l.unitPrice.minor })),
        { transaction: t },
      );
    });
  }
}

Production scenario

A payments module with three gateway adapters (Stripe for cards, Razorpay for UPI, a bank adapter for net banking). The PAYMENT_GATEWAY token resolves to a router adapter that picks by payment method. When Razorpay has an outage at 19:30 on a sale day, the on-call flips a config flag that routes UPI through a backup provider adapter. No deploy, because the routing lives in an adapter driven by config, and the use case never knew which provider it was talking to.

Test suite numbers: 640 use-case and domain tests run in 4 seconds with in-memory fakes; 45 adapter integration tests run in 90 seconds against a real PostgreSQL in Docker. Before hexagonal, the same coverage took 11 minutes because every test bootstrapped the whole NestJS module and a database.

Failure scenario

A team adopts hexagonal architecture but lets the TypeORM OrderEntity double as the domain Order "to avoid mapping code". Six months in, someone adds @ManyToOne(() => CustomerEntity, { eager: true }) to load the customer name for an email. Now every findById in the use case pulls the customer row, and order.customer.passwordHash is reachable from domain code. A junior serialises the domain object in an event payload. The password hash ends up in Kafka, retained for 7 days, readable by every consumer team. The mapping code they skipped would have cost two hours; the incident cost a week and a security review.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Anaemic domain. Ports and adapters exist, but all rules still live in the use case as if chains and the domain objects are bags of fields. You paid for the ceremony and got no domain model.
  • Leaky ports. OrderRepository.queryBuilder(): SelectQueryBuilder<OrderEntity> is not a port; it is TypeORM with an interface hat on.
  • Port explosion. One interface per method. Group by capability, not per method.
  • Mapping drift. Domain gains a field, the adapter mapper forgets it, data is silently dropped on save. Round-trip tests catch this.
  • Transactions across ports. Two save() calls through two repositories are two transactions unless a Unit of Work (Part 6) wraps them.
  • Over-abstracting infrastructure that will never change. You are not going to swap PostgreSQL for MongoDB. The value of the port is testability and clarity, not "database independence".

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They apply hexagonal architecture where the domain has rules worth protecting: orders, payments, pricing, inventory allocation, subscriptions. They do not apply it to a settings CRUD module or a webhook that writes a row. They measure success by one question: Can I test the rule that matters with no I/O?

They accept that mapping code is boring and write it anyway. They keep ports narrow and adapter-shaped, and they enforce the "no framework in domain" rule with a lint plugin, not a code review comment.

Common mistakes

  • Using the ORM entity as the domain entity.
  • Ports that expose ORM types.
  • Putting @Entity decorators in domain/ because "it's just metadata".
  • Creating a BaseRepository<T> with 30 generic methods and calling it a port.
  • Applying the full pattern to every module including three-endpoint CRUD.

Interview questions

  1. What is a port and what is an adapter? Give one inbound and one outbound example. Expected: interface defined by the core vs implementation; HTTP controller (inbound), TypeORM repository (outbound).
  2. Why must the domain have no @nestjs or typeorm imports? Expected: dependency direction; testability; portability across entry points.
  3. How do you wire a port to an adapter in NestJS? Expected: injection token (Symbol or string) with useClass/useFactory in the module; @Inject(TOKEN) in the consumer.
  4. What is the cost of hexagonal architecture and when is it not worth paying? Expected: mapping code, more files, indirection; not worth it for thin CRUD.
  5. How do you keep a repository port from leaking the ORM? Expected: return domain objects; accept domain objects; no QueryBuilder or FindOptions in the interface; specifications for complex queries.

Practical exercise

Refactor a layered OrdersService into hexagonal form: domain/order.ts with markPaid() and cancel() rules, application/ports/, application/place-order.use-case.ts, and two adapters (TypeormOrderRepository, InMemoryOrderRepository). Add an ESLint no-restricted-imports rule that forbids typeorm, sequelize and @nestjs/* (except @nestjs/common for Inject/Injectable) inside domain/ and application/.

Acceptance criteria: the use-case test suite runs with no database and completes in under 1 second; switching the module's useClass to the in-memory adapter passes the same e2e tests; a typeorm import inside domain/ fails lint.

5.9 Clean architecture

Concept

Clean architecture (Robert C. Martin) draws the system as concentric rings. Innermost: entities (enterprise business rules). Next: use cases (application business rules). Next: interface adapters (controllers, presenters, gateways, repositories). Outermost: frameworks and drivers (NestJS, TypeORM, PostgreSQL, Kafka, the web).

The one rule: source code dependencies point inward. Nothing in an inner ring knows the name of anything in an outer ring.

Why does it exist?

Same reason as hexagonal: protect business rules from infrastructure churn and make them testable. Clean architecture adds a stronger vocabulary for the layers and for what crosses their boundaries: use cases as first-class objects with explicit input and output models, and the insistence that data crossing a boundary is a simple structure (a DTO), never an entity or a database row.

Mental model

Imagine a medieval city. The keep in the centre holds the treasure (business rules). Around it, an inner wall (use cases), then the merchants' quarter (adapters), then the outer wall facing the fields and roads (frameworks). Traffic from the roads must pass through gates at each wall, showing papers (DTOs). Nobody in the keep has ever seen a road.

How it works

flowchart TB
  F["Frameworks and drivers\nNestJS, TypeORM, PostgreSQL, Kafka, Express"]
  A["Interface adapters\nControllers, Presenters, Repositories, Gateways"]
  U["Use cases\nPlaceOrder, CancelOrder, RefundOrder"]
  E["Entities\nOrder, Money, OrderStatus, policies"]
  F --> A
  A --> U
  U --> E

The rings map to a NestJS folder structure:

Ring Folder Contains May import
Entities domain/ Order, Money, value objects, domain errors, domain events nothing outside domain/ and shared-kernel/
Use cases application/ use cases, ports (interfaces), input/output models domain/
Interface adapters infrastructure/, presentation/ TypeORM repositories, Stripe gateway, controllers, DTOs, mappers application/, domain/, frameworks
Frameworks main.ts, modules, config wiring everything

Use cases are the application's verbs. One class per use case with a single execute() method is the common style. It reads as a table of contents of what the system does: PlaceOrderUseCase, CancelOrderUseCase, RefundOrderUseCase, ListOrdersForCustomerUseCase.

DTO mapping boundaries. Three different shapes exist for "an order", and they must not be the same class:

  1. The request DTO (CreateOrderDto, class-validator decorated) at the HTTP edge.
  2. The domain entity (Order, with behaviour) inside.
  3. The persistence entity (OrderEntity, TypeORM decorated) at the database edge.

Plus a response DTO for what goes back to the client. Mapping happens in the adapters: the controller maps request DTO to use-case input; the repository maps domain to persistence and back; the controller (or a presenter) maps use-case output to response DTO.

// src/modules/orders/presentation/http/orders.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Post, HttpCode } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PlaceOrderUseCase } from '../../application/place-order.use-case';
import { CreateOrderDto } from './dto/create-order.dto';
import { OrderCreatedResponse } from './dto/order-created.response';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly placeOrder: PlaceOrderUseCase) {}

  @Post()
  @HttpCode(201)
  async create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto): Promise<OrderCreatedResponse> {
    // Boundary 1: request DTO -> use-case input model (plain object)
    const result = await this.placeOrder.execute({
      orderId: dto.idempotencyKey ?? randomUUID(),
      customerId: dto.customerId,
      lines: dto.lines.map((l) => ({ productId: l.productId, qty: l.qty, unitPriceMinor: l.unitPriceMinor })),
    });
    // Boundary 2: use-case output -> response DTO
    return { orderId: result.orderId, status: 'PAID' };
  }
}

Domain errors are translated to HTTP at the edge with an exception filter, so the domain never throws HttpException:

// src/shared/http/domain-error.filter.ts
import { ArgumentsHost, Catch, ExceptionFilter, HttpStatus } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Response } from 'express';
import { DomainError } from '../../shared-kernel/domain-error';

const STATUS_BY_CODE: Record<string, number> = {
  ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE: HttpStatus.CONFLICT,
  ORDER_NOT_PAYABLE: HttpStatus.CONFLICT,
  ORDER_EMPTY: HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY,
  INSUFFICIENT_STOCK: HttpStatus.CONFLICT,
};

@Catch(DomainError)
export class DomainErrorFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  catch(err: DomainError, host: ArgumentsHost) {
    const res = host.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    const status = STATUS_BY_CODE[err.code] ?? HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST;
    res.status(status).json({ code: err.code, message: err.message });
  }
}

Production scenario

A subscription billing service: 14 use cases, 6 domain entities, 3 repositories, 2 gateways. The pricing rules (proration, trials, coupons, tax) live in domain/ and have 300 unit tests that run in 2 seconds. Finance changes the proration rule quarterly; each change is a domain-only PR reviewed by one engineer and one finance analyst who can read the plain TypeScript. Nothing in infrastructure/ changes. That is the payoff.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Use-case explosion. Sixty use-case classes with three lines each. Some teams group closely related operations into one application service; that is fine if the boundary rules hold.
  • Presenters and interactors ceremony. The original book's InputBoundary/OutputBoundary/Presenter structure is rarely worth it in TypeScript. Returning a plain output object from execute() is enough.
  • Mapping fatigue. Four representations of the same data. Use small mapper classes and round-trip tests; do not merge the representations.
  • Domain events swallowed. The domain records events, but nobody publishes them because the use case forgot. Make the repository or unit of work publish recorded events after commit.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see clean architecture as hexagonal architecture with a clearer vocabulary and a stricter DTO rule. They adopt the vocabulary (domain, application, infrastructure, presentation) as the team standard and apply the full ceremony only where the rules are rich. They are ruthless about the DTO boundary because that is where security incidents come from.

Interview questions

  1. Name the rings and the one rule. Expected: entities, use cases, adapters, frameworks; dependencies point inward.
  2. Why are there three or four "order" classes and why not merge them? Expected: request DTO, domain, persistence, response; different change reasons and different consumers; merging leaks data and couples layers.
  3. Where does a domain error become an HTTP 409? Expected: at the edge, in an exception filter; domain never imports HTTP.
  4. How does a use case differ from a service in layered architecture? Expected: single verb, explicit input/output models, depends on ports not ORM.

5.10 Onion architecture

Concept

Onion architecture (Jeffrey Palermo, 2008) is the same idea drawn slightly differently: a domain model core, a domain services ring, an application services ring, and an outer ring of infrastructure, UI and tests. Again, dependencies point inward, and infrastructure is at the edge.

The onion vocabulary adds one useful distinction: domain services (logic that involves several entities and belongs to the domain, like PricingService.calculate(order, customer, promotions)) versus application services (orchestration of a use case: load, call domain, save, publish).

Why the three are basically the same idea

Hexagonal, clean and onion were proposed independently over about a decade, and they converge on one principle:

Put business rules in the centre. Make everything else depend on them. Never the reverse.

Concern Hexagonal Clean Onion
Centre Application core Entities + use cases Domain model + domain services
Orchestration Use cases / application Use cases (interactors) Application services
Interfaces owned by centre Ports Boundaries / gateways Repository interfaces
Outside Adapters Interface adapters + frameworks Infrastructure, UI, tests
Emphasis Pluggable I/O Dependency rule + DTO boundaries Domain model richness

Pick one vocabulary for your team and stick with it. The folder structure this book uses throughout (domain/, application/, infrastructure/, presentation/) satisfies all three.

Mental model

Imagine an onion. The core is the smallest and most protected. Each layer wraps the one inside it. You can peel the outer layers (swap the database, the web framework) without touching the core. Cutting from the outside in, you never find the core depending on the skin.

How it works in NestJS

The onion's "domain services" ring is where you place logic that needs multiple aggregates but no infrastructure:

// src/modules/orders/domain/services/pricing.service.ts
// Domain service: pure, no I/O, no framework. Injected into use cases or constructed directly.
import { Order } from '../order';
import { Money } from '../../../../shared-kernel/money';

export interface Promotion { code: string; percentOff: number; minTotalMinor: number }

export class PricingService {
  applyPromotions(order: Order, promos: Promotion[]): { total: Money; applied: string[] } {
    let total = order.total;
    const applied: string[] = [];
    for (const p of promos) {
      if (total.minor >= p.minTotalMinor) {
        total = total.subtract(total.percent(p.percentOff));
        applied.push(p.code);
      }
    }
    return { total, applied };
  }
}

The application service (use case) loads promotions through a port, calls the domain service, and saves. The domain service has no idea where promotions come from.

When this ceremony is worth it, and when it is over-engineering

Worth it when at least two of these hold:

  • The module has rules that change (pricing, eligibility, state transitions, allocation, tax, compliance).
  • The module has more than one entry point (HTTP plus Kafka plus cron).
  • The module has more than one infrastructure implementation now or soon (two payment providers, a migration from Sequelize to TypeORM, an in-memory adapter for fast tests).
  • The team is larger than three and needs a shared structure to review against.
  • The module is long-lived (years, not a campaign microsite).

Over-engineering when:

  • The module is CRUD with validation: settings, addresses, tags, admin lookups. A controller, a service and a repository with response DTOs is the correct architecture. Adding ports, use cases, domain objects and three mappers to PUT /users/:id/address produces 11 files for what should be 3, and every new engineer wastes a day tracing them.
  • The rules are in the database anyway (unique constraints, checks) and the service is a thin pass-through.
  • You are prototyping to learn the domain; the boundaries you draw now will be wrong.

A pragmatic rule many senior teams use: start every module as layered with strict DTO boundaries; promote it to hexagonal/clean when the first real domain rule shows up, and not before. The promotion is cheap if the DTO boundary was already there, because that is the part that is expensive to retrofit.

A decision table:

Module Rules Entry points Infra variants Recommended
User addresses validation only HTTP 1 Layered + response DTOs
Product catalog (read) none HTTP 1 (plus cache) Layered + cache adapter
Orders / checkout many, changing HTTP, Kafka, cron 2 (TypeORM, in-memory) Hexagonal / clean
Payments many, regulated HTTP, webhooks 3 providers Hexagonal / clean
Inventory allocation concurrency rules gRPC, Kafka 1 (plus in-memory) Hexagonal / clean
Admin reports none HTTP read replica Layered, raw SQL allowed
Notifications templates, throttling Kafka, cron 3 channels Hexagonal (ports per channel)

Common mistakes across all three

  • Confusing folder names with architecture. Having domain/ does not mean you have a domain model.
  • Applying it everywhere out of fear of being "unclean".
  • Skipping the DTO boundary and keeping the ceremony: the worst of both worlds.
  • Building "generic" abstractions (BaseUseCase<TIn, TOut>, BaseRepository<T>) that add nothing but hide types.

Interview questions

  1. Compare hexagonal, clean and onion. Expected: same dependency principle, different vocabulary and emphasis; be able to map folders.
  2. What is a domain service and how is it different from an application service? Expected: domain service is pure multi-entity logic; application service orchestrates I/O around a use case.
  3. When would you refuse to apply clean architecture? Expected: CRUD modules, prototypes, tiny teams; explain the cost.
  4. What is the one part you would keep even in the simplest module? Expected: the DTO boundary at the API edge; never return entities.

Practical exercise

Audit a NestJS codebase with at least five modules. For each, fill the decision table above (rules, entry points, infra variants) and recommend layered or hexagonal. Refactor exactly one module to hexagonal and leave one CRUD module layered, adding response DTOs to it.

Acceptance criteria: a written one-page rationale per module; the hexagonal module's use-case tests run without a database; the CRUD module returns no entity fields not declared in its response DTO.

5.11 When should I choose each architecture?

There is no best architecture. There is only the architecture that fits the team, the domain, the traffic and the money you have today, with a credible path to what you will need in eighteen months. This section gives you the decision tools senior engineers actually use.

Concept

Architecture choice is a function of five inputs: team size and shape, domain complexity and stability, scaling profile (traffic level, and whether different parts scale differently), operational budget (people and money for platform work), and time to first release. The styles from the previous sections each optimise for a different combination.

The decision matrix

Architecture Team size Complexity Scaling Operational cost Time to first release Best for
Monolith 1 to 8 Low to medium; domain still being discovered Vertical plus identical replicas; one DB Very low: 1 pipeline, 1 image, 1 DB Days to weeks MVPs, internal tools, early startups, small SaaS
Modular monolith 4 to 40 Medium to high; domain becoming clear Same as monolith plus read replicas, separate worker processes Low: 1 pipeline, some lint/boundary tooling Weeks Most products for most of their life; growth-stage startups; teams with 2 to 6 squads
Microservices 20 to 1,000+ High; well-understood bounded contexts Independent per service; heterogeneous High: N pipelines, tracing, contracts, platform team Months (for a real, operable system) Large organisations, many autonomous teams, very different scaling or compliance profiles
SOA with ESB Enterprise-scale High, legacy integration heavy Bus-limited High plus vendor cost Months to years Integrating dozens of legacy vendor systems; rarely chosen fresh
Serverless 1 to 10 per function set Low per function Automatic, to the concurrency limit; DB is the bottleneck Low for spiky loads; hidden costs at steady high load Days Webhooks, file processing, cron, glue, low-traffic APIs
Event-driven (overlay) Any Adds complexity; needs idempotency discipline Excellent for decoupling and burst absorption Medium: broker, lag monitoring, DLQs, replay tooling Adds weeks Side effects, integration between modules or services, audit trails, analytics feeds
Layered (code-level) Any Low to medium rules N/A None Fastest CRUD-dominant modules
Hexagonal / Clean / Onion (code-level) 3+ per module Rich, changing rules N/A Mapping and structure overhead Adds days per module Orders, payments, pricing, inventory; anything with real business rules

Two of these rows (event-driven; layered vs hexagonal) are not alternatives to the deployment shapes above them. They are overlays. You can have an event-driven modular monolith with hexagonal orders and layered settings. In fact, that combination is the recommended default for most teams.

Secondary decision factors

Factor Pushes toward monolith / modular monolith Pushes toward microservices
Domain clarity Boundaries still moving Bounded contexts stable for 12+ months
Deploy cadence Everyone can ship together several times a day One team is blocked by another's release freeze
Scaling profile Uniform: every request is similar Search needs 64 GB RAM nodes; checkout needs 20 small pods; ML inference needs GPUs
Failure isolation A shared process is acceptable with bulkheads A recommendation bug must never take down checkout
Compliance Single audit scope PCI or health data must be in an isolated scope with restricted access
Data consistency Cross-domain transactions are common Domains rarely need atomic writes across each other
Platform capability No dedicated platform/SRE team A platform team owns CI templates, service mesh, tracing, on-call tooling
Hiring Generalists Enough seniors to own services end-to-end

The decision flow

flowchart TB
  S["New product or major rebuild"] --> Q1{"Traffic spiky and low average?\nWebhooks, cron, file jobs?"}
  Q1 -->|yes| SL["Serverless for those edges"]
  Q1 -->|no| Q2{"Team larger than about 20 engineers\nin 4+ autonomous squads?"}
  SL --> Q2
  Q2 -->|no| Q3{"More than 3 engineers or\nexpected to grow?"}
  Q3 -->|no| M["Monolith with DTO boundaries"]
  Q3 -->|yes| MM["Modular monolith\nschema per module, facades, events"]
  Q2 -->|yes| Q4{"Bounded contexts stable?\nDifferent scaling or compliance profiles?"}
  Q4 -->|no| MM
  Q4 -->|yes| Q5{"Platform team and tracing in place?"}
  Q5 -->|no| MM2["Modular monolith now,\nbuild platform, extract later"]
  Q5 -->|yes| MS["Microservices for the contexts that need it,\nkeep the rest modular"]
  M --> R1{"Per module: rich rules?"}
  MM --> R1
  MM2 --> R1
  MS --> R1
  R1 -->|yes| HX["Hexagonal / clean for that module"]
  R1 -->|no| LY["Layered with response DTOs"]

Read this flow as a set of gates, not a scoring sheet. Most products exit at "modular monolith". That is not a consolation prize; it is where most successful systems live for most of their life.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask the uncomfortable questions in the first meeting:

  • How many engineers will we have in 12 months? (Not "how many do we hope for.")
  • Which parts of this system will change every week, and which will not change for years?
  • What is the one workload with a different shape? (Search, media processing, reporting, ML.)
  • What happens to revenue if module X is down for 30 minutes? For module Y?
  • Who is on call, and how many dashboards can they honestly watch?
  • What is our tolerance for eventual consistency in the checkout flow?

They refuse to choose microservices "because we will need to scale". Scale is a load number; ask for it. A modular monolith on ten pods handles 20,000 RPS. Most products never reach 2,000.

They also refuse the opposite trap: a 300-engineer company on one deploy train, where a Friday release freeze for one team freezes everyone.

To a product manager: "The architecture decision is really a team decision. Tell me how the team will be organised in a year and I will tell you the shape of the system."

Common mistakes

  • Choosing based on résumé value or conference talks.
  • Choosing based on a competitor's architecture, whose team is ten times larger.
  • Deciding once and never revisiting. Architecture should be reviewed quarterly against the signals in the next section.
  • Mixing up code architecture (hexagonal) with deployment architecture (microservices) and thinking one implies the other.

Interview questions

  1. A fintech startup with 6 engineers asks you to design their payments platform. What shape do you propose and why? Expected: modular monolith, hexagonal payments module, event-driven side effects with outbox, serverless for webhooks; explain each choice against the matrix.
  2. What would make you move from a modular monolith to microservices? Expected: the signals in 5.12; give at least three.
  3. How do team structure and architecture relate? Expected: Conway's law; architecture mirrors communication structure; design the team and the architecture together.
  4. What is the difference between "scaling" and "scaling independently", and why does it matter for this decision? Expected: replicas scale a monolith; independent scaling is about heterogeneous resource profiles.

Practical exercise

Write a one-page architecture decision record (ADR) for a hypothetical ride-booking backend with 12 engineers: choose a deployment shape, list which modules get hexagonal treatment, name the event flows, and state three concrete signals that would trigger extracting the first service.

Acceptance criteria: the ADR names the numbers you assumed (RPS, team growth), lists alternatives rejected with reasons, and includes the decision flow path you followed.

5.12 Why a modular monolith is often better than microservices

Concept

A modular monolith gives you the boundaries of microservices (clear ownership, contracts, independent evolution of code) without the network in between. For teams under roughly 20 to 40 engineers, it delivers most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost, and it is the best possible starting point if you do end up extracting services later.

What microservices actually cost

The honest list. Every item below is a thing you pay for with engineer-hours, latency, or incidents, and none of them exist in a modular monolith.

  1. Network calls replace method calls. An in-process call costs about 100 nanoseconds. An HTTP call between pods in the same cluster costs 1 to 5 ms; gRPC 0.5 to 2 ms; with TLS and service mesh sidecars, add 1 to 3 ms. A checkout that touches five modules goes from 0 ms of communication overhead to 10 to 40 ms.
  2. Partial failure. A method call either returns or throws. A network call can time out with the work done, done twice, or half done. Every cross-service interaction needs timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, idempotency keys, and a plan for the "unknown outcome" case.
  3. Data consistency. One ACID transaction becomes a saga with compensations and an outbox. "Reserve stock and charge card" goes from 12 lines in a transaction to two services, three events, a state machine and a reconciliation job.
  4. Observability. Logs from one process become logs from twenty. You need distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry), trace-id propagation through HTTP headers and Kafka message headers, centralised logging, and per-service dashboards. Without these, debugging a production issue means guessing.
  5. CI/CD times N. Twenty services means twenty pipelines, twenty Dockerfiles, twenty Helm charts, twenty sets of secrets, twenty dependency-upgrade PRs when a CVE lands in undici.
  6. Contracts and versioning. Types checked by the TypeScript compiler become API contracts checked by... nothing, unless you build consumer-driven contract tests and a schema registry.
  7. A platform team. Someone must own the CI templates, the service mesh, the tracing backend, the secrets management, the deployment tooling and the on-call for all of it. In practice this is 3 to 6 senior engineers who are not building product.
  8. Local development. docker compose up with two containers becomes twenty containers or a shared remote dev environment.
  9. Cross-team features are slower. A feature that touches orders and payments now needs two PRs in two repositories, a contract change, a coordinated deploy order, and a backward-compatible window.
  10. Security surface. Every service is a network endpoint that needs authentication (mTLS or service tokens), authorisation, and rate limiting. In a monolith, module calls are not attackable.

The distributed monolith trap

The worst outcome is not a monolith and not microservices. It is a distributed monolith: services that must be deployed together, share a database, and call each other synchronously in long chains. You pay every cost above and get none of the independence.

Symptoms:

  • Two or more services read and write the same tables.
  • A release requires deploying services in a specific order.
  • A change to one service's DTO breaks three others at runtime.
  • The "user service" is called synchronously by every other service on every request.
  • Integration tests must run the whole fleet.
  • On-call for any service requires understanding all services.

The trap is easy to fall into because splitting the code is easy and splitting the data is hard. Teams split the code first, keep the shared database "temporarily", and never finish.

The signals that tell you it is time to split

Extract a module into its own service when you observe at least two of these, and not before:

  1. Team scaling. A single module is owned by more than about two "two-pizza teams" (16+ engineers) and their merge queue on the shared repository is the bottleneck.
  2. Independent deploy cadence. One module needs to ship several times a day while another needs release freezes (payments during tax season, for example), and the shared pipeline forces the slower cadence on everyone.
  3. Different scaling profile. One module needs 10x the CPU, or GPUs, or 64 GB RAM for an in-memory index, and running the whole monolith on that hardware is wasteful; or one module's load pattern (nightly batch) disrupts another's (daytime checkout).
  4. Regulatory or security isolation. PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2 scope reduction: putting card handling in a separate service with a separate database and restricted access shrinks the audit scope from the whole company to one team.
  5. Fault isolation is worth more than consistency. A bug in recommendations must never take down checkout; and recommendations does not need atomic transactions with orders anyway.
  6. A different runtime. The ML team writes Python; the image pipeline wants Rust. That is a real service boundary.

If you see only one signal, look for a cheaper fix first: a separate worker process from the same codebase, a read replica, a separate connection pool, a feature flag, or a second deployment of the same image with a different entry point. Many "we need microservices" conversations end with "we needed a separate worker deployment".

The folder layout that can be split later

repo/
  package.json
  nest-cli.json
  apps/
    api/                          <- the monolith's HTTP entry point
      src/main.ts
      src/app.module.ts           <- imports every module below
    worker/                       <- same code, different entry point: consumers and cron only
      src/main.ts
  libs/
    shared-kernel/                <- tiny: Money, Ids, DomainError, Result, Clock port
      src/
    contracts/                    <- public DTOs and event schemas, versioned; NO logic
      src/
        events/
          orders/order-paid.v1.ts
          inventory/stock-reserved.v1.ts
        inventory/reserve-stock.dto.ts
        payments/charge.dto.ts
    platform/                     <- cross-cutting infrastructure: logging, tracing, outbox, kafka client, config
      src/
  src/modules/
    orders/
      orders.module.ts
      public/orders.facade.ts     <- the only export
      application/
      domain/
      infrastructure/             <- schema: orders
      presentation/
    payments/
      payments.module.ts
      public/payments.facade.ts
      application/
      domain/
      infrastructure/             <- schema: payments
      presentation/
    inventory/
      inventory.module.ts
      public/inventory.facade.ts
      application/
      domain/
      infrastructure/             <- schema: inventory
      presentation/
    notifications/
      ...
  db/
    migrations/
      orders/                     <- migrations per schema, so a schema can leave with its history
      payments/
      inventory/
  .dependency-cruiser.js          <- forbids cross-module deep imports and domain -> infra imports

The properties that make this splittable:

  • Each module depends only on contracts, shared-kernel and platform. Never on another module's internals.
  • Each module owns a PostgreSQL schema and its migrations folder. The day it leaves, pg_dump --schema=payments and its migrations go with it.
  • Cross-module calls go through facades that have the exact shape a network client would have: async methods, DTO in, DTO out, no shared entities, no passing EntityManager across.
  • Cross-module reactions go through events whose schemas already live in contracts/, so replacing EventEmitter2 with Kafka changes the publisher and subscriber adapters, not the contracts.
  • Two entry points already exist (api, worker), so the team is used to running the same code in different processes.

The extraction, step by step

flowchart LR
  subgraph Before["Modular monolith"]
    A1["orders module"] -->|"PaymentsFacade"| B1["payments module"]
    B1 -->|"EventEmitter2 order.paid"| A1
    A1 --> D1[("shared DB\nschema orders\nschema payments")]
    B1 --> D1
  end
  subgraph After["After extraction"]
    A2["orders module\nin monolith"] -->|"PaymentsHttpClient\nsame interface"| B2["payments-service"]
    B2 -->|"Kafka orders.order-paid.v1"| A2
    A2 --> D2[("monolith DB\nschema orders")]
    B2 --> D3[("payments DB")]
  end
  Before --> After
  1. Prove the boundary. Run dependency-cruiser; confirm zero deep imports into payments and zero cross-schema queries (grep migrations and pg_stat_statements for joins that touch both schemas).
  2. Move to a second database while still in-process. Register a second TypeORM DataSource named payments pointing at a new database; migrate the schema with pg_dump --schema=payments | psql payments_db. The module now has no shared transactions with anyone; if something breaks here, you found hidden coupling cheaply.
  3. Swap in-process events for the broker. Publish order.paid through the outbox to Kafka; subscribe from the payments module via a Kafka consumer instead of @OnEvent. Still one process, but the event path is now the production path.
  4. Create the new app. apps/payments-service/src/main.ts importing PaymentsModule, with its own health checks and config. Deploy it alongside the monolith, consuming from Kafka, but not yet receiving synchronous calls.
  5. Replace the facade with a client. Implement PaymentsFacade's interface as PaymentsHttpClient (or gRPC) with timeouts, retries on idempotent operations, and a circuit breaker. Switch the provider in OrdersModule behind a feature flag; run both paths in shadow mode if the volume justifies it.
  6. Remove the module from the monolith. Delete src/modules/payments from the monolith; the code lives only in the new service (or in a monorepo package it owns).
  7. Observe for two weeks. Latency, error rates, consumer lag, reconciliation reports. Only then extract the next module, if a signal exists for it.

Each step is reversible. That is what separates an extraction from a rewrite.

Production scenario

A B2B invoicing company ran a modular monolith with 11 modules and 34 engineers for four years. Peak 1,800 RPS, one PostgreSQL primary, 40 pods. In year four, the payments team hit two signals at once: PCI scope reduction and a deploy freeze conflict with the reporting team. They extracted payments in five weeks using the steps above. Nothing else was extracted for the following two years because no other module showed two signals. Their platform investment stayed at one SRE.

Failure scenario

A different company, same size, went straight to 18 microservices in year one "to be ready for scale". By year two: three engineers on a platform team, a shared PostgreSQL that seven services wrote to (the distributed monolith), a 45-minute end-to-end test suite that ran all services, and a checkout p99 of 1.4 seconds from six sequential hops. A feature that touched orders and invoices took three weeks instead of three days. They spent year three merging nine services back into a modular monolith. The scale they were "ready for" peaked at 300 RPS.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They treat the modular monolith as the default and microservices as an exception that must be justified per module, per signal. They keep the door open (schemas, facades, contracts) so that extraction is a five-week project, not a rewrite. They measure whether the door is still open with tooling, not trust.

They are equally clear about the limits: at 60 engineers with six squads that need different deploy cadences, a single deploy train is a real cost, and they will split. The point is to split for a reason you can name and measure.

Common mistakes

  • Extracting a service before the boundary exists in the monolith (a shared table becomes a shared database).
  • Extracting the wrong module first (the most-called one, which then becomes a synchronous dependency of everything).
  • Skipping step 2 (separate database while in-process), which is the cheapest way to find hidden coupling.
  • Removing the module from the monolith before the new service has run in production.
  • Not budgeting for the platform work, so the first service has no tracing, no DLQ, no runbook.

Interview questions

  1. List five concrete costs of microservices that a modular monolith does not have. Expected: network latency, partial failure handling, sagas/outbox, tracing, N pipelines, platform team, contracts.
  2. What is a distributed monolith and how do you detect one? Expected: shared DB, ordered deploys, synchronous chains, fleet-wide tests.
  3. Name the signals that justify extracting a service. Expected: team scaling, deploy cadence, scaling profile, compliance isolation, fault isolation, runtime.
  4. Describe the safe extraction sequence and why the database moves before the process. Expected: steps above; moving the DB first reveals hidden coupling while rollback is trivial.
  5. How does a facade in a modular monolith prepare for extraction? Expected: async DTO-in/DTO-out interface identical to a network client; swap via DI token.

Practical exercise

In your modular monolith, register a second DataSource for one module pointing at a separate database. Move that module's schema with pg_dump --schema. Run the full test suite and the app.

Acceptance criteria: the module works from the separate database with no code changes outside its infrastructure/ folder and module file; any failure identifies a hidden cross-module coupling, which you document and fix through the owning module's facade.

5.13 Edge cases & failure modes at the architecture level

Individual components fail in ways you can unit test. Architectures fail in ways you only see in production, usually at 02:00, usually because two reasonable local decisions combined into an unreasonable global one. This section catalogues the architecture-level failure modes a senior engineer must recognise on sight, with the mechanism, the detection signal, and the fix for each.

The distributed monolith

Mechanism. Services were split by code but not by data or by deployment. Service A writes to a table that service B reads. Deploys must happen in order. A DTO change in A breaks B at runtime.

How you meet it. A "simple" column rename in the users table breaks the orders service, the notifications service and a nightly report, none of which the users team knew about. Or: the release checklist says "deploy inventory before orders, wait five minutes, then deploy orders".

Detection. Query pg_stat_statements grouped by application name (SET application_name per service) and look for two services touching the same tables. Grep deploy runbooks for ordering instructions. Count how many repositories a single-feature PR touches.

Fix. Assign each table an owner. Other services get the data through the owner's API or by consuming events into a local projection. Re-merge services that cannot be separated at the data level; a modular monolith is better than a distributed one.

Shared database between services

Mechanism. A special case of the above and the most common. Two services with one PostgreSQL. It "works" until: a migration by one service locks a table the other needs; one service's runaway query exhausts the pool for both; one service's schema change silently breaks the other's ORM mapping; and neither service can be scaled or backed up independently.

How you meet it. At 09:00, the catalog team runs ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL DEFAULT ... on a 200-million-row table. It takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for 40 seconds on older PostgreSQL versions. The orders service, which joins to products for pricing, stops serving checkout for 40 seconds. Nobody on the orders team was told.

Detection. More than one database role, or more than one application_name, writing to the same schema. Cross-schema foreign keys.

Fix. Schema-per-module now; database-per-service only when extracting. Move cross-domain reads to projections fed by events, with the timestamp guard shown in section 5.3.

-- Find tables touched by more than one application
SELECT relname, array_agg(DISTINCT application_name)
FROM pg_stat_activity a
JOIN pg_locks l ON l.pid = a.pid
JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = l.relation
WHERE a.application_name <> ''
GROUP BY relname
HAVING count(DISTINCT application_name) > 1;

Chatty synchronous chains

Mechanism. Request enters the gateway, calls A, which calls B, which calls C, which calls D. Each hop adds latency (2 to 30 ms), and each hop multiplies failure probability. With four hops at 99.9% availability each, the chain is 99.6%: from 43 minutes of downtime a month to 2.9 hours. Retries at each hop multiply load on the leaf: three retries per hop over four hops can amplify one user request into 81 leaf calls in the worst case.

How you meet it. The "order details" page makes 14 sequential service calls; p99 is 2.1 seconds. Or: the gateway's thread pool fills up while every request waits on a chain that has a slow tail.

Detection. Trace depth histogram in your tracing backend; any critical-path trace deeper than 3 hops. Fan-out counts per request.

Fix. Limit the critical path to two synchronous hops. Aggregate with a BFF that fans out in parallel rather than serially. Replace chains with local projections (the orders service keeps the product name and price it needs). Set timeout budgets that shrink at each hop: gateway 2,000 ms, A 1,500 ms, B 800 ms, C 300 ms, so the innermost call cannot exceed the outer deadline.

// Propagate a shrinking deadline instead of a fixed per-hop timeout
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HttpService } from '@nestjs/axios';
import { firstValueFrom } from 'rxjs';

@Injectable()
export class DeadlineHttpClient {
  constructor(private readonly http: HttpService) {}

  async get<T>(url: string, deadlineAtMs: number, minBudgetMs = 50): Promise<T> {
    const remaining = deadlineAtMs - Date.now();
    if (remaining < minBudgetMs) throw new Error(`deadline exceeded before calling ${url}`);
    const res = await firstValueFrom(
      this.http.get<T>(url, {
        timeout: remaining - 20, // leave a little for serialisation
        headers: { 'x-deadline-at': String(deadlineAtMs) }, // downstream reads this
      }),
    );
    return res.data;
  }
}

One slow service taking down the gateway

Mechanism. Node.js handles concurrency with an event loop and a finite number of in-flight sockets and memory. A slow downstream does not consume CPU; it consumes waiting requests. Each waiting request holds a socket, a buffer, a promise chain and often a database connection. When the slow service holds thousands of them, the gateway runs out of file descriptors, memory, or connection pool slots, and healthy routes fail too.

How you meet it. The recommendations service degrades to 8-second responses. The gateway has no per-route timeout. Within a minute, every gateway pod has 5,000 pending requests, the Kubernetes liveness probe times out, pods restart, and the restarts drop all in-flight requests including checkout.

Detection. In-flight request count per upstream on the gateway; event loop lag; pool wait time. All should be dashboards, and the first should have an alert.

Fix. Bulkheads: a per-upstream concurrency limit (for example, at most 50 in-flight calls to recommendations; the 51st fails fast). Circuit breakers: after N failures or timeouts in a window, open the circuit and return a fallback (empty recommendations) without calling. Per-route timeouts shorter than the liveness probe. Never let a non-critical dependency share limits with a critical one.

// Minimal bulkhead + circuit breaker as a NestJS provider (production: use opossum or cockatiel)
import { Injectable, Logger, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class RecommendationsBulkhead {
  private inFlight = 0;
  private failures = 0;
  private openUntil = 0;
  private readonly log = new Logger(RecommendationsBulkhead.name);

  constructor(private readonly maxInFlight = 50, private readonly failureThreshold = 20, private readonly openMs = 10_000) {}

  async run<T>(call: () => Promise<T>, fallback: () => T): Promise<T> {
    if (Date.now() < this.openUntil) return fallback();            // circuit open: fail fast
    if (this.inFlight >= this.maxInFlight) return fallback();      // bulkhead full
    this.inFlight++;
    try {
      const result = await call();
      this.failures = 0;
      return result;
    } catch (err) {
      if (++this.failures >= this.failureThreshold) {
        this.openUntil = Date.now() + this.openMs;
        this.log.warn(`circuit opened for ${this.openMs} ms`);
      }
      return fallback();
    } finally {
      this.inFlight--;
    }
  }
}

Event storms

Mechanism. One action produces many events; each event produces more. A bulk import of 500,000 products emits 500,000 ProductUpdated events. Five consumers each recompute a projection per event, hitting the database 2.5 million times. Or a feedback loop: A emits on change, B reacts and updates A, A emits again.

How you meet it. Consumer lag climbs to millions; the database CPU pins at 100% from projection updates; unrelated consumers on the same broker are starved; the on-call cannot tell whether the storm is finishing or growing.

Detection. Produce rate per topic with alerts on 10x baseline; consumer lag per partition; a causation-id chain length metric (how many hops from the original trigger).

Fix. Batch: emit ProductsBulkUpdated { ids: [...] } or let consumers process in batches (eachBatch in KafkaJS). Coalesce: a projection updater that debounces per key. Rate-limit consumers to protect the database. Break loops with causation ids and a maximum depth. Separate broker clusters or topics for bulk versus interactive traffic.

Schema drift between services

Mechanism. The producer changes a field's meaning, type or name. Consumers deployed against the old shape either crash (strict parsing), silently ignore the field (lenient parsing), or worse, misinterpret it (amount changing from rupees to paise without a name change).

How you meet it. Payments starts sending amount in minor units. Notifications still formats it as major units. Customers receive "Your order of 1,250,000 INR has been confirmed" for a 12,500 INR order. Support is flooded; the error is invisible in dashboards because nothing failed.

Detection. A schema registry with compatibility checks in CI; consumer-driven contract tests (each consumer publishes the shape it depends on; the producer's CI runs them). Diffs on contract packages that require reviewers from consuming teams.

Fix. Rules: never change a field's meaning; add a new field with a new name (amountMinor), deprecate the old one, remove it only after all consumers have migrated (checked by usage metrics). Validate events at the consumer with class-validator or zod and send invalid ones to a dead-letter topic instead of guessing.

Versioning events

Mechanism. Events are stored for days (Kafka retention) or forever (event sourcing). A consumer today may read an event produced by a version of the producer from last week. Every consumer must be able to read every version that exists in the topic.

Rules that work in practice.

  1. Put a version integer in the envelope and in the topic name for breaking changes: orders.order-paid.v1, orders.order-paid.v2.
  2. Additive changes (new optional fields) stay in v1. Consumers ignore unknown fields.
  3. For a breaking change, produce both v1 and v2 for a deprecation window (typically weeks), monitor v1 consumer group lag, and drop v1 when no group is reading it.
  4. Upcasting: a consumer library that transforms v1 payloads into v2 shape at read time, so handler code only ever sees the latest shape.
// libs/contracts/src/events/orders/order-paid.ts
export interface OrderPaidV1 { version: 1; id: string; orderId: string; amount: number }           // amount in major units (legacy)
export interface OrderPaidV2 { version: 2; id: string; orderId: string; amountMinor: number; currency: string }

export type OrderPaid = OrderPaidV1 | OrderPaidV2;

// Upcaster: consumers always handle V2
export function upcastOrderPaid(e: OrderPaid): OrderPaidV2 {
  if (e.version === 2) return e;
  return { version: 2, id: e.id, orderId: e.orderId, amountMinor: Math.round(e.amount * 100), currency: 'INR' };
}

Detection. Consumer errors spiking after a producer deploy; a schema registry rejecting an incompatible schema in CI (the good kind of detection).

Big-bang rewrites

Mechanism. The team decides the legacy system is unfixable and builds a replacement from scratch, feature-freezing the old one. The rewrite takes twice as long as estimated because the old system encoded years of edge cases nobody documented. Meanwhile the business needs features, so the old system is changed anyway, and the rewrite chases a moving target. The most common end state: two half-systems in production forever.

How you meet it. "We will replace the monolith with microservices by Q3." In Q3 of the following year, 40% of traffic is on the new system, 60% on the old, and every feature must be built twice.

Fix. The strangler fig approach: put a routing layer (gateway) in front of the old system. Build one capability at a time in the new system. Route that capability's traffic to the new system, keep the rest on the old. Remove the old capability's code once the new one is proven. Repeat. Each step ships value and is reversible. The old system shrinks until it disappears. Combined with the extraction sequence from section 5.12, this is how large migrations actually succeed.

flowchart LR
  C["Clients"] --> G["Gateway / router"]
  G -->|"/orders/*"| N["New orders service"]
  G -->|"/catalog/*, /users/*, everything else"| L["Legacy monolith"]
  N -->|"reads user data via API"| L
  N --> ND[("orders DB")]
  L --> LD[("legacy DB")]

A compact reference table

Failure mode First signal Root cause Fix
Distributed monolith Ordered deploys, multi-repo PRs Split code, not data Table ownership, projections, or re-merge
Shared database Cross-service lock waits, surprise migration breakage No data ownership Schema per module, DB per service on extraction
Chatty chains Trace depth > 3, p99 >> sum of p50s Synchronous composition BFF fan-out, projections, deadline propagation
Slow service kills gateway In-flight count climbs, event loop lag No bulkheads or breakers Per-upstream limits, circuit breaker, fallbacks
Event storm Produce rate 10x, lag in millions Per-item events on bulk actions, loops Batch events, coalesce, causation depth limit
Schema drift Silent wrong values, consumer crashes after producer deploy No contract enforcement Registry, contract tests, additive changes only
Event versioning Old consumers break on new payloads Breaking change in place Versioned topics, upcasters, deprecation windows
Big-bang rewrite Rewrite past deadline, two systems in prod Replacing instead of strangling Strangler fig, one capability at a time

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They assume every one of these will be attempted by someone on the team, usually with good intentions and under deadline pressure. So they encode the defences in tooling: lint rules for boundaries, database roles for schemas, CI checks for contracts, default timeouts and bulkheads in the shared HTTP client, per-partition lag alerts in the standard dashboard template. A rule that lives only in a wiki is not a rule.

They also keep a short written list of "things we will not do": no shared tables across services, no synchronous chains deeper than two hops on the checkout path, no event without an id and a version, no rewrite without a strangler plan.

Interview questions

  1. How do you detect a distributed monolith in a system you have just joined? Expected: shared tables across application names, ordered deploys, multi-repo feature PRs, fleet-wide integration tests.
  2. Explain how a slow non-critical dependency can take down a critical path, and the three defences. Expected: in-flight resource exhaustion; bulkheads, circuit breakers, timeouts shorter than probes.
  3. How would you migrate a large monolith to services without a big-bang? Expected: strangler fig with a gateway; one capability at a time; extraction sequence with database first.
  4. How do you version events safely? Expected: version in envelope and topic, additive changes, dual-publish window, upcasters.
  5. Why do retries make an outage worse, and how do you retry safely? Expected: amplification across hops; retry budgets, exponential backoff with jitter, only on idempotent operations, circuit breakers to stop retrying a dead service.

Practical exercise

Build a three-hop synchronous chain (gateway -> orders -> pricing -> promotions) in NestJS with no timeouts. Load-test it while making promotions sleep for 10 seconds. Observe the cascade. Then add deadline propagation, a bulkhead of 20 in-flight calls to promotions, and a circuit breaker with a fallback of "no discount".

Acceptance criteria: with promotions down, checkout p99 stays under 500 ms and returns full-price orders; the gateway's in-flight count never exceeds the bulkhead limit; promotions recovering closes the circuit within 15 seconds without a restart.

Senior Checklist — Part 05

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can enforce module boundaries in a NestJS monolith with exports, facades, schema-per-module and a lint rule, and I can prove the boundary holds
  • I can list at least seven concrete costs of microservices and name the signals that justify paying them
  • I can extract a module into a service in reversible steps, moving the database before the process
  • I can implement the transactional outbox and an idempotent consumer, and explain why in-process events are not durable
  • I can structure a module as domain / application / infrastructure / presentation with no framework imports in the core, and I know when that ceremony is not worth it
  • I can configure NestJS on Lambda correctly (app.init(), cached handler, max: 1, RDS Proxy, callbackWaitsForEmptyEventLoop = false)
  • I can recognise a distributed monolith, a chatty chain, an event storm and schema drift from their first production signals
  • I can design deadline propagation, bulkheads and circuit breakers so one slow dependency cannot take down the gateway
  • I can plan a strangler-fig migration instead of a big-bang rewrite
  • I can fill in the architecture decision matrix for a new product and defend the row I chose

Part 05 — Key Takeaways

  • Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to change: process boundaries, data ownership, deploy units. Pick the least structure that meets today's need with a door open for tomorrow's.
  • A monolith is the right starting point for small teams; a modular monolith with enforced boundaries (facades, exports, schema-per-module, lint rules) is the right home for most products for most of their life.
  • Microservices solve organisational and heterogeneous-scaling problems, not code-quality problems. They cost network latency, partial failure, sagas, tracing, N pipelines and a platform team. Adopt them per module, per named signal.
  • The distributed monolith (split code, shared data, ordered deploys) is worse than either a monolith or real microservices. Data ownership is the boundary that matters.
  • Service-per-database is non-negotiable in microservices; get needed data via APIs or event-fed projections with out-of-order guards.
  • Serverless shines for spiky, event-driven edges (webhooks, file processing, cron) and needs a connection pooler in front of PostgreSQL; it is rarely the right choice for a steady, high-traffic core API.
  • Events are facts in the past tense with an id and a version; commands are requests with one handler. Publish through a transactional outbox, consume idempotently, dead-letter poison messages, and alert on per-partition lag.
  • Layered architecture is fine for CRUD; it breaks when business rules grow because the business layer depends on the ORM. Hexagonal, clean and onion fix this by inverting the dependency so the domain depends on nothing.
  • Keep the DTO boundary at the API edge in every module, even the simplest; that is where data leaks come from, and it is what makes later refactoring cheap.
  • Extract services in reversible steps: prove the boundary, move the schema to its own database while still in-process, move events to the broker, deploy the new app, swap the facade for a client, remove the module.
  • Every synchronous cross-service call needs a deadline, a bulkhead and a fallback; every event needs an id, a version and an idempotent consumer.
  • Never big-bang rewrite. Strangle: route one capability at a time to the new system behind a gateway.

Part 6 — Clean Code Principles and Design Patterns

Part 5 covered the shape of systems: which process runs what, who owns which data. This part goes one level down, to the shape of code inside a module. Principles like SOLID and DRY, and patterns like Repository, Strategy and Unit of Work, are the vocabulary senior engineers use to keep a NestJS codebase changeable after three years and thirty contributors.

Two warnings up front. First, every principle here can be over-applied; a codebase that follows all of them mechanically is often harder to read than one that follows none. Each section therefore includes a note on where juniors misapply the idea. Second, patterns are not features. You do not "add the Strategy pattern"; you notice a specific pain (a growing switch on payment provider) and reach for the pattern that removes it. Learn the pain first, then the pattern.

6.1 SOLID

SOLID is five principles collected by Robert C. Martin. They are about managing dependencies between classes so that change in one place does not ripple everywhere. We take them one at a time, each with a realistic NestJS before-and-after.

6.1.1 Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

Concept

A class should have one reason to change. Not "one method" or "does one thing", but one reason: one group of stakeholders whose requirement changes would force you to edit it.

Why does it exist?

When one class serves several masters, every change for one master risks breaking the others, and the class accumulates dependencies from all of them. A service that handles order creation, payment, email and inventory has four teams' worth of change pressure and thirty injected dependencies. Every test needs thirty mocks.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant employee who cooks, waits tables and does the accounting. When the menu changes, the accounts might break because the same person's routine changed. Give each job to a separate role and menu changes stay in the kitchen.

NestJS example

Before: the classic God service.

// BEFORE: one class, four reasons to change (orders, payments, email, inventory)
@Injectable()
export class OrderService {
  constructor(
    @InjectRepository(Order) private orders: Repository<Order>,
    @InjectRepository(Product) private products: Repository<Product>,
    private readonly stripe: Stripe,
    private readonly mailer: MailerService,
    private readonly config: ConfigService,
  ) {}

  async checkout(userId: string, items: { productId: string; qty: number }[]) {
    // inventory logic
    for (const it of items) {
      const p = await this.products.findOneByOrFail({ id: it.productId });
      if (p.stock < it.qty) throw new ConflictException('out of stock');
      p.stock -= it.qty;
      await this.products.save(p);
    }
    // order logic
    const order = await this.orders.save(this.orders.create({ userId, items, status: 'CREATED' }));
    // payment logic
    const intent = await this.stripe.paymentIntents.create({ amount: order.totalMinor, currency: 'inr' });
    order.paymentIntentId = intent.id;
    await this.orders.save(order);
