    // email logic
    await this.mailer.sendMail({
      to: await this.lookupEmail(userId),
      subject: 'Order confirmed',
      html: `<h1>Thanks!</h1><p>Order ${order.id}</p>`,
    });
    return order;
  }
}

After: each responsibility in its own provider, with the use case as a thin orchestrator.

// AFTER: PlaceOrderUseCase orchestrates; each collaborator has one reason to change
@Injectable()
export class PlaceOrderUseCase {
  constructor(
    @Inject(ORDER_REPOSITORY) private readonly orders: OrderRepository,
    private readonly inventory: InventoryFacade,      // owns stock rules
    @Inject(PAYMENT_GATEWAY) private readonly payments: PaymentGateway, // owns provider calls
    private readonly events: EventEmitter2,           // notifications react to events
  ) {}

  async execute(cmd: PlaceOrderCommand): Promise<{ orderId: string }> {
    const reservation = await this.inventory.reserve({ orderId: cmd.orderId, lines: cmd.lines });
    const order = Order.create(cmd.orderId, cmd.customerId, toLines(cmd.lines), new Date());
    await this.orders.save(order);
    const { paymentId } = await this.payments.charge({ orderId: order.id, amount: order.total, idempotencyKey: `order:${order.id}` });
    order.markPaid();
    await this.orders.save(order);
    await this.events.emitAsync('order.paid', new OrderPaidEvent({ orderId: order.id, paymentId, reservationId: reservation.reservationId }));
    return { orderId: order.id };
  }
}

Email now lives in NotificationsModule as an @OnEvent('order.paid') handler. The marketing team can change the template without touching checkout, and the checkout test needs three small fakes instead of a Stripe mock and a mailer mock.

Where juniors misapply this

They read "one responsibility" as "one method per class" and produce OrderCreator, OrderSaver, OrderValidator, OrderTotalCalculator, each with four lines, and a checkout that is impossible to read because the logic is scattered across twelve files. The unit is reason to change, not method. A use case that orchestrates five steps of one business operation has one reason to change: that business operation.

Interview questions

  1. Define SRP precisely. Expected: one reason to change, one group of stakeholders; not "one method".
  2. How do you recognise an SRP violation in a NestJS service? Expected: many constructor dependencies from unrelated areas, tests with many mocks, changes from different teams in the same file.

6.1.2 Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

Concept

Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add a new behaviour (a new payment provider, a new shipping method) by adding code, not by editing the existing, tested code.

Why does it exist?

Editing working code risks breaking it. If adding Razorpay means editing the Stripe code path's switch, every payment provider addition re-tests every provider. OCP is achieved through abstraction: the code depends on an interface, and new behaviour is a new implementation.

Mental model

Imagine a power strip. You add a new device by plugging it in; you do not rewire the strip. The socket standard is the abstraction.

NestJS example

Before: a switch that grows with every provider.

// BEFORE: every new provider edits this method and its tests
async charge(order: Order, method: 'card' | 'upi' | 'paypal') {
  switch (method) {
    case 'card': return this.stripe.paymentIntents.create({ amount: order.totalMinor, currency: 'inr' });
    case 'upi':  return this.razorpay.orders.create({ amount: order.totalMinor, currency: 'INR' });
    case 'paypal': return this.paypal.orders.create({ purchase_units: [{ amount: { value: order.totalMajor } }] });
  }
}

After: a PaymentGateway interface, one class per provider, and a registry that maps method to gateway. Adding PayPal is a new file plus one line in the module.

export interface PaymentGateway {
  readonly method: PaymentMethod;
  charge(input: ChargeInput): Promise<ChargeResult>;
}

@Injectable()
export class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway {
  readonly method = 'card' as const;
  constructor(private readonly stripe: Stripe) {}
  async charge(input: ChargeInput): Promise<ChargeResult> {
    const intent = await this.stripe.paymentIntents.create(
      { amount: input.amount.minor, currency: input.amount.currency.toLowerCase(), metadata: { orderId: input.orderId } },
      { idempotencyKey: input.idempotencyKey },
    );
    return { paymentId: intent.id, status: intent.status === 'succeeded' ? 'CAPTURED' : 'PENDING' };
  }
}

export const PAYMENT_GATEWAYS = Symbol('PAYMENT_GATEWAYS');

@Injectable()
export class PaymentGatewayRegistry {
  private readonly byMethod = new Map<PaymentMethod, PaymentGateway>();
  constructor(@Inject(PAYMENT_GATEWAYS) gateways: PaymentGateway[]) {
    for (const g of gateways) this.byMethod.set(g.method, g);
  }
  for(method: PaymentMethod): PaymentGateway {
    const g = this.byMethod.get(method);
    if (!g) throw new DomainError('PAYMENT_METHOD_UNSUPPORTED', `no gateway for ${method}`);
    return g;
  }
}

// payments.module.ts: the only line that changes when adding a provider
{ provide: PAYMENT_GATEWAYS, useFactory: (s: StripeGateway, r: RazorpayGateway, p: PaypalGateway) => [s, r, p], inject: [StripeGateway, RazorpayGateway, PaypalGateway] },

Where juniors misapply this

They abstract before there is a second implementation. An interface with one implementation and a factory for it is speculation, not OCP. The rule of thumb: introduce the abstraction when the second concrete case arrives, or when you know with certainty it is coming this quarter. Until then, a switch with two cases is honest code.

Interview questions

  1. How does OCP relate to the Strategy pattern? Expected: Strategy is the usual mechanism; interface plus implementations plus selection.
  2. When is a switch acceptable? Expected: few stable cases, no second implementation on the horizon, or when the switch is the single selection point (a factory).

6.1.3 Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

Concept

If code works with an interface, it must work with every implementation of that interface without knowing which one it got. Subtypes must honour the contract of the supertype: same inputs accepted, same guarantees on outputs, no surprising exceptions, no strengthened preconditions, no weakened postconditions.

Why does it exist?

Abstractions are only useful if callers can trust them. If PaymentGateway.charge() returns a paymentId for Stripe but returns null for a bank transfer adapter "because bank transfers are async", every caller must now check for null and, in effect, know which adapter it has. The abstraction has leaked and OCP is gone.

Mental model

Imagine renting a car. Any car from the rental company should have a steering wheel, brakes, and an accelerator that do the same things. If one car's brake pedal accelerates, "it's still a car" is not a defence.

NestJS example

A subtle LSP violation with payment provider adapters:

// The contract: charge() either captures funds and returns CAPTURED, or returns PENDING
// with a paymentId that a webhook will later resolve. It throws PaymentDeclinedError on decline.
export interface PaymentGateway {
  charge(input: ChargeInput): Promise<{ paymentId: string; status: 'CAPTURED' | 'PENDING' }>;
}

// VIOLATION: this adapter throws for a normal outcome and returns a different shape for "pending"
@Injectable()
export class BankTransferGateway implements PaymentGateway {
  async charge(input: ChargeInput) {
    if (input.amount.minor > 50_000_00) throw new Error('bank transfers over 50k need manual approval'); // new precondition
    return { paymentId: '', status: 'PENDING' as const }; // empty id breaks the "paymentId identifies the payment" guarantee
  }
}

Callers written against Stripe and Razorpay now break in two ways: the empty paymentId is stored and later fails a NOT NULL/unique constraint, and the manual-approval Error is not a PaymentDeclinedError, so the generic error handler returns a 500 and the order is left in limbo.

The fix keeps the contract honest:

@Injectable()
export class BankTransferGateway implements PaymentGateway {
  constructor(private readonly ids: IdGenerator, private readonly approvals: ManualApprovalQueue) {}

  async charge(input: ChargeInput) {
    const paymentId = this.ids.next('bt'); // a real identifier, always
    if (input.amount.minor > 50_000_00) {
      await this.approvals.enqueue({ paymentId, orderId: input.orderId, amount: input.amount });
    }
    // PENDING is a valid contract outcome; the webhook/approval flow resolves it later
    return { paymentId, status: 'PENDING' as const };
  }
}

If bank transfers genuinely cannot satisfy the contract, the right move is a different interface (DeferredPaymentGateway) and explicit handling, not a subtype that lies.

Where juniors misapply this

They think LSP is about class inheritance only. In TypeScript, it applies to every implements and every structural type. The most common violation is an adapter that throws a generic Error where the contract promises a typed domain error, or that returns undefined where the contract promises a value.

Interview questions

  1. Give an example of an LSP violation that does not involve inheritance. Expected: an adapter implementing an interface but breaking its guarantees (null return, new exception, stronger precondition).
  2. How do you test LSP compliance across adapters? Expected: a shared contract test suite run against every implementation (describe.each over adapters).

6.1.4 Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

Concept

Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. Prefer several small, role-specific interfaces over one large general-purpose one.

Why does it exist?

A fat interface couples every client to every method. A ProductRepository with 25 methods must be fully mocked in every test, fully implemented by every adapter (including the in-memory one), and any change to any method touches every implementation. It also hides what a use case actually needs.

Mental model

Imagine a TV remote with 80 buttons when you only use 5. Now imagine you have to learn all 80 to be allowed to use the 5. That is a fat interface. A small remote per purpose is ISP.

NestJS example

Before: one repository interface for everything.

// BEFORE: every consumer sees, mocks and depends on all of this
export interface ProductRepository {
  findById(id: string): Promise<Product | null>;
  findBySku(sku: string): Promise<Product | null>;
  search(filter: ProductFilter, page: Page): Promise<Product[]>;
  save(p: Product): Promise<void>;
  delete(id: string): Promise<void>;
  decrementStock(id: string, qty: number): Promise<boolean>;
  bulkImport(rows: ProductRow[]): Promise<void>;
  countByCategory(): Promise<Record<string, number>>;
  // ... 17 more
}

After: narrow, role-based interfaces; a use case depends only on the one it needs.

export interface ProductReader {
  findById(id: string): Promise<Product | null>;
}
export interface ProductSearcher {
  search(filter: ProductFilter, page: Page): Promise<Product[]>;
}
export interface ProductWriter {
  save(p: Product): Promise<void>;
}
export interface StockAdjuster {
  decrementStock(id: string, qty: number): Promise<boolean>;
}

export const PRODUCT_READER = Symbol('PRODUCT_READER');
export const STOCK_ADJUSTER = Symbol('STOCK_ADJUSTER');

// The TypeORM class can implement several; each token maps to the same instance.
@Injectable()
export class TypeormProductRepository implements ProductReader, ProductSearcher, ProductWriter, StockAdjuster { /* ... */ }

// products.module.ts
providers: [
  TypeormProductRepository,
  { provide: PRODUCT_READER, useExisting: TypeormProductRepository },
  { provide: STOCK_ADJUSTER, useExisting: TypeormProductRepository },
],

// A use case now declares exactly what it needs; its test fakes one method.
@Injectable()
export class ReserveStockUseCase {
  constructor(@Inject(STOCK_ADJUSTER) private readonly stock: StockAdjuster) {}
}

useExisting is the NestJS provider type that aliases one token to another provider's instance; it is exactly what ISP needs.

Where juniors misapply this

They create an interface per method for everything, ending up with FindProductByIdPort, FindProductBySkuPort, and a module with 40 tokens. Group by role (reader, writer, searcher), not per method. A role is a coherent set of operations one kind of client needs.

Interview questions

  1. What is the cost of a fat repository interface in tests? Expected: mocking every method; brittle tests; hidden dependencies.
  2. How does NestJS useExisting help with ISP? Expected: one implementation exposed under several narrow tokens.

6.1.5 Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

Concept

High-level modules (business rules) should not depend on low-level modules (database, HTTP clients). Both should depend on abstractions. And the abstraction is owned by the high-level side: the use case defines the PaymentGateway interface it needs; the Stripe adapter conforms to it.

Why does it exist?

Without DIP, the direction of dependency follows the direction of the call: use case calls Stripe, so use case imports Stripe. Now the most important code depends on the most volatile. DIP flips the import direction while keeping the call direction, which is the entire trick behind hexagonal architecture.

Mental model

Imagine a wall socket again, but notice who defined the standard: the building (high level) defines the socket; appliance makers (low level) conform. The building does not adapt to each appliance.

NestJS example

DIP in NestJS is expressed with injection tokens and interfaces, because TypeScript interfaces do not exist at runtime and cannot be injected by type.

// application/ports/payment.gateway.ts   (owned by the high-level side)
export const PAYMENT_GATEWAY = Symbol('PAYMENT_GATEWAY');
export interface PaymentGateway {
  charge(input: ChargeInput): Promise<ChargeResult>;
  refund(paymentId: string, amount: Money, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<void>;
}

// application/refund-order.use-case.ts   (imports the port, never Stripe)
@Injectable()
export class RefundOrderUseCase {
  constructor(
    @Inject(PAYMENT_GATEWAY) private readonly payments: PaymentGateway,
    @Inject(ORDER_REPOSITORY) private readonly orders: OrderRepository,
  ) {}
  async execute(orderId: string, reason: string): Promise<void> {
    const order = await this.orders.findById(orderId);
    if (!order) throw new DomainError('ORDER_NOT_FOUND', orderId);
    order.requestRefund(reason);                // domain rule: only PAID or SHIPPED orders
    await this.payments.refund(order.paymentId!, order.total, `refund:${orderId}`);
    order.markRefunded();
    await this.orders.save(order);
  }
}

// infrastructure/stripe/stripe-payment.gateway.ts   (imports Stripe AND the port)
@Injectable()
export class StripePaymentGateway implements PaymentGateway { /* ... */ }

// payments.module.ts   (the composition root: the only file that knows both)
providers: [{ provide: PAYMENT_GATEWAY, useClass: StripePaymentGateway }]

In tests:

const payments: PaymentGateway = { charge: jest.fn(), refund: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined) };
const useCase = new RefundOrderUseCase(payments, new InMemoryOrderRepository([paidOrder]));

No Test.createTestingModule, no Stripe SDK, no network.

Where juniors misapply this

They put the interface next to the implementation (infrastructure/stripe/payment-gateway.interface.ts), which means the use case still imports from infrastructure. The interface must live with the consumer (application/ports/). They also create interfaces for things that will never vary and have no test value, like ConfigService, adding indirection with no benefit.

Interview questions

  1. Why can you not inject a TypeScript interface directly in NestJS? Expected: interfaces are erased at compile time; use a Symbol/string token with @Inject.
  2. Who owns the abstraction under DIP, and why does it matter? Expected: the high-level consumer; otherwise the import direction still points at infrastructure.
  3. Show how DIP and hexagonal architecture relate. Expected: ports are DIP abstractions; adapters are the low-level implementations; the module is the composition root.

Practical exercise (SOLID as a whole)

Take a OrderService of at least 300 lines from a real or sample project. Produce a refactoring plan that names, for each SOLID letter, one concrete violation and the fix. Implement the SRP and DIP fixes.

Acceptance criteria: the resulting use case has at most four constructor dependencies, all injected via tokens with interfaces owned by application/ports/; its unit tests run without NestJS's testing module or a database; a contract test suite runs against every PaymentGateway implementation with describe.each.

6.2 DRY — Don't Repeat Yourself

Concept

DRY says every piece of knowledge should have a single, authoritative representation in the system. Note the word: knowledge, not code. Two functions that look identical but encode different business facts are not a DRY violation. Two places that both encode "orders over 50,000 INR need manual review" are, even if the code looks different.

Why does it exist?

When a rule lives in two places, they drift. Someone changes the threshold in the API validator and forgets the one in the Kafka consumer. Now the same order is accepted by one path and rejected by the other, and the bug is invisible until an auditor asks why.

Mental model

Imagine a company's holiday policy printed in the employee handbook, on the intranet, and in the onboarding slides. HR updates the handbook. Two years later, new hires still learn the old policy from the slides. DRY says: one source of truth, and everything else links to it.

How it works

Identify the knowledge: a business rule, a validation constraint, a mapping, a configuration value. Give it one home (a domain class, a value object, a constant, a shared validator). Make every consumer reference that home. Duplication of mechanism (two loops that look alike) is not the target; duplication of decisions is.

NestJS example

Before: the threshold appears in three places.

// dto: create-order.dto.ts
@Max(50_000_00, { message: 'orders over 50,000 need manual review' })
totalMinor!: number;

// service: orders.service.ts
if (order.totalMinor > 50_000_00) await this.review.enqueue(order);

// consumer: order-events.consumer.ts
if (event.amountMinor >= 5_000_000) { /* someone typed it differently: >= vs > */ }

After: one domain policy, referenced everywhere.

// domain/policies/manual-review.policy.ts
export const MANUAL_REVIEW_THRESHOLD = Money.of(50_000_00, 'INR');

export class ManualReviewPolicy {
  static requiresReview(total: Money): boolean {
    return total.greaterThan(MANUAL_REVIEW_THRESHOLD);
  }
}

// dto: no business threshold; only structural validation (positive integer)
@IsInt() @Min(1) totalMinor!: number;

// use case and consumer both call the policy
if (ManualReviewPolicy.requiresReview(order.total)) await this.review.enqueue(order.id);

The DTO stopped encoding a business rule. That is a separate principle (separation of concerns, section 6.5) working together with DRY.

The danger of the wrong abstraction

DRY has a famous failure mode. Two code blocks look 80% similar; someone extracts a shared function with a boolean parameter for the 20% difference. A third caller needs a slightly different 20%, so a second parameter appears. A year later the shared function has six flags, nobody understands all the paths, and every change to it risks all six callers. Sandi Metz's line captures it: duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

A concrete NestJS case: sendNotification(user, type, options) that started as "send order email" and grew to handle SMS, push, marketing opt-outs, template selection and retries through flags. The fix is usually to inline the abstraction back into its callers, look at what each actually does, and only then extract the genuinely shared pieces (template rendering, say) while leaving the differing pieces separate.

Rules of thumb:

  • Wait for the third occurrence before extracting (the "rule of three"). Two data points do not define a pattern.
  • Extract knowledge (a rule, a mapping), not shape (two loops that happen to look alike).
  • If the extracted function needs a boolean parameter to choose behaviour, you probably extracted two things.
  • Prefer small, composable pieces over one configurable mega-function.

Where juniors misapply this

They DRY up test code until tests are unreadable (a makeOrderTestCase(flags) helper that nobody can follow). Test code is allowed to repeat; clarity beats reuse there. They also DRY across module boundaries, creating libs/common that every module depends on, which quietly reintroduces coupling the modular monolith was trying to remove. Duplicating a five-line DTO across two modules is often the correct choice.

Interview questions

  1. Define DRY precisely and give a case where duplicated code is not a DRY violation. Expected: single representation of knowledge; two similar-looking functions encoding different rules.
  2. What is "the wrong abstraction" and how do you recover from it? Expected: over-generalised shared code with flags; inline back, then re-extract only the shared knowledge.
  3. Why is DRY across module boundaries dangerous? Expected: shared code becomes coupling; modules can no longer change independently.

Practical exercise

Find a shared helper in a codebase that takes at least two boolean parameters. Inline it into every caller. Identify which parts are genuinely shared knowledge and re-extract only those.

Acceptance criteria: no boolean "mode" parameters remain; each caller's behaviour is unchanged (existing tests pass); the extracted pieces are each under 20 lines with a single purpose.

6.3 KISS — Keep It Simple

Concept

KISS says: of all the designs that solve the problem, choose the simplest one that works. Simplicity is measured by how much a new engineer must hold in their head to change the code safely, not by line count.

Why does it exist?

Complexity is the main cost driver in software. Every layer, indirection, generic parameter and configuration option must be understood by everyone who touches the code, forever. Complexity also hides bugs: the more paths, the more untested paths.

Mental model

Imagine a kitchen gadget that peels, slices, dices and juliennes, with 14 attachments. Most people use a knife. The knife is KISS. The gadget is impressive and sits in a drawer.

NestJS example

Before: a "flexible" generic base service.

// BEFORE: a generic CRUD base that every service extends
export abstract class BaseCrudService<T extends ObjectLiteral, CreateDto, UpdateDto> {
  constructor(protected readonly repo: Repository<T>, protected readonly mapper: Mapper<T, CreateDto, UpdateDto>) {}
  async findAll(query: QueryOptions<T>): Promise<Paginated<T>> { /* 60 lines of generic filter/sort/paginate */ }
  async create(dto: CreateDto, hooks?: LifecycleHooks<T>): Promise<T> { /* beforeCreate, afterCreate, validation plugins */ }
  // ...
}

Every real service overrides half of it, hooks fight with transactions, and the generic QueryOptions<T> lets clients filter by any column including passwordHash.

After: write the three endpoints the module needs.

@Injectable()
export class AddressesService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(AddressEntity) private readonly repo: Repository<AddressEntity>) {}

  listForUser(userId: string): Promise<AddressEntity[]> {
    return this.repo.find({ where: { userId }, order: { isDefault: 'DESC', createdAt: 'DESC' }, take: 20 });
  }

  async create(userId: string, dto: CreateAddressDto): Promise<AddressEntity> {
    if ((await this.repo.countBy({ userId })) >= 10) throw new UnprocessableEntityException('max 10 addresses');
    return this.repo.save(this.repo.create({ ...dto, userId }));
  }

  async remove(userId: string, id: string): Promise<void> {
    const result = await this.repo.delete({ id, userId }); // ownership check in the WHERE
    if (result.affected === 0) throw new NotFoundException();
  }
}

Twenty lines a new engineer reads in a minute. The "flexibility" of the base class was never needed; addresses have three operations.

Where juniors misapply this

They use KISS to justify skipping structure that is needed: "just put the SQL in the controller, KISS". Simplicity is about the whole system's understandability, not about the fewest files in this PR. A controller with 200 lines of SQL is not simple to change safely. The test is: what does the next person need to understand to make the next change?

Interview questions

  1. How do you measure simplicity? Expected: cognitive load for the next change; number of concepts, not lines.
  2. Give an example of complexity disguised as flexibility. Expected: generic base classes, plugin systems, config-driven behaviour with one configuration ever used.

6.4 YAGNI — You Aren't Gonna Need It

Concept

Do not build functionality until it is actually needed. Not "might be needed next quarter", not "would be nice", not "the other team said they might want it".

Why does it exist?

Speculative features cost the same to build as real ones, plus they cost maintenance, plus they are usually wrong because the real requirement, when it arrives, differs from the guess. A study of feature usage in enterprise software regularly finds that most built features are rarely or never used.

Mental model

Imagine packing for a weekend trip and bringing a snow shovel because "you never know". You carry it all weekend. If it snows, you will find it was the wrong shovel anyway.

NestJS example

Before: speculative multi-tenancy, multi-currency and soft delete on day one of a single-tenant, single-currency product.

@Entity()
export class Order {
  @Column() tenantId!: string;          // one tenant exists
  @Column() currency!: string;          // INR only, for the foreseeable future
  @Column({ nullable: true }) deletedAt?: Date; // nothing deletes orders
  @Column('jsonb', { default: {} }) metadata!: Record<string, unknown>; // "for future flexibility"
}

Every query must now filter by tenantId; every money calculation must consider currency; every read must exclude soft-deleted rows; metadata becomes the dumping ground where real columns should have gone.

After: the columns the product needs today, with a migration path noted in the ADR.

@Entity()
export class Order {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid') id!: string;
  @Column('uuid') customerId!: string;
  @Column('integer') totalMinor!: number; // INR; add a currency column when a second currency is scheduled
  @Column({ type: 'text' }) status!: OrderStatus;
  @Index() @Column('timestamptz') createdAt!: Date;
}

Adding a column later costs one migration. Carrying an unused abstraction costs every developer, every day.

Where YAGNI does not apply

YAGNI is about features and abstractions, not about engineering fundamentals. You always need: idempotency on payment calls, timeouts on network calls, input validation, structured logging with a request id, a migration tool, and a DTO boundary. Those are not speculative; they are the cost of being in production. Juniors sometimes invoke YAGNI to skip them, which is how a system ends up with no way to trace a failed payment.

The other exception is irreversible decisions: primary key type (uuid vs bigint), timezone handling (always timestamptz), money as integer minor units. These are cheap to get right now and very expensive to change later. YAGNI does not apply to them.

Interview questions

  1. Give an example of YAGNI done right and one of YAGNI used as an excuse. Expected: skipping speculative multi-tenancy vs skipping idempotency keys.
  2. Which decisions should you make early even under YAGNI? Expected: irreversible ones: ids, time, money representation, DTO boundary.

6.5 Separation of concerns

Concept

Separation of concerns (SoC) means each part of the system deals with one kind of thing: HTTP concerns in controllers and pipes, business rules in the domain, persistence in repositories, cross-cutting behaviour (auth, logging, caching, rate limiting) in guards, interceptors and middleware. The concerns are separated so they can be reasoned about, tested and changed independently.

Why does it exist?

When concerns mix, changes to one force re-testing all of them, and reuse becomes impossible. A business rule embedded in an HTTP controller cannot be triggered from a Kafka consumer. A caching decision inside a repository method cannot be turned off for a batch job.

Mental model

Imagine a hospital where the surgeon also handles billing and parking. Every surgery would include a stop at the payment desk. Separate roles let each get better at its job and let the hospital change its billing system without retraining surgeons.

How NestJS is built for it

NestJS's request pipeline is a separation-of-concerns machine. Each stage has one job:

Request
  -> Middleware        (raw request: body parsing, correlation id, raw-body capture for webhooks)
  -> Guards            (authentication, authorisation: who is this and may they do this)
  -> Interceptors pre  (timing, logging, caching lookup)
  -> Pipes             (validation and transformation of params/body into typed DTOs)
  -> Controller        (translate HTTP into a use-case call; nothing else)
  -> Use case / domain (business rules)
  -> Repository        (persistence)
  -> Interceptors post (response mapping, caching store, metrics)
  -> Exception filters (map domain errors to HTTP status codes)
Response

NestJS example

Each concern in its home:

// Cross-cutting: correlation id middleware
@Injectable()
export class CorrelationIdMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
    const id = (req.headers['x-request-id'] as string) ?? randomUUID();
    req.headers['x-request-id'] = id;
    res.setHeader('x-request-id', id);
    next();
  }
}

// Authorisation concern: a guard, not an `if` in the controller
@Injectable()
export class OrderOwnerGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(@Inject(ORDER_READER) private readonly orders: OrderReader) {}
  async canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const order = await this.orders.findById(req.params.id);
    if (!order) throw new NotFoundException();
    return order.customerId === req.user.id || req.user.roles.includes('support');
  }
}

// HTTP concern: the controller translates and delegates
@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly cancelOrder: CancelOrderUseCase) {}

  @Post(':id/cancel')
  @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, OrderOwnerGuard)
  @HttpCode(200)
  async cancel(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string, @Body() dto: CancelOrderDto): Promise<OrderResponse> {
    const order = await this.cancelOrder.execute({ orderId: id, reason: dto.reason });
    return OrderResponse.from(order);
  }
}

// Domain concern: the rule itself, testable with no HTTP
cancel(reason: string): void {
  if (this._status === 'SHIPPED' || this._status === 'DELIVERED') throw new DomainError('ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE', this._status);
  this._status = 'CANCELLED';
  this._cancelReason = reason;
}

Where juniors misapply this

They separate by technical type instead of by concern: a validators/ folder for all validators across all modules, a helpers/ folder with 80 unrelated functions. That is sorting, not separating. Concerns are things like "authorisation", "pricing", "persistence of orders". They also over-separate trivial things: a dto/, mapper/, interface/, impl/ folder tree for a two-method module.

Interview questions

  1. Map each stage of the NestJS request pipeline to a concern. Expected: as in the diagram above.
  2. Why should authorisation be a guard rather than an if in the service? Expected: reuse across endpoints, testability, clear failure mode, no business logic contamination; note that data-dependent authorisation sometimes needs both.
  3. What is the difference between separating by concern and separating by technical type? Expected: concern is a reason to change; type is a syntactic category.

6.6 Dependency inversion (the principle, standalone)

Concept

Section 6.1.5 covered DIP as the "D" of SOLID. It deserves a standalone view because it is the single most important idea in this part: it is the mechanism behind hexagonal architecture, testability, and every pattern that swaps implementations (Strategy, Adapter, Repository).

Stated simply: the caller defines what it needs; the callee conforms. The import arrows point toward the abstraction, and the abstraction lives with the caller.

How it works, mechanically, in TypeScript and NestJS

  1. The high-level module declares an interface and a runtime token (Symbol) in its own folder.
  2. The low-level module imports that interface and implements it.
  3. A composition root (the NestJS module) binds the token to the implementation.
  4. The high-level code receives the implementation through its constructor (@Inject(TOKEN)), never constructing it.
flowchart LR
  UC["PlaceOrderUseCase\napplication"] -->|"imports"| P["PaymentGateway interface\napplication/ports"]
  ST["StripePaymentGateway\ninfrastructure"] -->|"imports and implements"| P
  M["PaymentsModule\ncomposition root"] -->|"binds PAYMENT_GATEWAY to"| ST
  M -->|"provides"| UC
  UC -.->|"calls at runtime"| ST

Notice the solid arrows (compile-time imports) all point at the port or are made by the module. The dashed arrow (runtime call) goes from use case to Stripe, but no import does.

Inversion without a DI container

DI containers are convenient, not required. Plain TypeScript inversion looks like this and is what your tests use:

const useCase = new PlaceOrderUseCase(new InMemoryOrderRepository(), new FakePaymentGateway(), new FakePublisher());

If your use case can be built this way, the inversion is real. If it can only be built by NestJS, something (a static import, a ModuleRef lookup, a decorator with side effects) is hiding a dependency.

What not to invert

Not everything deserves a port. Inverting Logger, ConfigService, Date, crypto is sometimes valuable (a Clock port makes time-based rules testable; a Logger port rarely earns its keep). The test: would a second implementation exist in production or in tests, and does the abstraction make an important test possible? If not, import the concrete thing.

Interview questions

  1. Explain dependency inversion without using the words "interface" or "abstract". Expected: the code that needs something defines the shape of what it needs; the thing that provides it adapts to that shape; wiring happens in one place.
  2. How do you verify inversion is real in a NestJS codebase? Expected: use cases constructible with new and fakes; lint rules on import direction.
  3. Name something you would not invert and why. Expected: something with one implementation and no test value.

Practical exercise

Introduce a Clock port (now(): Date) into an orders module and inject it wherever new Date() was called in domain or application code. Write a unit test for "reservations expire after 15 minutes" that advances the fake clock.

Acceptance criteria: no new Date() remains in domain/ or application/; the expiry test runs in under 10 ms with no timers or sleeps; production binds Clock to a system implementation via useValue.

6.7 Dependency injection and the NestJS container

Concept

Dependency injection (DI) means a class receives its collaborators from the outside (usually through its constructor) instead of creating them itself. A DI container is the piece of infrastructure that builds the object graph: it reads what each class needs, creates instances in the right order, and hands them in. NestJS ships such a container and builds the entire application from it at startup.

Dependency inversion (section 6.6) is the principle; dependency injection is one mechanism for achieving it.

Why does it exist?

Without DI, PlaceOrderUseCase would contain this.payments = new StripePaymentGateway(new Stripe(process.env.STRIPE_KEY)). Now the use case knows about Stripe, about environment variables, and about how to construct an SDK client. You cannot test it without Stripe, cannot swap the provider, and cannot share one Stripe client across the app. DI moves construction to one place (the module) and gives every class exactly what it declares.

Mental model

Imagine a film set. Actors (classes) do not build their own props. A props department (the container) reads the script (the metadata on each class), builds every prop once, and hands each actor what their scene needs. Change the prop supplier and the actors do not notice.

How it works

At NestFactory.create(AppModule), the container performs these steps:

  1. Scan modules. Starting from AppModule, it walks imports recursively and builds a module graph. Each module gets its own container scope.
  2. Register providers. For each module, every entry in providers and controllers is registered under a token. For a class provider, the token is the class itself. For { provide: X, ... }, the token is X (a class, a string, or a Symbol).
  3. Read constructor metadata. TypeScript's emitDecoratorMetadata writes the constructor parameter types into design:paramtypes. @Inject(TOKEN) overrides a parameter's token explicitly (necessary for interfaces and for string/symbol tokens).
  4. Resolve. For each provider, the container resolves each constructor parameter's token by looking in the current module's providers, then in providers exported by imported modules, then in global modules. If nothing matches, boot fails with Nest can't resolve dependencies of X (?, Y). The ? marks the unresolvable position.
  5. Instantiate in dependency order. Providers are singletons per module by default (Scope.DEFAULT): each is created once and cached.
  6. Run lifecycle hooks (onModuleInit, onApplicationBootstrap) in dependency order.
flowchart TB
  AM["AppModule"] --> OM["OrdersModule"]
  AM --> PM["PaymentsModule"]
  AM --> CM["ConfigModule global"]
  OM --> OC["OrdersController"]
  OM --> UC["PlaceOrderUseCase"]
  OM --> OR["ORDER_REPOSITORY\nuseClass TypeormOrderRepository"]
  OM -->|"imports"| PM
  PM --> PG["PAYMENT_GATEWAY\nuseClass StripePaymentGateway"]
  PM --> SC["STRIPE_CLIENT\nuseFactory"]
  PM -.->|"exports"| PG
  OC --> UC
  UC --> OR
  UC --> PG
  PG --> SC
  SC --> CS["ConfigService"]
  CM -.->|"exports"| CS

Solid arrows are "depends on" or "declares"; dashed arrows are exports. UC can see PG only because PaymentsModule exports it and OrdersModule imports PaymentsModule.

Provider types

Syntax What the container does Typical use
MyService (class) new MyService(...resolved deps) once The default; most providers
{ provide: T, useClass: Impl } new Impl(...) registered under token T Binding a port to an adapter; environment-specific implementations
{ provide: T, useValue: obj } Registers obj as-is Constants, config objects, pre-built SDK clients, test doubles
{ provide: T, useFactory: fn, inject: [A, B] } Calls fn(a, b) (may be async) and registers the result Anything needing construction logic: SDK clients with keys, connections, conditional bindings
{ provide: T, useExisting: U } Aliases T to whatever U resolves to (same instance) ISP: one implementation under several narrow tokens; backward-compatible renames 
// payments.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import Stripe from 'stripe';

export const STRIPE_CLIENT = Symbol('STRIPE_CLIENT');

@Module({
  imports: [ConfigModule],
  providers: [
    // useFactory: construct an SDK client from config, once, with a timeout
    {
      provide: STRIPE_CLIENT,
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService) =>
        new Stripe(config.getOrThrow<string>('STRIPE_SECRET_KEY'), { apiVersion: '2024-06-20', timeout: 8_000, maxNetworkRetries: 2 }),
      inject: [ConfigService],
    },
    // useClass: bind the port to the adapter chosen by environment
    {
      provide: PAYMENT_GATEWAY,
      useClass: process.env.PAYMENTS_FAKE === 'true' ? FakePaymentGateway : StripePaymentGateway,
    },
    // useValue: a constant policy object
    { provide: REFUND_POLICY, useValue: { windowDays: 14, maxAutoRefundMinor: 20_000_00 } },
    // useExisting: expose the same instance under a narrower token
    StripePaymentGateway,
    { provide: REFUND_PROCESSOR, useExisting: StripePaymentGateway },
  ],
  exports: [PAYMENT_GATEWAY, REFUND_PROCESSOR],
})
export class PaymentsModule {}

Scopes and their performance cost

NestJS providers have three scopes:

Scope Instances When created Cost
Scope.DEFAULT One per application (per module registration) At bootstrap None per request
Scope.REQUEST One per incoming request Lazily, per request, for the whole dependency subtree Allocation and resolution per request; every provider that depends on a request-scoped provider becomes request-scoped too
Scope.TRANSIENT One per injection point When the consumer is created Multiple instances; consumers of a transient in a default-scoped provider still get one instance (created once with that consumer)

The bubbling rule is the trap. If OrdersController injects PlaceOrderUseCase which injects TypeormOrderRepository which injects a request-scoped TenantContext, then all three become request-scoped. The container now constructs the controller, the use case and the repository for every request. At 2,000 RPS that is 6,000 object constructions per second plus resolution work, and TypeORM repositories are not cheap to build. Benchmarks on typical NestJS apps show 10 to 30% throughput loss and measurable p99 increase when a request-scoped provider sits low in the graph.

// A legitimate request-scoped provider: it genuinely holds per-request state
@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST })
export class RequestContext {
  readonly requestId: string;
  readonly userId?: string;
  constructor(@Inject(REQUEST) req: Request) {
    this.requestId = req.headers['x-request-id'] as string;
    this.userId = (req as any).user?.id;
  }
}

The senior alternative is AsyncLocalStorage (Node.js built-in, see nestjs-cls for a NestJS integration): a middleware stores request context in async-local storage, and any default-scoped provider reads it without changing scope. You get per-request context at zero DI cost.

// Default-scoped provider reading per-request context via AsyncLocalStorage
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';

export const requestStore = new AsyncLocalStorage<{ requestId: string; userId?: string }>();

@Injectable()
export class RequestContextMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, _res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
    requestStore.run({ requestId: req.headers['x-request-id'] as string }, () => next());
  }
}

@Injectable() // DEFAULT scope: constructed once
export class AuditLogger {
  log(action: string) {
    const ctx = requestStore.getStore();
    console.log(JSON.stringify({ action, requestId: ctx?.requestId, userId: ctx?.userId }));
  }
}

Scope.TRANSIENT has a narrower use: a Logger that should carry the class name of whoever injected it. Even then, NestJS's built-in Logger with new Logger(MyClass.name) is simpler.

Circular dependencies and forwardRef

A circular dependency is A needing B and B needing A. At the class level, TypeScript's metadata for A's constructor references B before B's module has finished evaluating (or vice versa), so the container sees undefined and fails with Nest can't resolve dependencies... A circular dependency between modules/providers. forwardRef(() => B) defers the reference until both classes exist.

// Works, but treat it as a warning sign
@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@Inject(forwardRef(() => PaymentsService)) private readonly payments: PaymentsService) {}
}
@Injectable()
export class PaymentsService {
  constructor(@Inject(forwardRef(() => OrdersService)) private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}
}
// Module-level cycles need it too:
@Module({ imports: [forwardRef(() => PaymentsModule)] })
export class OrdersModule {}

A circular dependency between two business services almost always means a missing third concept or a missing event. Orders needs to tell payments to charge (a call), and payments needs to tell orders it succeeded (an event, not a call back). Replace the back-edge with EventEmitter2 or extract the shared piece into a third provider both depend on. Use forwardRef to get unblocked, then fix the design.

Barrel files (index.ts re-exporting everything) cause many accidental cycles. Import from the concrete file inside a module.

Dynamic modules: forRoot, forRootAsync, forFeature

A dynamic module is a module whose providers are computed from arguments at import time. TypeOrmModule.forRoot(options), ConfigModule.forRoot(), JwtModule.registerAsync() and BullModule.forRootAsync() all follow this convention.

  • forRoot(options): configure once with static options; typically returns a global module.
  • forRootAsync({ useFactory, inject, imports }): configure with options that depend on other providers (usually ConfigService), possibly asynchronously (fetching secrets).
  • forFeature(...): register per-module pieces (entities, queues) against the root configuration.

Writing your own:

// libs/platform/src/kafka/kafka.module.ts
import { DynamicModule, Module, Provider } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Kafka, Producer } from 'kafkajs';

export interface KafkaModuleOptions { clientId: string; brokers: string[] }
export const KAFKA_PRODUCER = Symbol('KAFKA_PRODUCER');
export const KAFKA_OPTIONS = Symbol('KAFKA_OPTIONS');

@Module({})
export class KafkaModule {
  static forRoot(options: KafkaModuleOptions): DynamicModule {
    return {
      module: KafkaModule,
      global: true,
      providers: [{ provide: KAFKA_OPTIONS, useValue: options }, KafkaModule.producerProvider()],
      exports: [KAFKA_PRODUCER],
    };
  }

  static forRootAsync(opts: { imports?: any[]; useFactory: (...args: any[]) => Promise<KafkaModuleOptions> | KafkaModuleOptions; inject?: any[] }): DynamicModule {
    return {
      module: KafkaModule,
      global: true,
      imports: opts.imports ?? [],
      providers: [
        { provide: KAFKA_OPTIONS, useFactory: opts.useFactory, inject: opts.inject ?? [] },
        KafkaModule.producerProvider(),
      ],
      exports: [KAFKA_PRODUCER],
    };
  }

  private static producerProvider(): Provider {
    return {
      provide: KAFKA_PRODUCER,
      useFactory: async (options: KafkaModuleOptions): Promise<Producer> => {
        const producer = new Kafka(options).producer({ idempotent: true, maxInFlightRequests: 5 });
        await producer.connect(); // async factory: bootstrap waits for the connection
        return producer;
      },
      inject: [KAFKA_OPTIONS],
    };
  }
}

// app.module.ts
KafkaModule.forRootAsync({
  imports: [ConfigModule],
  useFactory: (c: ConfigService) => ({ clientId: c.getOrThrow('SERVICE_NAME'), brokers: c.getOrThrow<string>('KAFKA_BROKERS').split(',') }),
  inject: [ConfigService],
}),

The ConfigurableModuleBuilder in @nestjs/common generates this boilerplate for you in recent NestJS versions; the hand-written version above is what it produces.

Practical example

A checkout request resolves through this graph: OrdersController (default) -> PlaceOrderUseCase (default) -> ORDER_REPOSITORY (default, TypeORM) and PAYMENT_GATEWAY (default, Stripe, which holds a shared STRIPE_CLIENT built by a factory). Per-request data (user id, request id) flows through AsyncLocalStorage, not through scoped providers. Total DI work per request: zero allocations. At 2,000 RPS on four pods, the container is not on any flame graph.

Production scenario

A team introduced Scope.REQUEST on a TenantContext provider that most repositories injected. Throughput dropped from 1,900 RPS to 1,350 RPS on the same hardware, and p99 rose from 110 ms to 190 ms. The DI resolution showed up as 18% of CPU in a profile. Moving tenant context to AsyncLocalStorage restored the original numbers in one afternoon.

Failure scenario

At startup after a refactor, the app fails: Nest can't resolve dependencies of the PlaceOrderUseCase (ORDER_REPOSITORY, ?). Please make sure that the argument Symbol(PAYMENT_GATEWAY) at index [1] is available in the OrdersModule context. The token exists in PaymentsModule, but someone removed it from exports while cleaning up. The ? marks index 1. The fix is one line, but the lesson is that DI errors are boot-time and loud, which is far better than runtime and silent. Keep a smoke test that boots the full AppModule in CI.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Injecting an interface by type (constructor(private gw: PaymentGateway)) compiles but resolves to Object at runtime; the container cannot find it. Always @Inject(TOKEN) for interfaces.
  • Two modules registering the same class provider get two instances (one per module). Share by exporting from one module and importing it.
  • Async useFactory that never resolves hangs bootstrap; add timeouts to connection factories.
  • @Global() overuse makes the dependency graph invisible; anything can inject anything.
  • Request scope bubbling silently turning half the app request-scoped after one innocent change.
  • forwardRef masking a design cycle that later becomes an event-loop-level deadlock in onModuleInit ordering.
  • Provider side effects in constructors (opening connections) happen during boot, before health checks are live; move to onModuleInit.
  • Lifecycle hook ordering. onModuleInit runs per module in dependency order; onApplicationBootstrap runs after all modules are initialised. Start Kafka consumers in the latter so their dependencies are ready.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They keep everything Scope.DEFAULT unless proven otherwise, and they carry per-request state in AsyncLocalStorage. They treat forwardRef as a lint warning. They build SDK clients in useFactory providers with explicit timeouts, once, and never new Stripe() inside a service. They write module exports deliberately, as a public API, and they keep a boot smoke test.

They can also explain the DI container to a junior in one sentence: "It reads each class's constructor, builds what it asks for, and hands it in; you write classes that declare what they need and never construct their collaborators."

Common mistakes

  • Using ModuleRef.get() all over the codebase instead of constructor injection (service locator; see anti-patterns in section 6.23).
  • Request scope for convenience.
  • Exporting everything from every module.
  • Creating SDK clients per request.
  • Missing @Inject on token-based dependencies.
  • Constructor logic that throws or does I/O.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through what NestFactory.create does with the module graph. Expected: scan imports, register providers under tokens, read design:paramtypes, resolve via module scope then imported exports then globals, instantiate singletons, run hooks.
  2. Explain request scope bubbling and its cost. Expected: any provider depending on a request-scoped one becomes request-scoped; per-request construction; measurable throughput loss; alternative is AsyncLocalStorage.
  3. Compare useClass, useValue, useFactory and useExisting with a use case for each. Expected: as in the table.
  4. When is forwardRef acceptable? Expected: temporarily; a cycle between business providers signals a missing event or third concept.
  5. How would you write a forRootAsync for a custom module? Expected: async useFactory with inject, options token, provider built from the options.
  6. Why does injecting by interface type fail at runtime? Expected: interfaces are erased; metadata records Object; use tokens.

Practical exercise

Profile a NestJS app under load (autocannon, 60 seconds) with a request-scoped provider injected into a repository. Record RPS and p99. Replace the provider with an AsyncLocalStorage-based context and re-run.

Acceptance criteria: the request-scoped version shows measurable DI overhead in a CPU profile (node --cpu-prof); the AsyncLocalStorage version restores RPS to within 5% of a baseline with no per-request context; every provider in the app is back to Scope.DEFAULT.

6.8 Composition over inheritance

Concept

Composition means building behaviour by combining objects that each do one thing: an OrderPricer that has a TaxCalculator and a DiscountPolicy. Inheritance means building behaviour by extending a parent class: DiscountedTaxedOrderPricer extends TaxedOrderPricer extends OrderPricer. "Composition over inheritance" says: prefer the first.

Why does it exist?

Inheritance creates the tightest coupling in object-oriented code. A subclass depends on the parent's implementation details, not just its interface: which methods call which, what state is set when, which methods are safe to override. Change the parent and every subclass may break in ways the compiler cannot see (the "fragile base class" problem). Inheritance is also single-axis: you get one parent. Real behaviour varies on several axes at once (tax rules, discount rules, rounding rules), and a class hierarchy explodes combinatorially trying to cover them.

Mental model

Imagine building a meal. Inheritance is a fixed set menu: "Meal A", "Meal A with extra cheese", "Meal A with extra cheese and no onions", each a separate item on the menu. Composition is choosing a base, a protein and toppings independently. Three axes with four options each is 64 meals from 12 ingredients, versus 64 menu items.

NestJS example

Before: a hierarchy of notification senders.

// BEFORE: behaviour variation via inheritance; every combination is a new class
abstract class BaseNotifier {
  async send(userId: string, template: string, data: object) {
    const user = await this.loadUser(userId);
    if (!this.shouldSend(user)) return;
    const body = this.render(template, data);
    await this.deliver(user, body);
    await this.audit(user, template);
  }
  protected abstract deliver(user: User, body: string): Promise<void>;
  protected shouldSend(user: User) { return true; }
  protected render(template: string, data: object) { return renderHandlebars(template, data); }
  // ...
}
class EmailNotifier extends BaseNotifier { protected async deliver(u: User, body: string) { /* SES */ } }
class MarketingEmailNotifier extends EmailNotifier { protected shouldSend(u: User) { return u.marketingOptIn; } }
class ThrottledMarketingEmailNotifier extends MarketingEmailNotifier { protected shouldSend(u: User) { return super.shouldSend(u) && this.underLimit(u); } }
class SmsNotifier extends BaseNotifier { /* ... and now we need ThrottledMarketingSmsNotifier too */ }

After: small collaborators composed in a service.

export interface Channel { deliver(user: User, body: string): Promise<void> }
export interface SendPolicy { allows(user: User, kind: NotificationKind): Promise<boolean> }
export interface Renderer { render(template: string, data: object): string }

@Injectable()
export class Notifier {
  constructor(
    @Inject(CHANNELS) private readonly channels: Map<ChannelName, Channel>,   // email, sms, push
    @Inject(SEND_POLICIES) private readonly policies: SendPolicy[],          // opt-in, throttle, quiet hours
    @Inject(RENDERER) private readonly renderer: Renderer,
    private readonly audit: AuditLog,
  ) {}

  async send(user: User, kind: NotificationKind, channel: ChannelName, template: string, data: object): Promise<void> {
    for (const p of this.policies) if (!(await p.allows(user, kind))) return;
    const body = this.renderer.render(template, data);
    await this.channels.get(channel)!.deliver(user, body);
    await this.audit.record(user.id, kind, channel);
  }
}

// Adding "quiet hours" is a new SendPolicy class and one line in the module. No hierarchy changes.
@Injectable()
export class QuietHoursPolicy implements SendPolicy {
  constructor(private readonly clock: Clock) {}
  async allows(user: User, kind: NotificationKind) {
    if (kind === 'TRANSACTIONAL') return true;
    const hour = this.clock.nowIn(user.timezone).getHours();
    return hour >= 8 && hour < 21;
  }
}

Each policy and channel is independently testable. New combinations cost zero new classes.

Where inheritance is still fine

  • Framework base classes that exist to be extended: PassportStrategy(Strategy), AuthGuard('jwt'), ExceptionFilter implementations, TypeORM entity base classes for id/createdAt/updatedAt columns.
  • Domain error hierarchies: class InsufficientStockError extends DomainError. Shallow (one level), stable, and used for instanceof in filters.
  • DTO inheritance with PartialType, PickType, OmitType from @nestjs/mapped-types or @nestjs/swagger; these are compile-time conveniences, not behaviour hierarchies.

The rule: inherit for is-a relationships that are shallow and stable; compose for behaviour variation.

Where juniors misapply this

They read "composition over inheritance" as "inheritance is banned" and replace a two-level error hierarchy with a tag field and a switch. They also build BaseService<T> / BaseController<T> / BaseRepository<T> hierarchies "to reduce boilerplate" and end up with the exact fragile-base-class problem the principle warns about; every real service overrides half the base.

Interview questions

  1. What is the fragile base class problem? Expected: subclasses depend on parent implementation details; parent changes break subclasses invisibly.
  2. Show how to replace a three-level inheritance chain with composition in NestJS. Expected: extract axes into interfaces; inject implementations; iterate policies.
  3. Where is inheritance appropriate? Expected: framework extension points, shallow error hierarchies, entity base columns.

Practical exercise

Find a Base*Service or Base*Repository in a codebase with at least two subclasses. List the methods each subclass overrides. Replace the hierarchy with composed collaborators.

Acceptance criteria: no extends Base* remains; each behaviour axis is an interface with at least one implementation; tests for each axis run without the others.

6.9 Coupling

Concept

Coupling is the degree to which one module depends on another. High coupling means a change in A forces changes in B. Low coupling means A and B can change independently. Coupling is not binary; it has kinds and directions, and knowing them tells you which dependencies are dangerous.

Why does it exist as a concept?

Because "reduce coupling" is useless advice without knowing what kind. A use case depending on a port is coupling, and it is fine. A service depending on the order in which another service's methods are called is also coupling, and it is a production incident waiting to happen. The vocabulary lets you name the problem.

Mental model

Imagine two dancers. Holding hands lightly (they can each move freely, adjusting) is loose coupling. Being tied together at the ankles (any step by one forces the other) is tight coupling. Being tied together and having to step in a specific order or fall over is temporal coupling.

Kinds of coupling, from best to worst

Kind Meaning NestJS example Verdict
Data coupling Modules share only simple data through parameters inventory.reserve({ orderId, lines }) returning { reservationId } Ideal
Stamp (structure) coupling A whole structure is passed when only part is used Passing the entire OrderEntity to a function that needs orderId Acceptable; watch for hidden dependencies
Control coupling One module passes a flag telling the other what to do sendNotification(user, { asMarketing: true, skipThrottle: true }) Smell; usually two functions in disguise
Temporal coupling Correct behaviour depends on call order or timing repo.beginTx() must be called before repo.save(); a configure() that must run before charge() Dangerous; hard to see, easy to break
Common (global) coupling Modules share global mutable state A module-level let currentTenant set by middleware and read by services Dangerous
Content coupling One module reaches into another's internals OrdersService querying inventory.stock directly; importing another module's infrastructure/ Worst; the modular monolith rules exist to prevent this

Two more from a different axis:

  • Afferent coupling (Ca): how many modules depend on this one (incoming). A shared kernel has high Ca. High Ca means changes here are expensive and dangerous, so the module must be stable.
  • Efferent coupling (Ce): how many modules this one depends on (outgoing). A use case orchestrating five ports has Ce of 5. High Ce means this module changes whenever any dependency changes, so it should be the thing that is allowed to change (application layer, not domain).

Instability I = Ce / (Ca + Ce). Domain code should be stable (I near 0): many things depend on it, it depends on nothing. Adapters and controllers should be unstable (I near 1): they depend on much, nothing depends on them. If your domain has high Ce (it imports TypeORM, NestJS, Stripe), the arrows are backwards.

Temporal coupling in practice

// Temporal coupling: works only if you call the methods in the right order
const report = new ReportBuilder();
report.setDateRange(from, to);   // forget this and generate() throws or returns everything
report.setCurrency('INR');       // forget this and amounts are unformatted
const csv = report.generate();

// Fix: make invalid states unrepresentable; require everything at construction
const csv = new ReportBuilder({ from, to, currency: 'INR' }).generate();

A more expensive example: a TypeORM QueryRunner that must be connect()ed, then startTransaction()ed, then used, then commitTransaction()ed or rollbackTransaction()ed, then release()d. Miss release() on one error path and the pool leaks a connection per error until the app stalls. The Unit of Work pattern (section 6.22) exists to wrap that temporal coupling in a single method that cannot be misused.

Measuring coupling in a NestJS codebase

dependency-cruiser produces the module graph and can report Ca/Ce per folder. A practical weekly check:

npx depcruise src --include-only "^src/modules" --output-type json > deps.json
echo "then count incoming/outgoing edges per module folder; alert when domain/ has outgoing edges to infrastructure/"

Configure a rule that forbids src/modules/*/domain from importing anything outside domain/ and shared-kernel/, and a rule that forbids src/modules/A/** from importing src/modules/B/{application,domain,infrastructure}/**.

Where juniors misapply this

They reduce coupling by adding indirection everywhere (an interface, a factory and a token for each class), which increases the number of dependencies while claiming to reduce coupling. Coupling to a stable, well-designed abstraction is cheap. The goal is to couple to stable things and be decoupled from volatile things, not to minimise a number.

Interview questions

  1. Name three kinds of coupling from best to worst and give a code example of each. Expected: data, control, content (or temporal).
  2. What are afferent and efferent coupling and how should they differ between domain and adapters? Expected: domain high Ca low Ce; adapters low Ca high Ce.
  3. Give a real example of temporal coupling in a NestJS app and how you removed it. Expected: QueryRunner lifecycle wrapped in a unit of work; builder requiring all inputs at construction.

6.10 Cohesion

Concept

Cohesion is how strongly the elements inside one module belong together. High cohesion: everything in modules/inventory is about stock, reservations and allocation. Low cohesion: a utils module with date formatting, a retry helper, a CSV parser and a Stripe webhook verifier.

Coupling is about relationships between modules; cohesion is about relationships within one. You want high cohesion and low coupling, and they reinforce each other: a highly cohesive module has a small, focused public interface, which makes it easy for others to depend on loosely.

Why does it exist?

Low cohesion means a module changes for unrelated reasons, its tests cover unrelated things, and its name stops meaning anything ("common", "shared", "core", "utils", "helpers", "misc"). Those names are a reliable sign of low cohesion. A change to date formatting re-runs the Stripe webhook tests because they share a module.

Mental model

Imagine a toolbox where each drawer holds one kind of tool: screwdrivers together, wrenches together. High cohesion. Now imagine a drawer labelled "stuff" with a screwdriver, a stapler, three batteries and a takeout menu. Every time you need anything you open "stuff" and dig. That drawer is your utils folder.

Levels of cohesion, from worst to best

Level Elements are grouped because... Example Verdict
Coincidental no reason utils.ts Worst
Logical they are the same kind of thing validators/ for every validator in the app Weak
Temporal they run at the same time startup.ts doing DB connect, cache warm, feature flag fetch Weak
Procedural they follow one procedure checkoutSteps.ts with unrelated helpers used by checkout Moderate
Communicational they operate on the same data everything that touches orders rows Good
Sequential output of one is input to the next pricing pipeline: base price then discounts then tax Good
Functional they all contribute to one well-defined task InventoryModule: reserve, release, commit, expire reservations Best

NestJS example

Before: a "shared" module that is really a junk drawer.

src/shared/
  utils/date.ts, money.ts, retry.ts, slugify.ts, csv.ts
  services/email.service.ts, sms.service.ts, stripe-webhook.service.ts, s3.service.ts
  guards/jwt.guard.ts, roles.guard.ts, order-owner.guard.ts
  interceptors/logging.interceptor.ts, cache.interceptor.ts

OrderOwnerGuard belongs to orders; stripe-webhook.service.ts belongs to payments; email/sms belong to notifications. retry.ts and date.ts are genuinely cross-cutting and can live in libs/platform.

After: cohesive modules and a small, honest platform library.

src/modules/orders/presentation/guards/order-owner.guard.ts
src/modules/payments/presentation/webhooks/stripe-webhook.controller.ts
src/modules/notifications/infrastructure/channels/{email,sms}.channel.ts
libs/platform/src/{retry,clock,logging,http-client}/       <- cross-cutting, no business knowledge
libs/shared-kernel/src/{money,ids,domain-error}.ts          <- domain primitives, tiny

The test for whether something belongs in platform: does it know anything about orders, users, payments, or any business concept? If yes, it belongs in a business module.

Cohesion inside a class

The same idea applies to a single class. A class where every method uses every field is cohesive. A class where half the methods use fields A and B and the other half use C and D is two classes wearing one name. OrdersService with createOrder(), cancelOrder() (using the repository and the domain) and exportOrdersCsv(), emailMonthlyReport() (using a CSV writer and a mailer) is two classes: an order use-case group and a reporting job.

Where juniors misapply this

They confuse cohesion with size and split a cohesive 300-line inventory allocation algorithm into 12 files "for cohesion". Size is not the metric; belonging together is. A cohesive module can be large. A 20-line utils.ts is still incoherent.

Interview questions

  1. Define cohesion and its relation to coupling. Expected: within-module belonging vs between-module dependency; high cohesion enables low coupling.
  2. What do folder names like common, shared, utils tell you? Expected: likely coincidental cohesion; audit and redistribute.
  3. How do you decide whether something belongs in a platform library or a business module? Expected: business knowledge test.

Practical exercise

Audit a shared/ or common/ folder in a NestJS project. For each file, classify its cohesion level and decide its correct home (a business module, platform, or shared-kernel). Move at least five files.

Acceptance criteria: the shared/ folder is either gone or contains only files with no business knowledge; dependency-cruiser shows no business module importing another's internals; all tests pass.

6.11 Repository pattern

Concept

A repository is an object that gives domain code the illusion of an in-memory collection of aggregates: findById, save, findPendingOlderThan(date). Behind it sits the database and the ORM. The domain and application layers talk to the repository interface; they never see SQL, TypeORM entities, or a QueryBuilder.

Why does it exist?

The problem is the ORM leaking upward. When a use case holds a TypeORM Repository<OrderEntity>, it gets 40 methods (createQueryBuilder, increment, query, manager), it receives persistence entities with lazy relations and database columns, and its tests need the ORM. Every query written inline in a service is a hidden dependency on the schema. The Repository pattern draws a line: persistence knowledge lives in one place per aggregate, expressed in domain terms.

Mental model

Imagine a library. You ask the librarian for "the books by this author" or "this book by its number". You do not walk into the archive, learn the shelving system, and pull boxes. The librarian (repository) knows the shelving system (schema and ORM); you know books (domain objects).

The anti-pattern: leaking TypeORM into services

// ANTI-PATTERN: the "repository" is TypeORM's, and QueryBuilder is in the service
@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(OrderEntity) private readonly repo: Repository<OrderEntity>) {}

  async listForCustomer(customerId: string, status?: string) {
    const qb = this.repo.createQueryBuilder('o')
      .leftJoinAndSelect('o.lines', 'l')
      .where('o.customer_id = :customerId', { customerId });
    if (status) qb.andWhere('o.status = :status', { status });
    return qb.orderBy('o.created_at', 'DESC').take(50).getMany(); // returns OrderEntity[] with relations
  }
}

Why this hurts: the service knows column names (customer_id), knows the relation name (lines), returns persistence entities to the controller (which serialises whatever is loaded, including things you did not intend), cannot be tested without a database or a deep mock of SelectQueryBuilder, and the same query gets copy-pasted with small variations across the codebase until nobody knows which one is canonical.

How it works

  1. Define a repository interface in application/ports/ (or domain/ in stricter setups), in domain terms, returning domain objects.
  2. Implement it once per storage technology in infrastructure/. The implementation owns mapping between domain objects and persistence entities/models.
  3. Bind with a token in the module.
  4. Keep the interface narrow and intention-revealing: findPendingPaymentOlderThan(cutoff) rather than find(options: FindManyOptions). If the interface accepts ORM query options, it is not a repository; it is the ORM with an extra step.
  5. For complex, composable queries, pair the repository with the Specification pattern (section 6.21) rather than exposing a query builder.

NestJS example: interface with TypeORM and Sequelize implementations

The port:

// src/modules/orders/application/ports/order.repository.ts
import { Order } from '../../domain/order';

export const ORDER_REPOSITORY = Symbol('ORDER_REPOSITORY');

export interface OrderRepository {
  findById(id: string): Promise<Order | null>;
  findForCustomer(customerId: string, opts: { status?: OrderStatus; limit: number }): Promise<Order[]>;
  findPendingPaymentOlderThan(cutoff: Date, limit: number): Promise<Order[]>;
  save(order: Order): Promise<void>;
}

The TypeORM implementation, with an explicit mapper:

// src/modules/orders/infrastructure/typeorm/typeorm-order.repository.ts
@Injectable()
export class TypeormOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(OrderEntity) private readonly repo: Repository<OrderEntity>) {}

  async findById(id: string): Promise<Order | null> {
    const row = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { lines: true } });
    return row ? OrderMapper.toDomain(row) : null;
  }

  async findForCustomer(customerId: string, opts: { status?: OrderStatus; limit: number }): Promise<Order[]> {
    const rows = await this.repo.find({
      where: { customerId, ...(opts.status ? { status: opts.status } : {}) },
      relations: { lines: true },
      order: { createdAt: 'DESC' },
      take: Math.min(opts.limit, 100),
    });
    return rows.map(OrderMapper.toDomain);
  }

  async findPendingPaymentOlderThan(cutoff: Date, limit: number): Promise<Order[]> {
    const rows = await this.repo
      .createQueryBuilder('o')
      .leftJoinAndSelect('o.lines', 'l')
      .where('o.status = :status AND o.created_at < :cutoff', { status: 'CREATED', cutoff })
      .orderBy('o.created_at', 'ASC')
      .take(limit)
      .getMany();
    return rows.map(OrderMapper.toDomain);
  }

  async save(order: Order): Promise<void> {
    await this.repo.save(OrderMapper.toPersistence(order)); // cascade saves lines
  }
}

The Sequelize implementation of the same port:

// src/modules/orders/infrastructure/sequelize/sequelize-order.repository.ts
@Injectable()
export class SequelizeOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
  constructor(@InjectModel(OrderModel) private readonly orders: typeof OrderModel) {}

  async findById(id: string): Promise<Order | null> {
    const row = await this.orders.findByPk(id, { include: [OrderLineModel] });
    return row ? OrderMapper.fromModel(row) : null;
  }

  async findForCustomer(customerId: string, opts: { status?: OrderStatus; limit: number }): Promise<Order[]> {
    const rows = await this.orders.findAll({
      where: { customerId, ...(opts.status ? { status: opts.status } : {}) },
      include: [OrderLineModel],
      order: [['createdAt', 'DESC']],
      limit: Math.min(opts.limit, 100),
    });
    return rows.map(OrderMapper.fromModel);
  }

  async findPendingPaymentOlderThan(cutoff: Date, limit: number): Promise<Order[]> {
    const rows = await this.orders.findAll({
      where: { status: 'CREATED', createdAt: { [Op.lt]: cutoff } },
      include: [OrderLineModel],
      order: [['createdAt', 'ASC']],
      limit,
    });
    return rows.map(OrderMapper.fromModel);
  }

  async save(order: Order): Promise<void> {
    await this.orders.sequelize!.transaction(async (transaction) => {
      await this.orders.upsert(OrderMapper.toModelAttrs(order), { transaction });
      await OrderLineModel.destroy({ where: { orderId: order.id }, transaction });
      await OrderLineModel.bulkCreate(OrderMapper.toLineAttrs(order), { transaction });
    });
  }
}

The use case does not change between the two. The tests for the use case use an InMemoryOrderRepository (a Map<string, Order>), which is a third implementation of the same port and takes 20 lines.

PostgreSQL example

The findPendingPaymentOlderThan query needs an index that matches its shape, and the repository is the one place that knows this:

-- Partial index: only CREATED orders, ordered by created_at, small and hot
CREATE INDEX orders_pending_created_idx ON orders.orders (created_at)
WHERE status = 'CREATED';

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM orders.orders WHERE status = 'CREATED' AND created_at < now() - interval '15 minutes'
ORDER BY created_at ASC LIMIT 100;
--  Limit  (cost=0.29..12.41 rows=100 width=96) (actual time=0.031..0.188 rows=100 loops=1)
--    ->  Index Scan using orders_pending_created_idx on orders  (actual time=0.029..0.171 rows=100 loops=1)
--          Index Cond: (created_at < (now() - '00:15:00'::interval))
--  Buffers: shared hit=7
--  Planning Time: 0.140 ms
--  Execution Time: 0.221 ms

Because the query is encapsulated, the index and the query can be tuned together without touching application code.

When NOT to use it

  • Read-heavy reporting and admin screens. A report that joins six tables and returns 40 columns does not want to be mapped into aggregates. Use a separate query service that returns read DTOs directly from SQL or a QueryBuilder (this is the "Q" in CQRS). Do not force reports through the repository.
  • Thin CRUD modules with no domain model. Repository<AddressEntity> from TypeORM injected into a small service is fine; adding an interface and a mapper for addresses is ceremony.
  • When the "domain object" is the entity anyway and you have consciously chosen that (small service, small team). Then the pattern's cost exceeds its value; just keep the queries in one class.

Common mistakes

  • A generic BaseRepository<T> with find(options) that re-exposes the ORM.
  • Repositories returning persistence entities (no mapping) so the "boundary" is cosmetic.
  • Repositories that contain business logic (save() that also sends an email).
  • One repository per table instead of per aggregate (an OrderLineRepository used by the order use case; lines belong to the order).
  • Methods with boolean flags (findById(id, withLines: boolean)); make two methods or accept the cost of always loading.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a domain repository and TypeORM's Repository<T>? Expected: interface in domain terms returning domain objects vs ORM data-access API returning entities.
  2. Why should a repository be per aggregate rather than per table? Expected: consistency boundary; the aggregate is saved as a whole.
  3. Where do complex reports go? Expected: query services / read side; not the repository.
  4. How do you test a use case that depends on a repository? Expected: in-memory implementation of the port.

Practical exercise

Extract every TypeORM createQueryBuilder and find* call from a service into an interface-based repository with a mapper. Add an in-memory implementation and a Sequelize implementation.

Acceptance criteria: the service has no typeorm import; the same use-case test suite passes against in-memory, TypeORM (Docker PostgreSQL) and Sequelize implementations via describe.each; no method on the interface accepts ORM option types.

6.12 Service pattern: application service vs domain service

Concept

"Service" is the most overloaded word in backend code. Two distinct things hide behind it:

  • An application service (use case) orchestrates one business operation: load aggregates through repositories, call domain behaviour, save, publish events, manage the transaction. It is thin and procedural. It knows about ports. It contains no business rules of its own.
  • A domain service holds business logic that does not naturally belong to one entity because it involves several, or needs a policy that is not state: PricingService.price(order, customer, promotions), StockAllocationService.allocate(reservationRequests, warehouses). It is pure: no I/O, no ports, no framework.

The NestJS-generated OrdersService is usually neither; it is both, plus persistence, plus HTTP concerns. That is the God service anti-pattern (section 6.23).

Why does it exist?

Without the distinction, business rules leak into orchestration code where they are hard to test, and orchestration leaks into domain code where it drags I/O in. Naming the two kinds gives every line of code an obvious home.

Mental model

Imagine a wedding. The wedding planner (application service) calls the caterer, the florist and the venue in the right order, handles payments, and deals with the timeline. The chef (domain service) decides how to cook for 200 people with three dietary constraints; the chef does not call the venue.

NestJS example

// Domain service: pure, no injection needed beyond other pure things
export class ShippingEligibilityService {
