  constructor(private readonly clock: Clock) {}

  canShip(order: Order, stock: StockLevel[], warehouseCutoff: Date): ShipDecision {
    if (order.status !== 'PAID') return ShipDecision.reject('ORDER_NOT_PAID');
    const short = order.lines.filter((l) => (stock.find((s) => s.productId === l.productId)?.available ?? 0) < l.qty);
    if (short.length) return ShipDecision.reject('INSUFFICIENT_STOCK', short.map((l) => l.productId));
    const sameDay = this.clock.now() < warehouseCutoff;
    return ShipDecision.accept(sameDay ? 'SAME_DAY' : 'NEXT_DAY');
  }
}

// Application service (use case): orchestrates I/O around the domain decision
@Injectable()
export class ShipOrderUseCase {
  constructor(
    @Inject(ORDER_REPOSITORY) private readonly orders: OrderRepository,
    private readonly inventory: InventoryFacade,
    private readonly eligibility: ShippingEligibilityService,
    @Inject(EVENT_PUBLISHER) private readonly events: EventPublisher,
    private readonly uow: UnitOfWork,
  ) {}

  async execute(orderId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.uow.run(async () => {
      const order = await this.orders.findById(orderId);
      if (!order) throw new DomainError('ORDER_NOT_FOUND', orderId);
      const stock = await this.inventory.levelsFor(order.lines.map((l) => l.productId));
      const decision = this.eligibility.canShip(order, stock, await this.inventory.todayCutoff());
      if (!decision.ok) throw new DomainError(decision.reason, decision.details?.join(','));
      order.markShipped(decision.speed);
      await this.orders.save(order);
      await this.events.publish(new OrderShippedEvent({ orderId, speed: decision.speed }));
    });
  }
}

ShippingEligibilityService has a full unit test suite with no mocks except a fake clock. ShipOrderUseCase has a few tests that check orchestration (calls save, publishes event, rolls back on failure) with fakes.

Where juniors misapply this

They create a domain service for everything, including logic that belongs on the entity (OrderStatusService.canCancel(order) instead of order.canCancel()). Rule: if the logic needs only one entity's state, it belongs on that entity. Domain services are for logic spanning entities or requiring external policy objects.

They also let application services grow rules: if (order.total > 50000) requireReview = true inside the use case. That is a domain policy; move it.

Interview questions

  1. Distinguish application service, domain service and entity behaviour with one example each. Expected: as above.
  2. Which of the three may perform I/O? Expected: only the application service, through ports.
  3. How do you keep an application service thin? Expected: rules go to entities/domain services; persistence to repositories; side effects to events.

6.13 Factory pattern

Concept

A factory is an object or function whose job is to create other objects, hiding the decision of which concrete class to create and how to construct it. The caller asks for "a payment gateway for UPI" and receives something that satisfies PaymentGateway.

Why does it exist?

Construction logic is a concern. When the choice of implementation depends on runtime data (payment method, tenant, country, feature flag), scattering that if across callers means every caller knows every implementation. Centralising it in a factory keeps callers OCP-compliant and makes the selection rule testable on its own.

Mental model

Imagine a car rental desk. You say "I need something for five people and a mountain road". The desk hands you keys. You did not pick the model, and you did not learn the fleet's inventory system.

How it works

  1. Define the product interface (PaymentGateway).
  2. Implement each concrete product (Stripe, Razorpay, PayPal).
  3. The factory receives the selection input and returns the right product. In NestJS the factory is a provider that has all concrete products injected (so their own dependencies are resolved by the container), and it selects among them.
  4. Callers depend on the factory and the interface, never on concrete products.

NestJS example: payment provider factory

// src/modules/payments/application/ports/payment.gateway.ts
export type PaymentMethod = 'card' | 'upi' | 'paypal' | 'netbanking';
export interface PaymentGateway {
  readonly provider: 'stripe' | 'razorpay' | 'paypal';
  supports(method: PaymentMethod, currency: string): boolean;
  charge(input: ChargeInput): Promise<ChargeResult>;
  refund(paymentId: string, amount: Money, idempotencyKey: string): Promise<void>;
}

// src/modules/payments/application/payment-gateway.factory.ts
@Injectable()
export class PaymentGatewayFactory {
  constructor(
    private readonly stripe: StripeGateway,
    private readonly razorpay: RazorpayGateway,
    private readonly paypal: PaypalGateway,
    private readonly flags: FeatureFlags,
  ) {}

  for(method: PaymentMethod, currency: string): PaymentGateway {
    // Selection rules live here and only here. They are testable without any SDK.
    if (method === 'upi' || method === 'netbanking') return this.razorpay;
    if (method === 'paypal') return this.paypal;
    if (currency === 'INR' && this.flags.isOn('cards-via-razorpay')) return this.razorpay;
    return this.stripe;
  }

  byProvider(provider: PaymentGateway['provider']): PaymentGateway {
    const g = [this.stripe, this.razorpay, this.paypal].find((x) => x.provider === provider);
    if (!g) throw new DomainError('PAYMENT_PROVIDER_UNKNOWN', provider);
    return g; // used by webhook handlers and refunds, which know the original provider
  }
}

// Caller
const gateway = this.gateways.for(cmd.method, order.total.currency);
const result = await gateway.charge({ orderId: order.id, amount: order.total, idempotencyKey: `order:${order.id}` });
await this.orders.recordPayment(order.id, gateway.provider, result.paymentId); // persist provider for later refunds

Storing gateway.provider alongside the payment is essential: a refund six months later must go to the provider that took the money, regardless of what the selection rule says today.

Factory vs useFactory

NestJS's useFactory provider option is a construction-time factory: it runs once at bootstrap to build a provider (an SDK client, a connection). The Factory pattern above is a runtime factory: it selects per call based on data. They complement each other: useFactory builds the Stripe client once; PaymentGatewayFactory.for() picks among gateways per order.

When NOT to use it

  • One implementation exists and none is planned. A factory over one product is noise.
  • The selection is static per deployment (always Stripe in the EU deployment). Use useClass bound by environment in the module instead.
  • The "factory" would just call new with no decision. A constructor is already a factory.

Common mistakes

  • Abstract factory hierarchies (AbstractPaymentGatewayFactory, PaymentGatewayFactoryImpl) for a three-way selection.
  • Factories that also perform the operation ("create and charge"), mixing selection with behaviour.
  • Selection rules duplicated in callers because the factory's API was awkward.
  • Forgetting to persist which product was chosen, so later operations (refund, webhook) cannot find their way back.

Interview questions

  1. Why put provider selection in a factory rather than in the use case? Expected: OCP; single place for rules; testable selection; callers unaware of concrete types.
  2. How does the NestJS container help implement a factory? Expected: inject all concrete products, each with its own resolved dependencies; the factory only selects.
  3. What must you persist when a factory picks a provider at runtime? Expected: the chosen provider id, for refunds and webhooks.

Practical exercise

Implement PaymentGatewayFactory with three gateway classes (two can be fakes) and a feature flag. Write unit tests for every selection rule with no SDKs. Add a refund use case that uses byProvider from the persisted provider id.

Acceptance criteria: selection tests cover each branch and run in under 50 ms; adding a fourth gateway requires no change to any use case; refunds route to the provider recorded at charge time even when the selection rule has changed.

6.14 Strategy pattern

Concept

Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so the algorithm can be chosen at runtime without the caller knowing which one it got. Shipping cost calculation (flat, weight-based, distance-based, free over a threshold), pricing (list, tiered, negotiated), authentication (JWT, API key, OAuth) are all families of strategies.

Strategy and Factory are often used together: the factory picks the strategy; the strategy does the work.

Why does it exist?

Without it, the algorithm choice is a switch inside the calling code, and every new variant edits and re-tests the caller. Strategy moves each variant into its own class with its own tests, and the caller collapses to strategy.calculate(input).

Mental model

Imagine navigation apps offering "fastest", "shortest", "avoid tolls". Same input (origin, destination), same output (a route), different algorithm. You pick one; the map does not care how it computes.

NestJS example: shipping cost strategies

// domain/shipping/shipping-strategy.ts
export interface ShippingContext { weightGrams: number; distanceKm: number; subtotal: Money; isPrime: boolean }
export interface ShippingStrategy {
  readonly code: string;
  applies(ctx: ShippingContext): boolean;
  cost(ctx: ShippingContext): Money;
}

export class FreeOverThresholdStrategy implements ShippingStrategy {
  readonly code = 'FREE_OVER_THRESHOLD';
  constructor(private readonly threshold: Money) {}
  applies(ctx: ShippingContext) { return ctx.subtotal.greaterThanOrEqual(this.threshold); }
  cost() { return Money.zero('INR'); }
}

export class WeightBandStrategy implements ShippingStrategy {
  readonly code = 'WEIGHT_BAND';
  constructor(private readonly bands: { upToGrams: number; priceMinor: number }[]) {}
  applies() { return true; } // default
  cost(ctx: ShippingContext) {
    const band = this.bands.find((b) => ctx.weightGrams <= b.upToGrams) ?? this.bands[this.bands.length - 1];
    return Money.of(band.priceMinor, 'INR');
  }
}

export class PrimeStrategy implements ShippingStrategy {
  readonly code = 'PRIME';
  applies(ctx: ShippingContext) { return ctx.isPrime; }
  cost() { return Money.zero('INR'); }
}

// application: strategies are ordered; the first that applies wins
@Injectable()
export class ShippingCalculator {
  constructor(@Inject(SHIPPING_STRATEGIES) private readonly strategies: ShippingStrategy[]) {}
  quote(ctx: ShippingContext): { code: string; cost: Money } {
    const s = this.strategies.find((x) => x.applies(ctx));
    if (!s) throw new DomainError('NO_SHIPPING_STRATEGY', 'no strategy applies');
    return { code: s.code, cost: s.cost(ctx) };
  }
}

// module: order matters and is explicit
{ provide: SHIPPING_STRATEGIES, useFactory: (cfg: ConfigService) => [
    new PrimeStrategy(),
    new FreeOverThresholdStrategy(Money.of(cfg.get('FREE_SHIP_MINOR', 99_900), 'INR')),
    new WeightBandStrategy([{ upToGrams: 500, priceMinor: 4_900 }, { upToGrams: 2_000, priceMinor: 9_900 }, { upToGrams: 10_000, priceMinor: 19_900 }]),
  ], inject: [ConfigService] },

Pricing strategies follow the same shape: PricingStrategy.price(product, customer) with ListPrice, TieredVolumePrice, ContractPrice implementations, selected by customer type.

Strategy in Passport authentication

@nestjs/passport is the Strategy pattern as a library. Each PassportStrategy subclass is one authentication algorithm; AuthGuard('jwt') or AuthGuard('api-key') picks it by name.

// JWT strategy for users
@Injectable()
export class JwtStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy, 'jwt') {
  constructor(config: ConfigService) {
    super({ jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken(), secretOrKey: config.getOrThrow('JWT_PUBLIC_KEY'), algorithms: ['RS256'] });
  }
  async validate(payload: { sub: string; roles: string[] }) { return { id: payload.sub, roles: payload.roles }; }
}

// API key strategy for partner integrations
@Injectable()
export class ApiKeyStrategy extends PassportStrategy(HeaderAPIKeyStrategy, 'api-key') {
  constructor(private readonly partners: PartnerKeyReader) {
    super({ header: 'x-api-key', prefix: '' }, false);
  }
  async validate(key: string) {
    const partner = await this.partners.findByHashedKey(hashApiKey(key)); // never store raw keys
    if (!partner || partner.revokedAt) throw new UnauthorizedException();
    return { id: partner.id, roles: ['partner'] };
  }
}

// Controllers choose the strategy by name; the handler code is the same
@UseGuards(AuthGuard(['jwt', 'api-key'])) // tries jwt, then api-key
@Get('orders')
list(@Req() req) { return this.listOrders.execute(req.user.id); }

When NOT to use it

  • Two stable variants that will never grow: a well-named if is clearer than two classes and a token.
  • The variants differ in data, not algorithm (different thresholds): use one strategy with configuration.
  • The "strategy" needs to be chosen by the caller every time with full knowledge of implementations; then it is just polymorphism, and a factory is the missing piece.

Common mistakes

  • Strategies with side effects (a shipping strategy that also creates a shipment). Keep them pure.
  • Implicit ordering of an injected array; document and test the order.
  • Strategy interfaces that grow methods only some strategies implement (ISP violation).

Interview questions

  1. Strategy vs Factory: who does what? Expected: factory selects; strategy executes; often combined.
  2. How is Passport an example of Strategy? Expected: named strategies, guard selects by name, same downstream code.
  3. When would you replace a strategy family with configuration? Expected: when variants differ only in parameters.

6.15 Adapter pattern

Concept

An adapter converts the interface of a third-party or legacy component into the interface your code expects. Your domain defines SmsSender { send(to, body): Promise<SmsReceipt> }; the Twilio adapter, the MSG91 adapter and the AWS SNS adapter each translate that call into their SDK's shape and translate the SDK's responses and errors back into yours.

Hexagonal architecture's "adapters" are this pattern applied systematically.

Why does it exist?

Third-party SDKs have their own types, error classes, retry semantics, pagination styles and naming. If those leak into your use cases, switching vendors (or adding a fallback vendor) touches every caller, and every test must mock the vendor SDK. An adapter confines vendor knowledge to one class.

Mental model

Imagine a travel plug adapter. Your laptop charger has one plug shape. The wall in another country has another. The adapter sits between; neither the charger nor the wall changes.

NestJS example: SMS provider adapter

// application/ports/sms.sender.ts  (your shape)
export const SMS_SENDER = Symbol('SMS_SENDER');
export interface SmsReceipt { providerMessageId: string; provider: string; acceptedAt: Date }
export class SmsDeliveryError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly code: 'INVALID_NUMBER' | 'RATE_LIMITED' | 'PROVIDER_DOWN' | 'UNKNOWN', message: string, readonly retryable: boolean) { super(message); }
}
export interface SmsSender {
  send(input: { toE164: string; body: string; idempotencyKey: string }): Promise<SmsReceipt>;
}

// infrastructure/sms/twilio-sms.adapter.ts  (the vendor's shape, translated)
import { Twilio } from 'twilio';

@Injectable()
export class TwilioSmsAdapter implements SmsSender {
  private readonly log = new Logger(TwilioSmsAdapter.name);
  constructor(@Inject(TWILIO_CLIENT) private readonly client: Twilio, private readonly config: ConfigService) {}

  async send(input: { toE164: string; body: string; idempotencyKey: string }): Promise<SmsReceipt> {
    try {
      const msg = await this.client.messages.create({
        to: input.toE164,
        from: this.config.getOrThrow('TWILIO_FROM'),
        body: input.body,
      });
      return { providerMessageId: msg.sid, provider: 'twilio', acceptedAt: new Date() };
    } catch (err: any) {
      // Translate vendor error codes into YOUR error vocabulary, including retryability.
      const code = Number(err?.code);
      if (code === 21211 || code === 21614) throw new SmsDeliveryError('INVALID_NUMBER', err.message, false);
      if (err?.status === 429) throw new SmsDeliveryError('RATE_LIMITED', err.message, true);
      if (err?.status >= 500) throw new SmsDeliveryError('PROVIDER_DOWN', err.message, true);
      this.log.error(`twilio unknown error ${err?.code}: ${err?.message}`);
      throw new SmsDeliveryError('UNKNOWN', err?.message ?? 'unknown', false);
    }
  }
}

A second adapter for MSG91 translates a completely different HTTP API into the same SmsReceipt and SmsDeliveryError. A FailoverSmsSender (itself implementing SmsSender) can wrap two adapters and try the second when the first throws a retryable error. Callers only ever see SmsSender.

The error translation is the part juniors skip and the part that matters most in production: your retry logic must decide "retry or not" from your error type, not from a vendor-specific status buried in an SDK exception.

When NOT to use it

  • A library that already matches your needs well and will not be swapped (a UUID generator, a date library). Wrapping date-fns in a DateAdapter is ceremony.
  • When the "adapter" adds no translation and no error mapping; then it is a pass-through and you have added a file for nothing.

Common mistakes

  • Adapters that leak vendor types in their return values (returning Twilio's MessageInstance).
  • Adapters without error translation, so callers catch vendor exceptions anyway.
  • Putting business rules in the adapter ("don't send marketing SMS at night" belongs in a policy, not in Twilio's adapter).
  • No timeouts on the SDK client; adapters must configure them.

Interview questions

  1. What belongs in an adapter and what does not? Expected: shape and error translation, timeouts, vendor auth; no business rules.
  2. How does an adapter enable failover between two SMS vendors? Expected: both implement the port; a composite implementation tries the second on retryable errors.
  3. Why translate vendor errors? Expected: retry decisions and HTTP mapping should not depend on vendor codes.

6.16 Decorator pattern

Concept

The GoF Decorator pattern wraps an object with another object that has the same interface and adds behaviour before or after delegating: caching, logging, retries, metrics, authorisation. The caller cannot tell the difference. Decorators stack: Metrics(Cache(Retry(TypeormOrderRepository))).

This is not the same thing as TypeScript/NestJS @Decorators. Those are compile-time annotations that attach metadata or modify class definitions (@Injectable(), @Get(), @Column()). The GoF pattern is a runtime composition of objects. They share a name and nothing else.

Why does it exist?

Cross-cutting behaviour (caching a repository's reads) should not be written inside the repository (which is about persistence), and should not be written in every caller. A decorator adds it in one place, transparently, and can be turned on or off by wiring.

Mental model

Imagine gift wrapping. The gift is the same; each layer of wrapping adds something (a box, paper, a ribbon) and can be added or removed without changing the gift.

NestJS example: caching decorator over a repository

// infrastructure/cache/cached-product.reader.ts
import { Cache } from 'cache-manager';

@Injectable()
export class CachedProductReader implements ProductReader {
  constructor(
    private readonly inner: ProductReader,          // the wrapped implementation
    private readonly cache: Cache,                  // from @nestjs/cache-manager (CACHE_MANAGER)
    private readonly ttlMs = 30_000,
  ) {}

  async findById(id: string): Promise<Product | null> {
    const key = `product:${id}`;
    const hit = await this.cache.get<SerializedProduct>(key);
    if (hit) return ProductMapper.deserialize(hit);
    const product = await this.inner.findById(id);           // delegate
    if (product) await this.cache.set(key, ProductMapper.serialize(product), this.ttlMs);
    return product;
  }
}

// products.module.ts: wiring the stack. Callers inject PRODUCT_READER and see only the interface.
providers: [
  TypeormProductRepository,
  {
    provide: PRODUCT_READER,
    useFactory: (repo: TypeormProductRepository, cache: Cache) => new CachedProductReader(repo, cache),
    inject: [TypeormProductRepository, CACHE_MANAGER],
  },
],

A metrics decorator with the same shape:

export class TimedProductReader implements ProductReader {
  constructor(private readonly inner: ProductReader, private readonly histogram: Histogram) {}
  async findById(id: string) {
    const end = this.histogram.startTimer({ op: 'product.findById' });
    try { return await this.inner.findById(id); } finally { end(); }
  }
}
// wiring: new TimedProductReader(new CachedProductReader(repo, cache), histogram)

NestJS interceptors as decorators

NestJS interceptors (@UseInterceptors(CacheInterceptor)) are the framework's built-in decorator mechanism for controller handlers: they wrap the handler with before/after behaviour. Use them for HTTP-level concerns (response caching, timing, response mapping). Use the GoF pattern for provider-level concerns (repository caching, gateway retries), where there is no request pipeline.

When NOT to use it

  • When the behaviour is not truly cross-cutting and belongs inside the class (an order's total calculation is not a decorator).
  • When stacking more than three or four decorators makes the wiring unreadable; consider a middleware pipeline abstraction or, for HTTP, interceptors.
  • Cache decorators over write methods or over methods whose results depend on the caller (per-user data) unless the key includes that context.

Common mistakes

  • Decorator that changes the contract (returns cached stale data where the interface promises fresh reads) without documenting it.
  • Caching a method that returns mutable domain objects and then mutating the cached instance.
  • Confusing @Decorators with the pattern in code review.
  • Forgetting cache invalidation on write paths (see Part 14 — Caching for the strategies).

Interview questions

  1. Explain the difference between NestJS @Decorators and the GoF Decorator pattern. Expected: metadata annotation vs runtime wrapping with same interface.
  2. How would you add caching to a repository without editing it? Expected: decorator implementing the same port, wired via useFactory.
  3. What changes when you stack Retry outside Cache versus inside? Expected: retry-outside retries cache misses' inner calls; retry-inside is retried per inner call; order determines semantics.

6.17 Facade pattern

Concept

A facade is a single, simplified entry point over a set of more complex subsystems. CheckoutFacade.placeOrder(cmd) hides that the operation involves inventory reservation, pricing, payment, order persistence and event publishing across three modules. The caller sees one method.

In the modular monolith (Part 5), each module's public/*.facade.ts is this pattern applied at the module boundary.

Why does it exist?

Callers should not need to know the choreography of five subsystems to do one business thing. Without a facade, that choreography is duplicated in every caller (HTTP controller, GraphQL resolver, admin CLI, Kafka consumer) and drifts. A facade also defines the module's public surface, which is what keeps the rest of the module private.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel concierge. You say "I want dinner and a show tonight". The concierge calls the restaurant, the theatre and the taxi company. You made one request.

NestJS example: checkout facade over inventory, payment, shipping

// src/modules/checkout/public/checkout.facade.ts
@Injectable()
export class CheckoutFacade {
  constructor(
    private readonly placeOrder: PlaceOrderUseCase,
    private readonly quoteShipping: ShippingCalculator,
    private readonly inventory: InventoryFacade,     // another module's facade
    private readonly pricing: PricingFacade,
  ) {}

  // One call for the client; the facade sequences the subsystems and shapes the result.
  async quote(cmd: QuoteCommand): Promise<QuoteResult> {
    const [availability, prices] = await Promise.all([
      this.inventory.availability(cmd.lines.map((l) => l.productId)),
      this.pricing.priceLines(cmd.customerId, cmd.lines),
    ]);
    const unavailable = cmd.lines.filter((l) => (availability.get(l.productId) ?? 0) < l.qty);
    const subtotal = prices.reduce((s, p) => s.add(p.lineTotal), Money.zero('INR'));
    const shipping = this.quoteShipping.quote({ weightGrams: prices.reduce((w, p) => w + p.weightGrams, 0), distanceKm: cmd.distanceKm, subtotal, isPrime: cmd.isPrime });
    return { subtotal, shipping: shipping.cost, shippingCode: shipping.code, unavailable: unavailable.map((l) => l.productId) };
  }

  async place(cmd: PlaceOrderCommand): Promise<{ orderId: string }> {
    return this.placeOrder.execute(cmd);
  }
}

The HTTP controller, the GraphQL resolver and a partner API controller all call CheckoutFacade. None of them knows that pricing and availability are fetched in parallel or which shipping strategy applied.

Facade vs use case

A use case is one operation. A facade is a module's public API, which may expose several use cases and some queries. Small modules often skip the facade and export use cases directly; that is fine as long as the export list stays deliberate. Use a facade when the module has many use cases, when you want one stable type for other modules to depend on, or when extraction to a service is on the horizon (the facade's interface becomes the client's interface).

When NOT to use it

  • A module with one or two use cases; export them directly.
  • As a place to put logic. A facade that contains business rules is a God service with a nicer name.
  • To hide a design problem (a facade over a tangle of circular dependencies does not remove the tangle).

Common mistakes

  • Facades that expose internal types (entities, ORM models) instead of DTOs.
  • Facades that grow to 40 methods (that is a module boundary problem, not a facade problem).
  • Calling one module's use cases directly from another module, bypassing the facade, "just this once".

Interview questions

  1. How does a facade support later extraction into a service? Expected: async DTO-in/DTO-out interface identical to a network client; swap implementation via DI.
  2. What should never appear in a facade's signature? Expected: entities, ORM types, EntityManager.
  3. Facade vs use case? Expected: module API vs single operation.

Practical exercise (patterns 6.14 to 6.17 together)

Build a notifications module with: an SmsSender port with two adapters (one real or realistic, one fake) and a FailoverSmsSender decorator; a SendPolicy strategy list (opt-in, quiet hours, throttle); and a NotificationsFacade exposing notify(userId, kind, payload). Consume it from an @OnEvent('order.paid') handler.

Acceptance criteria: the facade is the module's only export; the quiet-hours strategy is unit-tested with a fake clock; failover is tested by making the first adapter throw a retryable SmsDeliveryError; no vendor type appears outside infrastructure/.

6.18 Observer pattern

Concept

Observer lets one object (the subject) notify many others (observers) when something happens, without knowing who they are. In backend code this appears as domain events: an order emits OrderPaid; inventory, notifications and analytics each have a handler; the order code does not import any of them.

Inside one NestJS process, @nestjs/event-emitter (built on the eventemitter2 library) is the standard implementation. Across processes, the same idea becomes a message broker (Part 5.6).

Why does it exist?

It exists to decouple the cause from its effects. Every new reaction to "order paid" (a loyalty points award, a fraud check, a warehouse pick list) becomes a new handler instead of a new line in the checkout use case. It also lets side effects be turned on and off, tested in isolation, and moved out of the request path.

Mental model

Imagine a doorbell wired to several chimes: kitchen, garage, upstairs. Pressing the bell rings all of them. Add a chime in the garden by connecting it; the bell button does not change.

How it works with @nestjs/event-emitter

  1. EventEmitterModule.forRoot() in AppModule registers a singleton EventEmitter2.
  2. Providers with methods decorated @OnEvent('order.paid') are discovered at bootstrap and subscribed.
  3. emitter.emit('order.paid', payload) calls every listener synchronously, in registration order, on the emitter's call stack. emitAsync awaits async listeners and returns their results as an array.
  4. Options on @OnEvent: { async: true } runs the listener via setImmediate, detached from the emitter's flow; { promisify: true } makes emitAsync await it; wildcard patterns (order.*) require wildcard: true in forRoot.
// app.module.ts
EventEmitterModule.forRoot({ wildcard: true, maxListeners: 20, verboseMemoryLeak: true })

// contracts/events/order-paid.event.ts
export class OrderPaidEvent {
  static readonly name = 'order.paid';
  constructor(readonly payload: { id: string; orderId: string; paymentId: string; amountMinor: number; occurredAt: string }) {}
}

// modules/loyalty/application/on-order-paid.handler.ts
@Injectable()
export class AwardPointsOnOrderPaid {
  private readonly log = new Logger(AwardPointsOnOrderPaid.name);
  constructor(private readonly award: AwardPointsUseCase) {}

  @OnEvent(OrderPaidEvent.name, { async: true, promisify: true })
  async handle(event: OrderPaidEvent): Promise<void> {
    try {
      await this.award.execute({ orderId: event.payload.orderId, amountMinor: event.payload.amountMinor, eventId: event.payload.id });
    } catch (err) {
      // Listeners must never throw into the emitter; log with context and rely on reconciliation.
      this.log.error(`award points failed for order ${event.payload.orderId}: ${(err as Error).message}`);
    }
  }
}

Node EventEmitter pitfalls

@nestjs/event-emitter inherits the semantics of Node's EventEmitter, and those semantics surprise people in production.

  1. Listeners run synchronously by default. emit() calls each listener on the current stack. A listener that does 200 ms of work adds 200 ms to the emitting request. A listener that throws synchronously throws inside emit(), into the emitter's code path, potentially after the emitter's database transaction has already committed. Use { async: true } for anything with I/O.

  2. Unhandled errors in async listeners vanish. An async listener that rejects produces an unhandled promise rejection: nothing in the emitter's flow sees it. In Node 15+, an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default (--unhandled-rejections=throw). Every listener needs a try/catch that logs and, ideally, records a failure for reconciliation.

  3. error event semantics. On a plain Node EventEmitter, emitting 'error' with no listener throws. Do not name a domain event error.

  4. Memory leaks from listeners added per request. Code that calls emitter.on(...) inside a request handler adds a listener every request and never removes it. Node warns at 11 listeners (MaxListenersExceededWarning); with verboseMemoryLeak: true the warning includes the event name. Listeners belong on singleton providers registered once at boot, which @OnEvent guarantees.

  5. Ordering and partial failure. With four listeners, if the second throws (sync) the third and fourth never run. With async listeners, all run but there is no transaction across them. An in-process event is a best-effort fan-out.

  6. No durability. If the process dies after emit(), listeners that had not finished are gone. If you need durability, write an outbox row (Part 5.6) and let a relay publish to a broker; treat in-process events as a notification mechanism for recoverable work.

  7. Emitting inside a transaction. If the use case emits before COMMIT, a listener may read the database and not see the change, or the transaction may roll back after the listener already acted. Emit after commit, or collect events on the aggregate and dispatch them from the unit of work after commit (section 6.22).

Practical example

An order use case emits after its transaction commits:

@Injectable()
export class MarkOrderPaidUseCase {
  constructor(private readonly uow: UnitOfWork, @Inject(ORDER_REPOSITORY) private readonly orders: OrderRepository, private readonly emitter: EventEmitter2) {}

  async execute(orderId: string, paymentId: string): Promise<void> {
    const event = await this.uow.run(async () => {
      const order = await this.orders.findById(orderId);
      if (!order) throw new DomainError('ORDER_NOT_FOUND', orderId);
      if (order.status === 'PAID') return null; // idempotent
      order.markPaid(paymentId);
      await this.orders.save(order);
      return new OrderPaidEvent({ id: randomUUID(), orderId, paymentId, amountMinor: order.total.minor, occurredAt: new Date().toISOString() });
    });
    if (event) await this.emitter.emitAsync(OrderPaidEvent.name, event); // AFTER commit
  }
}

Failure scenario

A team adds a @OnEvent('order.paid') listener without async: true that calls the loyalty provider's HTTP API. The provider's p99 climbs to 4 seconds during an incident. Now checkout's p99 is 4 seconds too, because the listener runs on the checkout request's stack. Then the provider starts returning 500s; the listener throws synchronously inside emit(), which is called after the commit, so checkout returns 500 to the customer after charging the card and saving the order. Support handles 300 tickets of "I was charged but got an error". Two flags (async: true and a try/catch) would have prevented all of it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Listener throws synchronously and aborts remaining listeners.
  • Async listener rejects with no catch; process crash on unhandled rejection.
  • Listeners registered per request leak memory.
  • Emit before commit; listener sees stale data or acts on rolled-back state.
  • Lost events on process crash; use the outbox for anything that must happen.
  • A listener that re-emits the same event type (loops); include causation ids.
  • Test suites that forget EventEmitterModule and silently have zero listeners.

When NOT to use it

  • When the "observer" must succeed for the operation to be correct (reserve stock before confirming). That is a command with a return value, not an event.
  • When ordering across handlers matters. Observers are independent by design.
  • Across processes. Use a broker.

Common mistakes

  • Using events to avoid a direct call that should be direct (the caller needs the result).
  • Listeners with business-critical side effects and no reconciliation.
  • Naming events as commands (SendEmailEvent).
  • Emitting from inside repositories or entities directly (they should record events; the use case or unit of work dispatches them).

Interview questions

  1. What happens if a synchronous @OnEvent listener throws? Expected: it throws inside emit(), in the emitter's flow, and skips later listeners.
  2. How do you keep listeners from slowing the request? Expected: async: true; move I/O-heavy reactions to a queue or broker.
  3. Why emit after commit? Expected: listeners may read uncommitted data or act on a rolled-back change.
  4. When is EventEmitter2 the wrong tool? Expected: durability, cross-process, ordering guarantees, required outcomes.
  5. How does a listener leak memory? Expected: on() in request scope; MaxListenersExceededWarning.

Practical exercise

Add three @OnEvent('order.paid') listeners (loyalty, email, analytics) to a checkout flow. Make the email listener slow (2 s) and the analytics listener throw. Observe checkout latency and error behaviour. Then fix with async: true, try/catch with structured logging, and an outbox row for loyalty points (which must not be lost).

Acceptance criteria: checkout p99 is unaffected by the slow listener; the throwing listener never surfaces as a checkout error; killing the process mid-event does not lose loyalty points (the outbox relay replays them).

6.19 Command pattern

Concept

A command is an object that represents a request to do something: PlaceOrderCommand { orderId, customerId, lines }. A command handler executes it. Separating "the request" from "the execution" lets you validate, log, queue, retry, authorise and audit commands uniformly, and it makes each business operation a named, first-class thing.

In NestJS, @nestjs/cqrs provides CommandBus, @CommandHandler, QueryBus, @QueryHandler, EventBus and sagas. Commands mutate; queries read; the two are handled by different classes (CQRS: Command Query Responsibility Segregation).

Why does it exist?

Without it, an operation is a method call whose intent is scattered across parameters. With it, the operation is data: it can be serialised into a queue, replayed, inspected in logs, and given an idempotency key. Handlers become small, focused classes with one execute method, which lines up naturally with use cases.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant order ticket. The waiter writes the order (the command) on a ticket and puts it on the rail. The kitchen (handler) takes tickets in order. The ticket can be checked, prioritised, or voided without talking to the waiter. Compare with the waiter shouting the order at the chef and hoping.

How it works with @nestjs/cqrs

  1. CqrsModule in the module's imports registers the buses.
  2. A command is a plain class (often readonly fields). A handler class decorated @CommandHandler(PlaceOrderCommand) implements ICommandHandler<PlaceOrderCommand, Result>.
  3. commandBus.execute(new PlaceOrderCommand(...)) finds the handler by the command's class and calls execute. Exactly one handler per command; two is a boot error.
  4. Handlers can publish events on EventBus; @EventsHandler classes react; sagas (@Saga) turn event streams into new commands with RxJS.
// application/commands/place-order.command.ts
export class PlaceOrderCommand {
  constructor(
    readonly orderId: string,            // client-generated or idempotency-derived
    readonly customerId: string,
    readonly lines: { productId: string; qty: number }[],
    readonly idempotencyKey: string,
  ) {}
}

// application/commands/place-order.handler.ts
@CommandHandler(PlaceOrderCommand)
export class PlaceOrderHandler implements ICommandHandler<PlaceOrderCommand, { orderId: string }> {
  constructor(
    @Inject(ORDER_REPOSITORY) private readonly orders: OrderRepository,
    private readonly inventory: InventoryFacade,
    private readonly idempotency: IdempotencyStore,
    private readonly eventBus: EventBus,
  ) {}

  async execute(cmd: PlaceOrderCommand): Promise<{ orderId: string }> {
    // Idempotent command: same key returns the stored result without redoing side effects.
    const previous = await this.idempotency.find<{ orderId: string }>(cmd.idempotencyKey);
    if (previous) return previous;

    const reservation = await this.inventory.reserve({ orderId: cmd.orderId, lines: cmd.lines });
    const order = Order.create(cmd.orderId, cmd.customerId, toLines(cmd.lines), new Date());
    await this.orders.save(order);
    const result = { orderId: order.id };
    await this.idempotency.store(cmd.idempotencyKey, result, { ttlSeconds: 24 * 3600 });
    this.eventBus.publish(new OrderPlacedEvent(order.id, reservation.reservationId));
    return result;
  }
}

// presentation/orders.controller.ts
@Post()
async create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto, @Headers('idempotency-key') key: string) {
  if (!key) throw new BadRequestException('Idempotency-Key header required');
  return this.commandBus.execute(new PlaceOrderCommand(deriveOrderId(key), dto.customerId, dto.lines, key));
}

Idempotent commands

Commands arrive more than once: client retries after a timeout, load balancer retries, a queue redelivers. An idempotent command produces the same effect and the same result no matter how many times it is executed. Techniques:

  • Idempotency key store. Persist (key) -> result in PostgreSQL or Redis with a TTL. Check before executing; store after. Race: two concurrent requests with the same key both miss the check. Fix with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on the key before doing work, and have the loser wait or return 409.
  • Natural idempotency. Use the command's identity as the aggregate's identity (orderId derived from the key) so a second insert conflicts on the primary key.
  • Conditional updates. UPDATE orders SET status='PAID' WHERE id=$1 AND status='CREATED'; zero rows affected means already done.
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  key          text PRIMARY KEY,
  scope        text NOT NULL,             -- e.g. 'place-order'
  result       jsonb,
  status       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'IN_PROGRESS',
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- Claim the key first; the second concurrent request gets 0 rows and must wait or 409.
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (key, scope) VALUES ($1, 'place-order') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

Commands vs use cases vs events

Thing Shape Handlers Can fail? Direction
Command Imperative object (PlaceOrder) Exactly one Yes, returns a result or error Caller to handler
Use case Class with execute() It is the handler Yes Same as command handler
Event Past-tense fact (OrderPlaced) Zero or many No; it happened Handler to the world
Query Read request (GetOrderById) Exactly one Yes Caller to read side

A use case without @nestjs/cqrs and a command handler with it are the same idea. The bus adds: uniform middleware (logging, validation, authorisation across all commands), decoupling of the caller from the handler class, and a place to plug in a queue later. It costs indirection and a bus that hides the call graph from IDE navigation.

When NOT to use it

  • Small modules where useCase.execute() is already clear; the bus adds nothing.
  • When you need the handler's type for compile-time safety; commandBus.execute is loosely typed unless you wrap it.
  • As a substitute for a message queue. CommandBus is in-process and synchronous; it is not durable or distributed.
  • Full CQRS with separate read models and eventual consistency for a CRUD app. The "S" in CQRS is a big architectural step; the command pattern alone is not.

Common mistakes

  • Commands that carry entities or ORM models instead of plain data.
  • Handlers that call other handlers through the bus in chains, building an invisible call graph.
  • Non-idempotent handlers behind retrying callers.
  • Sagas that issue commands without correlation ids, so failures cannot be traced.
  • Using EventBus from @nestjs/cqrs as a durable event system (it has the same in-memory semantics as EventEmitter2).

Interview questions

  1. What does the command pattern give you over a direct method call? Expected: request as data; uniform middleware; queueability; audit; idempotency handling in one place.
  2. How do you make a command idempotent under concurrent duplicate requests? Expected: claim the key with an insert-on-conflict before work; conditional updates; aggregate id derived from the key.
  3. Command vs event: differences in handlers, failure and naming. Expected: one vs many; can fail vs cannot; imperative vs past tense.
  4. What does CQRS add beyond the command pattern, and when is it justified? Expected: separate read models; justified by very different read and write shapes or scale; not for CRUD.

Practical exercise

Implement PlaceOrderCommand with @nestjs/cqrs, an IdempotencyStore backed by PostgreSQL using INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING to claim keys, and a controller requiring an Idempotency-Key header. Fire 50 concurrent identical requests.

Acceptance criteria: exactly one order row and one inventory reservation exist; 49 requests return the same orderId (or 409 while in progress, then the same result on retry); the handler's unit tests cover "key already stored" and "key claimed by another in-flight request".

6.20 State pattern

Concept

The State pattern models an object whose behaviour depends on which state it is in, with an explicit list of states and an explicit list of legal transitions between them. An order is CREATED, then PAID, then SHIPPED, then DELIVERED; or it is CANCELLED from some of those states but not others. "Can this order be cancelled?" is answered by the state machine, not by a chain of if statements scattered across services.

Why does it exist?

Without it, status is a string column that anything can set to anything. order.status = 'SHIPPED' runs from a controller, a Kafka consumer and an admin script, each with its own idea of what is allowed. Eventually an order goes from DELIVERED back to CREATED because a retry replayed an old message, and a customer is charged twice. The State pattern centralises the rules: one table of legal transitions, one method to apply them, one error when they are violated.

Mental model

Imagine a traffic light. It has exactly three states and exactly three legal transitions: green to yellow, yellow to red, red to green. It never goes red to yellow. The wiring enforces this; no driver, no operator and no bug can make it happen. Your order's status column deserves the same wiring.

How it works

  1. Enumerate the states. Keep the list small and business-meaningful.
  2. Enumerate the legal transitions as a table: from state, event or action, to state.
  3. Implement a transition() method on the aggregate that consults the table, throws a typed error for an illegal transition, and records what happened.
  4. Persist the transition history (who, when, why) in addition to the current state; it is the audit trail and the debugging tool.
  5. Protect against concurrent transitions with optimistic locking (a version column) or a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status = :expected.
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> CREATED
  CREATED --> PAID: pay
  CREATED --> CANCELLED: cancel
  PAID --> SHIPPED: ship
  PAID --> CANCELLED: cancel with refund
  SHIPPED --> DELIVERED: deliver
  SHIPPED --> RETURN_REQUESTED: request return
  DELIVERED --> RETURN_REQUESTED: request return
  RETURN_REQUESTED --> REFUNDED: refund
  DELIVERED --> [*]
  CANCELLED --> [*]
  REFUNDED --> [*]

The legal transitions table

From Action To Guard Side effects
CREATED pay PAID payment captured OrderPaid event; commit stock reservation
CREATED cancel CANCELLED none release reservation
CREATED expire CANCELLED older than 15 minutes, unpaid release reservation
PAID ship SHIPPED stock committed; shipment created OrderShipped event
PAID cancel CANCELLED refund succeeded release stock; OrderCancelled event
SHIPPED deliver DELIVERED carrier confirmation OrderDelivered event
SHIPPED requestReturn RETURN_REQUESTED within return window create return ticket
DELIVERED requestReturn RETURN_REQUESTED within 14 days of delivery create return ticket
RETURN_REQUESTED refund REFUNDED goods received OrderRefunded event
any other combination any (illegal) throw IllegalTransitionError

Note what is not in the table: SHIPPED to CANCELLED. Once goods leave the warehouse, cancellation becomes a return. Encoding that rule here means no code path can cancel a shipped order by accident.

TypeScript implementation

// domain/order-status.ts
export type OrderStatus = 'CREATED' | 'PAID' | 'SHIPPED' | 'DELIVERED' | 'CANCELLED' | 'RETURN_REQUESTED' | 'REFUNDED';
export type OrderAction = 'pay' | 'cancel' | 'expire' | 'ship' | 'deliver' | 'requestReturn' | 'refund';

// The single source of truth for legal transitions.
const TRANSITIONS: Record<OrderStatus, Partial<Record<OrderAction, OrderStatus>>> = {
  CREATED: { pay: 'PAID', cancel: 'CANCELLED', expire: 'CANCELLED' },
  PAID: { ship: 'SHIPPED', cancel: 'CANCELLED' },
  SHIPPED: { deliver: 'DELIVERED', requestReturn: 'RETURN_REQUESTED' },
  DELIVERED: { requestReturn: 'RETURN_REQUESTED' },
  RETURN_REQUESTED: { refund: 'REFUNDED' },
  CANCELLED: {},
  REFUNDED: {},
};

export class IllegalTransitionError extends DomainError {
  constructor(readonly from: OrderStatus, readonly action: OrderAction) {
    super('ORDER_ILLEGAL_TRANSITION', `cannot ${action} an order in ${from}`);
  }
}

export function nextStatus(from: OrderStatus, action: OrderAction): OrderStatus {
  const to = TRANSITIONS[from][action];
  if (!to) throw new IllegalTransitionError(from, action);
  return to;
}

export function canTransition(from: OrderStatus, action: OrderAction): boolean {
  return TRANSITIONS[from][action] !== undefined;
}

The aggregate uses the table and records each transition as history plus a domain event:

// domain/order.ts (excerpt)
export interface OrderTransition { from: OrderStatus; to: OrderStatus; action: OrderAction; at: Date; actor: string; reason?: string }

export class Order {
  private _status: OrderStatus;
  private readonly _transitions: OrderTransition[] = [];
  private readonly _events: DomainEvent[] = [];
  readonly version: number; // for optimistic locking; copied from persistence

  get status() { return this._status; }
  get pendingEvents(): readonly DomainEvent[] { return this._events; }
  get transitions(): readonly OrderTransition[] { return this._transitions; }

  private apply(action: OrderAction, actor: string, now: Date, reason?: string): void {
    const from = this._status;
    const to = nextStatus(from, action); // throws IllegalTransitionError
    this._status = to;
    this._transitions.push({ from, to, action, at: now, actor, reason });
  }

  pay(paymentId: string, actor: string, now: Date): void {
    this.apply('pay', actor, now);
    this._paymentId = paymentId;
    this._events.push(new OrderPaidEvent({ orderId: this.id, paymentId, amountMinor: this.total.minor, occurredAt: now.toISOString() }));
  }

  cancel(actor: string, now: Date, reason: string): void {
    // Guards beyond the table live here: a PAID order needs a refund before it is CANCELLED.
    const wasPaid = this._status === 'PAID';
    this.apply('cancel', actor, now, reason);
    this._events.push(new OrderCancelledEvent({ orderId: this.id, refundRequired: wasPaid, reason, occurredAt: now.toISOString() }));
  }

  ship(shipmentId: string, actor: string, now: Date): void {
    this.apply('ship', actor, now);
    this._shipmentId = shipmentId;
    this._events.push(new OrderShippedEvent({ orderId: this.id, shipmentId, occurredAt: now.toISOString() }));
  }

  requestReturn(actor: string, now: Date, deliveredAt: Date | null): void {
    if (this._status === 'DELIVERED' && deliveredAt && now.getTime() - deliveredAt.getTime() > 14 * 86_400_000) {
      throw new DomainError('RETURN_WINDOW_CLOSED', 'returns accepted within 14 days of delivery');
    }
    this.apply('requestReturn', actor, now);
  }
}

Unit tests for the state machine need no database and are exhaustive: iterate every state and every action, assert that exactly the table's entries succeed.

describe('order transitions', () => {
  const states: OrderStatus[] = ['CREATED', 'PAID', 'SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED', 'CANCELLED', 'RETURN_REQUESTED', 'REFUNDED'];
  const actions: OrderAction[] = ['pay', 'cancel', 'expire', 'ship', 'deliver', 'requestReturn', 'refund'];
  it.each(states.flatMap((s) => actions.map((a) => [s, a] as const)))('%s + %s', (from, action) => {
    if (canTransition(from, action)) expect(() => nextStatus(from, action)).not.toThrow();
    else expect(() => nextStatus(from, action)).toThrow(IllegalTransitionError);
  });
});

PostgreSQL example: persisting state and transitions

CREATE TABLE orders.orders (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  status       text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('CREATED','PAID','SHIPPED','DELIVERED','CANCELLED','RETURN_REQUESTED','REFUNDED')),
  version      integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  payment_id   text,
  shipment_id  text,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Append-only history; the audit trail and the debugging tool
CREATE TABLE orders.order_transitions (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES orders.orders(id),
  from_status  text NOT NULL,
  to_status    text NOT NULL,
  action       text NOT NULL,
  actor        text NOT NULL,             -- user id, 'system:expiry-job', 'webhook:stripe'
  reason       text,
  occurred_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX order_transitions_order_idx ON orders.order_transitions (order_id, occurred_at);

-- Optimistic concurrency: only apply if nobody else moved the order since we loaded it
UPDATE orders.orders
SET status = 'PAID', payment_id = $2, version = version + 1, updated_at = now()
WHERE id = $1 AND version = $3;
-- rowCount 0 means a concurrent transition happened: reload and re-evaluate, or reject.

With TypeORM, @VersionColumn() on the entity makes repository.save() add WHERE version = :expected automatically and throw OptimisticLockVersionMismatchError on conflict. With Sequelize, version: true on the model does the same and throws OptimisticLockError. The repository catches these and re-throws a domain ConcurrentModificationError, which the HTTP layer maps to 409 Conflict.

Production scenario

An order service processes 300 transitions per second. Payment webhooks (pay), carrier webhooks (deliver), an expiry cron (expire) and customer actions (cancel, requestReturn) all arrive concurrently and out of order. The state table rejects the ones that no longer apply: a delayed expire for an order that was paid 200 ms earlier hits CREATED -> expire on an order that is now PAID and throws IllegalTransitionError, which the cron logs at info level and moves on. A replayed Stripe webhook for an already PAID order is recognised the same way. Illegal-transition counts are a dashboard metric; a sudden spike means a producer is replaying or a clock is wrong.

Failure scenario

Before the state machine existed, the carrier webhook handler wrote UPDATE orders SET status = 'DELIVERED' WHERE id = $1 with no guard. A carrier bug replayed 40,000 old delivery webhooks over one night. Orders that had been returned and refunded went back to DELIVERED. The refund reconciliation job, which selects REFUNDED orders, no longer saw them, and finance closed the month with 40,000 refunds unaccounted for. The fix was a transition table plus WHERE status = 'SHIPPED' in the update; the cleanup was three days of manual reconciliation.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Concurrent transitions on the same order: two admins cancel at once; a webhook and a cron race. Optimistic locking or conditional updates are mandatory.
  • Out-of-order events: deliver arrives before ship because two carrier integrations report independently. Decide explicitly: reject (and let the retry succeed later) or allow a skip transition with an audit entry.
  • Idempotent replays: applying pay to an already PAID order should be a no-op for the same payment id and an error for a different one.
  • State explosion: sub-states (PAID_AWAITING_STOCK, PAID_PARTIALLY_SHIPPED) multiply transitions. Consider a second, smaller machine for fulfilment rather than one giant table.
  • Time-based transitions (expiry) require a job that is itself idempotent and uses the machine, never raw updates.
  • Migration of existing rows to a new state set; add the state, migrate data, then remove the old state, never rename in place.

When NOT to use it

  • A boolean lifecycle (active/inactive) does not need a machine; a well-named method does.
  • Read-only status projections (a dashboard colour) do not transition anything.
  • When the workflow is genuinely user-defined at runtime (a configurable approval flow); then you want a workflow engine or a data-driven machine, not a hard-coded table.

Common mistakes

  • status as a free string with no CHECK constraint and no central transition function.
  • Transition rules duplicated in a controller if, a service if and a database trigger, each slightly different.
  • No transition history, so "how did this order end up here?" is unanswerable.
  • Emitting the domain event before the transition is persisted.
  • Guards that need I/O (refund succeeded) placed inside the pure domain method; put them in the use case, and let the domain method assume the guard has passed.

Interview questions

  1. How do you prevent an order from being cancelled after shipping? Expected: a transition table that has no SHIPPED to CANCELLED entry; a domain method that throws; a conditional update or version check for concurrency.
  2. Why store transition history in addition to current status? Expected: audit, debugging, reconciliation, analytics (time in state).
  3. How do you handle a replayed webhook that tries an already-applied transition? Expected: distinguish same-payment replay (no-op) from a genuine illegal transition (error); count both.
  4. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking for state transitions: when each? Expected: optimistic for low contention (most orders); SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for hot rows or when a read-then-write must be serialised.
  5. How do you unit-test a state machine exhaustively? Expected: cross product of states and actions against the table.

Practical exercise

Implement the order state machine above with @VersionColumn() in TypeORM. Write a Kafka consumer for carrier events and a cron for expiry, both going through the aggregate. Replay 10,000 old carrier events during a load test.

Acceptance criteria: no order ever leaves REFUNDED or CANCELLED; the exhaustive transition test passes; concurrent cancel and pay on the same order result in exactly one winner and one 409; order_transitions shows a complete, ordered history for every order.

6.21 Specification pattern

Concept

A specification is an object that encapsulates a business rule as a predicate: "is this product eligible for free shipping?", "does this order match the fraud review criteria?", "which products satisfy this customer's filter?". Specifications compose with and, or, not, so complex rules are built from small named ones. The same specification can be evaluated in memory against a domain object and translated into a database query.

Why does it exist?

Filtering logic tends to end up in two places at once: an if chain in a service for in-memory checks, and a hand-built WHERE clause in a repository for queries. They drift. Specifications give the rule one name and one definition, and they let query construction stay composable without exposing the ORM's QueryBuilder to callers (which the Repository pattern forbids).

Mental model

Imagine a job posting's requirements: "5+ years experience AND (TypeScript OR Go) AND NOT currently employed by a competitor". Each requirement is a small rule. The posting is a combination. A recruiter can check one candidate against it by hand (in-memory) or ask the database for everyone who matches (query). The requirements list is the specification.

How it works

  1. Define Specification<T> with isSatisfiedBy(candidate: T): boolean for in-memory evaluation.
  2. Give each specification a second capability: contributing its condition to a query. In TypeORM that is a method that adds a WHERE fragment to a SelectQueryBuilder; in Sequelize it returns a WhereOptions fragment.
  3. Provide and, or, not combinators that compose both capabilities.
  4. The repository accepts a specification: products.findMatching(spec, page). Callers compose rules; the repository translates them.

NestJS example: composable product filters

// domain/specifications/specification.ts
import { SelectQueryBuilder } from 'typeorm';

export interface Specification<T, Q = SelectQueryBuilder<any>> {
  isSatisfiedBy(candidate: T): boolean;
  applyTo(qb: Q, alias: string): Q; // query-side translation
  and(other: Specification<T, Q>): Specification<T, Q>;
  or(other: Specification<T, Q>): Specification<T, Q>;
  not(): Specification<T, Q>;
}

export abstract class CompositeSpecification<T> implements Specification<T> {
  abstract isSatisfiedBy(candidate: T): boolean;
  abstract applyTo(qb: SelectQueryBuilder<any>, alias: string): SelectQueryBuilder<any>;
  and(other: Specification<T>) { return new AndSpecification(this, other); }
  or(other: Specification<T>) { return new OrSpecification(this, other); }
  not() { return new NotSpecification(this); }
}

// Parameter names must be unique per specification instance to avoid collisions when composing.
let paramSeq = 0;
const param = (name: string) => `${name}_${++paramSeq}`;

class AndSpecification<T> extends CompositeSpecification<T> {
  constructor(private readonly a: Specification<T>, private readonly b: Specification<T>) { super(); }
  isSatisfiedBy(c: T) { return this.a.isSatisfiedBy(c) && this.b.isSatisfiedBy(c); }
  applyTo(qb: SelectQueryBuilder<any>, alias: string) {
    return qb.andWhere(new Brackets((w) => { this.a.applyTo(w as any, alias); this.b.applyTo(w as any, alias); }));
  }
}

class OrSpecification<T> extends CompositeSpecification<T> {
  constructor(private readonly a: Specification<T>, private readonly b: Specification<T>) { super(); }
  isSatisfiedBy(c: T) { return this.a.isSatisfiedBy(c) || this.b.isSatisfiedBy(c); }
  applyTo(qb: SelectQueryBuilder<any>, alias: string) {
    return qb.andWhere(new Brackets((w) => {
      w.where(new Brackets((x) => this.a.applyTo(x as any, alias)));
      w.orWhere(new Brackets((y) => this.b.applyTo(y as any, alias)));
    }));
  }
}

class NotSpecification<T> extends CompositeSpecification<T> {
  constructor(private readonly inner: Specification<T>) { super(); }
  isSatisfiedBy(c: T) { return !this.inner.isSatisfiedBy(c); }
  applyTo(qb: SelectQueryBuilder<any>, alias: string) {
    return qb.andWhere(new NotBrackets((w) => this.inner.applyTo(w as any, alias)));
  }
}

Concrete product specifications:

// domain/specifications/product.specs.ts
export class InCategory extends CompositeSpecification<Product> {
  constructor(private readonly categoryId: string) { super(); }
  isSatisfiedBy(p: Product) { return p.categoryId === this.categoryId; }
  applyTo(qb: SelectQueryBuilder<any>, alias: string) {
    const k = param('category');
    return qb.andWhere(`${alias}.category_id = :${k}`, { [k]: this.categoryId });
  }
}

export class PriceBetween extends CompositeSpecification<Product> {
  constructor(private readonly minMinor: number, private readonly maxMinor: number) { super(); }
  isSatisfiedBy(p: Product) { return p.price.minor >= this.minMinor && p.price.minor <= this.maxMinor; }
  applyTo(qb: SelectQueryBuilder<any>, alias: string) {
    const lo = param('pmin'), hi = param('pmax');
    return qb.andWhere(`${alias}.price_minor BETWEEN :${lo} AND :${hi}`, { [lo]: this.minMinor, [hi]: this.maxMinor });
  }
}

export class InStock extends CompositeSpecification<Product> {
  isSatisfiedBy(p: Product) { return p.available > 0; }
  applyTo(qb: SelectQueryBuilder<any>, alias: string) { return qb.andWhere(`${alias}.available > 0`); }
}

export class HasAnyTag extends CompositeSpecification<Product> {
  constructor(private readonly tags: string[]) { super(); }
  isSatisfiedBy(p: Product) { return p.tags.some((t) => this.tags.includes(t)); }
  applyTo(qb: SelectQueryBuilder<any>, alias: string) {
    const k = param('tags');
    return qb.andWhere(`${alias}.tags && :${k}::text[]`, { [k]: this.tags }); // PostgreSQL array overlap
  }
}

Composition in a use case, and translation in the repository:

// application/search-products.use-case.ts
const spec = new InCategory(q.categoryId)
  .and(new PriceBetween(q.minMinor ?? 0, q.maxMinor ?? Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER))
  .and(q.inStockOnly ? new InStock() : new InStock().or(new HasAnyTag(['preorder'])));
const page = await this.products.findMatching(spec, { limit: 24, cursor: q.cursor });

// infrastructure/typeorm/typeorm-product.repository.ts
async findMatching(spec: Specification<Product>, page: { limit: number; cursor?: string }): Promise<Product[]> {
  let qb = this.repo.createQueryBuilder('p').orderBy('p.id', 'ASC').take(Math.min(page.limit, 100));
  qb = spec.applyTo(qb, 'p');
  if (page.cursor) qb = qb.andWhere('p.id > :cursor', { cursor: page.cursor });
  const rows = await qb.getMany();
  return rows.map(ProductMapper.toDomain);
}

The same specification is used to validate a single product in memory (for example, "does this product still satisfy the promotion's rules at checkout time?"), so the promotion rule and the promotion listing can never disagree.

Sequelize variant

With Sequelize, applyTo returns a WhereOptions fragment and the combinators use Op.and, Op.or, Op.not:

export class PriceBetweenSeq implements SeqSpecification<Product> {
  constructor(private readonly minMinor: number, private readonly maxMinor: number) {}
  isSatisfiedBy(p: Product) { return p.price.minor >= this.minMinor && p.price.minor <= this.maxMinor; }
  toWhere(): WhereOptions { return { priceMinor: { [Op.between]: [this.minMinor, this.maxMinor] } }; }
}
// and: { [Op.and]: [a.toWhere(), b.toWhere()] }   or: { [Op.or]: [...] }   not: { [Op.not]: inner.toWhere() }

PostgreSQL example

The specification's SQL is only as fast as the indexes behind it. A category-plus-price filter with cursor pagination wants a composite index:

CREATE INDEX products_category_price_id_idx ON catalog.products (category_id, price_minor, id);
CREATE INDEX products_tags_gin_idx ON catalog.products USING gin (tags);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM catalog.products p
WHERE p.category_id = 'c1' AND p.price_minor BETWEEN 50000 AND 200000 AND p.available > 0 AND p.id > 'p_00001234'
ORDER BY p.id LIMIT 24;
-- Index Scan using products_category_price_id_idx on products p (actual time=0.041..0.412 rows=24 loops=1)
--   Index Cond: ((category_id = 'c1') AND (price_minor >= 50000) AND (price_minor <= 200000))
--   Filter: ((available > 0) AND (id > 'p_00001234'))
--   Rows Removed by Filter: 61
-- Buffers: shared hit=19
-- Execution Time: 0.451 ms

Because specifications compose freely, watch for combinations that produce un-indexable predicates (OR across different columns often forces a sequential scan). The repository is the place to log slow specification shapes and add indexes.

When NOT to use it

  • A fixed set of two or three query shapes. Named repository methods (findActiveInCategory) are simpler and easier to index deliberately.
  • Reports and analytics. Write SQL.
  • When the query side and the in-memory side would never both be used; then you only need a query object, not a specification.
  • When callers would need to build arbitrary specifications from HTTP input (a generic filter API). That leads to unbounded query shapes and SQL cost you cannot predict; whitelist the composable rules instead.

Common mistakes

  • Parameter name collisions when the same specification class is used twice in one query (fixed above with unique parameter names).
  • Specifications that hit the database inside isSatisfiedBy; they must be pure.
  • Exposing SelectQueryBuilder to callers "because specifications already use it"; the builder stays inside the repository and the specifications.
  • Building specifications from raw request bodies without validation.

Interview questions

  1. What problem does Specification solve that a repository method does not? Expected: composable rules with one definition for both in-memory and query evaluation.
  2. How do you keep composed specifications from breaking the query? Expected: bracketed sub-conditions, unique parameter names, tests per combinator.
  3. When is Specification over-engineering? Expected: few fixed queries; reports; no in-memory reuse.
  4. What is the performance risk of composable predicates? Expected: un-indexable combinations; monitor slow shapes; whitelist compositions.

Practical exercise

Implement InCategory, PriceBetween, InStock and HasAnyTag with and/or/not, a findMatching repository method with cursor pagination, and an in-memory check used at checkout to confirm a promotion still applies.

Acceptance criteria: a property-based test asserts that for random products and random specification trees, isSatisfiedBy agrees with the database query result; EXPLAIN for the three most common compositions shows index scans; no controller can construct a specification the whitelist does not allow.

6.22 Unit of Work

Concept

A Unit of Work (UoW) defines a transaction boundary around a business operation: everything inside either commits together or rolls back together, even when it spans several repositories and aggregates. It also collects domain events raised during the operation and dispatches them only after a successful commit.

In TypeORM, the mechanism is a QueryRunner or a transactional EntityManager; in Sequelize, a Transaction object. The pattern's job is to make sure every repository call inside the operation uses the same transaction without every method signature carrying a manager parameter.

Why does it exist?

A use case that saves an order, decrements stock and writes an outbox row through three repositories must not end with two of the three done. Without a UoW, each repository.save() is its own transaction; a crash between them leaves the system inconsistent. Passing an EntityManager into every repository method works but couples the application layer to TypeORM and turns every signature into save(order, manager). The UoW hides the transaction while guaranteeing it.

Mental model

Imagine a shopping trolley at a supermarket. You pick up items from many aisles (repositories). Nothing is bought until you pay at the till (commit). If your card is declined, everything goes back (rollback). Nobody in the aisles needs to know about the till.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
  participant UC as PlaceOrderUseCase
  participant UoW as UnitOfWork
  participant CLS as AsyncLocalStorage
  participant OR as OrderRepository
  participant IR as StockRepository
  participant OB as OutboxRepository
  participant PG as PostgreSQL
  participant EM as EventEmitter
  UC->>UoW: run(work)
  UoW->>PG: BEGIN
  UoW->>CLS: store EntityManager for this async context
  UoW->>UC: invoke work()
  UC->>OR: save(order)
  OR->>CLS: get EntityManager
  OR->>PG: INSERT INTO orders ...
  UC->>IR: decrement(productId, qty)
  IR->>CLS: get EntityManager
  IR->>PG: UPDATE stock ... WHERE available >= qty
  UC->>OB: append(OrderPaid)
  OB->>PG: INSERT INTO outbox ...
  UC-->>UoW: work() resolves
  UoW->>PG: COMMIT
  UoW->>EM: dispatch collected domain events
  UoW-->>UC: result
  1. The use case calls uow.run(async () => { ... }).
  2. The UoW acquires a QueryRunner, starts a transaction, and stores the transactional EntityManager in AsyncLocalStorage (CLS: continuation-local storage) for the current async context.
  3. Repositories, when they need a manager, ask a small helper for "the current manager", which returns the transactional one if a UoW is active or the default one if not.
  4. When the callback resolves, the UoW commits, releases the runner, and dispatches any domain events collected from aggregates during the operation.
  5. If the callback throws, the UoW rolls back, releases the runner, discards the collected events, and re-throws.
  6. Nested run() calls join the outer transaction (or create a savepoint) rather than opening a second one.

TypeORM implementation with AsyncLocalStorage

// libs/platform/src/persistence/transaction-context.ts
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
import { EntityManager } from 'typeorm';

export interface TxContext { manager: EntityManager; events: DomainEvent[] }
export const txStorage = new AsyncLocalStorage<TxContext>();

// libs/platform/src/persistence/typeorm-unit-of-work.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { EventEmitter2 } from '@nestjs/event-emitter';

@Injectable()
export class TypeormUnitOfWork implements UnitOfWork {
  private readonly log = new Logger(TypeormUnitOfWork.name);
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource, private readonly emitter: EventEmitter2) {}

  async run<T>(work: () => Promise<T>, opts: { isolation?: 'READ COMMITTED' | 'REPEATABLE READ' | 'SERIALIZABLE' } = {}): Promise<T> {
    const existing = txStorage.getStore();
    if (existing) return work(); // nested call joins the outer transaction

    const runner = this.dataSource.createQueryRunner();
    await runner.connect();
    await runner.startTransaction(opts.isolation ?? 'READ COMMITTED');
    const ctx: TxContext = { manager: runner.manager, events: [] };
    try {
      const result = await txStorage.run(ctx, work); // everything awaited inside sees ctx
      await runner.commitTransaction();
      await this.dispatch(ctx.events); // after commit, never before
      return result;
    } catch (err) {
      await runner.rollbackTransaction().catch((e) => this.log.error(`rollback failed: ${e.message}`));
      throw err;
    } finally {
      await runner.release(); // ALWAYS: leaking runners exhausts the pool
    }
  }

  collect(events: readonly DomainEvent[]): void {
    const ctx = txStorage.getStore();
    if (ctx) ctx.events.push(...events);
    else void this.dispatch([...events]); // outside a UoW: dispatch immediately
  }

  private async dispatch(events: DomainEvent[]): Promise<void> {
    for (const e of events) {
      try { await this.emitter.emitAsync(e.name, e); }
      catch (err) { this.log.error(`listener failed for ${e.name}: ${(err as Error).message}`); }
    }
  }
}

Repositories resolve the manager from context:

// libs/platform/src/persistence/current-manager.ts
@Injectable()
export class CurrentManager {
  constructor(private readonly dataSource: DataSource) {}
  get(): EntityManager { return txStorage.getStore()?.manager ?? this.dataSource.manager; }
}

// modules/orders/infrastructure/typeorm/typeorm-order.repository.ts
@Injectable()
export class TypeormOrderRepository implements OrderRepository {
  constructor(private readonly current: CurrentManager, private readonly uow: TypeormUnitOfWork) {}

  async save(order: Order): Promise<void> {
    const repo = this.current.get().getRepository(OrderEntity); // transactional if inside run()
    await repo.save(OrderMapper.toPersistence(order));
    this.uow.collect(order.pendingEvents); // dispatched after commit
    order.clearEvents();
  }

  async findById(id: string): Promise<Order | null> {
    const row = await this.current.get().getRepository(OrderEntity).findOne({ where: { id }, relations: { lines: true } });
    return row ? OrderMapper.toDomain(row) : null;
  }
}

The use case is now free of transaction plumbing:

async execute(cmd: PlaceOrderCommand): Promise<{ orderId: string }> {
  return this.uow.run(async () => {
    const order = Order.create(cmd.orderId, cmd.customerId, toLines(cmd.lines), this.clock.now());
    const ok = await this.stock.decrementIfAvailable(cmd.lines); // same transaction
    if (!ok) throw new DomainError('INSUFFICIENT_STOCK', 'one or more lines unavailable');
    order.pay(cmd.paymentId, cmd.actor, this.clock.now());
    await this.orders.save(order);                                // same transaction; events collected
    await this.outbox.append(order.pendingEvents);                // same transaction; durable publish
    return { orderId: order.id };
  }, { isolation: 'READ COMMITTED' });
}

The nestjs-cls package with its TypeORM transactional plugin (@nestjs-cls/transactional) implements exactly this shape and is the production-grade option; the hand-written version above shows what it does underneath.

Sequelize implementation

Sequelize has CLS support built in: Sequelize.useCLS(namespace) (with cls-hooked) makes every query inside sequelize.transaction(async (t) => ...) automatically use t without passing { transaction: t }. The modern equivalent with AsyncLocalStorage is the same idea:

// libs/platform/src/persistence/sequelize-unit-of-work.ts
import { Sequelize, Transaction } from 'sequelize';

export const seqTx = new AsyncLocalStorage<{ transaction: Transaction; events: DomainEvent[] }>();

@Injectable()
export class SequelizeUnitOfWork implements UnitOfWork {
  constructor(private readonly sequelize: Sequelize, private readonly emitter: EventEmitter2) {}

  async run<T>(work: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    if (seqTx.getStore()) return work();
    let events: DomainEvent[] = [];
    // sequelize.transaction with a callback commits on resolve and rolls back on throw
    const result = await this.sequelize.transaction({ isolationLevel: Transaction.ISOLATION_LEVELS.READ_COMMITTED }, async (transaction) => {
      const ctx = { transaction, events: [] as DomainEvent[] };
      const r = await seqTx.run(ctx, work);
      events = ctx.events;
      return r;
    });
    for (const e of events) await this.emitter.emitAsync(e.name, e).catch(() => undefined);
    return result;
  }
}

// Repository: pass the current transaction explicitly (or rely on useCLS)
async save(order: Order) {
  const transaction = seqTx.getStore()?.transaction;
  await OrderModel.upsert(OrderMapper.toModelAttrs(order), { transaction });
}

Pessimistic row locks inside the unit of work use lock: Transaction.LOCK.UPDATE on findOne/findAll (Sequelize) or setLock('pessimistic_write') (TypeORM) and must happen within the same transaction, which the UoW guarantees.

PostgreSQL example

What the database sees for one run():

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
UPDATE inventory.stock SET available = available - 2 WHERE product_id = 'p1' AND available >= 2;  -- rowCount must be 1
INSERT INTO orders.orders (id, customer_id, status, version, ...) VALUES (...);
INSERT INTO orders.order_lines (...) VALUES (...), (...);
INSERT INTO orders.order_transitions (...) VALUES (...);
INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_id, topic, payload) VALUES (...);
COMMIT;

Everything or nothing. The stock decrement's WHERE available >= 2 is the atomic guard; if rowCount is 0 the use case throws, and the whole transaction rolls back including any earlier inserts.

Transaction duration matters: the UoW holds a connection and row locks for its whole duration. Keep network calls (payment provider, email) outside run() or the pool drains under load. The pattern in section 6.19 (charge first with an idempotency key, then run a short transaction to record it) is the usual shape.

Production scenario

A checkout endpoint at 400 RPS with a pool of 20 connections per pod. Each UoW holds a connection for 6 to 12 ms (four statements, local PostgreSQL). Pool utilisation sits around 40%. A developer moves the Stripe call inside run() to "keep it atomic". Stripe p50 is 180 ms, p99 is 1.5 s. Connections are now held 200 ms to 1.5 s each; the pool saturates at about 100 RPS; requests queue for connections; p99 climbs to 9 s and the pods fail health checks. Reverting the change fixes it in one deploy. Rule: no external I/O inside a unit of work.

Failure scenario

An early version of the UoW forgot runner.release() on the rollback path. Every failed checkout (about 2% of traffic, mostly insufficient stock) leaked one connection. After 1,000 failed checkouts across the fleet, every pod's pool was exhausted. Checkout returned 503 for everyone while pg_stat_activity showed hundreds of idle in transaction sessions holding row locks on popular products. The fix was the finally block; the detection was an alert on idle in transaction sessions older than 30 seconds, which has been on the standard dashboard ever since.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Leaked query runners on error paths; always finally { release() }.
  • Long transactions holding locks and connections; keep I/O out.
