  • Nested run(): join the outer transaction; be explicit about whether an inner failure should roll back everything (usually yes) or use a savepoint (SAVEPOINT/ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT, supported by TypeORM's nested transaction() and Sequelize's nested transactions).
  • Context loss: AsyncLocalStorage context does not survive some callback-style APIs or EventEmitter listeners registered outside the context; verify with a test that a repository called from inside run() sees the transactional manager.
  • Events dispatched before commit (a listener reading uncommitted data); the UoW must dispatch after COMMIT.
  • Events lost after commit if the process dies before dispatch; for critical reactions, write to the outbox inside the transaction as well.
  • Deadlocks when two UoWs lock rows in different orders; always lock in a consistent order (sort product ids) and let PostgreSQL's deadlock detector abort one; retry the whole run() on 40P01.
  • Serialization failures under REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE (40001); retry the whole unit with backoff.
  • Read replicas: reads inside a UoW go to the primary (the transactional manager); do not route them elsewhere or you will read stale data inside your own transaction.

When NOT to use it

  • Single-statement operations; the statement is already atomic.
  • Read-only queries; a transaction adds nothing (except when you need a consistent snapshot across several reads, where REPEATABLE READ inside a UoW is exactly right).
  • Operations that span services; there is no cross-service transaction. Use a saga (Part 5.3).
  • Batch jobs processing millions of rows; one giant transaction bloats the WAL and holds locks for hours. Chunk into many small units.

Common mistakes

  • Passing EntityManager through every method signature instead of using context.
  • Opening the transaction in a controller or interceptor that does not know the business boundary.
  • Catching errors inside run() and swallowing them, so the transaction commits partial work.
  • External HTTP calls inside the transaction.
  • Forgetting that repository.save() outside run() still works (auto-commit), which hides missing boundaries; add a lint or a test that critical use cases call uow.run.

Interview questions

  1. What is a Unit of Work and what two guarantees does it provide? Expected: atomic commit/rollback across repositories; post-commit event dispatch.
  2. How do repositories find the current transaction without a manager parameter? Expected: AsyncLocalStorage/CLS holding the transactional manager; fallback to the default manager.
  3. Why must external calls stay outside the unit of work? Expected: connection and lock hold time; pool exhaustion under load.
  4. What happens on a nested run()? Expected: join outer transaction or savepoint; explain the choice.
  5. How do you detect leaked transactions in production? Expected: idle in transaction sessions, pool wait time, pg_stat_activity age.
  6. How do TypeORM and Sequelize differ in transaction propagation? Expected: TypeORM QueryRunner/EntityManager plus CLS; Sequelize transaction object, useCLS, or explicit { transaction }.

Practical exercise

Implement TypeormUnitOfWork with AsyncLocalStorage, wire OrderRepository, StockRepository and OutboxRepository through CurrentManager, and make PlaceOrderUseCase use uow.run. Write an integration test against Docker PostgreSQL that throws after the order insert and before the stock update.

Acceptance criteria: after the failing test, both orders and stock are unchanged and no outbox row exists; pg_stat_activity shows zero idle in transaction sessions after 1,000 failed runs; a listener on order.paid observes the committed order (a findById from the listener returns it); moving a fake 500 ms HTTP call inside run() makes a pool-saturation test fail, and moving it out makes it pass.

6.23 Anti-patterns in NestJS code

Every principle and pattern in this part has an evil twin: the shortcut that looks reasonable in a pull request and costs a week six months later. This section names the ones that show up most often in NestJS codebases, with how to recognise each, why it hurts, and the fix. Treat it as a code-review checklist.

The God service

What it looks like. OrdersService with 1,800 lines, 25 constructor dependencies, and methods for creating orders, charging cards, sending emails, generating invoices, exporting CSV and syncing with the warehouse. Every feature touches it; every PR conflicts in it.

Why it hurts. It violates SRP by definition; its tests need 25 mocks; it cannot be split across teams; a bug in the CSV export deploys with the checkout code; its dependency list makes it the most-coupled thing in the system (highest efferent coupling), so it changes whenever anything changes.

Fix. Split by business operation into use cases (PlaceOrderUseCase, CancelOrderUseCase) and by concern into domain services, repositories and adapters. Move reactions to events. A service should fit on two screens.

The fat controller

What it looks like.

// ANTI-PATTERN
@Post()
async create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto, @Req() req) {
  const product = await this.productRepo.findOneBy({ id: dto.productId });
  if (!product) throw new NotFoundException();
  if (product.stock < dto.qty) throw new ConflictException('out of stock');
  product.stock -= dto.qty;
  await this.productRepo.save(product);
  const order = await this.orderRepo.save({ userId: req.user.id, ...dto, status: 'CREATED' });
  await this.stripe.paymentIntents.create({ amount: order.total, currency: 'inr' });
  return order;
}

Why it hurts. The business rule is trapped behind HTTP: a Kafka consumer or a cron job cannot reuse it; the test needs an HTTP context; there is no transaction; the controller returns a persistence entity. Controllers should translate protocol into a use-case call and translate the result back; nothing else.

Fix. One line of delegation: return OrderResponse.from(await this.placeOrder.execute(toCommand(dto, req.user.id))).

Business logic in controllers, guards, pipes and interceptors

A close cousin. "Just a small check" in a guard (if (order.total > 50000 && !user.isVip) return false) is a business rule hidden in the HTTP layer where the domain tests never see it. Guards decide who may call; pipes validate shape; interceptors handle cross-cutting HTTP concerns. Business decisions belong in the domain and application layers.

Entities as DTOs

What it looks like. @Entity() class User with @Column() passwordHash used as the request body type, the response type and the domain model. @Post() create(@Body() user: User) and return this.repo.find().

Why it hurts. Mass assignment: a client posts { "email": "...", "role": "admin" } and the entity happily accepts it. Data leaks: the response includes passwordHash, mfaSecret, and every eager relation. Schema coupling: renaming a column changes the public API. Validation confusion: class-validator decorators on an entity apply to database rows too.

Fix. Separate CreateUserDto (validated, whitelisted with ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true })), User domain object, UserEntity persistence, and UserResponse. Yes, four classes. The alternative is a security incident.

Service locator via ModuleRef everywhere

What it looks like. constructor(private readonly moduleRef: ModuleRef) and then this.moduleRef.get(PaymentsService, { strict: false }) inside methods.

Why it hurts. Dependencies become invisible: the constructor says "I need ModuleRef", which means "I might need anything". Tests cannot see what to fake. Boot-time DI errors become runtime errors. Circular dependencies are hidden rather than fixed. strict: false bypasses module encapsulation entirely, so the modular monolith's walls disappear.

Fix. Constructor injection with explicit tokens. ModuleRef has legitimate uses (resolving request-scoped providers in a default-scoped context, dynamic plugin lookup by name in a registry), all rare and all at the composition edge, never inside business code.

Request-scoped everything

What it looks like. @Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST }) on services and repositories "so we can access the current user".

Why it hurts. Scope bubbles: every dependent provider becomes request-scoped; the container constructs the whole subtree per request; throughput drops 10 to 30% and p99 rises; some framework features (lifecycle hooks, @Cron, Kafka consumers) do not have a request to scope to and break in confusing ways.

Fix. AsyncLocalStorage (or nestjs-cls) for per-request context; keep providers default-scoped.

Static helpers instead of providers

What it looks like. export class DateUtils { static now() { return new Date(); } }, export const sendSlack = (msg) => axios.post(...), PriceUtils.calculate(order) with hidden reads from process.env.

Why it hurts. Static functions with side effects or hidden dependencies cannot be replaced in tests (you end up mocking modules with jest.mock, which is brittle and global). They read config from the environment at call time, so behaviour depends on where and when they run. They are invisible to the DI graph, so the dependency is real but undeclared.

Fix. Pure functions with no side effects and no hidden inputs can stay static (Money.add, slugify). Anything touching time, network, config, randomness or the database becomes a provider with an interface (Clock, SlackNotifier, PricingService).

Catching and swallowing errors

What it looks like.

// ANTI-PATTERN
try {
  await this.payments.charge(order);
} catch (e) {
  console.log('payment failed', e);
  // continues; order is saved as PAID anyway
}

Why it hurts. The system lies about its state. The order says PAID; the customer was not charged (or was charged and the exception was a timeout, so you do not know). Logs go to console.log without a request id. The next engineer cannot tell whether the catch was deliberate.

Fix. Catch only what you can handle, and handle it explicitly: translate (adapter turns vendor errors into domain errors), compensate (release the reservation), or record and retry (outbox, DLQ). Let everything else propagate to the exception filter, which maps it to a response and a structured log with the correlation id. Never catch {} with an empty body; never log-and-continue on a write path.

More anti-patterns worth naming

Anti-pattern Signal Fix
Anaemic domain Entities with only fields and getters; all rules in services Move behaviour onto aggregates; domain services for multi-entity rules
Leaky repository findAll(options: FindManyOptions), getQueryBuilder() on the interface Intention-revealing methods; specifications
Global modules everywhere @Global() on business modules Explicit imports and exports
Barrel-file cycles index.ts re-exporting everything; forwardRef sprouting Import from concrete files; events instead of back-edges
Transactions in interceptors @Transactional() on every controller method Unit of Work at the use-case boundary
Boolean parameters send(user, true, false) Separate methods or an options object with named fields
Config read at call time process.env.X inside services ConfigService injected; validated at boot with a schema
Missing timeouts axios.get(url) with defaults Explicit timeout on every outbound call; deadline propagation
Fire-and-forget promises this.email.send(...) without await in a request handler Await, or hand off to a queue with persistence
Logic in database triggers Business rules in BEFORE UPDATE triggers nobody remembers Rules in the domain; triggers only for invariants and auditing
Copy-pasted validation The same @IsEmail() rules in five DTOs with slight drift Shared validator classes or composed DTOs with PickType/IntersectionType

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They know that every anti-pattern above was written by someone reasonable under time pressure, so they do not rely on willpower. They add lint rules (no-restricted-imports for typeorm in domain/, a rule against ModuleRef outside platform/), CI checks (dependency-cruiser for boundaries, ValidationPipe whitelist on by default in main.ts), and review templates ("Does the controller contain an if on business data? Does any method return an entity?"). They also keep a written list of these anti-patterns in the repository so code review comments can link to the rule rather than re-arguing it.

Interview questions

  1. A controller method is 80 lines. What do you look for and what do you do? Expected: business logic, repository calls, vendor SDK calls, entities returned; delegate to a use case; response DTOs.
  2. Why is ModuleRef.get in business code a problem? Expected: hidden dependencies, runtime DI errors, broken encapsulation.
  3. What is wrong with catching an error and logging it in a payment flow? Expected: state lies; unknown outcome; must translate, compensate or retry explicitly.
  4. How does using entities as DTOs lead to a security incident? Expected: mass assignment and data leaks.

libs/shared-kernel/

The smallest folder in the repository and the most carefully guarded. It holds domain primitives that every module needs and that almost never change: Money (integer minor units plus currency, with add, subtract, multiply, percent, comparison), branded id types, the base DomainError with a stable code, the DomainEvent base shape (id, name, occurredAt, causationId), a Result type if the team prefers results over exceptions, and the Clock port. It imports nothing from any module and nothing from any framework. Every addition is reviewed as if it were a public API change, because it is one: everything depends on it, so its afferent coupling is the highest in the codebase.

libs/contracts/

The published surface of each module: event schemas (versioned in the file name and the payload), the DTOs facades accept and return, and nothing else. No logic, no classes with behaviour, no ORM types. When a module is extracted into a service, this folder becomes the shared package both sides depend on, so it must already look like one: additive changes only, deprecation before removal. Consumers of an event import its type from here, never from the producing module's internals.

libs/platform/

Cross-cutting infrastructure with no business knowledge: config loading and validation (a schema checked at boot so a missing variable fails fast), the logger and correlation-id middleware, the HTTP client factory with default timeouts and deadline propagation, the TypeORM root module and the Unit of Work, the outbox relay, the Kafka module and idempotent-consumer helper, tracing and metrics setup, and the health controller for @nestjs/terminus. The test for whether a file belongs here is whether it knows the words "order", "payment" or "customer"; if it does, it belongs in a module. Platform code is owned by whoever owns the platform (often the same team in a small company), and every module depends on it, so it changes rarely and carefully.

apps/

Entry points. api/main.ts boots AppModule with HTTP; worker/main.ts boots WorkerModule with Kafka consumers and cron jobs and no HTTP listener beyond health. Both import the same modules from src/modules; the difference is which presentation adapters are wired. A third entry point (lambda.ts for serverless, cli.ts for operational scripts using nest-commander) follows the same shape. Keeping entry points separate from modules is what allows the same code to run in different deployment shapes without forks.

src/modules/<name>/

One folder per bounded context. Each has its own NestJS module file, its own PostgreSQL schema and migrations folder, and the four inner folders below. A module may import shared-kernel, contracts, platform, and other modules' public/ facades; nothing else. dependency-cruiser enforces this.

public/

The module's facade: the single exported provider other modules may inject. Its methods take and return contract DTOs, are all async, and never expose entities, domain objects or EntityManager. It is deliberately shaped like a network client so that extraction to a service means replacing this one class with an HTTP or gRPC implementation of the same interface.

application/

The use cases (one class, one execute), the ports they depend on (ports/, interfaces plus injection tokens, owned here because this is the consumer), commands and queries if @nestjs/cqrs is used, event handlers that react to other modules' events by invoking use cases, and read-side query services that return DTOs directly (allowed to use the ORM's query builder because they are read-only projections, not domain operations). This layer orchestrates: load, call domain, save, publish. It contains no business rules of its own and no framework imports beyond @Inject/@Injectable. Transactions begin and end here, through the Unit of Work.

domain/

The reason the module exists. Aggregates and entities with behaviour (Order.pay(), Order.cancel()), value objects, the state machine and its transition table, domain events the aggregates record, domain services for multi-entity rules, specifications, and the module's typed errors. No imports from @nestjs/*, typeorm, sequelize, stripe, kafkajs or any I/O library; only shared-kernel and itself. Tests here are pure unit tests that run in milliseconds and cover every rule exhaustively. If this folder is empty or contains only interfaces, the module is CRUD and probably does not need the full layout; use layered structure with response DTOs instead.

infrastructure/

Outbound adapters that implement the ports: the TypeORM (or Sequelize) entities, mappers between persistence and domain, the repository implementation, an in-memory repository for fast tests, the payment provider adapter, the Kafka publisher. This is the only place that knows column names, vendor SDK types and error codes. Each adapter translates errors into domain errors and configures timeouts. Integration tests here run against real infrastructure in Docker and are the slowest tests in the module, so they are few and focused on mapping and query correctness.

presentation/

Inbound adapters: HTTP controllers with their request DTOs (validated with class-validator), response DTOs, module-specific guards; Kafka consumers that translate messages into use-case calls with idempotency; cron jobs that invoke use cases on a schedule. Each adapter is thin: authenticate, validate, translate, call, translate back. Domain errors are converted to protocol responses by the platform's exception filter, not here. If a controller method contains an if about business data, it belongs one layer down.

__tests__/ and test/

Module tests live beside the module, split by layer so their speed profiles are obvious: domain/ (pure, milliseconds), application/ (use cases with in-memory adapters, milliseconds), infrastructure/ (integration, seconds). Repository-wide test/e2e boots the API against Docker services for a handful of golden-path scenarios, and test/contract holds the shared contract suites run against every implementation of a port (describe.each over adapters) and the consumer-driven contract tests for events.

How to adopt this without stalling

Do not convert a whole codebase to this layout in one PR. Start with the DTO boundary in every module (that is the security-critical part and the cheap part). Then, when a module gains its first real rule, create its domain/ and move the rule there with a test. Then add ports and an in-memory adapter when the use-case tests get slow. Layered CRUD modules can stay layered indefinitely; the layout above is for modules that earn it.

Senior Checklist — Part 06

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can identify a concrete SOLID violation in a real NestJS service for each of the five letters and refactor it, and I can say where each principle is commonly over-applied
  • I can explain DRY as "one representation of knowledge" and recognise the wrong abstraction (flag-parameter helpers) when I see it
  • I can describe how the NestJS DI container resolves a provider, what useClass/useValue/useFactory/useExisting do, and why request scope bubbling costs throughput
  • I can replace request-scoped providers with AsyncLocalStorage and I treat forwardRef as a design smell
  • I can write a forRootAsync dynamic module
  • I can classify coupling (data, control, temporal, content; afferent vs efferent) and cohesion levels, and measure them with dependency-cruiser
  • I can implement an interface-based repository with TypeORM, Sequelize and in-memory adapters, and I know when a query service should bypass it
  • I can implement Factory, Strategy, Adapter, Decorator and Facade in NestJS with injection tokens, and name the situation where each is not worth it
  • I can list the Node EventEmitter pitfalls (sync listeners, unhandled rejections, leaks, no durability, emit-before-commit) and mitigate each
  • I can make a command idempotent under concurrent duplicates with a claimed key and conditional updates
  • I can implement an order state machine with a transition table, exhaustive tests, persisted history and optimistic locking
  • I can compose specifications that evaluate both in memory and as SQL, with unique parameter names and index-aware shapes
  • I can implement a Unit of Work with AsyncLocalStorage, dispatch events after commit, always release the runner, and keep external I/O outside the transaction
  • I can spot the NestJS anti-patterns (God service, fat controller, entities as DTOs, ModuleRef locator, request-scoped everything, static helpers, swallowed errors) in review and point to the fix
  • I can lay out a production NestJS module as public / application / domain / infrastructure / presentation and explain the import rules for each folder

Part 06 — Key Takeaways

  • Principles manage change: SRP limits reasons to change, OCP adds behaviour without editing, LSP keeps abstractions trustworthy, ISP keeps interfaces narrow, DIP points imports at abstractions the consumer owns.
  • DRY is about knowledge, not code; the rule of three applies, and duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction. KISS and YAGNI cut speculative structure, but never cut idempotency, timeouts, validation or the DTO boundary.
  • The NestJS container builds singletons from constructor metadata and tokens; interfaces need @Inject(TOKEN); keep everything Scope.DEFAULT and carry request context in AsyncLocalStorage.
  • Compose behaviour from small collaborators; reserve inheritance for framework extension points and shallow error hierarchies.
  • Couple to stable abstractions, not volatile implementations; the domain should have high afferent and near-zero efferent coupling. Folders named utils, common or shared are a cohesion smell.
  • A repository speaks domain language and returns domain objects; the moment its interface accepts ORM options it has stopped being a boundary. Reports go to query services.
  • Factory selects, Strategy executes, Adapter translates vendor shapes and errors, Decorator wraps with the same interface, Facade is a module's public API shaped like a future network client.
  • In-process events are synchronous, non-durable and error-prone by default: use async: true, catch inside listeners, emit after commit, and write an outbox for anything that must happen.
  • Commands are requests with one handler and an idempotency key; events are facts with many handlers. @nestjs/cqrs adds a bus, not durability.
  • Model lifecycles as explicit state machines with a transition table, exhaustive tests, persisted transitions and optimistic locking; illegal transitions are errors and a metric.
  • A Unit of Work is the transaction boundary of one business operation: all repositories share it through context, events dispatch after commit, the runner is always released, and no network call lives inside it.
  • Encode the rules in tooling (lint, dependency-cruiser, ValidationPipe whitelist, boot smoke tests) rather than in wiki pages; anti-patterns are written by reasonable people under deadline pressure.

Part 7 — Domain-Driven Design

Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is a way of building software where the business problem shapes the code, not the database schema and not the framework. It was described by Eric Evans in 2003, and twenty years later it is still the most useful vocabulary we have for organising a large backend.

Throughout this part we use one running example: an e-commerce platform with Order, Payment, Inventory, Shipping and Customer, plus Catalog and Notifications on the side. By the end you will have seen a complete PlaceOrder use case in NestJS with an Order aggregate, a repository, a TypeORM mapper, a unit of work, domain events dispatched after commit, and the PostgreSQL schema that backs the invariants.

A warning before we begin. DDD has two halves. The strategic half (domains, bounded contexts, context maps) is about deciding where the boundaries go. The tactical half (entities, value objects, aggregates, repositories) is about how to write the code inside a boundary. Most teams jump straight to the tactical patterns and end up with folders called domain/ full of classes that do nothing. The strategic half is where the real leverage is. We start there.

7.1 Domain, subdomain, and core vs supporting vs generic

Concept

The domain is the whole area of business your software serves. For us it is "selling physical goods online". A domain is too big to reason about in one piece, so we split it into subdomains: natural sub-areas that a business person would recognise. Our subdomains are Ordering, Payments, Inventory, Shipping, Customer management, Catalog and Notifications.

Not every subdomain matters equally. DDD names three kinds:

Kind Meaning E-commerce examples Build or buy?
Core What makes the business win. Complex, changes often, competitive advantage. Ordering (pricing rules, promotions, bundles), Inventory allocation across warehouses Build. Put your best engineers here.
Supporting Needed for the business to run, specific to you, but not a differentiator. Shipping (carrier selection, label generation), Customer profiles Build simply, or thin wrapper over a vendor.
Generic Every company needs it; solved problems. Payments (card processing), Notifications (email/SMS), Authentication Buy or use a library/SaaS: Stripe, SES, Auth0/Keycloak.

Why does it exist?

Without this classification, engineering effort is spread evenly. Teams spend three sprints building a beautiful email templating engine (generic) while the promotion engine that actually drives revenue (core) is a 900-line if/else in a controller. Classifying subdomains tells you where to invest design effort, where to accept "good enough", and where to pay a vendor.

It also tells you which parts to protect. Core domain code should be the most tested, the most isolated from frameworks, and the last to be outsourced.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant. The core is the kitchen and the menu: it is why customers come. Supporting is the reservation book: needed, custom to how this restaurant seats people, but nobody chooses the restaurant for it. Generic is the card terminal: every restaurant has one and none of them builds their own. You would never let the chef spend a week choosing card terminals, and you would never buy a kitchen "as a service".

How it works

Classifying subdomains is a conversation, not a code task. A senior engineer runs it like this:

  1. List every capability the business needs. Write them on cards: "accept an order", "charge a card", "reserve stock", "print a shipping label", "send order confirmation", "search products".
  2. Group cards into subdomains by asking "which business person owns this?" Sales owns ordering, Finance owns payments, Warehouse owns inventory and shipping, Marketing owns catalog.
  3. For each subdomain ask two questions: Would the company lose to a competitor if this were mediocre? (core if yes) and Could we buy this off the shelf tomorrow? (generic if yes). Everything else is supporting.
  4. Revisit yearly. Subdomains move. Shipping is supporting for a small shop; for Amazon it became core, which is why they built their own logistics.

Practical example

Our e-commerce classification, and the reasoning:

  • Ordering — core. Pricing, promotions, cart rules, B2B credit terms and multi-currency are complex and unique. A bug here costs money on every order. This is where the richest domain model lives.
  • Inventory — core. Multi-warehouse allocation, backorders and reservation expiry directly affect whether we can promise delivery dates. Competitors with better allocation sell more.
  • Shipping — supporting. We must pick carriers and produce labels, but the interesting logic lives inside carriers' APIs. We build a thin service that maps our shipment to their formats.
  • Customer — supporting. Addresses, preferences, loyalty tier. Custom enough that a generic CRM does not fit, simple enough for a straightforward model.
  • Payments — generic. We never touch card numbers. We integrate Stripe or Razorpay. Our "Payment" context stores intents, captures and refunds, and talks to the provider.
  • Catalog — supporting leaning generic. Product data and search. Many teams use a headless PIM or Elasticsearch.
  • Notifications — generic. Templated email/SMS/push over SES, Twilio, FCM.

NestJS example

Subdomain classification shows up in how you lay out modules and how thick each one is.

// src/app.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OrderingModule } from './ordering/ordering.module';        // core: rich domain model
import { InventoryModule } from './inventory/inventory.module';     // core: rich domain model
import { ShippingModule } from './shipping/shipping.module';        // supporting: thin service over carrier APIs
import { CustomerModule } from './customer/customer.module';        // supporting: simple CRUD + a few rules
import { PaymentsModule } from './payments/payments.module';        // generic: adapter over Stripe
import { NotificationsModule } from './notifications/notifications.module'; // generic: adapter over SES/Twilio

@Module({
  imports: [
    OrderingModule,
    InventoryModule,
    ShippingModule,
    CustomerModule,
    PaymentsModule,
    NotificationsModule,
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

Inside ordering/ you will find domain/, application/, infrastructure/ folders. Inside notifications/ you will find one service and one provider. That asymmetry is deliberate and correct.

Production scenario

A mid-size retailer processes 40,000 orders a day, about 0.5 orders per second on average and 15 per second during a sale. The ordering domain handles pricing for 120 promotion types. The notifications system sends 200,000 emails a day through SES. Which one gets a dedicated three-person team and a domain model with 400 unit tests? Ordering. Notifications is one engineer's part-time job and a 300-line adapter.

Failure scenario

A team spent four months building an in-house payment gateway abstraction with retry logic, fraud scoring and settlement reconciliation. It was elegant. Meanwhile the checkout page (core) still had a bug where a promotion could apply twice, costing roughly 2% of revenue on discounted orders. The post-mortem finding was not "bad engineers"; it was "no subdomain classification, so effort went to the interesting problem instead of the valuable one".

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

  • "Which subdomain is this ticket in?" is the first question before estimating.
  • Core gets the full DDD treatment: aggregates, invariants, domain events, exhaustive tests.
  • Supporting gets a clean service layer and DTOs; a rich domain model is optional.
  • Generic gets an adapter with a clear interface so the vendor can be swapped.
  • They refuse to let the team build a generic subdomain from scratch without a written reason (regulatory, cost at scale, or vendor lock-in risk).

Common mistakes

  • Treating every module as equally important, so the codebase has uniform mediocre quality.
  • Calling everything "core" because it feels important. If everything is core, nothing is.
  • Building generic subdomains (auth, email, payments) by hand and then owning security patches forever.
  • Never revisiting the classification as the business changes.

Interview questions

  1. How do you decide whether a subdomain is core, supporting or generic? Expected: the two questions (competitive advantage, buy-able off the shelf); give an example where the answer changed over time. Follow-up: what changes in how you build each kind?
  2. Payments is critical to an e-commerce business. Why is it usually classified as generic, not core? Expected: critical is not the same as differentiating; card processing is a solved, regulated problem; you build the adapter and orchestration, not the processor.
  3. Where would you put your most experienced engineers and why?
  4. A startup with five engineers wants to "do DDD". Which half of DDD would you start with? Expected: strategic; name subdomains and boundaries first, tactical patterns only in the core.

Practical exercise

Take a system you know (or the e-commerce example). List 15 capabilities, group them into subdomains and classify each as core, supporting or generic with one sentence of justification. Acceptance criteria: at most two subdomains are core; each generic subdomain names a vendor or library you would use instead of building; at least one classification includes a note on when it might change.

7.2 Ubiquitous language

Concept

The ubiquitous language is a shared vocabulary between developers and domain experts, used everywhere: in conversations, in tickets, in class names, in table names, in API paths. If the warehouse manager says "pick list", the code has a PickList class, not a FulfillmentItemsCollection.

The word "ubiquitous" means "the same everywhere". The point is not politeness; it is that every translation between a business term and a code term is a place for a bug to hide.

Why does it exist?

Consider the word order in our company:

  • Sales means "what the customer asked for and agreed to pay": lines, prices, discounts, payment status.
  • Warehouse means "what has to be picked, packed and shipped": SKUs, quantities, bin locations, box sizes. Prices are irrelevant.
  • Finance means "a revenue event with tax, invoice number and settlement date". Which bin the item was in is irrelevant.

If you build one Order class that satisfies all three, it has 80 fields, three lifecycles tangled together, and nobody can change it without breaking someone. The ubiquitous language forces you to notice that these are three different concepts that happen to share a word, and to give each a precise name inside its own boundary (which is exactly what bounded contexts are for in section 7.3).

Mental model

Imagine a hospital where doctors say "discharge" and the billing office says "close the account" and IT says "set status = 4". A nurse asks IT "was the patient discharged?" and IT says "status is 4" and the nurse does not know if that is yes. Everyone is translating. Now imagine the whole hospital agrees on "discharged" and the database column is literally discharged_at. Questions become answerable without translation.

How it works

  1. Listen to domain experts. Write down the nouns and verbs they use. "We allocate stock to an order." "A shipment can be split." "A payment is captured, not charged."
  2. Challenge ambiguity. When one word means two things, or two words mean one thing, stop and resolve it. "Is a cancelled order the same as a rejected order?" (No: cancelled is by the customer; rejected is by fraud review.)
  3. Put the words in code. order.cancel() not order.setStatus('CANCELLED'). StockAllocation not InventoryRecordLink.
  4. Put the words in the schema. Table stock_allocations, column captured_at, enum value SPLIT.
  5. Put the words in the API. POST /orders/{id}/cancellations not POST /orders/{id}/status.
  6. Keep a glossary per bounded context. A short markdown file is enough. Review it when new terms appear.

Practical example

Before the language was agreed, a ticket read: "When the order is done, update inventory". Three engineers read "done" as paid, shipped and delivered. Inventory was decremented at three different points depending on which code path ran. After the glossary existed, the ticket read: "When an order is Placed (customer confirmed and payment authorised), reserve stock. When the shipment is Dispatched, consume the reservation." Two precise verbs, two precise events, one implementation.

NestJS example

The language appears directly in method names, event names and DTOs.

// src/ordering/domain/order.ts (excerpt)
export class Order {
  // Verbs from the glossary, not generic setters.
  place(): void { /* validates lines, moves to PLACED, raises OrderPlaced */ }
  cancel(reason: CancellationReason): void { /* raises OrderCancelled */ }
  markPaid(paymentId: PaymentId): void { /* raises OrderPaid */ }
}

// src/inventory/domain/stock-item.ts (excerpt)
export class StockItem {
  reserve(qty: Quantity, forOrder: OrderId): StockReservation { /* ... */ }
  consume(reservation: StockReservation): void { /* on dispatch */ }
  release(reservation: StockReservation): void { /* on cancellation or expiry */ }
}

// src/ordering/application/events/order-placed.event.ts
export class OrderPlaced {
  constructor(
    public readonly orderId: string,
    public readonly customerId: string,
    public readonly lines: ReadonlyArray<{ sku: string; quantity: number }>,
    public readonly occurredAt: Date,
  ) {}
}

A reviewer who is not a developer can read order.cancel(reason) and stockItem.reserve(qty, forOrder) and confirm they match the business process.

PostgreSQL example

The same words in the schema. Note that the ordering context and the inventory context each use their own table names, and the words match the glossary.

-- Ordering context
CREATE TYPE order_status AS ENUM ('DRAFT', 'PLACED', 'PAID', 'CANCELLED', 'FULFILLED');

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  status       order_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'DRAFT',
  placed_at    timestamptz,
  cancelled_at timestamptz,
  cancellation_reason text
);

-- Inventory context: the glossary says "reserve", "consume", "release"
CREATE TYPE reservation_status AS ENUM ('ACTIVE', 'CONSUMED', 'RELEASED', 'EXPIRED');

CREATE TABLE stock_reservations (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  sku           text NOT NULL,
  warehouse_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  order_id      uuid NOT NULL,        -- reference by id, not FK across contexts
  quantity      integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  status        reservation_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
  expires_at    timestamptz NOT NULL,
  consumed_at   timestamptz,
  released_at   timestamptz
);

Production scenario

On a team of 12 engineers and 3 product managers, a glossary of about 60 terms lived in the repository under docs/glossary/ordering.md. New engineers reported that reading the glossary plus the aggregate classes was enough to understand the checkout flow in an afternoon. Support tickets referenced statuses by the same names the UI showed, so engineers could search logs for status=PLACED and find exactly what the customer saw.

Failure scenario

At 09:40 a product manager asked "how many orders were completed yesterday?" The analyst ran a query on status = 'COMPLETED'. The number was 30% lower than the dashboard. The dashboard counted FULFILLED. Finance counted PAID. Three definitions of complete, three numbers, a two-hour meeting to reconcile. The fix was a glossary entry and a rename: COMPLETED was removed from the enum entirely because nobody could define it.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

  • They treat renaming as a legitimate engineering task, not cosmetics. If the business now says "fulfilment" instead of "delivery", they rename the module.
  • They spot translation layers (a mapStatusToUiLabel() with 14 cases) as a smell that the language is not shared.
  • They keep the language per context. "Product" in Catalog is allowed to be a different word from "SKU" in Inventory, as long as each is precise within its boundary.

Common mistakes

  • Using technical words for business concepts: OrderDTO, OrderEntity, OrderRecord used interchangeably in conversation with product people.
  • Generic verbs (update, process, handle) that hide business meaning.
  • One giant global glossary that tries to force Sales, Warehouse and Finance to mean the same thing by "order".
  • Enum values that no domain expert recognises (STATUS_3, PENDING_2).

Interview questions

  1. What is the ubiquitous language and where does it have to appear? Expected: everywhere including code, schema, API and tickets; the point is eliminating translation.
  2. The sales team and the warehouse use "order" differently. What do you do? Expected: recognise two concepts, separate bounded contexts, precise names in each, an explicit mapping between them.
  3. Give an example of a bug caused by ambiguous language.
  4. How do you keep a glossary alive after the first month? Expected: it lives in the repo, is reviewed in PRs that add enum values or events, and product people can edit it.

Practical exercise

Pick one entity in a codebase you work on. List every status or verb applied to it in code, database and UI. Find at least two that are ambiguous or duplicated. Propose a glossary with precise definitions and the code/schema renames required. Acceptance criteria: each term has one sentence of definition, one owner (a role), and the rename list is complete enough to become a PR.

7.3 Bounded contexts

Concept

A bounded context is a boundary inside which a model and its language are consistent. Inside the Ordering context, "Order" means one precise thing and the Order class has exactly the fields ordering needs. Inside the Shipping context, "Shipment" is the concept, and if it references an order it does so by id and with only the fields shipping cares about.

Each bounded context owns its data. No other context reads or writes its tables directly. Communication happens through APIs or events.

A bounded context is not the same as a microservice. A monolith can have five bounded contexts as five NestJS modules that talk through interfaces and events. A microservice should contain one bounded context (or a few small ones), but a bounded context does not require a microservice. Boundaries are a design decision; deployment is a separate decision.

Why does it exist?

Without bounded contexts, you get the single shared Product class problem. Catalog needs marketing description, images, SEO slug and variant options. Inventory needs SKU, weight, dimensions, warehouse bins and reorder point. Ordering needs SKU, display name and price at the moment of ordering. Put all of that in one class and one table, and:

  • A change to how images are stored requires regression-testing the order pipeline.
  • Inventory's nightly stock sync locks rows that the checkout is trying to read.
  • The products table has 70 columns and nobody knows which ones are safe to null.
  • Teams block each other on every migration.

Bounded contexts turn one giant tangled model into several small consistent ones with explicit contracts between them.

Mental model

Imagine a large office building where each department has its own filing system. Sales files by customer name. The warehouse files by shelf location. Finance files by invoice number. The same physical item appears in all three systems, described differently. When Sales needs to know if something shipped, they do not walk into the warehouse and rummage; they ask at the counter, and the warehouse answers in Sales' terms. Each department is a bounded context. The counter is the API. The internal filing system is private.

How it works

  1. Find the seams. Where does the language change? Where does a word start meaning something else? Where does one team's change break another team's code? Those are boundaries.
  2. Give each context one model. Its own classes, its own tables (or schema), its own module.
  3. Reference across contexts by id only. Ordering stores customerId: string, not a Customer object and definitely not a foreign key into the customer context's table in a way that couples migrations.
  4. Duplicate data deliberately. Ordering copies productName and unitPrice into the order line at placement time. It is not a bug; it is a snapshot. If Catalog renames the product next week, the order still shows what the customer bought.
  5. Communicate by contract. Synchronous API calls for questions ("is this customer allowed to order on credit?"); asynchronous events for facts ("OrderPlaced").
  6. Protect the boundary. Lint rules, module encapsulation in NestJS (exports on modules), separate PostgreSQL schemas or databases, separate DB users with grants.

Here is the e-commerce system as bounded contexts:

flowchart TB
  subgraph Ordering
    O["Order aggregate"]
    OL["OrderLine"]
    O --- OL
  end
  subgraph Payments
    PI["PaymentIntent"]
    CAP["Capture / Refund"]
    PI --- CAP
  end
  subgraph Inventory
    SI["StockItem per SKU per warehouse"]
    RES["StockReservation"]
    SI --- RES
  end
  subgraph Shipping
    SH["Shipment"]
    PKG["Package"]
    SH --- PKG
  end
  subgraph Customer
    CU["Customer profile"]
    AD["Address book"]
    CU --- AD
  end
  subgraph Catalog
    PR["Product with variants and media"]
  end
  subgraph Notifications
    NT["Templated messages"]
  end
  O -->|"OrderPlaced event"| PI
  O -->|"OrderPlaced event"| SI
  PI -->|"PaymentCaptured event"| O
  SI -->|"StockReserved event"| O
  O -->|"OrderPaid event"| SH
  SH -->|"ShipmentDispatched event"| NT
  O -->|"customerId lookup"| CU
  PR -->|"price and name snapshot at placement"| O

Notice that Ordering never reaches into Inventory's tables. It publishes OrderPlaced; Inventory decides how to reserve; Inventory publishes StockReserved; Ordering reacts.

Practical example

The same "Product" in three contexts:

Field Catalog Inventory Ordering (OrderLine)
Identity productId, slug sku, warehouseId sku
Name Marketing title, translations Short pick name Name snapshot at order time
Price List price, sale price, price history none unitPrice snapshot with currency
Physical none weight, dimensions, bin none
Media images, videos, 3D none thumbnail URL snapshot (optional)
Quantity none on hand, reserved, reorder point quantity ordered

Three classes, three tables, three lifecycles. Catalog can rewrite its media pipeline without touching Inventory or Ordering.

NestJS example

A bounded context is a NestJS module with a narrow public surface. Only the application service and a few read models are exported. Entities, repositories and internal services stay private.

// src/inventory/inventory.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { StockItemOrmEntity } from './infrastructure/stock-item.orm-entity';
import { StockReservationOrmEntity } from './infrastructure/stock-reservation.orm-entity';
import { TypeOrmStockItemRepository } from './infrastructure/typeorm-stock-item.repository';
import { STOCK_ITEM_REPOSITORY } from './domain/stock-item.repository';
import { ReserveStockService } from './application/reserve-stock.service';
import { StockAvailabilityQuery } from './application/stock-availability.query';
import { OrderPlacedHandler } from './application/handlers/order-placed.handler';

@Module({
  imports: [TypeOrmModule.forFeature([StockItemOrmEntity, StockReservationOrmEntity])],
  providers: [
    { provide: STOCK_ITEM_REPOSITORY, useClass: TypeOrmStockItemRepository },
    ReserveStockService,
    StockAvailabilityQuery,
    OrderPlacedHandler, // reacts to events from Ordering
  ],
  // Only the public contract leaves the module. No repositories, no ORM entities.
  exports: [StockAvailabilityQuery],
})
export class InventoryModule {}

If OrderingModule needs to know availability, it injects StockAvailabilityQuery, which returns a plain DTO. It cannot inject TypeOrmStockItemRepository because it is not exported; NestJS will refuse to resolve it.

PostgreSQL example

Separate schemas per context in one database is the pragmatic middle ground for a modular monolith. Each context gets a database role with grants only on its schema, so a "quick join" across contexts fails at the database instead of silently coupling two teams.

CREATE SCHEMA ordering;
CREATE SCHEMA inventory;
CREATE SCHEMA catalog;

CREATE ROLE ordering_app LOGIN PASSWORD '...';
CREATE ROLE inventory_app LOGIN PASSWORD '...';

GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA ordering TO ordering_app;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA ordering TO ordering_app;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA ordering GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON TABLES TO ordering_app;

GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA inventory TO inventory_app;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA inventory TO inventory_app;

-- ordering_app cannot read inventory.stock_items. A cross-context join is a permission error.
-- Cross-context references are plain columns, not foreign keys:
CREATE TABLE ordering.orders (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id uuid NOT NULL,   -- id from the customer context; no REFERENCES customer.customers
  status      text NOT NULL
);

The missing foreign key is intentional. A foreign key across contexts means Customer cannot archive or re-key a customer without coordinating with Ordering's tables. Referential integrity across contexts is enforced by process (events, reconciliation jobs), not by the database.

TypeORM example

Two TypeORM entities named "product-ish", in two contexts, in two schemas. They do not share a base class.

// src/catalog/infrastructure/product.orm-entity.ts
import { Entity, PrimaryColumn, Column } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ schema: 'catalog', name: 'products' })
export class ProductOrmEntity {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column() slug: string;
  @Column() title: string;
  @Column('text') description: string;
  @Column('jsonb') media: { url: string; kind: 'image' | 'video' }[];
  @Column('bigint') listPriceMinor: string; // stored as minor units, see Money in 7.5
  @Column({ length: 3 }) currency: string;
}

// src/inventory/infrastructure/stock-item.orm-entity.ts
import { Entity, PrimaryColumn, Column, Index, VersionColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ schema: 'inventory', name: 'stock_items' })
@Index(['sku', 'warehouseId'], { unique: true })
export class StockItemOrmEntity {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column() sku: string;
  @Column('uuid') warehouseId: string;
  @Column('int') onHand: number;
  @Column('int') reserved: number;
  @Column('int') reorderPoint: number;
  @Column('numeric', { precision: 8, scale: 3 }) weightKg: string;
  @VersionColumn() version: number; // optimistic locking, see 7.15
}

Sequelize example

The same boundary in Sequelize: each context has its own Sequelize instance or at least its own schema option, and models are registered per module.

// src/inventory/infrastructure/stock-item.model.ts
import { Table, Column, Model, DataType, Index } from 'sequelize-typescript';

@Table({ schema: 'inventory', tableName: 'stock_items', version: true, timestamps: true })
export class StockItemModel extends Model {
  @Column({ type: DataType.UUID, primaryKey: true }) declare id: string;
  @Index({ name: 'ux_stock_sku_wh', unique: true }) @Column(DataType.STRING) declare sku: string;
  @Index({ name: 'ux_stock_sku_wh', unique: true }) @Column(DataType.UUID) declare warehouseId: string;
  @Column(DataType.INTEGER) declare onHand: number;
  @Column(DataType.INTEGER) declare reserved: number;
  @Column(DataType.INTEGER) declare reorderPoint: number;
}

// src/inventory/inventory.module.ts (Sequelize variant)
// SequelizeModule.forFeature([StockItemModel, StockReservationModel])

version: true gives Sequelize's optimistic locking column, analogous to TypeORM's @VersionColumn.

Production scenario

A modular monolith with seven bounded contexts ran as one NestJS process on 6 pods, one PostgreSQL primary with 7 schemas, and RabbitMQ for events between contexts. Total traffic 1,200 RPS. When Inventory needed to move to its own database because stock syncs from 40 warehouses were saturating I/O, the migration took three weeks instead of six months, because the schema was already separate, nothing joined across it, and all communication already went through events and one exported query service. That is the payoff of boundaries: you can change deployment later.

Failure scenario

The opposite story. A team had one products table shared by Catalog, Inventory and Ordering. Catalog added a trigger to update search_vector on every product update. Inventory's stock sync updated products.quantity_on_hand 500,000 times per night. Each update fired the trigger and rebuilt a tsvector. The nightly sync went from 12 minutes to 3 hours, and at 03:00 the checkout started timing out because the sync held row locks on products that customers were ordering. Root cause: three contexts sharing one table, so a change by one team silently changed the performance of the others.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Shared table across contexts. Any change is a cross-team change. Break it up: separate schemas, copy the needed fields.
  • Cross-context foreign keys. They block re-keying, archiving and independent deployment. Replace with id columns and a reconciliation job.
  • Chatty synchronous calls across contexts. Placing an order calls Customer, Catalog and Inventory synchronously; one slow context slows checkout. Prefer snapshots and events for anything that is not a hard precondition.
  • Boundary drawn along technical lines ("the database module", "the API module") instead of business lines. Those are layers, not contexts.
  • Too many tiny contexts. Fifteen contexts for a team of six means fifteen contracts to maintain. Merge until each context has an owner.
  • Stale snapshots. Ordering's copy of the product name is wrong after a rename. Decide explicitly which snapshots are meant to be historical (price at purchase: yes) and which should refresh (display name: maybe).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

  • They draw the context boundaries before the class diagram.
  • They ask "who owns this data?" for every table. One owner. If two contexts both write to it, the boundary is wrong.
  • They accept duplication of data across contexts and reject duplication of logic (two contexts both computing tax is a bug; two contexts both storing customerId is fine).
  • They keep contexts inside a monolith until there is a scaling, team or deployment reason to split, and they make sure that when the reason comes, the split is mechanical.
  • To a product manager: "Each team gets its own room with its own whiteboard. Rooms talk through the door, not through the wall. That is why the shipping team can change their whole system next quarter without the checkout breaking."

Common mistakes

  • Equating bounded context with microservice and splitting into services before the boundaries are understood.
  • Sharing ORM entities between modules "to avoid duplication".
  • Exporting repositories from NestJS modules so other modules can "just query".
  • Foreign keys everywhere, including across contexts, then discovering nothing can be deployed independently.
  • Drawing one context called "Core" that contains everything.

Interview questions

  1. What is a bounded context, and how does it differ from a microservice? Expected: a model/language boundary versus a deployment unit; contexts can live in a monolith.
  2. Why would you store the product name and price inside the order line instead of joining to the products table? Expected: snapshot semantics, boundary independence, historical accuracy. Follow-up: which fields should refresh and which should not?
  3. How do you enforce a boundary in a NestJS monolith? Expected: module exports, separate schemas, DB grants, lint rules on imports, events for cross-context communication.
  4. Two contexts need to be consistent (order paid and stock reserved). How do you handle that without a shared transaction? Expected: events, sagas/process managers (see Part 19 — Event-Driven Architecture), compensation, reconciliation.
  5. When is it wrong to split a context? Expected: no clear owner, high chatter, team too small.

Practical exercise

Take a products table with 40+ columns from a real or imagined system. Split it into Catalog, Inventory and Ordering views. For each column decide which context owns it and which contexts hold a snapshot of it. Write the three CREATE TABLE statements in three schemas and the NestJS module exports for each context. Acceptance criteria: no column has two owners; no foreign key crosses a schema; the only exported providers are query services or application services, never repositories or ORM entities.

7.4 Entities

Concept

An entity is an object defined by its identity, not by its attributes. Two customers with the same name, email and address are still two customers if they have different ids. An entity has a lifecycle: it is created, changes over time, and may eventually be archived or deleted, but it stays "the same thing" through all those changes.

In our domain: Order, Customer, Shipment, PaymentIntent, StockItem are entities.

Why does it exist?

Without the idea of identity, you cannot answer "is this the same order I saw five minutes ago?" after its status changed. You also cannot express "this order has changed" as opposed to "this is a different order". Identity is what lets you track, reference and audit something over time.

Mental model

Imagine a person. Their hair, weight and address change; their passport number does not. The passport number is identity. Two people can share a name and a birthday and still be two people. An entity is anything you would give a passport number to.

How it works

  1. Identity is assigned once, at creation, and never changes. Prefer generating it in the application (UUID v4, or UUID v7 / ULID for time-ordering) so the domain can create fully-formed entities without a database round trip. Database-generated serial ids force you to insert before you know who you are.
  2. Equality is by id. order1.equals(order2) compares ids, nothing else.
  3. Lifecycle is expressed as state transitions with rules. An Order goes DRAFT -> PLACED -> PAID -> FULFILLED, or -> CANCELLED from some states but not others. The entity enforces which transitions are legal.
  4. Behaviour lives on the entity. order.cancel(reason) not orderService.setStatus(order, 'CANCELLED').
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> DRAFT
  DRAFT --> PLACED: place
  PLACED --> PAID: markPaid
  PLACED --> CANCELLED: cancel
  PAID --> FULFILLED: fulfil
  PAID --> CANCELLED: cancel with refund
  FULFILLED --> [*]
  CANCELLED --> [*]

Practical example

A minimal entity base with identity equality, and the Order lifecycle rules. Note that the constructor is private and creation goes through a named factory, so an Order can never exist in an invalid state.

// src/shared/domain/entity.ts
export abstract class Entity<TId extends string> {
  protected constructor(public readonly id: TId) {}

  equals(other?: Entity<TId>): boolean {
    if (!other) return false;
    if (this === other) return true;
    return this.id === other.id; // identity, not attributes
  }
}

// src/ordering/domain/order.ts (lifecycle excerpt; lines and totals come in 7.6)
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { Entity } from '../../shared/domain/entity';
import { OrderStateError } from './errors';

export type OrderStatus = 'DRAFT' | 'PLACED' | 'PAID' | 'FULFILLED' | 'CANCELLED';

export class Order extends Entity<string> {
  private status: OrderStatus = 'DRAFT';
  private cancelledReason?: string;

  private constructor(id: string, public readonly customerId: string) {
    super(id);
  }

  static createDraft(customerId: string): Order {
    return new Order(randomUUID(), customerId);
  }

  get currentStatus(): OrderStatus {
    return this.status;
  }

  place(): void {
    this.assertStatus('DRAFT', 'place');
    this.status = 'PLACED';
  }

  markPaid(): void {
    this.assertStatus('PLACED', 'markPaid');
    this.status = 'PAID';
  }

  cancel(reason: string): void {
    if (this.status !== 'PLACED' && this.status !== 'PAID') {
      throw new OrderStateError(`Cannot cancel an order in status ${this.status}`);
    }
    this.status = 'CANCELLED';
    this.cancelledReason = reason;
  }

  private assertStatus(expected: OrderStatus, action: string): void {
    if (this.status !== expected) {
      throw new OrderStateError(`Cannot ${action} an order in status ${this.status}`);
    }
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Identity in the database is a primary key that never changes. Use uuid and let the application generate it. A CHECK on status transitions is hard to express in SQL, but you can at least constrain the set of values and record lifecycle timestamps.

CREATE TABLE ordering.orders (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,                 -- generated by the application
  customer_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  status        text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('DRAFT','PLACED','PAID','FULFILLED','CANCELLED')),
  placed_at     timestamptz,
  paid_at       timestamptz,
  cancelled_at  timestamptz,
  cancelled_reason text,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  -- lifecycle sanity: a cancelled order must have a reason and a timestamp
  CONSTRAINT chk_cancel_fields CHECK (
    (status <> 'CANCELLED') OR (cancelled_at IS NOT NULL AND cancelled_reason IS NOT NULL)
  )
);

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Database-generated ids force INSERT before the entity can be referenced, which pushes persistence concerns into the domain. Generate in the app.
  • Natural keys as identity (email as customer id). Emails change. Use a surrogate id and make email a unique attribute.
  • Mutable id fields on ORM entities. Mark them readonly in the domain class.
  • Equality by reference in tests: two Order instances loaded from the same row are equal by id but not by ===. Always use .equals().

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They ask "does this thing have a lifecycle and need to be tracked?" If yes, entity. If it is just a description (an amount, an address) it is probably a value object (next section). They keep entity ids opaque strings at the boundary and never expose numeric ids that leak row counts or allow enumeration (see Part 8 — API Design on id choice).

Common mistakes

  • Public setters on everything, so any code can put an entity in an invalid state.
  • Entities that are just bags of fields with all logic in services (the anemic model, section 7.13).
  • Comparing entities by all fields, so a status change makes it "a different order".

Interview questions

  1. What distinguishes an entity from a value object? Expected: identity and lifecycle versus value equality and immutability.
  2. Why generate ids in the application rather than with SERIAL? Expected: create valid entities before persistence, batch inserts, idempotency, no round trip, works across services.
  3. How do you stop an entity from being put into an invalid state? Expected: private constructor, factory, behaviour methods that check transitions, no public setters.

Practical exercise

Implement a Shipment entity with states PENDING -> PACKED -> DISPATCHED -> DELIVERED and a LOST state reachable only from DISPATCHED. Write Jest tests proving every illegal transition throws. Acceptance criteria: no public setters; all transitions are methods named with domain verbs; 100% branch coverage of the transition rules.

7.5 Value objects

Concept

A value object is an object defined entirely by its attributes. It has no identity. Two Money(1999, 'INR') values are the same value, full stop. Value objects are immutable: you never change one, you create a new one. They carry validation in the constructor so an invalid value object cannot exist.

Classic value objects in e-commerce: Money, Address, Email, Quantity, Sku, DateRange, Percentage.

Why does it exist?

Primitive obsession is the disease. When money is a number, the following bugs are all compile-time legal:

  • Adding 10 USD to 10 EUR.
  • 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.30000000000000004, so an invoice for three items at 0.1 each becomes 0.30000000000000004 and the payment provider rejects it.
  • Passing quantity where unitPrice was expected because both are number.
  • Validating an email in 14 controllers, differently in each.

Value objects put the rules in one place, make invalid states unrepresentable, and give the type system a chance to catch mistakes.

Mental model

Imagine a banknote. You do not care which 500-rupee note you hold; any 500-rupee note is as good as another. If someone swaps yours for a different 500-rupee note, nothing has changed. You cannot "modify" a note into a 1000-rupee note; you exchange it for a different note. That is a value object: interchangeable, immutable, defined by its value.

How it works

  1. Constructor validates and freezes. Throw a domain error on bad input. Use Object.freeze or readonly fields.
  2. Equality compares all attributes. Implement equals().
  3. Operations return new instances. money.add(other) returns a new Money.
  4. Never use floating point for money. Store integer minor units (paise, cents) as bigint or number within safe integer range, plus a currency code. In PostgreSQL use bigint minor units or numeric(19,4); never float/double precision.
  5. Persist as columns of the owning entity (embedded), not as a separate table with its own id.

Practical example

Money with currency, integer minor units and safe arithmetic:

// src/shared/domain/money.ts
import { DomainError } from './domain-error';

const MINOR_UNITS: Record<string, number> = { INR: 100, USD: 100, EUR: 100, JPY: 1, KWD: 1000 };

export class Money {
  private constructor(
    public readonly amountMinor: bigint,   // integer minor units, e.g. paise
    public readonly currency: string,      // ISO 4217
  ) {
    if (!(currency in MINOR_UNITS)) throw new DomainError(`Unsupported currency ${currency}`);
    Object.freeze(this);
  }

  static ofMinor(amountMinor: bigint | number, currency: string): Money {
    return new Money(BigInt(amountMinor), currency);
  }

  /** Parse "19.99" style decimal strings exactly, without ever touching a float. */
  static parse(decimal: string, currency: string): Money {
    const scale = MINOR_UNITS[currency];
    const m = /^(-)?(\d+)(?:\.(\d+))?$/.exec(decimal);
    if (!m) throw new DomainError(`Invalid amount ${decimal}`);
    const [, sign, whole, frac = ''] = m;
    const digits = Math.log10(scale);
    if (frac.length > digits) throw new DomainError(`Too many decimals for ${currency}`);
    const minor = BigInt(whole) * BigInt(scale) + BigInt(frac.padEnd(digits, '0') || '0');
    return new Money(sign ? -minor : minor, currency);
  }

  static zero(currency: string): Money {
    return new Money(0n, currency);
  }

  add(other: Money): Money {
    this.assertSameCurrency(other);
    return new Money(this.amountMinor + other.amountMinor, this.currency);
  }

  subtract(other: Money): Money {
    this.assertSameCurrency(other);
    return new Money(this.amountMinor - other.amountMinor, this.currency);
  }

  multiply(qty: number): Money {
    if (!Number.isInteger(qty) || qty < 0) throw new DomainError('Quantity must be a non-negative integer');
    return new Money(this.amountMinor * BigInt(qty), this.currency);
  }

  /** Percentage with banker's-free rounding to nearest minor unit, half up. */
  percent(basisPoints: number): Money {
    const scaled = this.amountMinor * BigInt(basisPoints);
    const rounded = (scaled + 5000n) / 10000n; // half-up on 10_000 basis points
    return new Money(rounded, this.currency);
  }

  isNegative(): boolean { return this.amountMinor < 0n; }
  isZero(): boolean { return this.amountMinor === 0n; }

  equals(other: Money): boolean {
    return this.currency === other.currency && this.amountMinor === other.amountMinor;
  }

  toString(): string {
    const scale = BigInt(MINOR_UNITS[this.currency]);
    const abs = this.amountMinor < 0n ? -this.amountMinor : this.amountMinor;
    const digits = Math.log10(Number(scale));
    const whole = abs / scale;
    const frac = (abs % scale).toString().padStart(digits, '0');
    return `${this.amountMinor < 0n ? '-' : ''}${whole}${digits ? '.' + frac : ''} ${this.currency}`;
  }

  private assertSameCurrency(other: Money): void {
    if (other.currency !== this.currency) {
      throw new DomainError(`Currency mismatch: ${this.currency} vs ${other.currency}`);
    }
  }
}

Email and Address:

// src/shared/domain/email.ts
export class Email {
  private static readonly RE = /^[^\s@]{1,64}@[^\s@]{1,255}\.[^\s@]{2,}$/;
  private constructor(public readonly value: string) { Object.freeze(this); }

  static of(raw: string): Email {
    const normalized = raw.trim().toLowerCase();
    if (normalized.length > 320 || !Email.RE.test(normalized)) {
      throw new DomainError('Invalid email address');
    }
    return new Email(normalized);
  }
  equals(other: Email): boolean { return this.value === other.value; }
}

// src/customer/domain/address.ts
export class Address {
  private constructor(
    public readonly line1: string,
    public readonly line2: string | null,
    public readonly city: string,
    public readonly postalCode: string,
    public readonly countryCode: string, // ISO 3166-1 alpha-2
  ) { Object.freeze(this); }

  static of(p: { line1: string; line2?: string; city: string; postalCode: string; countryCode: string }): Address {
    if (!p.line1?.trim()) throw new DomainError('line1 is required');
    if (!/^[A-Z]{2}$/.test(p.countryCode)) throw new DomainError('countryCode must be ISO alpha-2');
    if (p.countryCode === 'IN' && !/^\d{6}$/.test(p.postalCode)) throw new DomainError('Indian PIN must be 6 digits');
    return new Address(p.line1.trim(), p.line2?.trim() ?? null, p.city.trim(), p.postalCode.trim(), p.countryCode);
  }

  /** A new address with a changed line; the original is untouched. */
  withLine2(line2: string): Address {
    return new Address(this.line1, line2, this.city, this.postalCode, this.countryCode);
  }

  equals(o: Address): boolean {
    return this.line1 === o.line1 && this.line2 === o.line2 && this.city === o.city
      && this.postalCode === o.postalCode && this.countryCode === o.countryCode;
  }
}

NestJS example

Value objects are created at the boundary from validated DTOs. The DTO validates shape (is it a string, is it present); the value object validates meaning (is it a legal email, is the currency supported).

// src/ordering/api/dto/add-line.dto.ts
import { IsInt, IsString, Length, Matches, Min } from 'class-validator';

export class AddLineDto {
  @IsString() @Length(3, 64) sku: string;
  @IsInt() @Min(1) quantity: number;
  @Matches(/^\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$/) unitPrice: string;  // decimal string, never a JSON number
  @IsString() @Length(3, 3) currency: string;
}

// src/ordering/application/add-line.service.ts (excerpt)
const unitPrice = Money.parse(dto.unitPrice, dto.currency); // meaning-level validation here
order.addLine(new Sku(dto.sku), Quantity.of(dto.quantity), unitPrice);

Notice unitPrice: string. JSON numbers are IEEE doubles. If a client sends 19.99 as a JSON number, some serialisers will already have turned it into 19.989999999. Accept money as a string on the wire and parse it exactly.

PostgreSQL example

Money as two columns of the owning row. bigint minor units is the safest choice; numeric(19,4) is acceptable when you must store fractional minor units (interest, FX rates).

CREATE TABLE ordering.order_lines (
  id                uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id          uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES ordering.orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  sku               text NOT NULL,
  product_name      text NOT NULL,                     -- snapshot
  quantity          integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_price_minor  bigint NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price_minor >= 0),
  currency          char(3) NOT NULL,
  line_total_minor  bigint NOT NULL CHECK (line_total_minor >= 0),
  CONSTRAINT chk_line_total CHECK (line_total_minor = quantity * unit_price_minor)
);

-- Never this:
-- unit_price double precision   -- 0.1 + 0.2 problem, rounding drift over millions of rows

Why not money type? PostgreSQL's money type is locale-dependent and has fixed two-decimal precision; it breaks the moment you need JPY (0 decimals) or KWD (3 decimals). Use bigint plus currency.

TypeORM example

Embed the value object's fields into the entity with @Column(() => ...) embedded entities, or map manually in a mapper (section 7.7). The embedded approach is convenient but couples the ORM to the domain class shape.

// src/ordering/infrastructure/money.embedded.ts
import { Column } from 'typeorm';

export class MoneyColumns {
  @Column('bigint', { name: 'amount_minor' }) amountMinor: string; // TypeORM returns bigint as string
  @Column('char', { length: 3 }) currency: string;
}

// src/ordering/infrastructure/order-line.orm-entity.ts
@Entity({ schema: 'ordering', name: 'order_lines' })
export class OrderLineOrmEntity {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column('uuid', { name: 'order_id' }) orderId: string;
  @Column() sku: string;
  @Column('int') quantity: number;
  @Column(() => MoneyColumns, { prefix: 'unit_price_' }) unitPrice: MoneyColumns; // unit_price_amount_minor, unit_price_currency
}

TypeORM returns bigint columns as strings to avoid precision loss. Convert with BigInt(row.amountMinor) in the mapper.

Sequelize example

Sequelize has no embedded objects, so a mapper (or a getter/setter pair) converts between columns and the value object.

// src/ordering/infrastructure/order-line.model.ts
@Table({ schema: 'ordering', tableName: 'order_lines', timestamps: false })
export class OrderLineModel extends Model {
  @Column({ type: DataType.UUID, primaryKey: true }) declare id: string;
  @Column(DataType.UUID) declare orderId: string;
  @Column(DataType.STRING) declare sku: string;
  @Column(DataType.INTEGER) declare quantity: number;
  @Column({ type: DataType.BIGINT, field: 'unit_price_minor' }) declare unitPriceMinor: string;
  @Column(DataType.CHAR(3)) declare currency: string;

  get unitPrice(): Money {
    return Money.ofMinor(BigInt(this.unitPriceMinor), this.currency);
  }
}

Production scenario

A marketplace handled 12 currencies. Before value objects, there were 23 separate places that formatted or rounded prices, and quarterly reconciliation with the payment provider was off by a few hundred rupees every time (float drift across ~2 million line items). After Money was introduced with integer minor units and one rounding rule (half-up at the line level, documented), reconciliation matched to the paisa. The change touched 60 files and took one engineer two weeks; the cost of the bug had been a finance analyst's day every quarter, forever.

Failure scenario

At 11:20 a promotion "15% off" went live. Discount was computed as price * 0.85 in JavaScript floats and then Math.round()ed. For a price of 1005 paise, 1005 * 0.85 = 854.2499999999999, which rounded to 854 instead of the 854.25 -> 854 the finance team expected (fine here) but for 1015 paise, 862.75 came out as 862.7499999999999 and rounded to 862 instead of 863. Thousands of orders were one paisa short. The payment provider's amount validation compared against a server-side recalculation and rejected 4% of checkouts with "amount mismatch". Money as a value object with percent(basisPoints) on integers made this impossible.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Currency mismatch in arithmetic. Throw; never silently convert.
  • JSON numbers for money on the wire. Use strings.
  • bigint in JSON. JSON.stringify throws on bigint. Serialise Money explicitly (toJSON() returning { amount: '19.99', currency: 'INR' }).
  • Rounding rules differ by jurisdiction and by step (per line vs per order). Pick one, document it, test it.
  • Value objects with too much validation (address validation against a postal service API) belong in a domain service, not the constructor. Constructors must be pure and fast.
  • Mutable arrays inside "immutable" objects. Freeze deeply or expose ReadonlyArray.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They see a number typed as price or a string typed as email in a function signature and ask "who validated this?" If the answer is "the controller, probably", they introduce a value object. They treat Money as non-negotiable in any system that touches payments and will block a PR that adds a float money column.

Common mistakes

  • price: number everywhere, then toFixed(2) in random places.
  • Value objects with ids and their own tables ("addresses" table with address_id, then updating an address in place and changing history on old orders).
  • Validating in the DTO only, so internal code paths (imports, jobs) can create invalid values.
  • Sharing one Address object between two orders and mutating it.

Interview questions

  1. Why never use floating point for money? Show a concrete failing example. Expected: binary fractions, 0.1 + 0.2, rounding drift; use integer minor units plus currency.
  2. How do you represent money in PostgreSQL and why not the money type? Expected: bigint minor units plus char(3), or numeric; the money type is locale-bound with fixed two decimals.
  3. An address is stored on the customer. An order ships to that address. The customer later edits the address. What should the old order show? Expected: the order holds a snapshot value object; value objects are copied, not referenced.
  4. Where does validation of an email belong: DTO, value object, or database? Expected: shape in the DTO, meaning in the value object, uniqueness in the database; all three.

Practical exercise

Implement Money (as above), Quantity (positive integer, max 10,000) and Percentage (0 to 10000 basis points). Write property-based or table-driven Jest tests showing that sum of line totals equals order total for 10,000 random carts with two-decimal prices, and that the same carts computed with JavaScript floats disagree in at least some cases. Acceptance criteria: zero float arithmetic in the implementation; JSON.stringify of a Money produces { amount: string, currency: string }.

7.6 Aggregates and aggregate roots

Concept

An aggregate is a cluster of entities and value objects that are changed together and must stay consistent together. The aggregate root is the one entity through which all changes to the cluster go. Outside code holds a reference only to the root and calls its methods; it never reaches in and modifies a child directly.

Order is an aggregate root. OrderLine is a child entity inside the aggregate. Money, Sku, Quantity, ShippingAddress are value objects inside it. To add a line, you call order.addLine(...), never new OrderLine(...) followed by orderLines.push(...) from a service.

An aggregate is also the unit of consistency and the unit of transaction: one aggregate is loaded, changed and saved in one database transaction, and the invariants (rules that must always be true) inside it are guaranteed at the end of every transaction.

Why does it exist?
