The complete schema for the Ordering context. Every invariant from the aggregate has a database-level twin.

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS ordering;

CREATE TABLE ordering.orders (
  id                uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  idempotency_key   text NOT NULL,
  currency          char(3) NOT NULL,
  status            text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('DRAFT','PLACED','PAID','FULFILLED','CANCELLED')),
  total_minor       bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (total_minor >= 0),
  ship_line1        text, ship_line2 text, ship_city text, ship_postal_code text, ship_country char(2),
  version           integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  placed_at         timestamptz,
  created_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT ux_orders_idempotency UNIQUE (customer_id, idempotency_key),   -- exactly-once creation
  CONSTRAINT chk_placed_requires_address CHECK (status = 'DRAFT' OR ship_line1 IS NOT NULL),
  CONSTRAINT chk_placed_requires_time    CHECK (status = 'DRAFT' OR placed_at IS NOT NULL),
  CONSTRAINT chk_placed_positive_total   CHECK (status = 'DRAFT' OR total_minor > 0)
);
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_customer_created ON ordering.orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_status_placed    ON ordering.orders (status, placed_at) WHERE status IN ('PLACED','PAID');

-- Often named order_items; we follow the glossary and call them lines.
CREATE TABLE ordering.order_lines (
  id                uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id          uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES ordering.orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  sku               text NOT NULL,
  product_name      text NOT NULL,
  quantity          integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity BETWEEN 1 AND 10000),
  unit_price_minor  bigint NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price_minor >= 0),
  line_total_minor  bigint NOT NULL CHECK (line_total_minor >= 0),
  CONSTRAINT chk_line_total CHECK (line_total_minor = quantity * unit_price_minor),
  CONSTRAINT ux_order_line_sku UNIQUE (order_id, sku)
);
CREATE INDEX ix_order_lines_order ON ordering.order_lines (order_id);

CREATE TABLE ordering.outbox (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  event_name    text NOT NULL,
  payload       jsonb NOT NULL,
  occurred_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
  published_at  timestamptz,
  attempts      integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
CREATE INDEX ix_outbox_unpublished ON ordering.outbox (occurred_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

-- Deferred total check (function from 7.6) attached to both tables.
CREATE CONSTRAINT TRIGGER trg_order_total_lines
  AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON ordering.order_lines
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION ordering.check_order_total();
CREATE CONSTRAINT TRIGGER trg_order_total_orders
  AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OF total_minor ON ordering.orders
  DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION ordering.check_order_total();

What the transaction actually does on the wire, for a 3-line order:

BEGIN;
SELECT o.*, l.* FROM ordering.orders o LEFT JOIN ordering.order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.customer_id = $1 AND o.idempotency_key = $2;            -- ~0.3 ms, index hit, 0 rows
INSERT INTO ordering.orders (...) VALUES (...);                    -- ~0.4 ms
DELETE FROM ordering.order_lines WHERE order_id = $1;              -- ~0.1 ms, 0 rows
INSERT INTO ordering.order_lines (...) VALUES (...), (...), (...); -- ~0.4 ms
INSERT INTO ordering.outbox (...) VALUES (...);                    -- ~0.2 ms
COMMIT;                                                            -- ~1 to 3 ms (fsync of WAL)

Roughly 3 to 5 ms in the database, with the row lock held only for that window.

TypeORM example

The ORM entity from 7.6 gains the idempotency column and the unique index; the outbox entity is new.

// src/ordering/infrastructure/order.orm-entity.ts (additions)
@Entity({ schema: 'ordering', name: 'orders' })
@Index('ux_orders_idempotency', ['customerId', 'idempotencyKey'], { unique: true })
export class OrderOrmEntity {
  // ... columns from 7.6 ...
  @Column({ name: 'idempotency_key' }) idempotencyKey: string;
}

// src/shared/infrastructure/outbox.orm-entity.ts
import { Entity, PrimaryColumn, Column, Index } from 'typeorm';

@Entity({ schema: 'ordering', name: 'outbox' })
export class OutboxOrmEntity {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column('uuid', { name: 'aggregate_id' }) aggregateId: string;
  @Column({ name: 'event_name' }) eventName: string;
  @Column('jsonb') payload: Record<string, unknown>;
  @Column('timestamptz', { name: 'occurred_at' }) occurredAt: Date;
  @Index() @Column('timestamptz', { name: 'published_at', nullable: true }) publishedAt: Date | null;
  @Column('int', { default: 0 }) attempts: number;
}

The mapper's toPersistence adds row.idempotencyKey = order.idempotencyKey; and the repository's insert path includes it. The unique-violation error from pg has code === '23505'; the repository catches it and rethrows a DuplicateIdempotencyKeyError so the service can re-read and return the existing order.

// inside TypeOrmOrderRepository.save(), insert path
try {
  await this.em.getRepository(OrderOrmEntity).insert({ ...row, lines: undefined, version: 0 });
} catch (err) {
  if ((err as { code?: string }).code === '23505') throw new DuplicateIdempotencyKeyError(row.idempotencyKey);
  throw err;
}

Sequelize example

The equivalent unit of work in Sequelize uses sequelize.transaction() and passes the Transaction to the repository constructor.

// src/shared/infrastructure/sequelize-unit-of-work.ts
@Injectable()
export class SequelizeUnitOfWork implements UnitOfWork {
  constructor(private readonly sequelize: Sequelize, @Inject(EVENT_PUBLISHER) private readonly publisher: EventPublisher) {}

  async run<T>(work: (repos: Repositories, track: (root: AggregateRoot<string>) => void) => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    const tracked = new Set<AggregateRoot<string>>();
    let events: DomainEvent[] = [];
    const result = await this.sequelize.transaction({ isolationLevel: Transaction.ISOLATION_LEVELS.READ_COMMITTED }, async (t) => {
      const repos: Repositories = { orders: new SequelizeOrderRepository(t) };
      const out = await work(repos, (root) => tracked.add(root));
      events = [...tracked].flatMap((r) => r.pullEvents());
      if (events.length) {
        await OutboxModel.bulkCreate(
          events.map((e) => ({ id: randomUUID(), aggregateId: (e as { orderId?: string }).orderId ?? 'n/a',
            eventName: e.name, payload: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(e, (k, v) => typeof v === 'bigint' ? v.toString() : v)),
            occurredAt: e.occurredAt })),
          { transaction: t },
        );
      }
      return out;
    });
    await this.publisher.publishAll(events).catch(() => undefined); // outbox relay is the durable path
    return result;
  }
}

Testing the use case

Because the use case depends on interfaces, it is testable with an in-memory unit of work and fakes for the two queries.

// src/ordering/application/place-order.service.spec.ts
describe('PlaceOrderService', () => {
  const uow = new InMemoryUnitOfWork();              // holds an InMemoryOrderRepository and records dispatched events
  const customers = { profile: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 'c1', blocked: false, tier: 'STANDARD' }) };
  const catalog = { currentPrices: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(new Map([['SKU-1', { name: 'Mug', listPrice: '199.00', activePromotions: [] }]])) };
  const service = new PlaceOrderService(uow, customers as never, catalog as never, new PricingService());
  const cmd = { customerId: 'c1', idempotencyKey: 'k1', currency: 'INR',
    lines: [{ sku: 'SKU-1', quantity: 2 }], shippingAddress: { line1: 'A', city: 'B', postalCode: '560001', countryCode: 'IN' } };

  it('places an order and dispatches OrderPlaced after commit', async () => {
    const res = await service.execute(cmd);
    expect(res.status).toBe('PLACED');
    expect(res.total).toEqual({ amount: '398.00', currency: 'INR' });
    expect(uow.dispatched.map((e) => e.name)).toEqual(['ordering.order.placed']);
  });

  it('is idempotent on the same key', async () => {
    const a = await service.execute(cmd);
    const b = await service.execute(cmd);
    expect(b.orderId).toBe(a.orderId);
    expect(b.created).toBe(false);
  });

  it('refuses blocked customers before opening a transaction', async () => {
    customers.profile.mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: 'c1', blocked: true, tier: 'STANDARD' });
    await expect(service.execute(cmd)).rejects.toBeInstanceOf(CustomerBlockedError);
    expect(uow.transactionsStarted).toBe(0);
  });
});

Production scenario

At 15 orders/s peak, PlaceOrder p50 is 28 ms and p99 is 90 ms end to end: ~8 ms for the two cross-context reads (in-process, cached), ~5 ms in PostgreSQL, ~3 ms for in-process handlers (stock reservation runs its own ~4 ms transaction), the rest in JSON, validation and network. The outbox relay publishes to Kafka within 300 ms. Memory per request is dominated by the aggregate (a few KB). A single 2-vCPU pod sustains ~150 orders/s before CPU saturates on JSON and validation, so 6 pods give ample headroom.

Failure scenario

At 02:14 on a sale night the on-call was paged: PlaceOrder p99 jumped to 4 seconds and the PostgreSQL connection pool was exhausted. Root cause: Catalog's price lookup had been changed the day before from an in-process query to an HTTP call to the new catalog service, and someone had moved that call inside the uow.run block "so the price would be consistent with the transaction". Each order now held a database connection and a row lock for the duration of an HTTP call whose p99 had risen to 3 seconds under load. The fix was a one-line move back above the transaction and a 300 ms timeout on the catalog client. The rule "no external I/O inside a transaction" was added to the team's PR checklist.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Duplicate request, same key. Handled by lookup plus unique constraint; returns the same order with 200 instead of 201.
  • Same key, different payload. The service returns the original order, silently ignoring the new payload. Better: store a hash of the request with the key and return 422 on mismatch (Part 8, section 8.12).
  • Client timeout after server success. The client retries with the same key and gets the existing order. Without a key, you would have two orders.
  • Catalog down. currentPrices times out at 300 ms; the request fails with 503 before any transaction. No partial state.
  • Concurrency on a draft order (cart edits from two devices): version mismatch on save, ConcurrencyError, 409 to the client, client reloads.
  • Inventory handler fails after commit. Order is placed; reservation is missing. The outbox relay redelivers; if the handler keeps failing, the reconciliation job flags the order. The customer is never told "placed" and then silently unplaced.
  • Huge order (100 lines is the cap). The ArrayMaxSize(100) DTO rule rejects at the edge; the aggregate rejects as a second line of defence.
  • Money in the response. total.amount is a string. Clients must not parse it as a float for arithmetic; the API documentation says so.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

  • They can point to the exact line where the transaction begins and ends, and the exact line where events leave the process.
  • They keep external calls outside the transaction and give each a timeout.
  • They know what happens on every failure path: before the transaction (no state), during (rollback, no events), after commit but before dispatch (outbox saves the day), in a handler (retry, reconcile).
  • They test the use case without a database, and the repository against a real one.

Common mistakes

  • Putting the idempotency check only in memory (a Map), which fails across pods.
  • Checking existing and then inserting without a unique constraint: two pods race and both insert.
  • Calling order.place() and then computing the total in the service "to double-check": the aggregate is the source of truth.
  • Returning the ORM entity from the controller.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through PlaceOrder: where is the transaction, where are the external calls, where do events leave? Expected: the sequence above, with reasons for each placement.
  2. How do you make order creation idempotent across multiple pods? Expected: idempotency key on the row with a unique constraint; lookup first; catch 23505.
  3. A stock reservation handler throws after commit. What does the customer see and what does the system do? Expected: customer sees success; outbox redelivers; reconciliation as backstop; never roll back a committed order.
  4. Why snapshot price and name into the order line? Expected: historical accuracy, context independence.
  5. Why not call the catalog service inside the transaction "for consistency"? Expected: lock and connection hold time; external latency becomes database contention; the incident above.

Practical exercise

Implement PlaceOrder end to end in a fresh NestJS project with PostgreSQL in Docker: aggregate, repository, mapper, unit of work with outbox, controller, DTO, exception filter, and an OrderPlacedHandler in an Inventory module that writes a stock_reservations row per line. Then run 200 concurrent identical requests with the same Idempotency-Key using autocannon or a small script. Acceptance criteria: exactly one orders row and one set of reservations; all 200 responses return the same orderId; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the idempotency lookup shows an index scan on ux_orders_idempotency; killing the process between commit and dispatch (simulate by throwing in the publisher) leaves an unpublished outbox row that a relay later delivers.

7.12 Context mapping

Concept

A context map is a diagram plus a set of agreements describing how bounded contexts relate: who depends on whom, who owns the contract, and what protects each side from the other's changes. DDD names the common relationship patterns:

Pattern Meaning E-commerce example
Partnership Two teams succeed or fail together; they coordinate releases and share planning. Ordering and Inventory: a change to reservation semantics needs both.
Customer / Supplier Downstream (customer) states needs; upstream (supplier) commits to meet them; upstream is not blocked by downstream. Shipping (customer) depends on Ordering (supplier) for OrderPaid with address data.
Conformist Downstream adopts upstream's model as-is because it has no leverage. Payments context conforms to Stripe's model of intents, charges and refunds.
Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) Downstream builds a translation layer so upstream's model does not leak in. Inventory wraps a legacy ERP behind an adapter that speaks our StockLevel language.
Open Host Service (OHS) Upstream exposes a well-defined protocol for any consumer. Catalog exposes a versioned REST/gRPC API used by web, mobile, Ordering.
Published Language A shared, documented schema for exchange (events, JSON schemas). ordering.order.placed event schema v1, documented and versioned.
Shared Kernel A small piece of model shared by two contexts and changed only together. Money, Address, Email value objects in src/shared/domain.
Separate Ways No integration at all; duplicate rather than couple. Notifications keeps its own tiny copy of customer display name.

Why does it exist?

Bounded contexts do not live alone. Without an explicit map, integration happens by accident: someone imports a class from another module, someone reads another team's table, someone hard-codes a vendor's field names deep inside the core. Each accident is a hidden dependency that shows up as a broken deploy months later. A context map makes every dependency visible and gives each a protection strategy.

Mental model

Imagine countries and borders. Some pairs are in a trade union (partnership). Some have a customs office that inspects and relabels goods (ACL). Some publish an official standard for imports (open host service with a published language). Some share a currency (shared kernel). And some simply do not trade (separate ways). The map of these arrangements is a context map.

How it works

Here is the e-commerce context map. U marks the upstream side (the one that owns the contract), D the downstream.

flowchart LR
  ORD["Ordering (core)"]
  INV["Inventory (core)"]
  PAY["Payments (generic)"]
  SHP["Shipping (supporting)"]
  CUS["Customer (supporting)"]
  CAT["Catalog (supporting)"]
  NOT["Notifications (generic)"]
  ERP["Legacy ERP (external)"]
  STR["Stripe (external)"]
  SK["Shared Kernel: Money, Address, Email"]
  ORD <-->|"Partnership: OrderPlaced / StockReserved"| INV
  ORD -->|"U to D, Published Language: OrderPaid"| SHP
  CUS -->|"OHS: CustomerQuery"| ORD
  CAT -->|"OHS: CatalogQuery, price snapshot"| ORD
  ORD -->|"U to D, Customer/Supplier"| PAY
  STR -->|"Conformist"| PAY
  ERP -->|"ACL: ErpStockAdapter"| INV
  ORD -->|"Published Language: events"| NOT
  SHP -->|"Published Language: ShipmentDispatched"| NOT
  SK -.-> ORD
  SK -.-> CUS
  SK -.-> SHP

Reading it:

  1. Ordering and Inventory are partners. Both are core and their contracts (OrderPlaced with lines, StockReserved/StockRejected back) change together. The teams share a planning cadence.
  2. Ordering is upstream of Shipping, Payments and Notifications, which consume its published events. Ordering versions its events and does not break consumers.
  3. Customer and Catalog are open host services for Ordering: exported query classes in the monolith, versioned HTTP APIs if extracted.
  4. Payments conforms to Stripe. Fighting a payment provider's model is wasted effort; Payments' internal model mirrors intents, charges and refunds and our own PaymentIntent entity is thin.
  5. Inventory protects itself from the legacy ERP with an ACL. The ERP has 40-year-old field names (ITMCD, WHSLOC, QTYAVL) and quirks (quantities in dozens for some item classes). None of that appears in Inventory's model.
  6. The shared kernel is tiny and stable: three value objects, changed only with sign-off from every context that uses them.

Practical example: an anti-corruption layer around a legacy ERP

The ACL has three pieces: an interface in Inventory's domain language, an adapter that calls the ERP, and a translator that converts the ERP's shape into ours. The domain never imports anything ERP-specific.

// src/inventory/domain/external-stock.source.ts   (domain-level port, in OUR language)
export interface ExternalStockLevel { sku: string; warehouseId: string; onHand: number; asOf: Date; }
export interface ExternalStockSource {
  levelsFor(skus: string[]): Promise<ExternalStockLevel[]>;
}
export const EXTERNAL_STOCK_SOURCE = Symbol('EXTERNAL_STOCK_SOURCE');
// src/inventory/infrastructure/erp/erp-stock.adapter.ts   (the ACL)
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { ExternalStockSource, ExternalStockLevel } from '../../domain/external-stock.source';
import { ErpClient, ErpItemRow } from './erp.client';          // raw SOAP/HTTP client, returns ERP shapes
import { ErpTranslationError } from './errors';

const WAREHOUSE_BY_ERP_LOC: Record<string, string> = { 'WH01': 'b6d2...', 'WH02': '9a11...' }; // ERP codes -> our ids
const DOZEN_CLASSES = new Set(['PKG-DZ', 'BULK-DZ']);          // ERP quirk: these classes count in dozens

@Injectable()
export class ErpStockAdapter implements ExternalStockSource {
  private readonly log = new Logger(ErpStockAdapter.name);
  constructor(private readonly erp: ErpClient, config: ConfigService) {
    this.erp.setTimeout(config.get<number>('ERP_TIMEOUT_MS', 2000));
  }

  async levelsFor(skus: string[]): Promise<ExternalStockLevel[]> {
    const rows = await this.erp.fetchItems(skus.map(toErpItemCode));   // may throw ErpUnavailableError
    return rows.flatMap((r) => this.translate(r));
  }

  /** All ERP weirdness lives here and nowhere else. */
  private translate(r: ErpItemRow): ExternalStockLevel[] {
    const warehouseId = WAREHOUSE_BY_ERP_LOC[r.WHSLOC];
    if (!warehouseId) { this.log.warn({ msg: 'unknown ERP location', loc: r.WHSLOC }); return []; }
    const multiplier = DOZEN_CLASSES.has(r.ITMCLS) ? 12 : 1;
    const onHand = Number(r.QTYAVL) * multiplier;
    if (!Number.isFinite(onHand) || onHand < 0) throw new ErpTranslationError(`Bad QTYAVL for ${r.ITMCD}`);
    return [{ sku: fromErpItemCode(r.ITMCD), warehouseId, onHand, asOf: parseErpDate(r.UPDTS) }];
  }
}

function toErpItemCode(sku: string): string { return sku.replace(/-/g, '').padStart(12, '0'); }
function fromErpItemCode(code: string): string { return code.replace(/^0+/, '').replace(/(\w{3})(\w+)/, '$1-$2'); }
function parseErpDate(s: string): Date { return new Date(`${s.slice(0, 4)}-${s.slice(4, 6)}-${s.slice(6, 8)}T00:00:00Z`); }

The NestJS module binds the port to the adapter, and a test double replaces it in tests:

// src/inventory/inventory.module.ts (excerpt)
providers: [
  { provide: EXTERNAL_STOCK_SOURCE, useClass: ErpStockAdapter },
  ErpClient,
]
// in tests: { provide: EXTERNAL_STOCK_SOURCE, useValue: fakeStockSource }

When the ERP is replaced in three years, only infrastructure/erp/ changes.

Published language in a monolith

Ordering's domain/events.ts is its published language. To keep other modules from importing anything else, add a lint rule (with eslint-plugin-import or eslint-plugin-boundaries) that allows src/*/domain/events.ts and src/*/application/*.query.ts to be imported across contexts and forbids everything else. It is a five-line config that prevents a whole class of coupling.

Production scenario

A company had 9 contexts across 4 teams. The context map lived in docs/context-map.md with the Mermaid diagram above and a table listing, per edge, the contract (event names or query class), the owner, and the versioning rule. Every quarterly planning session started by reviewing the map. When the Shipping team wanted to add estimatedDelivery to the order confirmation email, the map showed that Notifications consumed ordering.order.placed, not anything from Shipping, so the right move was a new shipping.shipment.promised event rather than stuffing shipping data into Ordering's event.

Failure scenario

The ERP integration originally had no ACL. QTYAVL flowed straight into stock_items.on_hand. Then the ERP vendor changed PKG-DZ items to report in units instead of dozens. Overnight, 3,000 SKUs showed 12x less stock than reality, the site marked them out of stock, and revenue dropped 18% for a day before anyone connected the two. With the adapter above, the change would have been a one-line edit to DOZEN_CLASSES, discovered by the adapter's contract tests against a recorded ERP response.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Shared kernel that grows. Someone adds OrderSummary to shared/ "because two contexts need it". Now two contexts are coupled through a bag of shared types. Keep the kernel to primitives-with-rules.
  • Conformist by accident. The core domain adopts a vendor's field names and the vendor's quirks become business rules. Conform only in generic contexts; ACL in core.
  • Upstream breaks the published language. Renaming an event field breaks every consumer. Add fields, never remove; version the event name (ordering.order.placed.v2) for breaking changes.
  • ACL too thin (just renames fields) or too thick (contains business rules). It should translate and validate, nothing more.
  • Partnership between teams in different time zones with no shared cadence turns into two conformists resenting each other. Name a contract owner.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

  • Every arrow on the map has an owner and a protection strategy. If they cannot name both, the arrow is a risk.
  • They put an ACL in front of anything they do not control and expect to outlive: ERPs, partner APIs, old databases.
  • They treat events and query interfaces as public APIs with versioning rules.
  • To a product manager: "Between departments we agreed on forms. If the warehouse changes its internal system, the form stays the same, so checkout keeps working."

Common mistakes

  • Importing another context's repository or ORM entity.
  • Letting a third-party SDK's types appear in domain classes.
  • Drawing the map once and never updating it.
  • Making everything a partnership, so nobody can release without everybody.

Interview questions

  1. Explain anti-corruption layer with a concrete example and what goes wrong without it. Expected: adapter plus translator around a legacy system; vendor change incident.
  2. When is conformist the right choice? Expected: generic subdomain, no leverage over upstream, low value in fighting the model.
  3. What is a shared kernel and what are its risks? Expected: small shared model; risk of growing into coupling; change only together.
  4. How do you version a published language (events) without breaking consumers? Expected: additive changes, new event names for breaking changes, consumer-driven contract tests (Part 23).

Practical exercise

Draw the context map for a system you know with at least five contexts. For every edge, write the pattern, the contract (event or interface name), the owner and the versioning rule. Then implement one ACL around one external system with a contract test that replays a recorded response. Acceptance criteria: no external type appears outside the adapter folder; the contract test fails if the external format changes; the map is checked into the repository.

7.13 Anemic vs rich domain model

Concept

An anemic domain model is one where entities are bags of getters and setters and all behaviour lives in services. A rich domain model puts behaviour and invariants on the entities and aggregates, and services only orchestrate.

Anemic is the default output of most ORM tutorials and code generators. It is not always wrong (see 7.14), but in a core subdomain it produces bugs because invariants have no owner.

Why does it exist?

The rich model exists because rules need a home. When OrderService.cancel() checks the status and RefundService.process() also checks the status and AdminController.forceCancel() forgets to, the rule "cannot cancel a fulfilled order" is enforced in some places and not others. Putting the rule in Order.cancel() means every path enforces it, and the test for the rule is a unit test on Order.

Mental model

Imagine two kinds of bank vault. In the anemic one, the vault is a box with an open lid; a guard is supposed to check every hand that reaches in, but there are eleven guards and each has their own checklist. In the rich one, the vault has one door with one lock and the rules are built into the lock; there is no way to reach in that bypasses them.

Before: anemic

// order.entity.ts (anemic)
@Entity()
export class Order {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid') id: string;
  @Column() status: string;
  @Column('bigint') totalMinor: string;
  @OneToMany(() => OrderLine, (l) => l.order, { cascade: true }) lines: OrderLine[];
  // no methods
}

// orders.service.ts (anemic: every rule lives here, and in three other services)
@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private repo: Repository<Order>, private events: EventEmitter2) {}

  async addLine(orderId: string, sku: string, qty: number, priceMinor: number) {
    const order = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { id: orderId }, relations: ['lines'] });
    if (order.status !== 'DRAFT') throw new BadRequestException('not editable');
    const line = new OrderLine(); line.sku = sku; line.quantity = qty; line.unitPriceMinor = String(priceMinor);
    order.lines.push(line);
    order.totalMinor = String(order.lines.reduce((s, l) => s + Number(l.unitPriceMinor) * l.quantity, 0)); // float risk, duplicated elsewhere
    await this.repo.save(order);
  }

  async cancel(orderId: string) {
    const order = await this.repo.findOne({ where: { id: orderId } });
    // forgot to check FULFILLED; AdminService.forceCancel has a slightly different check
    order.status = 'CANCELLED';
    await this.repo.save(order);
    this.events.emit('order.cancelled', order); // emitted after save, but not tied to a transaction
  }
}

Problems: rules scattered and inconsistent, total recomputed by hand with Number() (float), events not transactional, Order can be constructed empty, tests need a database.

After: rich

// domain/order.ts (rich; see 7.6 for the full class)
export class Order extends AggregateRoot<string> {
  addLine(sku: string, productName: string, quantity: number, unitPrice: Money): void {
    this.assertMutable('add a line');
    /* currency, max lines, one-line-per-sku invariants */
    this.lines.push(OrderLine.create(sku, productName, quantity, unitPrice));
  }
  total(): Money { return this.lines.reduce((s, l) => s.add(l.lineTotal()), Money.zero(this.currency)); }
  cancel(reason: string, now = new Date()): void {
    if (this.status === 'FULFILLED') throw new OrderStateError('Cannot cancel a fulfilled order');
    if (this.status === 'CANCELLED') return;
    const wasPaid = this.status === 'PAID';
    this.status = 'CANCELLED';
    this.raise(new OrderCancelled(this.id, reason, wasPaid, now));
  }
}

// application/cancel-order.service.ts (thin orchestration; see 7.9)
async execute(cmd: CancelOrderCommand) {
  return this.uow.run(async ({ orders }, track) => {
    const order = await orders.findByIdForUpdate(cmd.orderId);
    if (!order) throw new OrderNotFoundError(cmd.orderId);
    track(order);
    order.cancel(cmd.reason);
    await orders.save(order);
    return { orderId: order.id, status: order.currentStatus };
  });
}

Every path that cancels an order goes through Order.cancel(). The rule is tested once. The event is transactional.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They look for invariants with no owner. If the same if (status !== ...) appears in three services, the model is anemic and that check needs to move onto the aggregate. They also know when anemic is fine: a Setting entity with two fields and no rules does not need a rich model.

Common mistakes

  • "Rich" models that still have public setters, so the rules can be bypassed.
  • Moving orchestration into entities (an aggregate that calls a repository or an HTTP client). Rich means business rules, not I/O.
  • Refactoring the whole codebase to rich at once. Do it one aggregate at a time, starting with the one with the most bugs.

Interview questions

  1. What is an anemic domain model and why is it considered a problem? Expected: behaviour in services, invariants without owner, duplication and inconsistency.
  2. Show how you would move one rule from a service into an aggregate and what test changes. Expected: before/after above; unit test on the aggregate replaces DB-backed service test.
  3. Is anemic always bad? Expected: no; fine for supporting/generic CRUD.

Practical exercise

Find a service in your codebase with the same status check in two or more places. Move the rule into the entity, replace the checks with a method call, and write one unit test for the rule. Acceptance criteria: the check exists in exactly one place; the service test that needed a database is replaced by a domain unit test.

7.14 When NOT to use DDD, and DDD-lite

Concept

DDD's tactical patterns cost code: two model shapes, mappers, unit of work, events, factories. That cost is repaid when the domain is complex and long-lived. It is wasted when the domain is simple.

Do not reach for full DDD when:

  • The subdomain is CRUD-heavy. An admin tool for editing product descriptions has no invariants beyond "title required". A DTO, a validation pipe and a repository are enough.
  • The domain is unclear. In the first months of a startup, nobody knows what "order" will mean. Aggregates designed now will be wrong; keep the model thin until the language stabilises.
  • The team is small and the system is small. Three engineers and 15 tables do not need seven bounded contexts and a context map.
  • The subdomain is generic. Do not write a rich domain model for email sending.

DDD-lite

Most teams get 80% of the value from a small subset:

Practice Keep in DDD-lite? Why
Ubiquitous language, glossary Yes Free, prevents the most expensive misunderstandings
Bounded contexts as NestJS modules with narrow exports Yes Cheap, prevents the shared-table disaster
Value objects for Money, Email, Address Yes Prevents real bugs; tiny cost
Entities with behaviour methods, no public setters Yes The core of "rules have an owner"
One repository per root, no child repositories Yes Keeps invariants enforceable
Domain events after commit Yes, for anything cross-context Prevents phantom-reservation incidents
Separate domain model plus mapper Only in core Elsewhere, ORM entity with methods is fine
Unit of work abstraction Only in core Elsewhere, dataSource.transaction() in the service is fine
Full context map with all seven patterns When more than 3 teams Otherwise a paragraph in the README
CQRS, event sourcing Rarely Separate decisions with their own costs (Part 19)

Decision matrix

Signal Suggests
Many invariants, several statuses with rules, money involved Rich aggregate, separate model, unit of work
Mostly create/read/update/delete with validation ORM entity with a few methods, service, DTO
Two or more teams touching the same tables Bounded contexts with separate schemas now
One team, one deployable, under 30 tables Modules with narrow exports; skip the context map
Domain experts disagree on terms Stop designing aggregates; run glossary sessions first
Vendor or legacy system in the loop ACL regardless of anything else

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They apply DDD per subdomain, not per codebase. The Ordering module has aggregates and a unit of work; the Settings module has a controller, a service and a TypeORM entity. Both are correct. They also resist "DDD" as a folder structure: domain/, application/, infrastructure/ folders with anemic classes inside are not DDD, they are ceremony.

Common mistakes

  • Applying the full tactical pattern set to every module because a blog post said so.
  • Skipping the strategic half (boundaries, language) and doing only the tactical half.
  • Refusing DDD entirely because "we are not that complex", then rediscovering invariants scattered across 40 services two years later.

Interview questions

  1. When would you advise against DDD? Expected: CRUD-heavy, unclear domain, small team, generic subdomain; and which subset you would still keep.
  2. What is the minimum set of DDD practices you always apply? Expected: the "yes" rows above.
  3. A team of four has domain/application/infrastructure folders but all logic is in services. Is that DDD? Expected: no; explain what would make it so and whether it is even needed.

Practical exercise

Audit one module in your codebase against the DDD-lite table. For each row decide "have it", "need it", or "do not need it" with one sentence. Acceptance criteria: at least one "do not need it" with justification (over-engineering is a real finding), and at least one concrete PR proposed for a "need it".

7.15 Edge cases & failure modes for DDD

This section gathers the sharp edges that bite teams in production, with the concrete fix for each.

Aggregates that grow too big

Customer with 10 million orders as children is the classic case. Symptoms: loading a customer takes seconds, memory spikes, every order placement locks the customer row so a busy B2B customer's staff block each other.

Fix: Order is its own aggregate with customerId. If you need "customer lifetime spend" as a rule (say, a credit limit), keep a summary on the customer (outstandingBalanceMinor) updated by an event handler with its own small transaction, and accept that it can lag by milliseconds. Enforce the hard limit at payment authorisation time, not at cart time.

A useful heuristic: if you would ever need to paginate the children to display them, they are not children; they are separate aggregates.

Concurrent modification of one aggregate

Two admins edit the same draft, or a customer taps "place order" twice on two tabs. Without protection, the last write wins and one edit silently disappears.

Fix: optimistic locking. TypeORM's @VersionColumn increments on every save() and throws OptimisticLockVersionMismatchError if the loaded version is stale; or do it by hand with WHERE id = :id AND version = :version and check affected (section 7.7). Sequelize: version: true on the model, catch OptimisticLockError. Map the error to HTTP 409 and let the client reload and retry. Use pessimistic FOR UPDATE instead when conflicts are frequent and the critical section is short (stock decrement is the classic case).

// Handling the version conflict at the application layer
try {
  await orders.save(order);
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof ConcurrencyError) throw new ConflictException('Order was modified; reload and retry');
  throw err;
}

Events emitted before commit

Covered in 7.10 with the phantom reservation incident. Fix: the unit of work is the only thing that dispatches, and only after COMMIT; the outbox row is written inside the transaction for durability.

Cross-aggregate invariants

"Total reserved across all warehouses must not exceed total on hand across all warehouses" spans many StockItem aggregates. Trying to enforce it atomically means locking all of them (deadlocks, contention) or one giant Warehouse aggregate (too big).

Fix options, in order of preference:

  1. Redefine the invariant per aggregate. Reserved per (sku, warehouse) must not exceed on-hand per (sku, warehouse). Each StockItem enforces its own rule with a CHECK (reserved <= on_hand) in the database. The cross-warehouse total is then automatically satisfied.
  2. Saga / process manager. Reserve warehouse by warehouse; if one fails, release the others (compensation). Eventual consistency for a few hundred milliseconds.
  3. Reconciliation. A periodic job that compares sums and flags or repairs drift.

Never option 4: one transaction across all warehouses.

Bounded contexts sharing tables

Two contexts writing the same table means neither can change it, and a "harmless" trigger from one takes the other down (the products incident in 7.3). Fix: separate schemas, separate database roles, id references instead of foreign keys, snapshots for the fields the other context needs, events for changes.

Other sharp edges

  • Mapper drift. New column, forgotten mapper line, silent data loss. Round-trip test on every mapper.
  • Rehydration through validating constructors. Loading 10,000 orders for a report runs Address.of() validation 10,000 times; worse, a historic row that violates a newer rule cannot be loaded at all. Use rehydrate factories that skip validation for persisted state, and never use aggregates for reports (read models).
  • Domain exceptions leaking as 500s. Map domain errors to HTTP in one global filter (Part 8, section 8.9).
  • Handlers assuming ordering. OrderCancelled arrives before OrderPlaced after a partition rebalance. Handlers check current state and tolerate out-of-order.
  • A "shared" module that becomes the real domain. If src/shared/domain has more than value objects and base classes, the boundaries have collapsed.
  • Transactions spanning HTTP calls. Pool exhaustion under load (the 02:14 incident in 7.11). No external I/O inside uow.run.

Senior Checklist — Part 07

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can classify subdomains as core, supporting or generic and say what to build vs buy
  • I can draw the bounded contexts and the context map for a system I work on, with a protection pattern on every edge
  • I can explain why "Product" is three different models in Catalog, Inventory and Ordering
  • I can implement Money with integer minor units and a currency, and I refuse float money columns
  • I can design an aggregate around its invariants, keep it small, and reference other aggregates by id
  • I can write one repository per aggregate root with a mapper and optimistic locking
  • I can write an application service with a unit of work that commits first and dispatches events after
  • I can add an outbox so events survive a crash between commit and dispatch
  • I can put an anti-corruption layer around a legacy or vendor system
  • I can recognise an anemic model and move a rule onto the aggregate with a unit test
  • I can say when DDD is overkill and what DDD-lite subset I would still keep

Part 07 — Key Takeaways

  • Strategic DDD (subdomains, language, bounded contexts, context map) gives more leverage than tactical patterns; do it first and do it per subdomain.
  • Core gets the full treatment; supporting gets a clean service layer; generic gets bought or wrapped.
  • One word, one meaning, per context. "Order" is three concepts; give each its own model, table and name.
  • Each bounded context owns its data: separate schema, id references instead of cross-context foreign keys, snapshots of what it needs, events for the rest.
  • Entities have identity and lifecycle; value objects are immutable and compared by value. Money is integer minor units plus currency, never a float.
  • Aggregates are drawn around invariants, kept small, loaded whole, modified through the root, and saved in one transaction with a version column.
  • Repositories exist per aggregate root only, participate in the caller's transaction, and hide the ORM behind a mapper in the core.
  • Domain services hold rules that span aggregates; application services orchestrate load, change, save, commit, publish and never hold business rules.
  • Domain events are raised inside the aggregate, written to an outbox inside the transaction, and dispatched only after commit; every handler is idempotent.
  • Cross-aggregate rules are handled by redefining the invariant, by sagas with compensation, or by reconciliation, never by one giant transaction.
  • Wrap anything you do not control (ERP, partner API, vendor SDK) in an anti-corruption layer; conform only in generic subdomains.
  • DDD-lite (language, modules with narrow exports, value objects, behaviour on entities, root-only repositories, post-commit events) is usually enough; full ceremony belongs in the core only.

Part 8 — API Design (REST first)

An API is a contract you will be held to for years. The database schema behind it can change every sprint; the API cannot, because mobile apps stuck on last year's release and partner integrations nobody remembers are calling it right now. That asymmetry is why API design deserves more care than almost any other backend decision.

This part covers REST thoroughly, with NestJS code for everything: resource modeling, URIs, verbs, status codes, pagination, filtering, bulk operations, partial updates, versioning, errors, validation, idempotency, rate limiting, contracts, long-running operations and webhooks. It ends with a complete OrdersController and an API design review checklist. GraphQL and gRPC are covered in Part 9; the principles here (resources, idempotency, errors, versioning) carry over.

8.1 Resource modeling

Concept

A REST API exposes resources: named things a client can address and manipulate. Order, Customer, Shipment, Payment. A resource is identified by a URI and manipulated with HTTP verbs. Resources are modelled around business capabilities and the ubiquitous language (Part 7), not around database tables.

Resource kinds:

  • Collection: /orders (many orders).
  • Item: /orders/8f3c... (one order).
  • Sub-resource: /orders/8f3c.../lines (the lines that belong to that order).
  • Action as a resource: /orders/8f3c.../cancellations (the fact that a cancellation happened), created with POST, instead of an RPC-style /orders/8f3c.../cancel.

Why does it exist?

Modelling around resources gives clients a uniform interface: once they know how /orders works, they know how /shipments works. It gives caches, proxies and gateways something to reason about (a GET on a URI is cacheable; a POST is not). And it forces you to name business concepts, which is exactly the discipline that keeps an API stable while the implementation churns.

Modelling around tables, by contrast, ties the contract to the schema. Every normalisation, rename or split of a table becomes a breaking change.

Mental model

Imagine a well-run post office. There are counters (resources) with clear signs: "Parcels", "Letters", "Complaints". You do not ask the clerk to "run procedure 47 with these parameters". You go to the "Complaints" counter and file a complaint (create a complaint resource). Later you can ask "what happened to complaint 123?" (read the resource). The counters are organised by what customers want to do, not by which filing cabinet the clerk uses.

How it works

Bad, table-driven API. It exposes the schema and pushes logic to the client:

GET    /order_header?id=42
GET    /order_detail?order_header_id=42
POST   /order_header          body: { status_id: 1, cust_id: 9 }
POST   /order_detail          body: { order_header_id: 42, prod_id: 7, qty: 2 }   (repeat per line)
PUT    /order_header/42       body: { status_id: 4 }                               (client "cancels" by setting a magic number)
GET    /status_lookup                                                                (client fetches what 4 means)

Problems: five round trips to place an order; no atomicity (line 3 fails, lines 1 and 2 are orphaned); the client knows that status 4 means cancelled; renaming order_header breaks everyone; the invariant "cannot cancel a fulfilled order" is enforced by hoping the client checked.

Good, resource-driven API. It speaks the business language and keeps invariants server-side:

POST   /orders                          body: { currency, lines: [...], shippingAddress }   -> 201 + Location
GET    /orders/{id}
GET    /orders?status=PAID&cursor=...
PATCH  /orders/{id}                     body: { shippingAddress }                          (draft only)
DELETE /orders/{id}                     (draft only; placed orders are cancelled, not deleted)
POST   /orders/{id}/cancellations       body: { reason }                                   -> 201 with the cancellation
GET    /orders/{id}/cancellations       (history: who cancelled, when, why)
POST   /orders/{id}/payments            body: { method, ... }                              -> 202 (async capture)
GET    /orders/{id}/shipments

One call places an order atomically. Cancelling is creating a cancellation resource, which naturally has an id, a timestamp, a reason and an actor, and which you can list. The client never sees status codes as magic integers.

Why POST /orders/{id}/cancellations and not POST /orders/{id}/cancel? Three reasons:

  1. It is a noun. The cancellation is a thing that exists after the fact, can be looked up, and can carry data (reason, refund amount, who did it).
  2. It is idempotent-friendly. Creating a second cancellation for an already-cancelled order can return the existing one (200) instead of failing.
  3. It stays consistent. /cancel, /approve, /ship, /refund sprawl into an RPC API with a different shape per verb. Sub-resources keep one shape.

When a verb resource truly has no state to keep (a /search with a large body, a /validate that returns a result without side effects), an action endpoint is acceptable. Use it rarely and document why.

Practical example

The Ordering API's resource model, derived from the aggregate and events in Part 7:

Resource Backed by Verbs
/orders Order aggregate POST (place), GET (list)
/orders/{id} Order aggregate GET, PATCH (draft edits), DELETE (draft only)
/orders/{id}/lines OrderLine inside the aggregate POST, PATCH /{lineId}, DELETE /{lineId} (draft only)
/orders/{id}/cancellations OrderCancelled event, cancellations table POST, GET
/orders/{id}/payments Payments context via events POST (initiate), GET
/orders/{id}/shipments Shipping context read model GET

Notice that /orders/{id}/shipments is served from a read model fed by Shipping's events, not by joining into Shipping's tables. The API boundary respects the bounded context boundary.

NestJS example

The controller structure follows the resource tree. Sub-resources get their own controller with a prefix.

// src/ordering/api/orders.controller.ts (shape only; full version in 8.18)
@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  @Post() create() {}
  @Get() list() {}
  @Get(':id') getOne() {}
  @Patch(':id') update() {}
  @Delete(':id') remove() {}
}

// src/ordering/api/order-cancellations.controller.ts
@Controller('orders/:orderId/cancellations')
export class OrderCancellationsController {
  constructor(private readonly cancelOrder: CancelOrderService) {}

  @Post()
  @HttpCode(201)
  async create(@Param('orderId', ParseUUIDPipe) orderId: string, @Body() dto: CreateCancellationDto,
               @CurrentUser() user: { id: string }, @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response) {
    const result = await this.cancelOrder.execute({ orderId, reason: dto.reason, requestedBy: user.id });
    if (result.alreadyCancelled) res.status(200);   // idempotent: return the existing cancellation
    res.setHeader('Location', `/orders/${orderId}/cancellations/${result.cancellationId}`);
    return result;
  }

  @Get()
  list(@Param('orderId', ParseUUIDPipe) orderId: string) { /* history */ }
}

PostgreSQL example

Actions-as-resources usually earn their own table. It doubles as an audit log.

CREATE TABLE ordering.order_cancellations (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id      uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES ordering.orders(id),
  reason        text NOT NULL,
  requested_by  uuid NOT NULL,
  refund_minor  bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (refund_minor >= 0),
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT ux_one_cancellation_per_order UNIQUE (order_id)   -- an order is cancelled at most once
);

Production scenario

A marketplace API served 2,000 RPS across 60 resources. Because every resource followed the same shape (GET list with cursor, GET item, POST create with Idempotency-Key, sub-resources for actions), the mobile team built one generic client layer and new resources needed zero client changes. Partner onboarding time dropped from three weeks to three days because the OpenAPI document was predictable.

Failure scenario

A team exposed POST /orders/{id}/setStatus with { status: 'CANCELLED' }. The iOS app cached the status list and, after a backend change renamed CANCELLED to CANCELED (American spelling, a "harmless" cleanup), every cancel from iOS was rejected with 400 for six weeks until the app store release caught up. With POST /orders/{id}/cancellations there is no status string on the wire to break.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Resource that maps to two aggregates. /orders/{id}/shipments reads Shipping data. Serve it from a read model; do not let the Ordering controller call Shipping's repository.
  • Deeply nested URIs mirroring the object graph: /customers/{c}/orders/{o}/lines/{l}/product. Stop at two levels; orders have their own top-level collection.
  • Actions that are really queries (POST /orders/search). Acceptable when filters are too large for a query string; document it as a query.
  • Deleting vs cancelling. DELETE /orders/{id} on a placed order would erase history. Only drafts are deletable; placed orders are cancelled.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They start from the ubiquitous language and the aggregate boundaries, list the nouns, decide which are top-level collections, and turn every business verb into either a state-changing PATCH or a sub-resource POST. They ask "what will a client want to read back after doing this?" If the answer is anything (a reason, a timestamp, an actor), it is a resource.

Common mistakes

  • Generating controllers from tables.
  • /getOrder, /createOrder, /updateOrderStatus.
  • Exposing internal enums as integers.
  • One PUT /orders/{id} that accepts any field and lets the client change status, total and customerId.

Interview questions

  1. Why POST /orders/{id}/cancellations instead of POST /orders/{id}/cancel? Expected: noun, has data and history, idempotent-friendly, consistent shape.
  2. Show a table-driven API and explain what breaks when the schema changes. Expected: the bad example above; atomicity, magic values, renames.
  3. How do you expose data from another bounded context through this API? Expected: read model fed by events; no cross-context repository calls.
  4. When is an action endpoint acceptable? Expected: stateless operations like search or validate; rare and documented.

Practical exercise

Take a SHIPMENTS table with columns id, order_id, carrier_code, status_id, tracking_no, dispatched_ts, delivered_ts. Design the resource model: collection, item, sub-resources for dispatch and delivery confirmation, and a read model for tracking events. Acceptance criteria: no status integers on the wire; every state change is either a PATCH of a draft or a POST to a sub-resource; the URI tree is at most two levels deep.

8.2 URI design

Concept

A URI names a resource. Good URIs are predictable, stable and boring: plural nouns, lowercase kebab-case, no verbs, no trailing slashes, no file extensions, ids that are safe to expose.

Why does it exist?

Clients hard-code URIs. Search engines, logs, dashboards and alerting rules match on them. A URI is the most public part of your contract, and inconsistency (some singular, some plural, some camelCase) is the first thing a partner notices and the last thing you can fix.

Mental model

Imagine street addresses. "12 Baker Street" works because every street follows the same pattern. If some streets used "Baker St. #12", some "Baker-12", and some "House twelve on the road of bakers", the postal service would grind to a halt. URIs are addresses; make them uniform.

How it works

Rules, with reasons:

Rule Example Why
Plural nouns for collections /orders, /customers GET /orders reads naturally as "the orders"; /orders/{id} as "one of the orders"
Lowercase, kebab-case for multi-word /order-cancellations, /shipping-addresses URIs are case-sensitive; kebab-case survives copy-paste and is readable in logs
No verbs /orders/{id}/cancellations not /cancelOrder The verb is the HTTP method
No trailing slash /orders not /orders/ Two URIs for one resource confuse caches and routers; redirect one to the other
At most two levels of nesting /orders/{id}/lines/{lineId} Deeper paths duplicate ids and couple the client to the object graph
Query params for filters, sorts, pages /orders?status=PAID&sort=-placedAt Path is identity; query is selection
No file extensions /orders/{id} with Accept: application/json Content negotiation, not filenames
Version prefix if using URI versioning /v1/orders Section 8.11
Ids are opaque strings /orders/8f3c2b1e-... See below

Choosing ids. Three options:

Id type Example Pros Cons
Sequential integer /orders/10482 Small, fast B-tree, human-readable Leaks volume ("they have 10k orders"); enumerable (/orders/10483); requires DB round trip before you know the id
UUID v4 /orders/8f3c2b1e-4a5b-... Generated anywhere, not enumerable, no volume leak 36 chars; random inserts fragment B-trees (UUID v7 / ULID fix this by being time-ordered)
Public id / prefixed id /orders/ord_7Yq3kLp2Xz Self-describing, short, not enumerable, internal id can change Needs a mapping or a generator; must be unique-indexed

Recommendation: internal primary key can be uuid (v7 if your PostgreSQL stack supports it, otherwise v4), and the API exposes the same value. If you want Stripe-style prefixed ids (ord_, cus_), store them as a separate unique column. Never expose sequential integers for anything a user could enumerate (orders, invoices, users).

NestJS example

Enforce the rules mechanically. A ParseUUIDPipe on every id param rejects junk before it reaches the service, and a global prefix plus versioning is set once in main.ts.

// src/main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { VersioningType } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  app.setGlobalPrefix('api');
  app.enableVersioning({ type: VersioningType.URI, defaultVersion: '1' }); // /api/v1/orders
  await app.listen(3000);
}
bootstrap();

// src/ordering/api/order-lines.controller.ts
@Controller('orders/:orderId/lines')
export class OrderLinesController {
  @Patch(':lineId')
  changeQuantity(
    @Param('orderId', new ParseUUIDPipe({ version: '4' })) orderId: string,
    @Param('lineId', new ParseUUIDPipe({ version: '4' })) lineId: string,
    @Body() dto: ChangeQuantityDto,
  ) { /* ... */ }
}

Express (NestJS's default adapter) treats /orders and /orders/ as the same route by default (strict routing off). Keep it that way, and make sure your gateway does not add or strip slashes inconsistently.

PostgreSQL example

Time-ordered UUIDs avoid the random-insert problem. PostgreSQL 17 does not ship a UUID v7 generator natively (it arrives in 18 as uuidv7()); until then generate in the application (uuidv7 npm package) or with a small SQL function. The difference matters at scale:

-- Random UUID v4 primary key: inserts land on random leaf pages, cache misses, index bloat.
-- Time-ordered UUID v7 primary key: inserts append to the right-hand leaf, like a serial.
-- Measured on a 50M-row orders table: v4 insert throughput ~35% lower than v7, index 20% larger.

CREATE TABLE ordering.orders (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY,           -- v7 generated by the app
  public_id  text NOT NULL UNIQUE,       -- optional: 'ord_7Yq3kLp2Xz' for the API
  ...
);
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_public_id ON ordering.orders (public_id);

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Case sensitivity. /Orders and /orders are different URIs. Enforce lowercase at the gateway with a redirect.
  • URL-encoded ids with slashes or spaces. Reject ids that do not match the expected pattern.
  • Id enumeration attacks. GET /orders/10483 with someone else's order. Non-enumerable ids reduce the blast radius; authorisation is still required (Part 21 — Security).
  • Very long query strings (> 8 KB) rejected by proxies. Move large filters to POST /orders/search.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They write the URI table before the code and review it with the mobile and partner teams. They pick UUIDs or prefixed ids by default and reserve integers for internal joins. They put lint rules or an OpenAPI linter (Spectral) in CI to catch camelCase paths and verbs.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing /order/{id} and /orders.
  • /api/v1/getOrderById?id=42.
  • Exposing auto-increment ids and then discovering a competitor scraped growth numbers.
  • /orders/{id}/ with a trailing slash returning 404 on one router and 200 on another.

Interview questions

  1. UUID vs sequential integer vs public id for API identifiers? Expected: the table above; enumeration, volume leak, B-tree behaviour, v7/ULID.
  2. How deep should URI nesting go and why? Expected: two levels; deeper duplicates ids and couples clients.
  3. Why no verbs in URIs? Expected: method is the verb; uniform interface; caching.

Practical exercise

Write an OpenAPI linter config (Spectral) that fails on: verbs in paths, uppercase letters, trailing slashes, nesting deeper than two levels, path params not matching a UUID or prefixed-id pattern. Run it against an existing spec. Acceptance criteria: at least five real violations found and fixed; the linter runs in CI.

8.3 HTTP verbs

Concept

HTTP methods carry standard semantics that clients, caches, proxies and retries depend on:

Method Meaning Safe (no side effects) Idempotent (repeat = same result) Request body Typical response
GET Read a resource Yes Yes No 200, 404
HEAD Headers only Yes Yes No 200
OPTIONS Capabilities, CORS preflight Yes Yes No 204
POST Create, or non-idempotent action No No Yes 201, 202, 200
PUT Replace the whole resource No Yes Yes 200, 204, 201
PATCH Partial update No Not by default (can be made so) Yes 200
DELETE Remove No Yes Usually no 204, 404, 409

Safe means the client can call it without changing anything; browsers prefetch and caches store safe responses. Idempotent means calling it N times has the same effect as once; a client or proxy can retry it without fear.

Why does it exist?

Retries. Every network call can time out with the server having done the work. If the client knows the method is idempotent, it can retry blindly. If not, it must not, unless the server gives it a way (an Idempotency-Key, section 8.12). Getting verbs right is what makes reliable clients possible.

Mental model

Imagine a vending machine. Looking at the display (GET) is safe; do it all day. Pressing "return coins" (DELETE) twice returns the coins once; idempotent. Inserting a coin (POST) twice inserts two coins; not idempotent, so if you are not sure the first coin registered, you need a receipt (idempotency key) before inserting another.

How it works

PUT vs PATCH. PUT /orders/{id}/shipping-address with a full address replaces the address entirely: omitted fields become null. PATCH /orders/{id} with { "shippingAddress": { "line2": "Flat 4" } } changes only line2. PUT is idempotent by definition; PATCH is idempotent only if the patch is absolute ("set quantity to 3") and not relative ("increase quantity by 1"). Prefer absolute patches. Section 8.8 covers JSON Merge Patch vs JSON Patch.

POST for creation. Creating a new order must mint a new id, so POST /orders is not idempotent by default. Two ways to make creation safe to retry: (a) client-supplied ids with PUT /orders/{clientGeneratedUuid} (idempotent by construction), or (b) POST with an Idempotency-Key header. Most public APIs use (b).

DELETE semantics. The first DELETE returns 204; a repeat may return 404 (resource gone) or 204 (still gone, which is the more retry-friendly choice). Both are idempotent: the end state is the same.

NestJS example

Method decorators map one to one. Note @HttpCode where the default (200 for everything except POST, which defaults to 201) is wrong.

@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  @Get(':id')                       // safe, idempotent, cacheable
  getOne(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) { /* ... */ }

  @Post()                           // non-idempotent by default; Idempotency-Key makes it safe (8.12)
  @HttpCode(201)
  create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto) { /* ... */ }

  @Put(':id/shipping-address')      // replace whole sub-resource; idempotent
  @HttpCode(200)
  replaceAddress(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string, @Body() dto: AddressDto) { /* ... */ }

  @Patch(':id')                     // partial; keep patches absolute so repeats are harmless
  update(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string, @Body() dto: UpdateOrderDto) { /* ... */ }

  @Delete(':id')                    // idempotent; second call also 204
  @HttpCode(204)
  async remove(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) {
    await this.deleteDraft.execute({ orderId: id }); // no-op if already gone
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

Idempotent DELETE and PUT at the SQL level:

-- DELETE: affected rows 0 on repeat is fine; still return 204.
DELETE FROM ordering.orders WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'DRAFT';

-- PUT replace-address: same statement, same end state on repeat.
UPDATE ordering.orders
SET ship_line1 = $2, ship_line2 = $3, ship_city = $4, ship_postal_code = $5, ship_country = $6,
    updated_at = now(), version = version + 1
WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'DRAFT';

-- PATCH relative update is NOT idempotent; avoid on retryable paths:
-- UPDATE order_lines SET quantity = quantity + 1 WHERE id = $1;
-- Absolute is:
UPDATE ordering.order_lines SET quantity = $2 WHERE id = $1;

Failure scenario

A mobile app used POST /cart/items to add items and retried on timeout. At 19:00 on a Friday the API's p99 crossed the app's 5-second timeout, so every add was retried once or twice. Carts filled with duplicate lines; 4% of orders that evening had double quantities, and the refund queue took two days to clear. The fix was twofold: PUT /cart/items/{sku} with an absolute quantity (idempotent by design), and Idempotency-Key on POST /orders.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • GET with side effects (GET /orders/{id}/cancel). Crawlers and prefetchers will trigger it. Never.
  • POST used for everything because "it is easier". Clients cannot retry anything safely.
  • PATCH with relative operations on retryable paths.
  • DELETE with a body. Many proxies drop it. Put parameters in the query string or use a sub-resource.
  • HEAD not mirroring GET headers (Content-Length, ETag) confuses download managers and caches.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

For every endpoint they ask: Can it timeout? Can it fail? Can it duplicate? Can it partially succeed? Then they pick the method whose semantics tell the truth, and they add an idempotency key wherever the method alone cannot make retries safe. They refuse GET with side effects and POST for reads with no justification.

Common mistakes

  • POST /orders/{id}/get.
  • PUT that only updates the provided fields (that is PATCH).
  • Returning 200 with { success: false } on a DELETE failure.
  • Relying on PATCH being idempotent without checking the operations are absolute.

Interview questions

  1. Define safe and idempotent; give an HTTP method that is idempotent but not safe. Expected: DELETE, PUT.
  2. Is PATCH idempotent? Expected: not by definition; absolute patches are; relative are not; design accordingly.
  3. How do you make POST creation safe to retry? Expected: client-generated id with PUT, or Idempotency-Key.
  4. Second DELETE on the same resource: 204 or 404? Expected: both valid; 204 is more retry-friendly; be consistent.

Practical exercise

Audit ten endpoints in a codebase. For each, record method, whether it is actually safe/idempotent as implemented, and what a client retry would do. Fix at least two mismatches. Acceptance criteria: every GET is side-effect free; every PUT/DELETE is provably idempotent in SQL; every non-idempotent POST either has an idempotency key or a documented reason not to.

8.4 Status codes

Concept

The status code is the first thing a client reads. It decides whether to parse the body as a result or as an error, whether to retry, whether to re-authenticate, whether to back off. Using the right code is not pedantry; it is the difference between a client that self-heals and one that pages you.

Why does it exist?

Generic clients (SDKs, gateways, browsers, monitoring) act on the code without reading your documentation. A 401 triggers token refresh; a 429 triggers backoff with Retry-After; a 503 is retried; a 400 is not. Return 200 with { "error": ... } and none of that works, and your dashboards say everything is fine while customers cannot pay.

Mental model

Imagine traffic lights. Green (2xx): proceed. Amber (3xx): change course. Red with a "you" sign (4xx): you did something wrong, fix it before trying again. Red with a "road closed" sign (5xx): not your fault, try another time. A driver who gets a green light with a note saying "actually the bridge is out" will crash.

How it works

The decision, as a flowchart:

flowchart TB
  S["Request handled"] --> A{"Auth present and valid?"}
  A -->|no| C401["401 Unauthorized"]
  A -->|yes| B{"Allowed for this user?"}
  B -->|no| C403["403 Forbidden"]
  B -->|yes| D{"Body or params well formed?"}
  D -->|no| C400["400 Bad Request"]
  D -->|yes| E{"Semantically valid?"}
  E -->|no| C422["422 Unprocessable Content"]
  E -->|yes| F{"Resource exists?"}
  F -->|no| C404["404 Not Found"]
  F -->|yes| G{"State allows it?"}
  G -->|no| C409["409 Conflict"]
  G -->|yes| H{"Completed now?"}
  H -->|"no, queued"| C202["202 Accepted"]
  H -->|"yes, created"| C201["201 Created"]
  H -->|"yes, no body"| C204["204 No Content"]
  H -->|"yes, body"| C200["200 OK"]

The full table for our API:

Situation Code Notes
Read succeeded 200 Body is the resource
Created synchronously 201 Location header points to the new resource
Accepted for async processing 202 Body or Location points to a status resource (8.16)
Succeeded, nothing to return 204 DELETE, some PUT
Idempotent replay of a create 200 Same resource as before; some APIs use 201 again; be consistent
Malformed JSON, wrong types, missing required field 400 Syntax/shape problem
Valid shape, invalid meaning (unknown SKU, quantity above stock, bad state transition data) 422 Semantic problem; the client must change the content
Not authenticated / token expired 401 Include WWW-Authenticate
Authenticated but not permitted 403 Do not reveal whether the resource exists if that leaks data; some APIs return 404 instead
Resource missing 404 Also for resources the user may not know exist
Method not supported on this resource 405 With Allow header
Cannot satisfy Accept 406
State conflict (cancel a fulfilled order), optimistic lock mismatch, duplicate unique key 409 Body says which
Precondition failed (If-Match mismatch) 412 Section 8.8
Payload too large 413 Section 8.19
Unsupported media type 415 Client sent XML
Rate limited 429 Retry-After header
Unexpected server error 500 Never leak details; correlation id in body
Upstream (payment provider, catalog service) failed or timed out 502 / 504 Client may retry with backoff
Overloaded or in maintenance 503 Retry-After

400 vs 422. Use 400 when the request could not be understood: broken JSON, quantity: "two", missing currency. Use 422 when it was understood but cannot be processed: sku does not exist, countryCode is not served, promotion expired. Both mean "do not retry unchanged". The distinction helps client developers know whether the bug is in serialisation or in business data.

409 vs 422. 409 is about state: the request would be fine if the resource were in a different state (cancelling a fulfilled order, version mismatch, duplicate key). 422 is about content: the request would never be fine.

202 for async. When placing a payment takes seconds (3-D Secure, bank calls), return 202 with a Location of a status resource the client can poll, or a webhook registration. Section 8.16.

NestJS example

NestJS ships the HttpException family. Use them from controllers and guards; map domain errors to them in one global filter (8.9). Never throw new Error('not found') from a controller.

import {
  BadRequestException, UnauthorizedException, ForbiddenException, NotFoundException,
  ConflictException, UnprocessableEntityException, PayloadTooLargeException,
  ServiceUnavailableException, GatewayTimeoutException, HttpException, HttpStatus,
} from '@nestjs/common';

// Direct use in a controller/guard (rare; most mapping happens in the filter):
if (!user) throw new UnauthorizedException();                        // 401
if (!can(user, 'orders:read', order)) throw new ForbiddenException(); // 403
if (!order) throw new NotFoundException(`Order ${id} not found`);    // 404

// Custom with explicit status and a structured body:
throw new HttpException(
  { type: 'https://errors.example.com/order-not-cancellable', title: 'Order cannot be cancelled', status: 409 },
  HttpStatus.CONFLICT,
);

// 202 for async work:
@Post(':id/payments')
@HttpCode(202)
async initiatePayment(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string, @Body() dto: InitiatePaymentDto,
                      @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response) {
  const { paymentId } = await this.initiate.execute({ orderId: id, ...dto });
  res.setHeader('Location', `/api/v1/payments/${paymentId}`);
  return { paymentId, status: 'PENDING' };
}

The mapping from domain errors (Part 7) to HTTP, applied by the filter in 8.9:

Domain error HTTP
OrderNotFoundError 404
OrderStateError (bad transition) 409
ConcurrencyError (version mismatch) 409
DuplicateIdempotencyKeyError (payload mismatch) 422
OrderInvariantError, UnknownSkuError, InsufficientStockError 422
CustomerBlockedError 403
ErpUnavailableError, catalog timeout 503 / 504
Anything else 500

Production scenario

An API gateway retried any 5xx up to three times with jittered backoff and never retried 4xx. Because the app returned 503 for "payment provider timed out" and 422 for "card declined", the gateway automatically retried the transient failures (which succeeded 70% of the time on retry) and never retried declines. When the app briefly returned 500 for declines due to a bug, the gateway retried each decline three times, tripling load on the provider and triggering their rate limit. Status codes are control signals for the whole chain.

Failure scenario

At 10:05 the checkout success rate dashboard showed 99.8%, while support tickets said "cannot pay". The API returned 200 { "ok": false, "message": "payment failed" } on decline and on provider outage alike. The dashboard counted 200s. The provider had been down for 40 minutes. After the fix (503 for provider failures, 422 for declines, 200 only for success), the same outage would have paged within two minutes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • 200 for errors. Monitoring, retries and caches all lie.
  • 500 for client errors. Gateways retry them; load triples during a bad deploy.
  • 404 vs 403 information leak. Returning 403 for an order that exists but is not yours tells an attacker the id is valid. For sensitive resources, return 404 for both.
  • 201 without Location. Clients cannot find what they created.
  • 204 with a body. Some HTTP stacks choke. @HttpCode(204) and return nothing.
  • 429 without Retry-After. Clients retry immediately and make it worse.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They can name the code for any situation without thinking, and they make sure the gateway's retry policy, the SDK's retry policy and the app's codes agree. They treat a wrong code as a bug with the same priority as wrong data, because downstream automation depends on it.

Common mistakes

  • Wrapping every response in { success, data, error } with status 200.
  • Using 400 for everything from bad JSON to "order already shipped".
  • Throwing raw Error from services and letting NestJS turn it into a 500 with a stack trace in development mode that leaks in production.

Interview questions

  1. 400 vs 422 vs 409: give one example of each in an order API. Expected: malformed JSON; unknown SKU; cancelling a fulfilled order or version mismatch.
  2. Why does returning 200 with an error body cause operational problems? Expected: retries, caches, monitoring, SDK behaviour.
  3. When do you return 202 and what must accompany it? Expected: async work; Location of a status resource or a webhook.
  4. 403 or 404 for someone else's order? Expected: depends on leak tolerance; 404 hides existence; be consistent.

Practical exercise

Write a Jest e2e test suite for POST /orders and POST /orders/{id}/cancellations that asserts the exact status for: malformed JSON, missing currency, unknown SKU, blocked customer, unknown order, cancelling a fulfilled order, version conflict, catalog timeout. Acceptance criteria: eight distinct assertions, at least six distinct status codes, and no test accepts "any 4xx".

8.5 Pagination

Concept

Pagination splits a large collection into pages a client can fetch one at a time. Two families:

  • Offset pagination: GET /orders?limit=20&offset=400 (or page=21). The client asks for "rows 401 to 420". Simple, supports "jump to page N" and total counts, and gets slower the further you go.
  • Cursor (keyset) pagination: GET /orders?limit=20&cursor=eyJ.... The client says "give me 20 rows after the last one I saw". The cursor encodes the sort key of the last row. Constant cost per page regardless of depth, stable under inserts, no "jump to page N".

Why does it exist?

GET /orders on a 50-million-row table without pagination is a denial-of-service against yourself: the database scans and sorts everything, Node serialises hundreds of megabytes of JSON, and the client's parser dies. Pagination bounds the work per request. Cursor pagination additionally bounds the work per page no matter how deep the client goes, which is what keeps the 10,000th page as cheap as the first.

Mental model

Imagine a paper phone book. Offset pagination is "open to page 400 and read 20 names": to find page 400 you count through 399 pages every time. Cursor pagination is a bookmark: "start after 'Patel, Rahul' and read 20 names". The book falls open at the bookmark instantly, and if a new name is inserted earlier in the book, your bookmark still points at the right place.

How it works

Offset, what the database does:

SELECT * FROM ordering.orders
WHERE customer_id = $1
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000;

PostgreSQL must walk the index (or sort the heap) through 200,020 rows and discard 200,000. Cost grows linearly with offset. On a 50M-row table:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM ordering.orders ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000;

Limit  (cost=8412.33..8413.17 rows=20 width=312) (actual time=182.410..182.437 rows=20 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=61234 read=13890
  ->  Index Scan Backward using ix_orders_created_id on orders
        (cost=0.56..2103417.02 rows=50000000 width=312) (actual time=0.031..171.884 rows=200020 loops=1)
        Buffers: shared hit=61234 read=13890
Planning Time: 0.140 ms
Execution Time: 182.468 ms

200,020 rows read to return 20; 75,000 buffer pages touched; 182 ms. Page 1 of the same query is 0.05 ms. Page 500,000 would be seconds. Under load this is what takes the database down: one analytics client paging through everything.

The total-count problem. Offset UIs want "page 21 of 2,500", which needs SELECT count(*). On a big table with a WHERE, that is a full index or heap scan (hundreds of ms to seconds) on every page request. Options: cache the count for a minute; return an estimate from pg_class.reltuples or EXPLAIN; return hasMore instead of a total; or drop totals entirely (which is what cursor APIs do).

Cursor / keyset, what the database does:

SELECT * FROM ordering.orders
WHERE customer_id = $1
  AND (created_at, id) < ($2, $3)          -- row comparison: strictly after the cursor row
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 21;                                  -- fetch one extra to know if there is a next page

With an index on (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC), PostgreSQL seeks directly to the cursor position and reads 21 rows, whatever the depth:

Limit  (cost=0.56..24.91 rows=21 width=312) (actual time=0.038..0.071 rows=21 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=6
  ->  Index Scan using ix_orders_customer_created_id on orders
        (cost=0.56..57934.10 rows=49978 width=312) (actual time=0.036..0.066 rows=21 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((customer_id = $1) AND (ROW(created_at, id) < ROW($2, $3)))
        Buffers: shared hit=6
Execution Time: 0.092 ms

Six buffer pages instead of 75,000. That is the whole argument.

Why the composite (created_at, id)? Because created_at is not unique: two orders can share a timestamp, and paging by created_at < $2 alone would skip or repeat them. Adding the unique id as a tiebreaker makes the ordering total and the cursor unambiguous. The row-value comparison (created_at, id) < ($2, $3) is exactly "later rows in the sort order" and PostgreSQL can use the composite index for it directly.

The flow:

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant API as OrdersController
  participant Q as OrdersQuery
  participant PG as PostgreSQL
  C->>API: GET /orders?limit=20
  API->>Q: list(limit 21, cursor null)
  Q->>PG: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 21
