  1. Compare URI, header and media-type versioning. Expected: the table; visibility, caching, routing, tooling.
  2. What changes require a new version and what do not? Expected: removing/renaming/retyping/meaning change vs additive.
  3. How do you sunset a version safely? Expected: deprecation headers, usage dashboard, notice period, 410 with migration link.
  4. A field's meaning must change but its name stays. What do you do? Expected: new field name or new version; never silent semantic change.

Practical exercise

Add a v2 of GET /orders/{id} that returns total as { amount, currency } while v1 keeps totalPaise, both served by one query service. Add the deprecation interceptor to v1 and a per-version request counter metric. Acceptance criteria: both versions pass e2e tests against the same database row; v1 responses carry Deprecation, Sunset and Link headers; /api/orders/{id} without a version returns v2; a Grafana-style query (or a log aggregation) can show calls per version per API key.

8.12 Idempotency

Concept

An idempotent operation produces the same result no matter how many times it is applied. For HTTP, GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST is not. The Idempotency-Key pattern makes POST safe to retry: the client sends a unique key per logical operation; the server remembers the key and the response; a repeat with the same key returns the stored response instead of doing the work again.

The pattern is standard practice at Stripe, Adyen, Razorpay and most payment and ordering APIs, and there is an IETF draft (Idempotency-Key header) describing it.

Why does it exist?

Networks lose responses. The server charges the card, commits the order, and the response is lost in a proxy timeout. The client sees an error and retries. Without idempotency the customer is charged twice or has two orders. With it, the retry returns the first order. Every endpoint that creates money movement or a unique business event needs this: payments, order placement, refunds, transfers, sending a message, creating a shipment.

Mental model

Imagine handing a bank teller a deposit slip with a serial number. If you are unsure whether the first slip was processed and hand over a copy with the same serial, the teller checks the log, sees the serial, and hands you the original receipt instead of depositing again. A slip with a new serial is a new deposit.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant I as IdempotencyInterceptor
  participant R as Redis
  participant H as Handler
  participant PG as PostgreSQL
  C->>I: POST /orders with Idempotency-Key K
  I->>I: fingerprint = sha256 of method path user body
  I->>R: SET idem:user:K in-progress NX PX 60000
  alt key is new
    R-->>I: OK
    I->>H: run handler
    H->>PG: transaction commit
    H-->>I: 201 body
    I->>R: SET idem:user:K completed status body fingerprint PX 86400000
    I-->>C: 201 body
  else key exists and completed with same fingerprint
    R-->>I: existing record
    I-->>C: replay stored status and body plus Idempotent-Replayed true
  else key exists and completed with different fingerprint
    I-->>C: 422 idempotency key reused
  else key exists and still in progress
    I-->>C: 409 request in progress with Retry-After 1
  end

Design decisions:

  1. Scope the key to the authenticated principal (user:K or apiKey:K). Two customers may both send K=1.
  2. Fingerprint the request (method, path, canonicalised body hash). A replay with the same key but different body is a client bug; return 422, never execute it.
  3. Reserve the key atomically before doing the work. Redis SET key value NX PX ttl or a PostgreSQL INSERT into a table with a unique constraint. This is what stops two concurrent identical requests from both executing.
  4. Store the response (status, headers you care about, body) after the handler completes. TTL of 24 hours is conventional; payments often keep 7 days.
  5. Replay exactly: same status, same body, plus a header (Idempotent-Replayed: true) so clients and logs can tell.
  6. On handler failure with a 5xx, delete the reservation so the client can retry and actually execute. On 4xx, store the error too; a retry with the same broken payload should get the same answer.
  7. Concurrent duplicate (key reserved, work in progress): return 409 with Retry-After: 1. The client waits and retries; by then the response is stored.

Redis vs PostgreSQL for the store:

Redis PostgreSQL
Atomic reservation SET NX PX INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING under a unique index
Latency ~0.3 ms ~1 to 2 ms
TTL Native Cron delete or partitioned table
Survives Redis restart Only with persistence; a lost key means a possible duplicate Yes
Same transaction as the business write No (two systems) Yes: the key row and the order row commit together
Use when Volume is high, and the business write already has its own unique constraint as a backstop Money movement where losing a key is unacceptable, or no Redis in the stack

The belt-and-braces approach used in Part 7's PlaceOrder: the interceptor in Redis for fast replay, plus UNIQUE (customer_id, idempotency_key) on the orders row as the durable guarantee.

NestJS example

An interceptor with Redis (ioredis), a decorator to opt endpoints in, and request fingerprinting.

// src/shared/api/idempotent.decorator.ts
import { SetMetadata } from '@nestjs/common';
export const IDEMPOTENT_KEY = 'idempotent';
export const Idempotent = (opts: { ttlSeconds?: number } = {}) => SetMetadata(IDEMPOTENT_KEY, { ttlSeconds: 86_400, ...opts });
// src/shared/api/idempotency.interceptor.ts
import {
  BadRequestException, CallHandler, ConflictException, ExecutionContext, HttpException, Injectable, NestInterceptor,
  UnprocessableEntityException,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { Observable, from, of, throwError } from 'rxjs';
import { catchError, mergeMap, tap } from 'rxjs/operators';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import Redis from 'ioredis';
import { IDEMPOTENT_KEY } from './idempotent.decorator';

interface StoredResponse { state: 'in-progress' | 'completed'; fingerprint: string; status?: number; body?: unknown; }

@Injectable()
export class IdempotencyInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(private readonly redis: Redis, private readonly reflector: Reflector) {}

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const opts = this.reflector.get<{ ttlSeconds: number } | undefined>(IDEMPOTENT_KEY, ctx.getHandler());
    if (!opts) return next.handle();

    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse();
    const key: string | undefined = req.headers['idempotency-key'];
    if (!key || key.length > 128) throw new BadRequestException('Idempotency-Key header is required (1-128 chars)');

    const principal = req.user?.id ?? req.apiKeyId;
    if (!principal) throw new BadRequestException('Idempotency requires an authenticated principal');
    const redisKey = `idem:${principal}:${key}`;
    const fingerprint = fingerprintOf(req.method, req.route?.path ?? req.path, req.body);

    return from(this.reserve(redisKey, fingerprint)).pipe(
      mergeMap((existing) => {
        if (!existing) {
          // We own the key. Run the handler, then store the outcome.
          return next.handle().pipe(
            tap(async (body) => {
              const status = res.statusCode ?? 200;
              await this.store(redisKey, { state: 'completed', fingerprint, status, body }, opts.ttlSeconds);
            }),
            catchError((err) => from(this.onError(redisKey, fingerprint, err, opts.ttlSeconds)).pipe(mergeMap(() => throwError(() => err)))),
          );
        }
        if (existing.fingerprint !== fingerprint) {
          throw new UnprocessableEntityException({ code: 'IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED', message: 'Idempotency-Key was already used with a different request' });
        }
        if (existing.state === 'in-progress') {
          res.setHeader('Retry-After', '1');
          throw new ConflictException({ code: 'REQUEST_IN_PROGRESS', message: 'A request with this Idempotency-Key is still being processed' });
        }
        // Replay.
        res.status(existing.status!);
        res.setHeader('Idempotent-Replayed', 'true');
        return of(existing.body);
      }),
    );
  }

  /** Returns null if we reserved the key, or the existing record otherwise. Atomic via SET NX. */
  private async reserve(redisKey: string, fingerprint: string): Promise<StoredResponse | null> {
    const placeholder: StoredResponse = { state: 'in-progress', fingerprint };
    const ok = await this.redis.set(redisKey, JSON.stringify(placeholder), 'PX', 60_000, 'NX');
    if (ok === 'OK') return null;
    const raw = await this.redis.get(redisKey);
    return raw ? (JSON.parse(raw) as StoredResponse) : null;   // expired between SET and GET: treat as new on retry
  }

  private async store(redisKey: string, rec: StoredResponse, ttlSeconds: number): Promise<void> {
    await this.redis.set(redisKey, JSON.stringify(rec), 'EX', ttlSeconds);
  }

  private async onError(redisKey: string, fingerprint: string, err: unknown, ttlSeconds: number): Promise<void> {
    const status = err instanceof HttpException ? err.getStatus() : 500;
    if (status >= 500) { await this.redis.del(redisKey); return; }            // let the client retry for real
    const body = err instanceof HttpException ? err.getResponse() : { message: 'error' };
    await this.store(redisKey, { state: 'completed', fingerprint, status, body }, ttlSeconds);  // deterministic 4xx replays
  }
}

function fingerprintOf(method: string, path: string, body: unknown): string {
  return createHash('sha256').update(`${method}\n${path}\n${canonical(body)}`).digest('hex');
}
/** Stable JSON: sorted keys so { a, b } and { b, a } fingerprint the same. */
function canonical(v: unknown): string {
  if (Array.isArray(v)) return `[${v.map(canonical).join(',')}]`;
  if (v && typeof v === 'object') {
    return `{${Object.keys(v as object).sort().map((k) => `${JSON.stringify(k)}:${canonical((v as Record<string, unknown>)[k])}`).join(',')}}`;
  }
  return JSON.stringify(v);
}

Usage:

@Post()
@HttpCode(201)
@Idempotent({ ttlSeconds: 86_400 })
@UseInterceptors(IdempotencyInterceptor)
create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto) { /* ... */ }

Note the ordering: the interceptor must run after authentication (it needs req.user) and before the handler. NestJS runs guards, then interceptors, then pipes, then the handler; so a JwtAuthGuard on the controller satisfies that. Also note res.statusCode inside tap: because @HttpCode(201) is applied by NestJS before the handler's result is sent, the value is correct when tap runs.

PostgreSQL example

The durable variant, when Redis is not acceptable as the source of truth. The reservation is an insert with a unique index; the response is stored on the same row; the business write can share the transaction.

CREATE TABLE ops.idempotency_keys (
  principal_id     text NOT NULL,
  idem_key         text NOT NULL,
  fingerprint      char(64) NOT NULL,
  state            text NOT NULL CHECK (state IN ('in-progress', 'completed')),
  response_status  smallint,
  response_body    jsonb,
  locked_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() + interval '24 hours',
  PRIMARY KEY (principal_id, idem_key)
);
CREATE INDEX ix_idem_expires ON ops.idempotency_keys (expires_at);   -- for the cleanup job

-- Reserve (atomic). Zero rows returned means someone else holds the key.
INSERT INTO ops.idempotency_keys (principal_id, idem_key, fingerprint, state)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, 'in-progress')
ON CONFLICT (principal_id, idem_key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING principal_id;

-- Complete, in the same transaction as the order insert:
UPDATE ops.idempotency_keys
SET state = 'completed', response_status = $4, response_body = $5
WHERE principal_id = $1 AND idem_key = $2;

-- Stale in-progress reservations (process died mid-request) are released by a job:
DELETE FROM ops.idempotency_keys WHERE state = 'in-progress' AND locked_at < now() - interval '2 minutes';
DELETE FROM ops.idempotency_keys WHERE expires_at < now();

Which endpoints need it

Endpoint Idempotency-Key? Why
POST /orders Yes Duplicate orders cost money and trust
POST /orders/{id}/payments Yes, mandatory Double charge
POST /refunds Yes, mandatory Double refund
POST /orders/{id}/cancellations Optional; naturally idempotent via unique constraint Second cancel returns the first
POST /notifications Yes Duplicate emails/SMS
POST /inventory/adjustments/batch Per item (8.7) Retried batch
PUT, DELETE, GET No Already idempotent
POST /orders/search No Read-only

Production scenario

An ordering API at 15 orders/s peak saw a 1.8% retry rate from mobile clients (flaky networks). Before idempotency keys that was roughly 1,000 duplicate orders a week, each needing a refund and a support touch. After: zero duplicates; 1.8% of POST /orders responses carried Idempotent-Replayed: true; Redis handled the extra ~30 operations per second without noticing. The interceptor added about 0.8 ms per request.

Failure scenario

At 21:10 during a sale, Redis was restarted by an operator to apply a config change, losing in-memory keys (no AOF). For the next 60 seconds, retried POST /orders requests found no key and executed again. The UNIQUE (customer_id, idempotency_key) constraint on orders caught all 43 of them as 23505 unique violations, which the repository turned into a re-read of the existing order. No duplicates. This is why the durable backstop exists even when Redis is the fast path.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Same key, different payload. Reject with 422; never execute the second.
  • Concurrent duplicates. SET NX makes exactly one winner; the other gets 409 and retries after a second.
  • Process crash after reservation, before storing the response. The 60-second in-progress TTL (or the 2-minute cleanup) releases the key; the client's retry executes; the business unique constraint prevents a duplicate if the first actually committed.
  • Response stored but business transaction rolled back (store-before-commit bug). Store only after the handler returns, which is after commit in the unit-of-work design from Part 7.
  • Key reuse across endpoints. The fingerprint includes method and path, so reuse yields 422.
  • Huge stored bodies. Cap stored response size (for example 64 KB); for bigger ones store a reference (the created resource id) and re-fetch on replay.
  • Clock skew is not an issue for TTLs in Redis (server-side clock), but is for signed requests (8.19).
  • Client generates keys badly (same key for every request). Document: one UUID v4 per logical operation, reused only for retries of that operation.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They make idempotency mandatory on any endpoint that moves money or creates a business event, reserve the key atomically before doing work, fingerprint the payload, replay faithfully, and keep a database unique constraint as the last line of defence. They document the client contract in three sentences and put it in the OpenAPI description of the header.

Common mistakes

  • Checking "does the key exist" and then inserting, without atomic reservation.
  • Storing the response before the transaction commits.
  • Ignoring the payload; a client bug then returns a wrong order as if it were the new one.
  • Making the key optional on payments.
  • In-memory Map for keys, which does not work with two pods.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through the Idempotency-Key flow including concurrent duplicates and a crash mid-request. Expected: the diagram; SET NX; TTLs; durable constraint.
  2. Where do you store keys and why? Expected: Redis fast path vs PostgreSQL durable; both in critical paths.
  3. Same key, different body: what do you return? Expected: 422, never execute.
  4. Which endpoints must have idempotency and which must not? Expected: the table; reads and already-idempotent verbs excluded.
  5. How does the interceptor know the response status to store? Expected: res.statusCode after @HttpCode; or handler returns a tuple; store after completion.

Practical exercise

Implement the interceptor with Redis and the PostgreSQL backstop, then run three tests: 50 concurrent identical POST /orders (expect 1 executed, 49 replays or 409s that then replay), same key with a different body (422), and a simulated handler crash (throw 500) followed by a retry that executes. Acceptance criteria: exactly one order row; replays carry Idempotent-Replayed: true and byte-identical bodies; FLUSHALL on Redis mid-test still results in exactly one order row thanks to the unique constraint.

8.13 Rate limiting

Concept

Rate limiting caps how many requests a client may make in a window: 100 requests per minute per user, 1,000 per minute per API key, 20 login attempts per hour per IP. Exceeding the cap returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header. It protects the service from abuse, from runaway clients, and from itself (one tenant cannot starve the others).

Three algorithms you will meet:

Algorithm How Pros Cons
Fixed window Counter per key per window (user:123:2026-09-07T10:05) Trivial, one INCR Burst of 2x at the window boundary
Sliding window log/counter Count requests in the trailing N seconds (sorted set or two-window interpolation) Smooth, accurate More memory or a little math
Token bucket Bucket refills at R tokens/s up to capacity B; each request takes a token Allows short bursts up to B while enforcing average R Needs a Lua script for atomic refill-and-take

@nestjs/throttler implements a sliding-window style counter with configurable storage; gateways and reverse proxies (NGINX, Envoy, cloud API gateways) usually implement token buckets.

Why does it exist?

Without limits, one misbehaving client (a retry loop, a scraper, a load test pointed at production, a credential-stuffing bot) consumes all capacity. Rate limiting turns "the site is down for everyone" into "one client gets 429s". It also enforces commercial tiers (free: 60/min; paid: 6,000/min) and protects expensive endpoints (search, exports, login).

Mental model

Imagine a nightclub with a bouncer counting people in per minute. Above the limit, the bouncer says "wait two minutes" (429 with Retry-After) instead of letting the club overflow. VIP cards (API tiers) get a higher count. The bouncer at the street entrance (gateway) handles the crowd; the bartender (application) enforces "two drinks per person per hour" (business-aware limits).

How it works

Where to limit. Two layers, different jobs:

Layer Knows Good for Not good for
Gateway / load balancer / CDN IP, path, API key header, coarse volume Absorbing floods before they reach Node; per-IP limits; DDoS mitigation Per-user or per-tenant rules that need authentication; business-specific limits
Application (NestJS) Authenticated user, tenant, plan, endpoint cost Per-user and per-plan limits; expensive endpoints; login attempts per account Absorbing floods (the request has already cost a connection and a JSON parse)

Use both: coarse at the edge, precise in the app.

Keys. Per IP (anonymous traffic; beware NAT and mobile carriers sharing IPs), per user id (authenticated), per API key (partners), per tenant (multi-tenant SaaS), and often per endpoint group (login: strict; reads: generous; writes: moderate).

Storage. Counters must be shared across pods, so Redis, not process memory. Each check is one or two Redis operations (~0.3 ms). Use a Lua script or MULTI so the increment and TTL set are atomic.

Response. 429, Retry-After: <seconds>, and the informational headers X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset (the IETF draft standardises these as RateLimit-*). A problem+json body with code: RATE_LIMITED.

NestJS example

@nestjs/throttler with Redis storage and a per-user tracker.

// src/app.module.ts
import { ThrottlerModule, ThrottlerGuard, seconds, minutes } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { ThrottlerStorageRedisService } from '@nest-lab/throttler-storage-redis';
import { APP_GUARD } from '@nestjs/core';
import Redis from 'ioredis';

@Module({
  imports: [
    ThrottlerModule.forRootAsync({
      inject: [ConfigService],
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({
        throttlers: [
          { name: 'short', ttl: seconds(1), limit: 20 },        // burst protection
          { name: 'long', ttl: minutes(1), limit: 300 },        // sustained
        ],
        storage: new ThrottlerStorageRedisService(new Redis(config.getOrThrow('REDIS_URL'))),
        errorMessage: 'Too many requests',
      }),
    }),
  ],
  providers: [{ provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: UserOrIpThrottlerGuard }],
})
export class AppModule {}
// src/shared/api/user-or-ip-throttler.guard.ts
import { ExecutionContext, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ThrottlerGuard, ThrottlerException, ThrottlerLimitDetail } from '@nestjs/throttler';

@Injectable()
export class UserOrIpThrottlerGuard extends ThrottlerGuard {
  /** Key by authenticated user or API key when present; fall back to IP. */
  protected async getTracker(req: Record<string, any>): Promise<string> {
    if (req.user?.id) return `user:${req.user.id}`;
    if (req.apiKeyId) return `key:${req.apiKeyId}`;
    const fwd = (req.headers['x-forwarded-for'] as string | undefined)?.split(',')[0]?.trim();
    return `ip:${fwd ?? req.ip}`;
  }

  /** Emit a problem+json-compatible 429 and a Retry-After header. */
  protected async throwThrottlingException(ctx: ExecutionContext, detail: ThrottlerLimitDetail): Promise<void> {
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse();
    res.setHeader('Retry-After', Math.ceil(detail.timeToBlockExpire || detail.timeToExpire));
    throw new ThrottlerException(JSON.stringify({ code: 'RATE_LIMITED', title: 'Too Many Requests' }));
  }
}

Per-endpoint overrides:

@Post('auth/login')
@Throttle({ short: { limit: 5, ttl: seconds(10) }, long: { limit: 20, ttl: minutes(15) } })  // credential stuffing
login() {}

@Get('health')
@SkipThrottle()
health() {}

@Post('orders/export')
@Throttle({ long: { limit: 5, ttl: minutes(60) } })     // expensive
exportOrders() {}

When the guard runs before authentication (guards run in registration order; APP_GUARD providers run in the order declared), req.user is not yet set. Either register the auth guard first, or apply the throttler at the controller level after @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard); the tracker then sees the user.

The trust in X-Forwarded-For above is only safe if your gateway overwrites it. Configure app.set('trust proxy', 1) for Express to derive req.ip correctly, and never trust the header from the open internet.

PostgreSQL example

Rate limiting belongs in Redis, not PostgreSQL; a database round trip per request for a counter is a bad trade. Where PostgreSQL does appear is in plan configuration and audit:

CREATE TABLE ops.api_plans (
  api_key_id     uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  plan           text NOT NULL CHECK (plan IN ('free','standard','enterprise')),
  per_minute     integer NOT NULL,
  burst          integer NOT NULL
);
-- Loaded into memory at startup and refreshed every minute; the guard reads the cached plan per key.

CREATE TABLE ops.rate_limit_events (
  occurred_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  tracker      text NOT NULL,
  route        text NOT NULL,
  limit_name   text NOT NULL
);
-- Written asynchronously (queue) on each 429 for abuse review, not on the request path.

A Redis token bucket, for the record, is a ~15-line Lua script executed with EVALSHA: read tokens and ts, refill min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) * rate), take one if available, write back with a TTL, return allowed and the wait time. It is atomic because Redis runs Lua scripts single-threaded.

Production scenario

A public API served 5,000 RPS with three tiers. The edge (a cloud API gateway) enforced 2,000 requests per minute per IP and dropped SYN floods. NestJS enforced per-API-key plan limits with Redis (p99 overhead 0.6 ms). On a typical day 0.4% of requests were 429s, nearly all from two integrations with retry loops; both were contacted with their own X-RateLimit data. During a scraping incident the edge absorbed 40,000 RPS from 800 IPs and the app never saw more than 5,200.

Failure scenario

At 08:00 on the day of a marketing push, the login endpoint had no specific limit, only the global 300/min per IP. A credential-stuffing bot ran 250 logins per minute per IP from 2,000 IPs. Each login did a bcrypt compare (~80 ms of CPU). The pods hit 100% CPU, real users got timeouts, and the autoscaler added pods that were immediately saturated too. The fix was a 5-per-10-seconds limit on /auth/login per IP and per account, plus a progressive delay after failures. Rate limits must be endpoint-aware because endpoints are not equally expensive.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Redis down. Decide: fail open (no limits, service still works; safe against outage, unsafe against abuse) or fail closed (429 for everyone). Most choose fail open with an alarm, and rely on the edge limit as the backstop. @nestjs/throttler will throw if the storage errors, so wrap the storage or catch in the guard.
  • Shared IPs (corporate NAT, mobile carriers): per-IP limits punish thousands of users. Prefer per-user once authenticated; keep per-IP generous.
  • Window boundary bursts with fixed windows: 2x the limit in two seconds. Sliding windows or token buckets fix it.
  • Retry storms. Clients that retry 429s immediately amplify the problem. Retry-After plus documented exponential backoff with jitter; consider blocking repeat offenders for longer (blockDuration in throttler).
  • Limits on health checks or webhooks you receive from partners: exempt them or you will throttle your own monitoring and lose events.
  • Clock skew between pods does not matter (Redis owns the counters); skew between client and server matters only for X-RateLimit-Reset as an absolute timestamp; prefer seconds-until-reset.
  • Cost-based limits. A search costs 50x a read. Weight requests (take N tokens) rather than counting them equally.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They limit at the edge for volume and in the app for meaning, with Redis as the shared counter. They set stricter limits on expensive and security-sensitive endpoints, return 429 with Retry-After, expose remaining quota so good clients can self-regulate, and decide the Redis-down behaviour deliberately. They watch the 429 rate per client as an early warning of broken integrations.

Common mistakes

  • Process-memory counters that reset on deploy and differ per pod.
  • One global limit for all endpoints.
  • Trusting X-Forwarded-For from the internet, letting attackers pick their own key.
  • No Retry-After, so clients hammer harder.
  • Rate limiting before authentication and then keying by IP only.

Interview questions

  1. Fixed window vs sliding window vs token bucket: when does each fit? Expected: the table; boundary bursts; burst allowance.
  2. Where do you rate limit and why both places? Expected: edge for volume/IP; app for user/plan/endpoint.
  3. Redis is down. What does your rate limiter do? Expected: deliberate fail-open or fail-closed with an alarm; edge as backstop.
  4. How would you protect a login endpoint? Expected: per-IP and per-account limits, progressive delay, lockout policy, monitoring.
  5. How do you avoid punishing users behind a shared corporate IP? Expected: per-user keys after auth; generous IP limits; API keys for partners.

Practical exercise

Configure @nestjs/throttler with Redis storage and a user-or-IP tracker, strict limits on /auth/login, and @SkipThrottle on health. Write a load test (autocannon -c 50 -d 10) against /orders and /auth/login and capture the 429 rate, Retry-After values and X-RateLimit-Remaining decreasing. Then stop Redis and prove the chosen fail-open or fail-closed behaviour. Acceptance criteria: two pods share counters (same Redis); login is limited per IP and per account independently; a 429 body is problem+json with code: RATE_LIMITED; Redis outage behaviour is tested and alarmed.

8.14 API contracts (OpenAPI)

Concept

An API contract is a machine-readable description of every endpoint, parameter, request body, response and error: for REST that is an OpenAPI document (3.0 or 3.1, YAML or JSON). It is the single source of truth that documentation, client SDKs, mock servers, contract tests and gateways are generated from.

Two ways to produce it:

  • Code-first: decorate NestJS controllers and DTOs with @nestjs/swagger and generate the document at build time. The code is the truth; the spec follows.
  • Contract-first (design-first): write the OpenAPI document by hand (or with a designer tool), review it with consumers, then generate server stubs or validate the implementation against it. The spec is the truth; the code follows.

Why does it exist?

Without a contract, the API is whatever the code happens to do today. Frontend and mobile teams read the source or guess; partners email questions; changes are discovered by breakage. A contract lets consumers build in parallel against mocks, lets you generate typed clients instead of hand-writing them, and gives you something to diff in CI to catch breaking changes before they ship.

Mental model

Imagine architectural blueprints. Builders, electricians and inspectors all work from the same drawing. If the drawing is derived from the finished house (code-first), it is always accurate but you only see problems after the walls are up. If the house is built from the drawing (contract-first), you can argue about the kitchen before pouring concrete, but the drawing and the house can drift unless someone checks.

How it works

Code-first (@nestjs/swagger) Contract-first
Source of truth Decorated code OpenAPI file in the repo
Drift risk Low (generated) but decorators can lie (wrong @ApiResponse) High unless validated at runtime or in CI
Review before build Hard; the code exists first Natural; consumers review the YAML
Parallel work Consumers wait for a deployable Consumers mock from the spec on day one
Tooling in NestJS First-class Generate DTOs with openapi-typescript/openapi-generator; validate with express-openapi-validator
Best for Small teams, internal APIs, fast iteration Public/partner APIs, multiple consumer teams, regulated changes

A pragmatic hybrid that works: code-first generation, the generated spec committed to the repo, and a CI step that diffs it against the previous version (oasdiff, openapi-diff) and fails on breaking changes. You get accuracy from generation and review from the diff.

Generating clients. From the spec, openapi-generator-cli produces TypeScript (typescript-fetch, typescript-axios), Kotlin, Swift and more. The mobile team never hand-writes a request again; a renamed field becomes a compile error in their build, not a runtime crash in production.

Contract tests. The contract is only valuable if the implementation honours it. Provider-side: run the e2e suite through an OpenAPI validator middleware that fails any response not matching the schema. Consumer-side: consumer-driven contracts (Pact) let each consumer record what it actually uses, and the provider's CI verifies it never breaks those expectations. Part 23 — Testing covers the full setup.

NestJS example

Swagger setup and the decorators that make the document accurate.

// src/main.ts (excerpt)
import { DocumentBuilder, SwaggerModule } from '@nestjs/swagger';
import { writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const config = new DocumentBuilder()
  .setTitle('Orders API')
  .setDescription('Place, read and cancel orders. All money values are decimal strings.')
  .setVersion('2.0.0')
  .addBearerAuth()
  .addServer('https://api.example.com', 'production')
  .build();
const document = SwaggerModule.createDocument(app, config, { ignoreGlobalPrefix: false });
if (process.env.WRITE_OPENAPI === '1') writeFileSync('openapi.json', JSON.stringify(document, null, 2)); // committed and diffed in CI
SwaggerModule.setup('api/docs', app, document);   // interactive UI at /api/docs, disabled in production behind a flag
// src/ordering/api/dto/order-response.dto.ts
import { ApiProperty, ApiPropertyOptional } from '@nestjs/swagger';

export class MoneyDto {
  @ApiProperty({ example: '1299.00', description: 'Decimal string, never a float' }) amount: string;
  @ApiProperty({ example: 'INR', minLength: 3, maxLength: 3 }) currency: string;
}
export class OrderResponseDto {
  @ApiProperty({ format: 'uuid' }) id: string;
  @ApiProperty({ enum: ['DRAFT', 'PLACED', 'PAID', 'FULFILLED', 'CANCELLED'], description: 'Open enum: clients must tolerate unknown values' }) status: string;
  @ApiProperty({ type: MoneyDto }) total: MoneyDto;
  @ApiPropertyOptional({ format: 'date-time' }) placedAt?: string;
  @ApiProperty({ description: 'Optimistic concurrency token; send back as If-Match', example: 12 }) version: number;
}
export class ProblemDetailsDto {
  @ApiProperty({ example: 'https://errors.example.com/order-not-cancellable' }) type: string;
  @ApiProperty({ example: 'Order cannot be cancelled' }) title: string;
  @ApiProperty({ example: 409 }) status: number;
  @ApiPropertyOptional() detail?: string;
  @ApiProperty({ example: 'ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE' }) code: string;
  @ApiPropertyOptional() correlationId?: string;
}
// controller decorators (full controller in 8.18)
@ApiTags('orders')
@ApiBearerAuth()
@Controller({ path: 'orders', version: '2' })
export class OrdersController {
  @Post()
  @ApiOperation({ summary: 'Place an order', description: 'Idempotent via Idempotency-Key. Replays return 200 with Idempotent-Replayed: true.' })
  @ApiHeader({ name: 'Idempotency-Key', required: true, description: 'UUID v4 per logical operation; reuse only for retries' })
  @ApiCreatedResponse({ type: OrderResponseDto, headers: { Location: { schema: { type: 'string' } } } })
  @ApiResponse({ status: 200, description: 'Idempotent replay', type: OrderResponseDto })
  @ApiBadRequestResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto })
  @ApiUnprocessableEntityResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto, description: 'Unknown SKU, insufficient stock, key reused' })
  @ApiResponse({ status: 429, type: ProblemDetailsDto, description: 'Rate limited; see Retry-After' })
  create() {}
}

The class-validator decorators already carry constraints; @nestjs/swagger's CLI plugin (@nestjs/swagger/plugin in nest-cli.json) reads them and the TypeScript types, so most @ApiProperty boilerplate disappears and the spec stays in sync with validation.

Production scenario

A public API with 80 endpoints generated its spec in CI on every merge, published it to a developer portal, and produced TypeScript, Kotlin and Swift SDKs automatically. A breaking-change diff gate (oasdiff breaking) blocked 11 PRs in a year that would have removed or retyped fields. Partner onboarding used the mock server generated from the same spec; partners integrated before the endpoints were finished.

Failure scenario

A controller's @ApiOkResponse({ type: OrderResponseDto }) was copy-pasted onto a list endpoint that actually returned { items, pageInfo }. The generated Kotlin client expected a single order, crashed on parse, and the Android release was pulled. The contract test that would have caught it (validate every e2e response against the spec) was added the next sprint. A decorator is a claim; only a test makes it true.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Decorators that lie. Response types not matching reality. Validate responses against the spec in e2e tests.
  • Spec published from a branch that never shipped. Publish from the deployed build's artefact.
  • Global prefix and versioning missing from the spec paths. Check ignoreGlobalPrefix and version handling in createDocument.
  • Swagger UI exposed in production with try it out against live data. Gate it behind auth or an environment flag.
  • Enums closed in the spec while the server adds values; clients generated with strict enums crash. Document enums as open or add values only with a version.
  • Money as number in the spec because a DTO used number. Strings, always.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

They pick code-first with a committed, diffed spec for most teams, and contract-first for partner-facing APIs where consumers must review before build. They treat the spec as an artefact of the release, generate clients from it, and gate CI on breaking-change detection. They make sure something executes the contract against the implementation.

Common mistakes

  • No spec, or a hand-maintained one that is two versions behind.
  • Spec with no error responses documented.
  • Hand-written client SDKs that drift.
  • any-typed DTOs that generate {} schemas.

Interview questions

  1. Code-first vs contract-first: tradeoffs and when you choose each. Expected: the table; hybrid with diff gate.
  2. How do you catch a breaking API change before it ships? Expected: committed spec, oasdiff in CI, consumer contract tests.
  3. How do you make sure the spec matches the implementation? Expected: response validation in e2e tests; generated from code; plugin reads validators.
  4. What do generated clients buy you and what do they cost? Expected: type safety and no hand-written requests; regeneration workflow and versioning.

Practical exercise

Enable the swagger CLI plugin, generate openapi.json in CI, commit it, add oasdiff breaking against the previous commit, and add an e2e test that validates every response against the spec with an OpenAPI validator. Then generate a typescript-fetch client and use it in one e2e test. Acceptance criteria: removing a response field fails CI; the generated client compiles and places an order; the spec documents 400, 401, 404, 409, 422 and 429 for the create endpoint.

8.15 HATEOAS (briefly)

Concept

HATEOAS (Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State) is the idea that responses include links to the next possible actions, so a client navigates the API by following links rather than by hard-coding URIs and rules:

{
  "id": "8f3c...", "status": "PLACED",
  "_links": {
    "self":   { "href": "/api/v2/orders/8f3c..." },
    "cancel": { "href": "/api/v2/orders/8f3c.../cancellations", "method": "POST" },
    "pay":    { "href": "/api/v2/orders/8f3c.../payments", "method": "POST" }
  }
}

A fulfilled order would have no cancel link; the client learns what is possible from the server, not from a copy of the business rules.

Why it is attractive

The server owns the state machine. Clients do not duplicate "can I cancel?" logic. URIs can change without breaking clients that follow links. It is what makes the web itself work: browsers know nothing about your site and still navigate it.

Why most teams skip it

  • Clients are not generic. A mobile app is built by people who read your docs and design a screen with a "Cancel" button; they still need to know the rules to design the UI, and they still hard-code the screens.
  • Tooling is thin. OpenAPI does not describe link semantics well; generated clients ignore _links.
  • Payload bloat for lists (links per item).
  • Format wars: HAL, JSON:API, Siren, Collection+JSON. Each has a small following.
  • The value is real but small compared to the cost, unless you are building a truly generic client (an admin console that renders any resource, a workflow engine).

The pragmatic middle

Keep two things from HATEOAS and drop the rest:

  1. Return a Location header on 201 and self where cheap.
  2. Return allowed actions as booleans or a list when the UI needs them: "actions": ["cancel", "pay"] or "canCancel": true. Clients get the server's decision on what is possible without a full link format. This is HATEOAS in spirit: the server, not the client, decides.
// in the response mapper
return { ...dto, actions: computeAllowedActions(order) };   // ['cancel'] for PLACED, [] for FULFILLED

Interview questions

  1. What is HATEOAS and why is it rarely implemented fully? Expected: links drive navigation; non-generic clients, tooling, bloat.
  2. What part of the idea is worth keeping? Expected: server-decided allowed actions; Location; self.

8.16 Long-running operations

Concept

Some requests cannot finish inside an HTTP timeout: generating a 200,000-row export, capturing a payment that requires a bank redirect, provisioning a tenant, bulk imports. The API accepts the work, returns 202 Accepted immediately with a way to track it, does the work in the background, and lets the client find out the result by polling a status resource or by receiving a webhook.

Why does it exist?

HTTP connections through gateways and load balancers have timeouts of 30 to 60 seconds, mobile networks less. Holding a connection open for minutes wastes a worker, fails unpredictably, and leaves the client unsure whether the work happened. The 202 pattern decouples "I accepted your request" from "the work is done".

Mental model

Imagine dropping off a car for service. You get a ticket number immediately (202 plus operation id). You can call and ask "is it ready?" (polling), or leave your phone number and be called when it is (webhook). You do not stand at the counter for four hours holding the line.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant API as ExportsController
  participant Q as Queue
  participant W as Worker
  participant PG as PostgreSQL
  C->>API: POST /orders/exports
  API->>PG: INSERT operations status PENDING
  API->>Q: enqueue export job
  API-->>C: 202 Accepted, Location /operations/op_123, Retry-After 5
  C->>API: GET /operations/op_123
  API-->>C: 200 status RUNNING, progress 40
  W->>PG: UPDATE operations status SUCCEEDED, result URL
  C->>API: GET /operations/op_123
  API-->>C: 303 See Other, Location /orders/exports/exp_9
  W-->>C: optional webhook operation.completed
  1. POST the request. Validate synchronously (a bad request should fail now, not five minutes later).
  2. Create an operation resource (operations row) in PENDING, enqueue a job with the operation id, and return 202 with Location: /operations/{id} and Retry-After.
  3. The client polls GET /operations/{id}. Return 200 with { status: PENDING | RUNNING | SUCCEEDED | FAILED, progress, result, error }. On success, either embed the result or return 303 See Other to the result resource.
  4. Optionally, on completion send a webhook (8.17).
  5. The operation is idempotent through the same Idempotency-Key mechanism as any POST.
  6. Operations expire (keep 7 days), and the job is retried with backoff; the status resource reflects retries.

NestJS example

Using @nestjs/bullmq for the queue. The controller returns 202; the processor updates the operation.

// src/ordering/api/exports.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, HttpCode, Param, Post, Res, ParseUUIDPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectQueue } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Queue } from 'bullmq';
import { Response } from 'express';

@Controller()
export class ExportsController {
  constructor(@InjectQueue('exports') private readonly queue: Queue, private readonly operations: OperationsService) {}

  @Post('orders/exports')
  @HttpCode(202)
  @Idempotent()
  @UseInterceptors(IdempotencyInterceptor)
  async start(@Body() dto: CreateExportDto, @CurrentUser() user: { id: string }, @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response) {
    const op = await this.operations.create({ kind: 'orders.export', requestedBy: user.id, input: dto });
    await this.queue.add('export', { operationId: op.id }, {
      jobId: op.id,                                            // dedupe: one job per operation
      attempts: 5, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 2_000 }, removeOnComplete: true,
    });
    res.setHeader('Location', `/api/v2/operations/${op.id}`);
    res.setHeader('Retry-After', '5');
    return { operationId: op.id, status: 'PENDING' };
  }

  @Get('operations/:id')
  async status(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string, @CurrentUser() user: { id: string }, @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response) {
    const op = await this.operations.getOwned(id, user.id);   // 404 if not yours
    if (op.status === 'SUCCEEDED' && op.resultLocation) {
      res.status(303); res.setHeader('Location', op.resultLocation);
    } else if (op.status === 'PENDING' || op.status === 'RUNNING') {
      res.setHeader('Retry-After', '5');
    }
    return { id: op.id, status: op.status, progress: op.progress, error: op.error, createdAt: op.createdAt, updatedAt: op.updatedAt };
  }
}
// src/ordering/application/export.processor.ts
import { Processor, WorkerHost } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Job } from 'bullmq';

@Processor('exports', { concurrency: 2 })
export class ExportProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  constructor(private readonly operations: OperationsService, private readonly exporter: OrdersExporter) { super(); }

  async process(job: Job<{ operationId: string }>): Promise<void> {
    const op = await this.operations.markRunning(job.data.operationId);   // no-op if already SUCCEEDED (idempotent retry)
    if (!op) return;
    try {
      const url = await this.exporter.run(op.input, async (pct) => this.operations.progress(op.id, pct));
      await this.operations.succeed(op.id, { resultLocation: url });
    } catch (err) {
      if (job.attemptsMade + 1 >= (job.opts.attempts ?? 1)) await this.operations.fail(op.id, toProblem(err));
      throw err;   // let BullMQ retry with backoff
    }
  }
}

PostgreSQL example

CREATE TABLE ops.operations (
  id               uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  kind             text NOT NULL,
  requested_by     uuid NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('PENDING','RUNNING','SUCCEEDED','FAILED')),
  progress         smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (progress BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
  input            jsonb NOT NULL,
  result_location  text,
  error            jsonb,
  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() + interval '7 days'
);
CREATE INDEX ix_operations_owner ON ops.operations (requested_by, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ix_operations_expiry ON ops.operations (expires_at);

-- Idempotent transition to RUNNING (a retried job must not restart a finished operation):
UPDATE ops.operations SET status = 'RUNNING', updated_at = now()
WHERE id = $1 AND status IN ('PENDING','RUNNING') RETURNING *;

Production scenario

An exports endpoint produced CSVs of up to 2 million rows (3 to 8 minutes). Synchronous attempts timed out at the load balancer's 60 s. With 202 plus polling every 5 s, clients saw progress climb, and the result was a pre-signed S3 URL returned via 303. Two worker pods with concurrency 2 handled 300 exports a day; the queue absorbed month-end spikes of 40 in an hour with no API impact.

Failure scenario

A payment capture that took 20 s (issuer slow) was implemented synchronously. The gateway timed out at 30 s roughly 3% of the time; the capture succeeded; the client saw a 504 and showed "payment failed"; customers paid again. Moving to 202 with Location: /payments/{id} and a status of PENDING until the provider's webhook arrived eliminated the double payments; the mobile app polls every 2 s for up to a minute and then falls back to "we will email you".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Polling storms. Thousands of clients polling every 200 ms. Return Retry-After; rate limit the status endpoint per operation; offer webhooks.
  • Worker crash mid-job. BullMQ re-delivers; markRunning is idempotent; the exporter must tolerate a restart (write to a temp key, move on success).
  • Operation visible to other users. Scope status reads by owner.
  • Result too large for the status body. Return a location, not the data.
  • Stuck in RUNNING forever after a crash with no retry. A sweeper marks operations older than N minutes as FAILED with a retryable error.
  • Client loses the operation id. Provide GET /operations?kind=... for the owner's recent operations.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Anything over a few seconds becomes 202 with an operation resource. They validate synchronously, enqueue with a deterministic job id, make the worker idempotent, expose progress, set Retry-After, expire operations, and offer webhooks for integrations that should not poll.

Interview questions

  1. Design an export endpoint for millions of rows. Expected: 202, operation resource, queue, worker, 303 to result, expiry.
  2. A payment provider takes up to 30 s. How does the API behave? Expected: 202 with status resource; provider webhook completes it; client polls or is notified.
  3. How do you stop polling from becoming a problem? Expected: Retry-After, per-operation rate limits, webhooks, long-polling or SSE for interactive cases.

Practical exercise

Implement POST /orders/exports and GET /operations/{id} with BullMQ. Kill the worker mid-export and prove the retry completes without producing two files. Acceptance criteria: 202 with Location and Retry-After; status shows progress; success returns 303; a stale RUNNING operation is failed by a sweeper after 10 minutes; another user gets 404 for your operation.

8.17 Webhooks

Concept

A webhook is an HTTP request you make to a URL the client registered, when something happens: order.paid, shipment.dispatched, operation.completed. It is the push alternative to polling. You are now the client, and everything that makes clients hard (timeouts, retries, duplicates, ordering, security) is your problem.

Why does it exist?

Polling wastes resources on both sides and adds latency equal to the polling interval. Integrations (ERPs, marketplaces, customer systems) want to know within seconds that an order was paid, without asking every second. Webhooks deliver that, at the cost of you operating a reliable delivery system.

Mental model

Imagine subscribing to a courier's SMS updates. The courier sends a message when the parcel moves. Sometimes the message is delayed, sometimes duplicated, and occasionally "out for delivery" arrives after "delivered". You still trust it because each message has a parcel number and a timestamp, and you can always check the tracking page (fetch current state) if in doubt.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
  participant D as Domain event
  participant O as Outbox relay
  participant Q as Webhook queue
  participant W as Webhook worker
  participant R as Receiver endpoint
  D->>O: order.paid written in outbox
  O->>Q: enqueue delivery per subscription
  W->>W: build payload, sign HMAC with timestamp
  W->>R: POST with X-Webhook-Signature and X-Webhook-Id
  alt 2xx within 5 s
    R-->>W: 200
    W->>Q: mark delivered
  else timeout or 5xx or 429
    R-->>W: 503
    W->>Q: retry with exponential backoff up to 24 h
  else 4xx other than 429
    R-->>W: 400
    W->>Q: mark failed, no retry, alert subscriber
  end

Design rules for the sender:

  1. Sign every delivery. HMAC-SHA256 over timestamp.rawBody with a per-subscription secret. Header: X-Webhook-Signature: t=1725700000,v1=<hex>. Including the timestamp prevents replay of an old captured request; receivers reject if |now - t| > 5 min.
  2. Include an event id (X-Webhook-Id, also in the body) so receivers can deduplicate. Delivery is at-least-once.
  3. Small payload with ids and the event type; the receiver fetches the current resource for details if it needs them. This also solves ordering: the fetched state is always current.
  4. Timeouts and retries. 5 s connect+response timeout. Retry on timeout, 5xx and 429 with exponential backoff and jitter: 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h, 12 h, 24 h. Do not retry on other 4xx (the receiver rejected it deliberately).
  5. Per-subscription circuit breaking. After N consecutive failures, pause the subscription, alert the subscriber, expose a "redeliver" endpoint.
  6. Durability. Deliveries originate from the outbox (Part 7, 7.10) so a crash never loses an event.
  7. Security of the destination. Only HTTPS; block private IP ranges (SSRF); resolve DNS once and pin; no redirects.
  8. Observability. A webhook_deliveries table with attempts, status codes and latencies; a dashboard per subscriber; a UI to replay.

Design rules for the receiver (you will write these too, for Stripe, Razorpay, shipping carriers):

  1. Verify the signature against the raw body (not re-serialised JSON), with timingSafeEqual.
  2. Check the timestamp tolerance.
  3. Return 200 fast (under a second), before doing the work; enqueue the work internally. Senders time out and retry otherwise.
  4. Deduplicate by event id in a table with a unique constraint; a duplicate is a 200 no-op.
  5. Tolerate out-of-order delivery: apply state transitions defensively, or fetch the current resource.
  6. Never trust the payload for authorisation; look up your own records by id.

NestJS example

Sender worker with signing and retry policy, and a receiver with raw-body verification.

// src/webhooks/application/webhook-delivery.processor.ts
import { Processor, WorkerHost } from '@nestjs/bullmq';
import { Job, UnrecoverableError } from 'bullmq';
import { createHmac } from 'node:crypto';

interface DeliveryJob { deliveryId: string; url: string; secret: string; eventId: string; body: string; }

@Processor('webhooks', { concurrency: 20 })
export class WebhookDeliveryProcessor extends WorkerHost {
  constructor(private readonly deliveries: WebhookDeliveriesRepository, private readonly guard: OutboundUrlGuard) { super(); }

  async process(job: Job<DeliveryJob>): Promise<void> {
    const { deliveryId, url, secret, eventId, body } = job.data;
    await this.guard.assertAllowed(url);                                 // https only, no private ranges, no redirects
    const t = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
    const sig = createHmac('sha256', secret).update(`${t}.${body}`).digest('hex');

    const controller = new AbortController();
    const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 5_000);
    let status = 0;
    try {
      const res = await fetch(url, {
        method: 'POST', redirect: 'manual', signal: controller.signal,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'X-Webhook-Id': eventId, 'X-Webhook-Signature': `t=${t},v1=${sig}`, 'User-Agent': 'example-webhooks/1.0' },
        body,
      });
      status = res.status;
    } catch (err) {
      await this.deliveries.recordAttempt(deliveryId, job.attemptsMade + 1, 0, String(err));
      throw err;                                                          // retry with backoff
    } finally { clearTimeout(timer); }

    await this.deliveries.recordAttempt(deliveryId, job.attemptsMade + 1, status);
    if (status >= 200 && status < 300) { await this.deliveries.markDelivered(deliveryId); return; }
    if (status === 429 || status >= 500) throw new Error(`Receiver returned ${status}`);            // retry
    await this.deliveries.markFailed(deliveryId, status);
    throw new UnrecoverableError(`Receiver rejected with ${status}`);                                // no retry
  }
}

// enqueue with the backoff policy (from the outbox relay):
// queue.add('deliver', job, { jobId: deliveryId, attempts: 8, backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 60_000 }, removeOnComplete: true });
// src/payments/api/provider-webhook.controller.ts  (we are the receiver)
import { Controller, Headers, HttpCode, Post, Req, UnauthorizedException, BadRequestException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { RawBodyRequest } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Request } from 'express';
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';

@Controller('webhooks/payments')
export class ProviderWebhookController {
  constructor(private readonly inbox: WebhookInboxService, private readonly config: ConfigService) {}

  @Post()
  @HttpCode(200)
  @SkipThrottle()                                         // never rate limit a provider's webhooks
  async receive(@Req() req: RawBodyRequest<Request>, @Headers('x-webhook-signature') sigHeader?: string) {
    const raw = req.rawBody;                              // requires NestFactory.create(AppModule, { rawBody: true })
    if (!raw || !sigHeader) throw new BadRequestException('Missing body or signature');
    const { t, v1 } = parseSignature(sigHeader);
    if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(t)) > 300) throw new UnauthorizedException('Stale signature');  // 5 min tolerance
    const expected = createHmac('sha256', this.config.getOrThrow('PAYMENT_WEBHOOK_SECRET')).update(`${t}.${raw.toString()}`).digest('hex');
    if (expected.length !== v1.length || !timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(v1))) throw new UnauthorizedException('Bad signature');

    const event = JSON.parse(raw.toString()) as { id: string; type: string; data: Record<string, unknown> };
    await this.inbox.enqueueOnce(event);                  // INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING, then a job
    return { received: true };                            // fast 200; the work happens in a worker
  }
}

function parseSignature(h: string): { t: string; v1: string } {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(h.split(',').map((kv) => kv.split('=') as [string, string]));
  if (!parts.t || !parts.v1) throw new BadRequestException('Malformed signature header');
  return { t: parts.t, v1: parts.v1 };
}

PostgreSQL example

Sender-side deliveries and receiver-side inbox.

CREATE TABLE webhooks.subscriptions (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id      uuid NOT NULL,
  url           text NOT NULL,
  secret        text NOT NULL,                       -- store encrypted at rest
  event_types   text[] NOT NULL,
  status        text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE' CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','PAUSED')),
  consecutive_failures integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE TABLE webhooks.deliveries (
  id               uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  subscription_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES webhooks.subscriptions(id),
  event_id         uuid NOT NULL,
  event_type       text NOT NULL,
  payload          jsonb NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING' CHECK (status IN ('PENDING','DELIVERED','FAILED')),
  attempts         integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  last_status_code integer,
  last_error       text,
  next_attempt_at  timestamptz,
  created_at       timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  delivered_at     timestamptz,
  CONSTRAINT ux_delivery_per_sub_event UNIQUE (subscription_id, event_id)   -- one delivery record per event per subscriber
);
CREATE INDEX ix_deliveries_pending ON webhooks.deliveries (next_attempt_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';

-- Receiver side: dedupe inbox
CREATE TABLE payments.webhook_inbox (
  event_id     text PRIMARY KEY,
  event_type   text NOT NULL,
  payload      jsonb NOT NULL,
  received_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  processed_at timestamptz
);

Production scenario

A platform delivered 1.2 million webhooks a day to 400 subscribers. First-attempt success was 97.5%; 2.1% succeeded on retry within an hour; 0.4% exhausted retries (dead subscribers) and were surfaced in the subscriber dashboard with a replay button. Median delivery latency from event to receiver 200 was 800 ms. Two subscribers with flapping endpoints were auto-paused and emailed; nobody was paged.

Failure scenario

A receiver (an ERP integration) processed each webhook synchronously in the handler: 12 s of ERP calls before returning 200. The sender timed out at 5 s and retried; the ERP received the same order three to eight times; duplicate purchase orders were raised. Fix on the receiver: return 200 immediately after writing to an inbox with a unique event id, process asynchronously, dedupe. Fix on the sender's docs: "respond within 5 s; we retry on timeout; deliveries are at-least-once".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Duplicates. At-least-once delivery. Receivers dedupe by event id.
  • Out of order. shipment.delivered before shipment.dispatched after a retry. Receivers apply defensively or fetch current state; senders include a sequence or occurredAt.
  • Clock skew between sender and receiver breaks timestamp tolerance. 5 minutes is standard; log skew when rejecting.
  • Secret rotation. Support two active secrets per subscription during rotation; sign with the new, verify with either.
  • SSRF via subscriber URL pointing at http://169.254.169.254/ or an internal service. Validate and block private ranges; resolve and pin DNS.
  • Slow receivers holding worker concurrency. Per-subscriber concurrency limits; timeouts.
  • Payload includes PII the subscriber should not have. Send ids; let them fetch with their own authorisation.
  • Retrying 4xx forever. Only retry timeouts, 5xx and 429.
  • Signature over re-serialised JSON fails because key order changed. Always sign and verify the raw bytes.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Webhooks are a distributed system they now operate. They sign with timestamps, deliver from the outbox with backoff, dedupe on both sides, keep payloads small, protect against SSRF, expose delivery logs and replay to subscribers, and write the receiver contract ("200 within 5 s, at-least-once, verify raw body") into the docs. As a receiver they verify, ack fast, inbox, dedupe, process async.

Common mistakes

  • No signature, or signature without timestamp.
  • Verifying against JSON.stringify(req.body) instead of the raw body.
  • Doing the work inside the receiver handler.
  • Retrying on 400.
  • Sending the full order with customer PII to every subscriber.

Interview questions

  1. Design outbound webhooks: security, retries, ordering, observability. Expected: HMAC with timestamp, backoff schedule, at-least-once with ids, small payloads with fetch, delivery log and replay, SSRF protection.
  2. How do you verify an incoming webhook safely? Expected: raw body, timingSafeEqual, timestamp tolerance, fast 200, inbox dedupe.
  3. Why include a timestamp in the signature? Expected: replay protection.
  4. A subscriber's endpoint is down for a day. What happens? Expected: backoff up to 24 h, pause after N failures, alert, manual replay.

Practical exercise

Build both sides: a sender that delivers order.paid from the outbox with signing and backoff, and a receiver for a mock payment provider with raw-body verification and an inbox. Test: tampered body (401), stale timestamp (401), duplicate event id (200, processed once), receiver returning 503 twice then 200 (delivered on attempt 3), receiver returning 400 (failed, no retry), subscriber URL http://10.0.0.1/ (rejected). Acceptance criteria: all six pass; the deliveries table shows attempts and status codes; a replay endpoint re-enqueues a failed delivery.

8.18 Worked example: the Orders API end to end

This section assembles the pieces from 8.1 to 8.17 into one complete slice: the OrdersController with all six endpoints, the DTOs, an OrdersService facade over the Part 7 use cases, the exception filter, the idempotency interceptor, swagger decorators and module wiring. Everything here is real NestJS code; the domain and application layer it calls is the one built in Part 7 — Domain-Driven Design.

The endpoints:

POST   /api/v2/orders                       place an order (idempotent via Idempotency-Key)
GET    /api/v2/orders/:id                   read one (ETag)
GET    /api/v2/orders?status=PAID&cursor=   list with filters and cursor pagination
PATCH  /api/v2/orders/:id                   edit a draft (merge-patch, If-Match)
DELETE /api/v2/orders/:id                   delete a draft (idempotent)
POST   /api/v2/orders/:id/cancellations     cancel a placed or paid order (action as resource)

DTOs

// src/ordering/api/dto/create-order.dto.ts
import { ApiProperty, ApiPropertyOptional } from '@nestjs/swagger';
import { Type } from 'class-transformer';
import { ArrayMaxSize, ArrayMinSize, IsArray, IsIn, IsInt, IsOptional, IsString, Length, Matches, Max, MaxLength, Min, ValidateNested } from 'class-validator';
import { UniqueBy } from '../../../shared/api/validators/unique-by.validator';

export class OrderLineDto {
  @ApiProperty({ example: 'MUG-BLU-01' }) @IsString() @MaxLength(64) @Matches(/^[A-Z0-9-]+$/) sku: string;
  @ApiProperty({ example: 2, minimum: 1, maximum: 10000 }) @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(10000) quantity: number;
}
export class AddressDto {
  @ApiProperty() @IsString() @Length(1, 200) line1: string;
  @ApiPropertyOptional() @IsOptional() @IsString() @MaxLength(200) line2?: string;
  @ApiProperty() @IsString() @Length(1, 100) city: string;
  @ApiProperty({ example: '560001' }) @IsString() @Length(3, 12) @Matches(/^[A-Za-z0-9 -]+$/) postalCode: string;
  @ApiProperty({ example: 'IN' }) @IsIn(['IN', 'US', 'GB', 'DE']) countryCode: string;
}
export class CreateOrderDto {
  @ApiProperty({ enum: ['INR', 'USD', 'EUR'] }) @IsIn(['INR', 'USD', 'EUR']) currency: string;
  @ApiProperty({ type: [OrderLineDto], minItems: 1, maxItems: 100 })
  @IsArray() @ArrayMinSize(1) @ArrayMaxSize(100) @ValidateNested({ each: true }) @Type(() => OrderLineDto) @UniqueBy('sku')
  lines: OrderLineDto[];
  @ApiProperty({ type: AddressDto }) @ValidateNested() @Type(() => AddressDto) shippingAddress: AddressDto;
  @ApiPropertyOptional({ maxLength: 500 }) @IsOptional() @IsString() @MaxLength(500) customerNote?: string;
}
// src/ordering/api/dto/update-order.dto.ts
import { PartialType, PickType } from '@nestjs/swagger';
import { CreateOrderDto } from './create-order.dto';

// Only the fields a draft may change. No currency, no lines (they have their own sub-resource), no status.
export class UpdateOrderDto extends PartialType(PickType(CreateOrderDto, ['shippingAddress', 'customerNote'] as const)) {}

// src/ordering/api/dto/create-cancellation.dto.ts
export class CreateCancellationDto {
  @ApiProperty({ maxLength: 500 }) @IsString() @Length(1, 500) reason: string;
}

// src/ordering/api/dto/list-orders.query.dto.ts   (from 8.6; limit, cursor, status[], placedAfter, placedBefore, sort, q)
// src/ordering/api/dto/order-response.dto.ts
export class MoneyDto { @ApiProperty({ example: '1299.00' }) amount: string; @ApiProperty({ example: 'INR' }) currency: string; }
export class OrderLineResponseDto {
  @ApiProperty({ format: 'uuid' }) id: string;
  @ApiProperty() sku: string;
  @ApiProperty() productName: string;
  @ApiProperty() quantity: number;
  @ApiProperty({ type: MoneyDto }) unitPrice: MoneyDto;
  @ApiProperty({ type: MoneyDto }) lineTotal: MoneyDto;
}
export class OrderResponseDto {
  @ApiProperty({ format: 'uuid' }) id: string;
  @ApiProperty({ enum: ['DRAFT', 'PLACED', 'PAID', 'FULFILLED', 'CANCELLED'], description: 'Open enum' }) status: string;
  @ApiProperty({ type: [OrderLineResponseDto] }) lines: OrderLineResponseDto[];
  @ApiProperty({ type: MoneyDto }) total: MoneyDto;
  @ApiProperty({ type: AddressDto }) shippingAddress: AddressDto;
  @ApiPropertyOptional() customerNote?: string | null;
  @ApiPropertyOptional({ format: 'date-time' }) placedAt?: string;
  @ApiProperty({ description: 'Send back as If-Match on PATCH' }) version: number;
  @ApiProperty({ type: [String], example: ['cancel'] }) actions: string[];
}
export class CancellationResponseDto {
  @ApiProperty({ format: 'uuid' }) id: string;
  @ApiProperty({ format: 'uuid' }) orderId: string;
  @ApiProperty() reason: string;
  @ApiProperty() refundRequired: boolean;
  @ApiProperty({ format: 'date-time' }) createdAt: string;
}

The service facade

OrdersService is the API layer's single entry point into the Ordering context. It delegates to the Part 7 use cases and the read-side query, and maps domain results to response DTOs. It contains no business rules.

// src/ordering/api/orders.service.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PlaceOrderService } from '../application/place-order.service';
import { UpdateDraftService } from '../application/update-draft.service';
import { DeleteDraftService } from '../application/delete-draft.service';
import { CancelOrderService } from '../application/cancel-order.service';
import { OrdersQuery, Page } from '../application/orders.query';
import { OrderNotFoundError } from '../domain/errors';
import { CreateOrderDto, UpdateOrderDto, ListOrdersQueryDto, OrderResponseDto, CancellationResponseDto } from './dto';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(
    private readonly placeOrder: PlaceOrderService,
    private readonly updateDraft: UpdateDraftService,
    private readonly deleteDraft: DeleteDraftService,
    private readonly cancelOrder: CancelOrderService,
    private readonly query: OrdersQuery,
  ) {}

  async create(customerId: string, idempotencyKey: string, dto: CreateOrderDto): Promise<{ order: OrderResponseDto; created: boolean }> {
    const result = await this.placeOrder.execute({ customerId, idempotencyKey, currency: dto.currency, lines: dto.lines,
      shippingAddress: dto.shippingAddress, customerNote: dto.customerNote });
    const order = await this.getOne(customerId, result.orderId);
    return { order, created: result.created };
  }

  async getOne(customerId: string, orderId: string): Promise<OrderResponseDto> {
    const view = await this.query.getForCustomer(customerId, orderId);   // read model; 404 hides other customers' orders
    if (!view) throw new OrderNotFoundError(orderId);
    return toResponse(view);
  }

  list(customerId: string, q: ListOrdersQueryDto): Promise<Page<OrderResponseDto>> {
    return this.query.listForCustomer(customerId, q).then((page) => ({ ...page, items: page.items.map(toResponse) }));
  }

  async update(customerId: string, orderId: string, expectedVersion: number, dto: UpdateOrderDto): Promise<OrderResponseDto> {
    await this.updateDraft.execute({ customerId, orderId, expectedVersion,
      shippingAddress: dto.shippingAddress, customerNote: dto.customerNote });   // undefined = unchanged, null = clear
    return this.getOne(customerId, orderId);
  }

  remove(customerId: string, orderId: string): Promise<void> {
    return this.deleteDraft.execute({ customerId, orderId });   // no-op if already gone
  }

  async cancel(customerId: string, orderId: string, reason: string): Promise<{ cancellation: CancellationResponseDto; created: boolean }> {
    const r = await this.cancelOrder.execute({ customerId, orderId, reason, requestedBy: customerId });
    return { created: r.created, cancellation: { id: r.cancellationId, orderId, reason: r.reason, refundRequired: r.refundRequired, createdAt: r.createdAt.toISOString() } };
  }
}

function toResponse(v: OrderView): OrderResponseDto {
  const actions: string[] = [];
  if (v.status === 'DRAFT') actions.push('edit', 'delete', 'place');
  if (v.status === 'PLACED') actions.push('pay', 'cancel');
  if (v.status === 'PAID') actions.push('cancel');
  return {
    id: v.id, status: v.status, version: v.version, placedAt: v.placedAt?.toISOString(), customerNote: v.customerNote,
    lines: v.lines.map((l) => ({ id: l.id, sku: l.sku, productName: l.productName, quantity: l.quantity,
      unitPrice: money(l.unitPriceMinor, v.currency), lineTotal: money(l.lineTotalMinor, v.currency) })),
    total: money(v.totalMinor, v.currency),
    shippingAddress: { line1: v.shipLine1, line2: v.shipLine2 ?? undefined, city: v.shipCity, postalCode: v.shipPostalCode, countryCode: v.shipCountry },
    actions,
  };
}
function money(minor: string, currency: string): MoneyDto {
  const digits = currency === 'JPY' ? 0 : 2;
  const s = BigInt(minor).toString().padStart(digits + 1, '0');
  return { amount: digits ? `${s.slice(0, -digits)}.${s.slice(-digits)}` : s, currency };
}

The controller

// src/ordering/api/orders.controller.ts
import {
  Body, Controller, Delete, Get, Headers, HttpCode, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Patch, Post, Query, Res,
  UseGuards, UseInterceptors, PreconditionRequiredException, BadRequestException,
} from '@nestjs/common';
import {
  ApiBadRequestResponse, ApiBearerAuth, ApiConflictResponse, ApiCreatedResponse, ApiHeader, ApiNoContentResponse,
  ApiNotFoundResponse, ApiOkResponse, ApiOperation, ApiPreconditionFailedResponse, ApiResponse, ApiTags,
  ApiUnprocessableEntityResponse,
} from '@nestjs/swagger';
import { Throttle, seconds } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { Response } from 'express';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser } from '../../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { Idempotent } from '../../shared/api/idempotent.decorator';
import { IdempotencyInterceptor } from '../../shared/api/idempotency.interceptor';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';
import { CreateOrderDto, UpdateOrderDto, CreateCancellationDto, ListOrdersQueryDto, OrderResponseDto, CancellationResponseDto, ProblemDetailsDto } from './dto';

type User = { id: string };

@ApiTags('orders')
@ApiBearerAuth()
@ApiBadRequestResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto })
@ApiResponse({ status: 401, type: ProblemDetailsDto })
@ApiResponse({ status: 429, type: ProblemDetailsDto, description: 'Rate limited; honour Retry-After' })
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
@Controller({ path: 'orders', version: '2' })
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Post()
  @HttpCode(201)
  @Idempotent({ ttlSeconds: 86_400 })
  @UseInterceptors(IdempotencyInterceptor)
  @Throttle({ short: { limit: 5, ttl: seconds(1) } })
  @ApiOperation({ summary: 'Place an order', description: 'Prices and names are snapshotted at placement. Idempotent per Idempotency-Key for 24 h.' })
  @ApiHeader({ name: 'Idempotency-Key', required: true, description: 'UUID v4 per logical operation; reuse only for retries' })
  @ApiCreatedResponse({ type: OrderResponseDto, headers: { Location: { schema: { type: 'string' } } } })
  @ApiOkResponse({ type: OrderResponseDto, description: 'Idempotent replay (Idempotent-Replayed: true)' })
  @ApiUnprocessableEntityResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto, description: 'UNKNOWN_SKU, INSUFFICIENT_STOCK, IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED' })
  @ApiResponse({ status: 403, type: ProblemDetailsDto, description: 'Customer blocked' })
  async create(
    @CurrentUser() user: User,
    @Headers('idempotency-key') idempotencyKey: string,
    @Body() dto: CreateOrderDto,
    @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response,
  ): Promise<OrderResponseDto> {
    const { order, created } = await this.orders.create(user.id, idempotencyKey, dto);
    res.setHeader('Location', `/api/v2/orders/${order.id}`);
    res.setHeader('ETag', `"${order.version}"`);
    if (!created) res.status(200);
    return order;
  }

  @Get()
  @ApiOperation({ summary: 'List my orders', description: 'Cursor pagination; cursors are opaque and expire with the sort spec.' })
  @ApiOkResponse({ description: 'items plus pageInfo' })
  list(@CurrentUser() user: User, @Query() q: ListOrdersQueryDto) {
    return this.orders.list(user.id, q);
  }

  @Get(':id')
  @ApiOperation({ summary: 'Get an order' })
  @ApiOkResponse({ type: OrderResponseDto, headers: { ETag: { schema: { type: 'string' } } } })
  @ApiNotFoundResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto })
  async getOne(@CurrentUser() user: User, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string, @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response): Promise<OrderResponseDto> {
    const order = await this.orders.getOne(user.id, id);
    res.setHeader('ETag', `"${order.version}"`);
    res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'private, no-cache');   // revalidate; never shared-cache a customer's order
    return order;
  }

  @Patch(':id')
  @ApiOperation({ summary: 'Edit a draft order', description: 'JSON merge-patch semantics: null clears, absent leaves unchanged. Requires If-Match.' })
  @ApiHeader({ name: 'If-Match', required: true, description: 'ETag from the last GET, e.g. "12"' })
  @ApiOkResponse({ type: OrderResponseDto })
  @ApiNotFoundResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto })
  @ApiConflictResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto, description: 'Order is not a draft' })
  @ApiPreconditionFailedResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto, description: 'Version mismatch; reload and retry' })
  @ApiResponse({ status: 428, type: ProblemDetailsDto, description: 'If-Match missing' })
  async update(
    @CurrentUser() user: User,
    @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string,
    @Headers('if-match') ifMatch: string | undefined,
    @Body() dto: UpdateOrderDto,
    @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response,
  ): Promise<OrderResponseDto> {
    if (!ifMatch) throw new PreconditionRequiredException('If-Match header is required');
    const m = /^(?:W\/)?"(\d+)"$/.exec(ifMatch.trim());
    if (!m) throw new BadRequestException('Malformed If-Match');
    const order = await this.orders.update(user.id, id, Number(m[1]), dto);
    res.setHeader('ETag', `"${order.version}"`);
    return order;
  }

  @Delete(':id')
  @HttpCode(204)
  @ApiOperation({ summary: 'Delete a draft order', description: 'Idempotent: deleting an already-deleted draft returns 204. Placed orders cannot be deleted; cancel them.' })
  @ApiNoContentResponse()
  @ApiConflictResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto, description: 'Order is not a draft' })
  async remove(@CurrentUser() user: User, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.orders.remove(user.id, id);
  }

  @Post(':id/cancellations')
  @HttpCode(201)
  @ApiOperation({ summary: 'Cancel an order', description: 'Creates a cancellation. Repeating returns the existing cancellation with 200.' })
  @ApiCreatedResponse({ type: CancellationResponseDto })
  @ApiOkResponse({ type: CancellationResponseDto, description: 'Already cancelled' })
  @ApiNotFoundResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto })
  @ApiConflictResponse({ type: ProblemDetailsDto, description: 'ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE: fulfilled orders cannot be cancelled' })
  async cancel(
    @CurrentUser() user: User,
    @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string,
    @Body() dto: CreateCancellationDto,
    @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response,
  ): Promise<CancellationResponseDto> {
    const { cancellation, created } = await this.orders.cancel(user.id, id, dto.reason);
    res.setHeader('Location', `/api/v2/orders/${id}/cancellations/${cancellation.id}`);
    if (!created) res.status(200);
    return cancellation;
  }
}

The exception filter (8.9) and the idempotency interceptor (8.12) are the ones already shown; the filter is registered globally in main.ts, the interceptor is applied per endpoint with @Idempotent().

Module wiring and bootstrap

// src/ordering/ordering.module.ts
@Module({
  imports: [TypeOrmModule.forFeature([OrderOrmEntity, OrderLineOrmEntity]), CustomerModule, CatalogModule, SharedInfrastructureModule],
  controllers: [OrdersController],
  providers: [
    OrdersService, OrdersQuery,
    PlaceOrderService, UpdateDraftService, DeleteDraftService, CancelOrderService, PricingService,
    IdempotencyInterceptor, CursorCodec,
  ],
})
export class OrderingModule {}

// src/main.ts (all the global pieces together)
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, { bodyParser: false, rawBody: true });
app.set('trust proxy', 1);
app.use(json({ limit: '1mb', strict: true }));
app.setGlobalPrefix('api');
app.enableVersioning({ type: VersioningType.URI, defaultVersion: '2' });
app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true, transform: true, forbidUnknownValues: true, validationError: { target: false, value: false } }));
app.useGlobalFilters(new ProblemDetailsFilter(app.get(HttpAdapterHost)));
app.use(correlationIdMiddleware);
app.enableShutdownHooks();

What a request looks like

Idempotency-Key: 6b1c1c5e-2f0e-4c7f-9d1a-0a9d3e2f1b11
Content-Type: application/json

{ "currency": "INR", "lines": [ { "sku": "MUG-BLU-01", "quantity": 2 } ],
  "shippingAddress": { "line1": "12 MG Road", "city": "Bengaluru", "postalCode": "560001", "countryCode": "IN" } }

ETag: "0"

  "total": { "amount": "398.00", "currency": "INR" }, "shippingAddress": { ... }, "placedAt": "2026-09-07T04:12:31.118Z",
