A retry of the same request returns the same body with 200 and Idempotent-Replayed: true. A cancel of a fulfilled order returns:

X-Correlation-Id: req_01J7Q8ZB77

  "detail": "Cannot cancel: order is FULFILLED", "instance": "/api/v2/orders/8f3c.../cancellations",

Production scenario

This shape ran at 1,200 RPS across six pods: 70% GET (list and item, p50 6 ms, served by the read query with the composite index), 25% POST /orders (p50 28 ms, p99 90 ms including the idempotency round trip to Redis), 5% everything else. The Idempotent-Replayed rate was 1.8%, the 412 rate on PATCH 0.4%, the 429 rate 0.3% (two integrations). Error bodies were uniform, the OpenAPI document was generated on every merge and diffed, and the mobile SDK was regenerated from it.

8.19 Edge cases & failure modes for APIs

Every item below has bitten a real system. For each: what happens, and the defence.

  • Duplicate request. The client sends the same POST twice (double-tap, retry loop). Defence: Idempotency-Key with atomic reservation and replay (8.12); unique constraints in the database as the durable backstop; naturally idempotent sub-resources (cancellations with UNIQUE (order_id)).
  • Client timeout after server success. The order committed; the response was lost; the client thinks it failed. Defence: idempotency keys so the retry returns the original; Location headers and GET so the client can reconcile; never make clients guess.
  • Retries of non-idempotent calls. SDKs and gateways retry 5xx and timeouts by default. Defence: every retryable path is idempotent by verb (PUT, DELETE) or by key (POST); return 4xx (not 5xx) for client faults so gateways do not retry them; document the retry contract.
  • Partial failure in bulk. Item 137 fails. Defence: per-item results with per-item keys (8.7); bounded concurrency; all-or-nothing only for related items.
  • Large payloads. A 40 MB body exhausts memory or hits the gateway limit. Defence: body limit (1 MB) at gateway and app returning 413; array size caps in DTOs; streaming uploads for files (multipart to object storage with pre-signed URLs, never buffered through Node); pagination for responses; async export for big results.
  • Malicious input. __proto__ keys (prototype pollution) neutralised by whitelist: true and a strict JSON parser; ReDoS by length caps and linear regexes; SQL injection through sort/filter by allow-lists; id enumeration by UUID/prefixed ids plus authorisation on every read (getForCustomer, not getById); path traversal in file names by never using client strings as paths; header injection by validating Location-influencing values.
  • Clock skew in signed requests. A client's clock is 8 minutes off; every signed request or webhook is rejected as stale. Defence: 5-minute tolerance is standard; return a problem body that says "clock skew" with the server time so the client can correct; monitor rejection reasons; use NTP everywhere you control.
  • Pagination drift when rows are inserted. Offset pages repeat or skip items when rows are inserted before the current page. Defence: keyset pagination on an immutable (created_at, id); opaque signed cursors; hasNextPage instead of totals.
  • Breaking changes in responses. Adding a field is safe (clients must ignore unknown fields; say so in the docs). Removing, renaming, retyping (number to string), changing meaning (paise to rupees), tightening validation, or changing a status code are breaking. Defence: additive evolution; a diffed OpenAPI document in CI; a new version for anything breaking; deprecation and sunset headers.
  • Mobile clients stuck on old versions. Some users never update. Defence: keep old versions alive per the sunset policy; per-version usage dashboards; tolerant readers on the client (ignore unknown fields, handle unknown enum values); a minimum-supported-version check that returns 426 Upgrade Required with a store link only for security-critical breaks.
  • Enum growth. A new status value crashes a client with an exhaustive switch. Defence: document enums as open; add values in minor releases only when clients are known to tolerate them; otherwise version.
  • Timeouts on the server side. A slow catalog lookup makes POST /orders hang. Defence: per-dependency timeouts (300 ms for in-request reads), 503/504 with Retry-After, circuit breakers (Part 18 — Resilience), no external I/O inside transactions.
  • Thundering retries after an outage. All clients retry at once when you come back. Defence: Retry-After with jittered values; rate limits at the edge; documented exponential backoff with jitter in SDKs.
  • Authorisation by URL only. GET /orders/{id} checks the token but not ownership. Defence: every read and write is scoped by the principal in the query itself.
  • Caching mistakes. A CDN caches GET /orders/{id} and serves one customer's order to another. Defence: Cache-Control: private, no-cache on anything user-specific; Vary: Authorization; only cache public resources.
  • Correlation lost. An error in a worker cannot be tied to the request that queued it. Defence: propagate the correlation id through queue messages and webhook headers.
  • Inconsistent error shapes between the gateway (429, 503), the framework (404 for unknown routes) and the app. Defence: configure the gateway's error bodies; catch-all route in NestJS returning problem+json; contract tests on error responses.

8.20 API design review checklist

Use this table in design reviews and PR reviews. A "no" needs a written reason.

Area Question Reference
Resources Are endpoints modelled around business resources and capabilities, not tables? 8.1
Resources Are state changes expressed as PATCH of writable fields or POST to a sub-resource (/cancellations), not /cancel? 8.1
URIs Plural nouns, kebab-case, no verbs, no trailing slashes, at most two levels deep? 8.2
URIs Are ids non-enumerable (UUID/prefixed) and validated with a pipe? 8.2
Verbs Is every GET side-effect free? Every PUT/DELETE provably idempotent? Every POST either idempotent-keyed or documented as not retryable? 8.3
Status codes Is 400 vs 422 vs 409 used consistently? 201 with Location? 202 for async? 429 with Retry-After? Never 200 for errors? 8.4
Pagination Cursor-based for lists that can grow? Composite (created_at, id) key with a matching index? Opaque, signed cursors? Limit capped? 8.5
Filtering Are filter and sort fields allow-listed and index-backed? Unknown params rejected? Search uses full-text/trigram, not ILIKE? 8.6
Bulk Batch size capped? Partial success with per-item results and per-item keys? Bounded concurrency? 8.7
Partial updates Merge-patch semantics documented (null vs absent)? If-Match required with 412 on mismatch? Writable fields whitelisted? 8.8
Errors RFC 9457 problem+json from one global filter? Stable code catalogue? Correlation id in body and logs? No stack traces? 8.9
Validation Global ValidationPipe with whitelist, forbidNonWhitelisted, transform? Length and array caps? No nested-quantifier regexes? Body size limit? 8.10
Versioning Version strategy chosen and applied consistently? Additive changes preferred? Deprecation and Sunset headers on old versions? Usage per version measured? 8.11
Idempotency Idempotency-Key mandatory on money-moving and creating POSTs? Atomic reservation? Fingerprint check? Replay identical? Database unique constraint as backstop? 8.12
Rate limiting Limits at the edge and in the app? Keyed by user/API key after auth? Stricter on login and expensive endpoints? 429 with Retry-After? Redis-down behaviour decided? 8.13
Contracts OpenAPI generated and committed? Breaking-change diff in CI? Responses validated against the spec in tests? Clients generated, not hand-written? 8.14
Async Operations over a few seconds return 202 with a status resource and Retry-After? Workers idempotent? Operations expire? 8.16
Webhooks HMAC with timestamp? At-least-once with event ids? Backoff schedule? SSRF protection? Delivery log and replay? Receiver acks fast and dedupes? 8.17
Security Every read/write scoped by principal? Cache-Control: private on user data? No PII in webhooks or error details? 8.19
Money All amounts are decimal strings with currency, never floats? Part 7, 7.5
Compatibility Clients told to ignore unknown fields and enum values? Nothing removed or renamed without a version? 8.19

Senior Checklist — Part 08

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can model an API around resources and business capabilities and explain why table-driven APIs break
  • I can turn a business action into a sub-resource (POST /orders/{id}/cancellations) and say why it beats /cancel
  • I can pick the right status code for any situation, including 400 vs 422 vs 409 and 202 for async
  • I can read the EXPLAIN for OFFSET 200000 and implement keyset pagination with a composite index, opaque signed cursors and backward paging
  • I can allow-list filter and sort fields so dynamic ORDER BY can never become injection or a full sort
  • I can design a bulk endpoint with partial success, per-item idempotency and bounded concurrency
  • I can implement merge-patch with correct null/undefined semantics and If-Match/412
  • I can write one global RFC 9457 exception filter that maps domain errors to HTTP without leaking internals
  • I can configure ValidationPipe to prevent mass assignment, prototype pollution and ReDoS
  • I can implement an idempotency interceptor with atomic reservation, fingerprinting, replay and a database backstop
  • I can rate limit at the edge and in the app with Redis, keyed by principal, with 429 and Retry-After
  • I can version an API, evolve it additively, and sunset a version with headers and usage data
  • I can design 202-based long-running operations and secure, retried, deduplicated webhooks on both sides
  • I can run an API design review with the checklist above

Part 08 — Key Takeaways

  • An API is a long-lived contract; design it around business resources and the ubiquitous language, never around tables.
  • Business actions become sub-resources (/cancellations), which gives them ids, history, idempotency and a uniform shape.
  • Verbs carry semantics that retries depend on: GET safe, PUT/DELETE idempotent, POST needs an Idempotency-Key when it creates money or business events.
  • Status codes are control signals for gateways, SDKs and monitoring; 200-with-error breaks all three.
  • Offset pagination costs grow with depth; keyset pagination on (created_at, id) with a matching index is constant-time and drift-free; cursors are opaque and signed.
  • Every filter and sort field is an allow-listed promise that an index exists; client strings never reach ORDER BY.
  • Bulk endpoints cap size, bound concurrency, and return per-item results with per-item idempotency.
  • PATCH is merge-patch with null-clears/absent-unchanged semantics and requires If-Match; lost updates are a bug, not a feature.
  • One global filter emits RFC 9457 problem+json with a stable code catalogue and a correlation id; stack traces never leave the server.
  • ValidationPipe with whitelist, forbidNonWhitelisted and transform, plus length caps and linear regexes, is a security control before it is a UX feature.
  • Idempotency is reserve-atomically, fingerprint, execute, store, replay, with a unique constraint in PostgreSQL as the durable backstop.
  • Rate limit coarse at the edge and precise in the app with Redis; stricter on login and expensive endpoints; always send Retry-After.
  • Version at the URI, evolve additively, keep one implementation behind thin adapters, and sunset with Deprecation/Sunset headers and usage dashboards.
  • Anything slower than a few seconds is 202 plus an operation resource; webhooks are signed with timestamps, delivered at-least-once with backoff, deduplicated by event id, and acknowledged fast by receivers.
  • Adding fields is safe; removing, renaming, retyping or changing meaning is a new version, because some client somewhere will never update.

Part 61 — GraphQL and gRPC

REST (Part 8) is the default API style in this book, and for good reason: it is simple, universal and predictable. But it is not the only style, and a senior engineer chooses the right one for each situation. This Part covers the two most important alternatives: GraphQL, a query language that lets clients ask for exactly the data they need in one request, and gRPC, a fast binary protocol for service-to-service communication. We teach what each is, how to build it in NestJS, its specific performance and security traps, and — most importantly — when each wins over REST.

The running scenario ties them together: an order service that exposes REST publicly (simple, cacheable, universal), GraphQL for the mobile app (one round trip for a screen's worth of nested data), and gRPC internally between services (fast, typed, efficient). That is a realistic architecture, and the point of the Part is the judgment to choose each, not dogma that one is best.

This Part builds on REST (Part 8), API style decisions (Part 49), schema compatibility (Part 32), and microservices communication (Part 5). NestJS supports all three styles with real modules, which we use.

61.1 GraphQL

61.1.1 What GraphQL is

Concept

GraphQL is a query language for APIs. Instead of many fixed endpoints each returning a fixed shape (as in REST), a GraphQL API exposes a single endpoint and a schema of available types and fields, and the client sends a query describing exactly which fields it wants, including nested related data, in one request. The server returns precisely that shape — no more, no less.

Why does it exist?

REST has two shape problems for rich clients. Over-fetching: an endpoint returns fields the client does not need, wasting bandwidth. Under-fetching (the N+1 round trip problem): a client needs related data (an order, its items, each item's product) and must make several sequential REST calls to assemble one screen, which is slow, especially on mobile over a high-latency network. GraphQL solves both: the client asks for exactly the fields it needs, across relationships, in a single request. It exists because mobile and complex frontends needed to fetch tailored, nested data efficiently, and REST made that awkward.

Mental model

REST is a fixed-menu restaurant: each dish (endpoint) comes exactly as the kitchen prepares it, and if you want a bit from three dishes you order all three. GraphQL is a build-your-own plate: you describe on one order slip exactly what you want — "the order's total, its items' names, and each item's product image" — and the kitchen assembles that one plate. The schema is the list of ingredients available; the query is your order slip; the response is your custom plate.

How it works

A GraphQL API has three core operation types:

  • Query: read data (like GET).
  • Mutation: change data (like POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE).
  • Subscription: receive real-time updates over a persistent connection (like a WebSocket feed).

The schema defines types and their fields; resolvers are the server functions that fetch each field's data.

# Schema (what the server offers)
type Order {
  id: ID!
  status: String!
  totalCents: Int!
  items: [OrderItem!]!        # nested relationship
}
type OrderItem {
  quantity: Int!
  product: Product!           # nested relationship
}
type Product { id: ID!, name: String!, imageUrl: String }

type Query { order(id: ID!): Order }
# A client query: ask for exactly these fields, including nested ones, in ONE request.
query {
  order(id: "ord_1001") {
    status
    totalCents
    items {
      quantity
      product { name imageUrl }   # fetched in the same request
    }
  }
}

The response matches the query's shape exactly. The mobile app got everything for its order screen — the order, its items, each item's product name and image — in one round trip, fetching only the fields it asked for.

NestJS example

NestJS supports GraphQL two ways: code-first (you write TypeScript classes and decorators, and the schema is generated) and schema-first (you write the schema in GraphQL SDL and implement resolvers). Code-first is common in TypeScript projects because the types stay in sync with the code.

// order.model.ts -- code-first: decorators generate the GraphQL schema
import { ObjectType, Field, ID, Int } from '@nestjs/graphql';

@ObjectType()
export class Order {
  @Field(() => ID) id: string;
  @Field() status: string;
  @Field(() => Int) totalCents: number;
  @Field(() => [OrderItem]) items: OrderItem[];
}
// orders.resolver.ts -- resolvers fetch the data for each query/field
import { Resolver, Query, Args, ID, ResolveField, Parent } from '@nestjs/graphql';
import { Order } from './order.model';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';

@Resolver(() => Order)
export class OrdersResolver {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Query(() => Order, { nullable: true })
  order(@Args('id', { type: () => ID }) id: string) {
    return this.orders.findOne(id);              // resolves the top-level order
  }

  @ResolveField(() => [OrderItem])
  items(@Parent() order: Order) {
    return this.orders.itemsFor(order.id);       // resolves the nested items field
  }
}

The @Query resolver handles the top-level order query; the @ResolveField resolver handles the nested items field. This per-field resolution is GraphQL's power and also the source of its biggest trap (the N+1 problem, 61.1.2).

Production scenario

A mobile app's order-detail screen needs the order, its items, each item's product name and image, and the shipping address. Over REST that was four sequential calls (order, items, products, address), about 400 ms of round trips on a mobile network. With GraphQL it is one query returning exactly those fields, about 120 ms. The app also stopped over-fetching the dozen order fields it did not display. For a data-rich mobile client over high latency, the single-round-trip, exact-shape fetch is a real, measurable improvement.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior sees GraphQL as the right tool when clients need flexible, nested, tailored data in few round trips — classically a mobile app or a complex frontend (a backend-for-frontend). They also see its costs clearly: the per-field resolver model makes the N+1 problem easy to introduce (61.1.2), caching is harder than REST (61.1.3), and the flexible query surface is an attack surface (a client can ask for an enormous nested query). They do not adopt GraphQL reflexively; they adopt it when the client's data-fetching pain justifies the added server complexity, and they keep REST for simple, public, cacheable APIs where its simplicity wins (61.3).

Common mistakes

  • Adopting GraphQL for a simple public API where REST's simplicity and cacheability win.
  • Ignoring the N+1 problem that the resolver model invites (61.1.2).
  • Exposing an unbounded query surface with no depth/complexity limits (61.1.3).
  • Treating GraphQL as "REST but better" rather than a different tool with different tradeoffs.

Interview questions

  1. What problems does GraphQL solve over REST? Over-fetching (clients get only the fields they ask for) and under-fetching / multiple round trips (clients fetch nested related data in one request), which especially helps mobile and complex frontends.
  2. What are the three GraphQL operation types? Query (read), Mutation (write), Subscription (real-time updates over a persistent connection).
  3. What is a resolver? A server function that fetches the data for a field; GraphQL resolves fields individually, which is its power and the source of the N+1 problem.
  4. Code-first vs schema-first in NestJS? Code-first writes TypeScript decorated classes and generates the schema (types stay in sync with code); schema-first writes the SDL and implements resolvers against it.

Practical exercise

Build a NestJS code-first GraphQL API for orders with an order(id) query that returns the order, its items, and each item's product, and write a single client query that fetches the whole order-detail screen's data in one request. Acceptance criteria: the response shape matches the query exactly, and the query returns nested items and products in one round trip.

61.1.2 The N+1 problem and DataLoader batching

Concept

GraphQL's per-field resolution creates the N+1 problem: a query for a list of N orders, each needing its customer, triggers 1 query for the orders plus N queries for the customers — N+1 database queries for one GraphQL request. DataLoader solves this by batching: it collects all the individual customer-id lookups made during one request and issues a single batched query, turning N+1 into 2.

Why does it exist?

Because resolvers run per field per object, a naive customer resolver runs once for each order in a list, each issuing its own database query. For 100 orders that is 101 queries, which hammers the database and makes the request slow (the same N+1 problem that plagues ORMs, Part 15, now at the GraphQL layer). DataLoader exists to batch these per-request lookups into one query and to cache them within the request, so a field resolved many times does not hit the database many times.

Mental model

Imagine a mail room where each of 100 employees separately walks to the post office to pick up their one letter — 100 trips. DataLoader is the mail clerk who collects everyone's requests, makes one trip, and distributes the letters. It batches many small lookups made during a single request into one trip to the data source, and remembers results so the same lookup within that request is not repeated.

How it works

// A DataLoader batches customer-id lookups made during one GraphQL request.
import DataLoader from 'dataloader';

function createCustomerLoader(customers: CustomersService) {
  return new DataLoader<string, Customer>(async (ids: readonly string[]) => {
    // Called ONCE with all the ids collected during this tick -> one batched query.
    const rows = await customers.findManyByIds(ids as string[]);  // WHERE id = ANY($1)
    const byId = new Map(rows.map((r) => [r.id, r]));
    return ids.map((id) => byId.get(id)!);                        // return in the same order
  });
}
// In the resolver: use the loader instead of a direct per-order query.
@ResolveField(() => Customer)
customer(@Parent() order: Order, @Context() ctx: { customerLoader: DataLoader<string, Customer> }) {
  return ctx.customerLoader.load(order.customerId);   // batched + cached per request
}

Each load(id) call during the request is collected; DataLoader issues one WHERE id = ANY(...) query for all of them, so 100 orders produce 1 orders query plus 1 batched customers query — 2 total, not 101. Crucially, a DataLoader instance is created per request (not shared across requests), so its cache does not leak stale data between users; in NestJS you create the loaders in the GraphQL context for each request.

Production scenario

A GraphQL query for a list of 50 orders with their customers and item products ran 50 + 50 + 150 = 250 database queries without batching, taking 600 ms and loading the database heavily. With DataLoader on the customer and product fields, it dropped to a handful of batched queries and about 40 ms. On a busy endpoint, that is the difference between the database comfortably serving the traffic and the database falling over, and it is a one-time implementation of per-field loaders.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • No batching: the default N+1 explosion; a list query can issue hundreds of database queries and overload the database.
  • Sharing a DataLoader across requests: its per-request cache leaks one user's data into another's request; always create loaders per request.
  • Loader returns wrong order: the batch function must return results in the same order as the input ids (or map by id), or fields get mismatched data.
  • Batching hides, not fixes, a huge query: a deeply nested query can still fetch a vast amount; combine batching with depth/complexity limits (61.1.3).
  • Caching stale within a long request: for mutations within a request, you may need to clear the loader cache.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the N+1 problem as the default risk of GraphQL, not an edge case, and puts DataLoader (or an equivalent batching layer) on every field that fetches related data, created per request. They verify with query logs or EXPLAIN that a list query issues a handful of batched queries, not hundreds, because the resolver model makes it trivially easy to ship an N+1 explosion that passes functional tests and then overloads the database under load. They know batching improves efficiency but does not bound the total work, so they pair it with depth and complexity limits so a client cannot request an enormous nested result (61.1.3).

Common mistakes

  • No DataLoader, causing N+1 query explosions that overload the database.
  • Sharing a DataLoader across requests, leaking data between users.
  • Returning batch results in the wrong order, mismatching data to objects.
  • Assuming batching alone makes GraphQL safe without query limits.

Interview questions

  1. What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and why does it arise? A query for N objects each needing related data triggers 1 + N queries, because resolvers run per field per object; it is GraphQL's default performance trap.
  2. How does DataLoader solve it? It batches the per-field lookups made during one request into a single query and caches them within the request, turning N+1 into roughly 2.
  3. Why must a DataLoader be created per request? Its cache is request-scoped; sharing it across requests would leak one user's data into another's request and serve stale data.
  4. Does batching bound the total work a query does? No — it reduces query count but a deeply nested query can still fetch a huge amount; you also need depth and complexity limits.

Practical exercise

Add a customer field to the orders GraphQL API that, without batching, causes N+1 queries for a list of orders, confirm the explosion in the query log, then add a per-request DataLoader and confirm the query count drops to a handful. Acceptance criteria: a list query for 50 orders issues a constant small number of database queries regardless of list size, and loaders are created per request.

61.1.3 GraphQL performance, security and API evolution

Concept

GraphQL's flexibility — any client can ask for any shape — is also its risk. A malicious or careless client can send a deeply nested or hugely expensive query. Caching is harder than REST because every query can be different. And evolving the schema has its own rules (you add and deprecate rather than version). This section covers the guardrails and practices that make a GraphQL API safe and maintainable.

Why does it exist?

A REST endpoint does a bounded, known amount of work. A GraphQL query's cost depends on what the client asks for, so without limits a client can request order -> items -> product -> relatedProducts -> ... nested dozens of levels deep, or request thousands of objects, and make one request do enormous work — a denial-of-service by query. Caching, which REST gets largely for free via HTTP, is harder because the single endpoint receives varied POST queries. These guardrails and techniques exist to keep GraphQL's flexibility from becoming a liability.

How it works — security limits

Risk Defense
Deeply nested query Depth limit: reject queries nested beyond N levels
Hugely expensive query Complexity limit: assign each field a cost, cap the total per query
Many expensive queries (abuse) Rate limiting by cost, not just request count
Arbitrary queries from untrusted clients Persisted queries: only allow pre-registered query ids
Introspection revealing the whole schema Disable introspection in production for non-public APIs 
// Depth and complexity limits in NestJS (via validation rules / plugins).
GraphQLModule.forRoot({
  // reject queries deeper than 7 levels
  validationRules: [depthLimit(7)],
  // assign costs and cap total complexity (via a complexity plugin)
  // a query exceeding the cap is rejected before execution
});

Persisted queries are the strongest control for first-party clients: instead of the client sending an arbitrary query string, you pre-register the allowed queries (at build time) and the client sends only a query id. The server runs only known queries, which eliminates arbitrary expensive queries and shrinks the request size. For a public API where you cannot control clients, you rely on depth, complexity and cost-based rate limits instead.

How it works — caching

REST caches naturally: a GET /products/42 response can be cached by URL at the browser, CDN and server (Part 16). GraphQL is harder because requests are POSTs with varied query bodies to one endpoint, so URL-based HTTP caching does not apply directly. The approaches:

  • Per-field / entity caching on the server: cache the resolved data for an entity (a product by id) in Redis (Part 16), so resolvers hit the cache; DataLoader's per-request cache handles within-request reuse.
  • Persisted queries over GET: a persisted query with a stable id can be sent as a GET and cached by a CDN like REST.
  • Client-side caching (the GraphQL client libraries cache normalized entities), which reduces repeat requests.

The honest tradeoff: GraphQL gives clients flexibility at the cost of the easy HTTP caching REST enjoys, so you rebuild caching at the entity and client layers.

How it works — pagination, errors and evolution

  • Pagination uses connections (the Relay cursor pattern): a list field returns edges with cursors and a pageInfo, enabling stable cursor pagination (Part 8). Every list field is paginated, as in REST.
  • Errors: GraphQL can return partial data plus an errors array (a query touching several fields can succeed for some and fail for others), which clients must handle; this differs from REST's single status code.
  • Evolution without versions: GraphQL APIs evolve by adding fields and types (additive, non-breaking) and deprecating old fields (@deprecated) rather than minting /v2. Removing or changing a field is breaking, so you deprecate, monitor usage, and remove only when no client uses it — the same compatibility discipline as Part 32, applied field by field.

Federation and supergraphs

As an organization grows, one GraphQL schema can span many services. Federation lets each service own part of the graph (orders service owns Order, products service owns Product), and a gateway composes them into one supergraph the client queries as a single graph. This is powerful but adds operational complexity (the gateway, cross-service resolution, shared types), so it is for organizations with many teams and services where a single unified graph genuinely helps — not a starting point.

Failure scenario

A public GraphQL API had no depth or complexity limits. An attacker sent a query nesting order -> customer -> orders -> customer -> orders ... many levels deep, each level multiplying the work; one request consumed enormous CPU and database load, and a handful of such requests took the service down — a denial-of-service through a single crafted query. The fixes: a depth limit, a complexity limit with per-field costs, cost-based rate limiting, and persisted queries for the first-party clients so only known queries run. The lesson: GraphQL's open query surface must be bounded, or one request can do unbounded work.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats a GraphQL endpoint's open query surface as an attack surface and bounds it from day one: depth limits, complexity limits with per-field costs, cost-aware rate limiting, and persisted queries for first-party clients (disabling introspection on non-public APIs). They rebuild the caching that REST gave for free at the entity (Redis) and client layers, accepting that as the price of flexibility. They paginate every list with cursor connections, handle partial errors, and evolve the schema additively with deprecation and usage monitoring rather than versioning. They reach for federation only at the scale where many teams and services justify a gateway's complexity. Throughout, they keep REST for the simple, public, cacheable parts of the surface where its simplicity wins.

Common mistakes

  • No depth/complexity limits, allowing denial-of-service by query.
  • Allowing arbitrary queries from untrusted clients instead of persisted queries.
  • Expecting REST-style HTTP caching to work and getting none.
  • Unpaginated list fields; ignoring partial errors.
  • Breaking the schema by removing/changing fields instead of deprecating.
  • Reaching for federation before the scale justifies it.

Interview questions

  1. Why is a GraphQL endpoint a denial-of-service risk, and how do you defend it? A client controls the query's cost; a deeply nested or huge query does unbounded work. Defend with depth limits, complexity limits with per-field costs, cost-based rate limiting, and persisted queries.
  2. Why is caching harder in GraphQL than REST, and what do you do? Varied POST queries to one endpoint defeat URL-based HTTP caching; rebuild caching at the entity (Redis) and client layers, and use persisted queries over GET for CDN caching.
  3. How does a GraphQL API evolve without versioning? Add fields/types (non-breaking) and deprecate old fields with @deprecated, monitor usage, and remove only when unused — the compatibility discipline of Part 32, field by field.
  4. What is federation and when is it appropriate? Each service owns part of the graph, composed by a gateway into one supergraph; appropriate at organizational scale with many teams/services, not as a starting point.
  5. What are persisted queries and why use them? Pre-registered allowed queries referenced by id; they eliminate arbitrary expensive queries from first-party clients and enable GET/CDN caching.

Practical exercise

Add guardrails to the orders GraphQL API: a depth limit, a complexity limit with per-field costs, and cursor-based pagination on the orders list. Then demonstrate that a deeply nested or oversized query is rejected before execution. Add entity caching in Redis for the product resolver. Acceptance criteria: an abusive deep query is rejected, lists are cursor-paginated, and repeated product fetches hit the Redis cache.

61.2 gRPC

61.2.1 Protobuf, services and streaming

Concept

gRPC is a high-performance framework for service-to-service communication. You define services and messages in a protobuf (Protocol Buffers) schema, and gRPC generates typed client and server code. It uses a compact binary format over HTTP/2, making it fast and efficient, with a typed contract shared by both sides. It is the common choice for internal communication between microservices.

Why does it exist?

Between internal services, REST over JSON is wasteful: JSON is verbose text to serialize and parse, there is no enforced contract (a field rename breaks the caller at runtime), and each call is a separate HTTP/1.1 connection. gRPC fixes all three: binary protobuf is compact and fast, the .proto schema is a strict typed contract both sides generate code from, and HTTP/2 multiplexes many calls over one connection and supports streaming. It exists because internal service-to-service traffic — high volume, trusted, performance-sensitive — benefits enormously from a fast, typed, efficient protocol that a public browser-facing API does not need.

Mental model

REST-over-JSON between services is like two departments mailing each other long typed letters in plain language, re-reading and interpreting each one. gRPC is like them sharing a strict pre-printed form (the protobuf schema) and exchanging compact filled-in forms over a dedicated fast line (HTTP/2). The shared form guarantees both sides agree on the fields; the compact format and fast line make exchanges quick; and the line can carry many forms at once and even a continuous stream.

How it works — the protobuf contract

// orders.proto -- the shared, typed contract both sides generate code from
syntax = "proto3";
package orders;

service OrderService {
  rpc GetOrder (GetOrderRequest) returns (Order);              // unary (one request, one response)
  rpc ListOrders (ListOrdersRequest) returns (stream Order);  // server streaming
}

message GetOrderRequest { string id = 1; }                    // field numbers matter (see evolution)
message Order {
  string id = 1;
  string status = 2;
  int32 total_cents = 3;
  repeated OrderItem items = 4;
}
message OrderItem { string product_id = 1; int32 quantity = 2; }
message ListOrdersRequest { string user_id = 1; int32 limit = 2; }

The field numbers (= 1, = 2) are how protobuf identifies fields on the wire — not the names. This is central to schema evolution (61.2.2). gRPC supports four call types: unary (one request, one response, like a normal function call), server streaming (one request, a stream of responses), client streaming (a stream of requests, one response), and bidirectional streaming (both stream). Streaming over the persistent HTTP/2 connection is efficient for large result sets or continuous data.

NestJS example

NestJS has a gRPC microservice transport.

// orders.grpc.controller.ts -- implement the service defined in the .proto
import { Controller } from '@nestjs/common';
import { GrpcMethod } from '@nestjs/microservices';

@Controller()
export class OrdersGrpcController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @GrpcMethod('OrderService', 'GetOrder')     // maps to the rpc in the .proto
  async getOrder(data: { id: string }) {
    const order = await this.orders.findOne(data.id);
    return { id: order.id, status: order.status, totalCents: order.totalCents, items: order.items };
  }
}
// Calling the gRPC service from another NestJS service (the client side).
const order = await this.orderServiceClient.getOrder({ id: 'ord_1001' }); // typed, binary, HTTP/2

Deadlines and status codes

Like any network call, a gRPC call needs a deadline (timeout) — gRPC has first-class deadline propagation, where a caller's deadline flows to downstream calls, so a chain of services all respect the original budget (excellent for preventing cascading slowness, Part 38). gRPC has its own status codes (not HTTP status codes): OK, NOT_FOUND, INVALID_ARGUMENT, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, UNAVAILABLE, PERMISSION_DENIED, etc. You map your errors to these, and clients decide retry behavior from them (UNAVAILABLE is retryable, INVALID_ARGUMENT is not), the same reasoning as HTTP status codes (Part 71).

Production scenario

An order service calls an inventory service and a pricing service on every order placement, thousands of times per second internally. Over REST/JSON this was measurable serialization overhead and a separate connection per call. Switching the internal calls to gRPC cut serialization cost and per-call latency, multiplexed the calls over persistent HTTP/2 connections, and gave a typed contract so a field change in the inventory schema was caught at build time in the generated code rather than breaking at runtime. Deadline propagation meant the order placement's overall timeout budget flowed to the downstream calls automatically. For high-volume internal traffic, gRPC's efficiency and typed contract paid off clearly.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reaches for gRPC for internal, high-volume, performance-sensitive, trusted service-to-service communication, where its binary efficiency, typed contract, HTTP/2 multiplexing, streaming and deadline propagation are real advantages. They do not use it for public, browser-facing APIs, because browsers cannot speak gRPC directly (needing gRPC-Web and a proxy), it is not human-readable for easy debugging, and REST/GraphQL serve external clients better (61.3). They set deadlines on every call (relying on propagation through the chain), map errors to the right gRPC status codes so retry behavior is correct, and treat the .proto as a shared contract evolved carefully (61.2.2). gRPC is an internal-plumbing tool in their mind, not a public-API tool.

Common mistakes

  • Using gRPC for public browser-facing APIs where REST/GraphQL fit better.
  • No deadlines, losing gRPC's cascading-timeout protection.
  • Mapping all errors to one status code, breaking clients' retry logic.
  • Treating the .proto casually and breaking the contract (61.2.2).

Interview questions

  1. What is gRPC and why use it between services? A high-performance RPC framework using binary protobuf over HTTP/2 with a typed shared contract; it is efficient, strictly typed, multiplexed and supports streaming — ideal for high-volume internal service calls.
  2. What are the four gRPC call types? Unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional streaming.
  3. What is deadline propagation and why does it matter? A caller's deadline flows to downstream calls so a chain respects the original time budget, preventing cascading slowness.
  4. Why not use gRPC for a public browser API? Browsers cannot speak gRPC directly (need gRPC-Web + a proxy), the binary format is not human-readable, and REST/GraphQL serve external clients better.

Practical exercise

Define an OrderService in a .proto with a unary GetOrder and a server-streaming ListOrders, implement it as a NestJS gRPC microservice, and call it from another NestJS service as a typed client with a deadline. Map a not-found to the NOT_FOUND status code. Acceptance criteria: the call is typed end to end from the generated code, the deadline is enforced, and a missing order returns NOT_FOUND.

61.2.2 Schema evolution and gRPC operations

Concept

A protobuf schema is a contract between services that are deployed independently, so it must evolve without breaking either side. Protobuf's design — identifying fields by number, not name, and making fields optional — supports backward- and forward-compatible evolution if you follow the rules. The main operational concerns beyond the schema are load balancing (HTTP/2 is sticky), and reaching gRPC from the browser (gRPC-Web and gateways).

Why does it exist?

Services deploy on their own schedules, so at any moment an old client may talk to a new server or vice versa. If a schema change broke that, every change would require a lockstep deploy of all services — impossible at scale. Protobuf's field-number identity and optional fields make most changes compatible, so a new server with an extra field still works with an old client, and an old server ignores a new field it does not understand. The rules exist to preserve this, and breaking them causes exactly the cross-version failures Part 32 warns about.

How it works — the compatibility rules

message Order {
  string id = 1;
  string status = 2;
  int32 total_cents = 3;
  repeated OrderItem items = 4;
  string currency = 5;          // ADD: new fields get a new number; old code ignores it (safe)
  reserved 6;                    // RESERVE a retired number so it is never reused
  reserved "old_field_name";     // RESERVE a retired name too
}

The rules that keep protobuf compatible:

  • Never change a field's number. The number is its identity on the wire; changing it makes old and new code disagree about what the field is. This is the cardinal rule.
  • Never reuse a retired field's number. When you remove a field, reserved its number (and name) so a future field cannot accidentally reuse it and misinterpret old data.
  • Add new fields with new numbers. Old code ignores them (forward compatible); new code reading old data sees them as default (backward compatible).
  • Do not change a field's type incompatibly. Some type changes are compatible, many are not; treat a type change as potentially breaking.
  • Removing or renaming a field is a breaking-ish change to callers that use it; deprecate and migrate (Part 32), and reserve the number.

This is the same backward/forward compatibility discipline as Part 32 (schema and API compatibility), expressed through protobuf's field numbers. Follow it and services evolve independently; break it and you get subtle data corruption across versions.

How it works — load balancing and gRPC-Web

Load balancing: because gRPC runs over long-lived HTTP/2 connections that multiplex many calls, a naive connection-level load balancer sends all of one client's calls to one server (sticky), causing uneven load. gRPC load balancing is therefore done at the request level (client-side load balancing or an L7 proxy/service mesh that understands HTTP/2), so individual calls spread across servers. This is a known gRPC operational consideration (Part 26 on load balancing).

gRPC-Web and gateways: browsers cannot make raw gRPC calls (they lack the needed HTTP/2 control). gRPC-Web is a variant that works in browsers via a proxy that translates between gRPC-Web and gRPC. Alternatively, a gateway exposes a REST/JSON or GraphQL facade in front of gRPC services for external clients. The common pattern: gRPC internally between services, a gateway (REST or GraphQL) for the public and the browser (61.3).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the .proto as a shared contract under the same compatibility discipline as any API (Part 32): never change or reuse field numbers, add fields with new numbers, reserve retired numbers, and deprecate rather than remove. They know gRPC's HTTP/2 connections need request-level load balancing (client-side or an L7 proxy/mesh), not naive connection-level balancing, or load concentrates on a few servers. They expose gRPC to browsers only through gRPC-Web with a proxy or, more commonly, through a REST/GraphQL gateway, keeping raw gRPC internal. They apply deadlines and the right status codes so the whole mesh behaves well under failure (Part 38).

Common mistakes

  • Changing or reusing a field number, corrupting data across versions.
  • Removing a field without reserving its number, so a future field reuses it.
  • Connection-level load balancing of gRPC, concentrating load on few servers.
  • Trying to call raw gRPC from a browser without gRPC-Web or a gateway.

Interview questions

  1. What are the protobuf rules for compatible schema evolution? Never change or reuse field numbers, add fields with new numbers, reserve retired numbers and names, avoid incompatible type changes, and deprecate rather than remove — so independently deployed services stay compatible.
  2. Why is gRPC load balancing different from REST? gRPC uses long-lived multiplexed HTTP/2 connections, so connection-level balancing is sticky; you need request-level balancing (client-side or an L7 proxy/mesh) to spread calls.
  3. How do browsers use gRPC services? Not directly — via gRPC-Web through a translating proxy, or via a REST/GraphQL gateway in front of the gRPC services.
  4. Why do protobuf field numbers matter more than names? Numbers are the field identity on the wire; changing one makes old and new code disagree about the data, causing corruption.

Practical exercise

Evolve the Order protobuf by adding a currency field with a new number, then simulate removing an old field by reserving its number and name. Verify that an old client and a new server interoperate after the additive change. Then describe how you would load-balance this gRPC service and expose it to a browser. Acceptance criteria: the additive change is backward/forward compatible, the retired number is reserved, and you can explain request-level load balancing and the gRPC-Web/gateway options.

61.3 Choosing REST, GraphQL or gRPC

61.3.1 The decision and the combined architecture

Concept

REST, GraphQL and gRPC are three tools for three situations, not competitors where one wins. The senior skill is matching each to where it fits: REST for simple, public, cacheable APIs; GraphQL for flexible, nested data to rich clients (mobile, complex frontends); gRPC for fast, typed, high-volume internal service-to-service communication. A mature system often uses all three at once.

Why does it exist?

Each style optimizes for different things. REST optimizes for simplicity, universality and HTTP caching. GraphQL optimizes for client flexibility and few round trips. gRPC optimizes for internal performance and typed contracts. No single style is best at all three, so forcing one everywhere means paying its weaknesses where another's strengths were needed. Choosing per situation gives you each strength where it matters.

How it works — the decision matrix

Factor REST GraphQL gRPC
Best for Public APIs, simple CRUD Mobile/complex frontends needing tailored nested data Internal service-to-service
Format JSON (text, human-readable) JSON Binary protobuf (compact)
Transport HTTP/1.1 or 2 HTTP (usually POST) HTTP/2
Client flexibility Fixed shapes Client picks fields Fixed (typed contract)
HTTP caching Easy (by URL) Harder (rebuild at entity/client) Not applicable
Browser-native Yes Yes No (needs gRPC-Web/gateway)
Typed contract Via OpenAPI (optional) Via schema Strong (protobuf, generated)
Round trips for nested data Many One Few (and streaming)
Main risk Over/under-fetching N+1, query cost, caching Not for public/browser
Debuggability High (readable) Medium Lower (binary) 
Choose REST when:            Choose GraphQL when:          Choose gRPC when:
- public or third-party API  - mobile app / rich frontend  - internal service-to-service
- simple CRUD resources      - many client-specific shapes - high volume, perf-sensitive
- HTTP caching matters       - few round trips needed      - streaming between services
- maximum simplicity/        - a backend-for-frontend      - a strict typed contract
  compatibility/debuggability                              - deadline propagation in a mesh

The combined architecture (the worked example)

flowchart TB
    PUB["Third-party / public clients"] -->|REST + JSON| GW["API Gateway"]
    MOB["Mobile app"] -->|GraphQL| GW
    GW --> ORD["Order Service"]
    ORD -->|gRPC| INV["Inventory Service"]
    ORD -->|gRPC| PRC["Pricing Service"]
    ORD -->|gRPC| SHP["Shipping Service"]

The order service exposes REST publicly for third-party integrations and simple cacheable reads (its simplicity and HTTP caching win there), GraphQL for the mobile app so a screen's nested data comes in one round trip with only the fields it needs, and talks gRPC internally to inventory, pricing and shipping services for fast, typed, high-volume calls with deadline propagation. Each style is used exactly where its strengths apply and its weaknesses do not matter. This is not over-engineering; it is matching the tool to the job, and it is a common real architecture.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior chooses the API style per boundary, not per company. For the public edge they default to REST for its simplicity, universality, cacheability and debuggability, reaching for GraphQL only when a rich client's data-fetching pain (over/under-fetching, many round trips) genuinely justifies the added server complexity and the N+1/caching/query-cost work it brings. For internal service-to-service traffic at volume they reach for gRPC's efficiency and typed contracts, while keeping it off the public edge. They are comfortable running all three in one system, because that is often the right answer, and they resist both the dogma that REST is always enough and the hype that GraphQL or gRPC should be everywhere. The question is always "what does this specific boundary need?"

Common mistakes

  • Forcing one style everywhere out of dogma or hype.
  • Using GraphQL for a simple public API, taking on its complexity for no benefit.
  • Using gRPC at the public/browser edge, fighting its lack of browser support.
  • Using REST for high-volume internal calls where gRPC's efficiency and typing would help.
  • Not considering a combined architecture where each style serves its natural boundary.

Interview questions

  1. When do you choose REST, GraphQL and gRPC respectively? REST for simple, public, cacheable APIs; GraphQL for rich clients needing tailored nested data in few round trips; gRPC for high-volume, performance-sensitive, typed internal service-to-service communication.
  2. Why not use GraphQL everywhere? It adds server complexity (N+1, query-cost limits, rebuilt caching) and is overkill for simple public CRUD where REST's simplicity and HTTP caching win.
  3. Why keep gRPC internal? Browsers cannot speak it directly, its binary format is not human-readable, and it offers no HTTP caching; REST/GraphQL serve external clients better.
  4. Describe a realistic architecture using all three. REST for public/third-party, GraphQL for the mobile app via a gateway/BFF, gRPC internally between services — each at the boundary where its strengths fit.

Practical exercise

For the order system, write a one-page decision (an ADR, Part 49) specifying which API style serves the public/third-party edge, the mobile app, and the internal inventory/pricing/shipping calls, with justifications tied to each style's strengths and the concrete needs (caching, nested data, performance, typing, browser support). Acceptance criteria: each choice follows from stated requirements, and the decision explicitly rejects the styles not chosen for each boundary with reasons.

Senior Checklist — Part 61

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can build a GraphQL API in NestJS and explain queries, mutations, resolvers
  • I can identify and fix the N+1 problem with per-request DataLoader
  • I can secure a GraphQL API with depth/complexity limits and persisted queries
  • I can build a gRPC service in NestJS with protobuf, deadlines and status codes
  • I can evolve a protobuf schema compatibly (field numbers, reserved)
  • I can choose REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC for a given boundary and justify it
  • I can design a combined architecture using all three where each fits

Part 61 — Key Takeaways

  • GraphQL lets clients request exactly the fields they need, including nested data, in one request, solving REST's over-fetching and multiple-round-trip problems for rich clients.
  • GraphQL's per-field resolution invites the N+1 problem; fix it with a per-request DataLoader that batches lookups, and verify the query count stays small.
  • A GraphQL endpoint's open query surface is an attack surface; bound it with depth and complexity limits, cost-based rate limiting, and persisted queries for first-party clients.
  • GraphQL loses REST's easy HTTP caching; rebuild caching at the entity (Redis) and client layers, paginate with cursor connections, and evolve the schema additively with deprecation.
  • gRPC uses binary protobuf over HTTP/2 with a typed shared contract — fast, efficient, streaming-capable — ideal for high-volume internal service-to-service calls.
  • gRPC gives deadline propagation and its own status codes; set deadlines and map errors correctly so a service mesh behaves well under failure.
  • Evolve protobuf compatibly: never change or reuse field numbers, add fields with new numbers, reserve retired numbers, and deprecate rather than remove (the Part 32 discipline).
  • gRPC is internal plumbing; browsers need gRPC-Web with a proxy or a REST/GraphQL gateway, and gRPC needs request-level load balancing, not connection-level.
  • REST, GraphQL and gRPC are three tools for three situations; a mature system often uses REST publicly, GraphQL for rich clients, and gRPC internally.
  • Choose the API style per boundary based on its concrete needs (caching, nested data, performance, typing, browser support), resisting both REST dogma and GraphQL/gRPC hype.
